A.G.M. 1980 = COMMODORE'S REPORT

I have been asking myself whether beginning and ending a term of office with subscription increases has any particular significance, I don't think so, except that it highlights the relentless march of inflation and the inevitable effect it has upon us all,

Before we come to the proposals and elections tonight, your Officers and Committee are obliged to submit for your approval, reports on the state of the Club, its finances and activities over the past year,

o

The activities of the Club, as our constitution states, are concerned with the promotion of amateur sailing, social fellowship and the provision of all possible facilities to this end. I believe as a Club we have once again met these objectives, and I should like at this point to thank, on your behalf, the Officers, Committee and Members who have worked so hard to bring this about. The activities of course are divided between sailing and more domestic matters. Stan Oaker our Sailing Secretary will be reporting on the former whilst I must deal with the latter. However, as 0.0.D. at the Regatta I feel entitled to offer my thanks to whoever it was who organised the weather = please do it again next year!

Now to the main events of the yeare Two new features were the Inter Social Club's Sports Day, and the use of our Club by the British Canoe Union for the Blackwater Canoe Race. Only one team eventually made the journeyto Stansgate to compete in the Inter=Club event, but it was very enjoyable none the less. Also gratifying was the support given by members to the Maldon Little Ship Sponsored Rowing Race held in aid of the ReNeLeIe I am Sure we enrich the quality of our Club by socialising and joining in events with other Clubs on the
TIivere

On the more domestic side, our caretaker, Claude Emerson, assisted by his wife Ivy, have once again worked hard to maintain the Club and premises in a clean and tidy condition. The purchase of a vacuum cleaner which can pick up water from the floor has been a great help, The effluent arrangements worked well after repairs and modifications early on in the year. Under the able direction of Cyril Drakeford our Clubhouse Secretary, a number of other tasks were completed — a carpet was fitted in the galley; the rubbish collection point was moved away from the Clubhouse; a stile of unique and spontaneous design was constructed on the sea wall and a flag mast was erected = Mark 3 or is it Mark 4? will feature next year.

The trees have again been tended by Bug Bradley and June and Russell Fuller. We are now discovering the species which flourish at Stansgate, so our success rate should gradually improve,

The Club has continued to support 8.A.C.S.P.A. and 8.J.R.Ce. AS you could not fail to notice in the local press, 8.A.C.S.PeA. has been in the thick of the controversy over water skiers on the river. I have personally attended a number of meetings on this subject, one with the River Sub-Committee of the Maldon District Council, who are feeling the brunt of the complaints about water skiers. It has been the opinion of most Clubs on the river that there is room for us all, and that with a modicum of common sense and co-operation a solution could be found. Fortunately this has proved to be the case, and next year the Stone Ski Club have agreed to confine their Club racing to 1 hours duration ina designated area on the northside of the river and at a published time around mideday. They will also operate a voluntary speed limit elsewhere on the river, of 30 mpehe Of interest also is the intention of the Maldon District Council to call a meeting of all river users, at the beginning of each year where ideas and views can be freely expressed and it is hoped that any potential problems can be nipped in the bud.

The licence mentioned last year, for us to maintain the concrete apron, mete, groyne and scrubbing posts on the foreshore was formally agreed with the Maldon District Council. We are also currently engaged in negotiations with the Council in order to lease the area of foreshore where our moorings are positioned. The objective here is to give members greater influence and security of tenure over this important aspect of our Club. To this end the newly formed Moorings Sub=—Committee has done much useful work,

4 -

Security has continued to be a problem. Money has been taken from the changing rooms, and wheels, trailers, avon dinghies, petrol and various other items have also been stolen. It is a sad reflection on our times. I can only suggest that we take greater care and take home or lock away the more attractive and valuable items of equipment.

On the social side the Barbecue was again lucky with the weather, if a little on the draughty side. The Regatta Disco was as noisy and boistrous as The Christmas Dance was a little thin on the ground but was a considerable success. The Laying=Up Supper was well supported = the numbers being considerably up on last year. The Winter Lectures and Cruiser Evenings were interesting and well supported. Russell Fuller, Pat Harper and Social Committee are to be congratulated on their efforts.

Ann Allen has done good work as Editor of Navigans = I would however like to see more members contributing to make it more entertaining and newsy, as well as being the vehicle for the Commodores and Committees notices and exhortations.

The Galley Ladies have again worked against increasing odds to give us a pleasant and profitable service, It is well to remember that their efforts save us all nearly £2 per head on our subscriptions. The Bar has worked efficiently under the management of John and Mavis Weedon, and Jack & Joyce Reeve have given loyal and friendly service behind the counter every Sunday.

Camping has been well supported and trouble free. We must continue to keep this activity well disciplined and controlled if we are to be successful when we apply to renew our Planning Permission at the end of next year,

Throughout the year the M.A.S.C. Committee have been negotiating with the larger Sections, to try and find a fair and reasonable formula for arriving at Section contributions for the facilities and services they use. We have insisted throughout, that whatever criteria are arrived at to assess contribution, they must be applicable to all sections and accepted by the membership as being fair and reasonable. I believe we are very near to reaching such an agreement. The rent or contribution we now pay is fixed by our 6 year agreement with the M.A.S.C. at £2,000 per annum. This agreement has 1 more year to run. When it expires however, the M.A.S.C.e have made it clear that they will be expecting an increased contribution from use As a continuation of our policy of self sufficiency and as a gesture of goodwill the Committee have offered in the mean time to pay the insurance premiums on the Clubhouse.=<This item being the only Sailing Section cost currently paid for by the M.A.S.C. Whilst no figures are yet on the table
for 1982 it has been indicated that a rental in excess of £3,000 will be expected.

The proposals for increased subscriptions contain a provision to cushion a rise in contribution, but I should stress that it is only a relatively small proportion of what we need. The bulk is required to cover other items of expenditure we shall incur over the next 2 years. For example the road will need to be repaired and surfaced again = this alone will cost £2,000 at todays prices. We must replace the Rescue Boat Engine, paint and redecorate the Clubhouse, repair the hard and finish piping the ditch. In all we need to raise an additional £2,000 per annum. As you can see the Committee have chosen this time to allocate most of the increase on to the members who make the greatest use of the facilities, that is, the sailors. The increase proposed is essentially £3 for ordinary members, £4.50 for associates, plus £4 on the Hard Fee. I should stress also that even with these increases our subscription rates will still be appreciably lower than other Clubs on the river. I shall of course be pleased to answer any questions you may have when we come to consider the proposals later on in the
proceedings.

As you can see from the Agenda a number of well known members are taking a well deserved break from office. They arez= Cyril Drakeford, Alan Goss, Stan and Vera Oaker, Russ Fuller, Ann Allen, Mick Gray and Margaret Linquwood. I would ask you at this point to join with me in showing your appreciation for their generous services to the Club. Needless to say they are not going to disappear from the scene all together, all have expressed a willingness to help their replacements settle in.

We do however have 4 vacancies on the Committee. Two very important posts are going begging — namely Sailing Secretary and Clubhouse Secretary. Please come forward after this evenings proceedings if you would like to offer your services in any waye As one who was coaxed into being Club Bosun more years ago than I care to remember, I can ensure you it is a great team to belong to. John, Frank and David will make you most welcome,

Finally I should like you all to know that the Marconi Sailing Club is held in high regard by other Clubs and organisations on the rivers; That Mary and I have found it a pleasure and an honour representing you as your Commodore and Lady and that we wish John and Mavis every success and hope that they derive the same enjoyment and satisfaction as we have done,

Ron Greygoose.

POLICE REGISTER OF YACHTS

The police are compiling a register of yachts in order to help owners who are unfortunate enough to have their boats stolen and also, no doubt, with the idea of taking proceedings against those who offend the law of the sea, Members should therefore, in their own interests, and to collaborate in this commendable scheme, complete and return the forms which are available from clubs and police stations.

Care should be taken to ensure that the numbers of items which are specially liable to theft, such as, outboard engines and inflatable dinghies, are entered an the forms, It is also important to display clearly the names of our yachts, their port of registration or the letters indicating their home club. The same applies to tenders and inflatable dinghies carried uninflated on board,

Where is your yacht?

An amusing incident happened to me towards the end of the season. The Customs in London telephoned me to say that a yacht called Hullabaloo had suspiciously turned up at a WesteGerman port. From the Lloyd's register of Shipping they found that I was the owner of a yacht bearing this name and where was it? After checking, I was able to assure them that my Hullabaloo was indeed safely at her moorings. To date, I have not heard the sequel.

No doubt, other owner's yachts have an equally frivolous name, although, perhaps in my case, some people might consider it appropriate!

Eric Payne.

CALLING ALL RADIO OPERATORS

I am attending an operator's course of lectures at the Maldon Little Ship Club, which is proving very educational and entertaining.

I have suggested to the lecturer that the growing army of radio users in the MeSeCe Could warrant running a similar course for use He would be prepared to come along if there is enough demand. About 15 to 20 people are needed to make a course worthwhile.

Basically, all skippers of vessels fitted with VHF radio are required by law to hold a certificate of competency (issued by the Post Office). The course consists of five weekly lessons on radio procedure (largely practical work using two on closed circuit). At the end of the course there is an examination by a P.0. Inspector, who issues the certificate of competency
(hopefully).

Current cost of all this is £5.00 for the course, with an examination fee of £17.00 to keep Susby in bird seed. If you already own a radio, or are thinking about fitting one, or are just interested, then I am sure you will find the course interesting. You never know, one day it could prove to be the best investment you ever made? Please give me a ring on Chelmsford [redacted], and I will take it from there.

John Smith.

COLWYN STONE, DECEASED.

Members will be grieved to hear of the passing of our good friend Colwyn Stone in December, after a long period of heart trouble. In November, I had a long conversation with him when he seemed so much better that he was contemplating a return to work, when the relapse came on December 9th. RNLI ROWING RACE 1981

Sunday January 4th was crisp, sunny and cold = fair conditions for the
annual rowing race in aid of the RNLI organised by the Maldon Little Ship Club. This year competitors had a choice of course from the start, which was at the lock side at Heybridge Basin. Several chose the outside routs, down river and around Hilly Pool Point and then back up river into Colliers Reach and past Herring Point, with the finish at the quay side by the Queen's Head. This was by far the quickest way, taking some a mere twenty minutes to cover a distance of approximately 3 miles.

However, the majority opted in favour of "the pretty way", along the canal past Bentalls up to Beeleigh Weir, then into and down the river, under the Full bridge and back to the quaye Marconi were particularly well pepresented. The Fisherman immaculately turned out by Claude Emerson, with a new coat of varnish, dazzling white painted rubbing strake, and a pristine white burgee fluttering from the bow. Her crew, Pete Clayton, Grahem Mead, Ian Lindsey and Danny Lumley with Sarah Cant as coxswain soon sorted out a little problem with timing during the early stages, and although because of handicapping were one of the last boats to start, they were one of the first competitors to finish.

Pete Hall and Jim Campbell did well in the Queen Mary working off the excess's of the festive season, while there were two new "faces" on the scene, Steven Hodges and Nick Nice resplendent in war paint and pheasant feathers handled their canoe with flair and panache, and "bravely" paddled their way round the bend and up the creek. Following at a more sedate pace Vic Crisp and colleague were obviously more interested in viewing the scenery and as the Owl and the Pussy Cat in a real pea green boat they made a picturesque sight gliding up river,

Maldon Little Ship Club had a strong female entry with several boats under feminine command, but the most outstanding craft was "Macavon", an inflatable gaily decorated with balloons, crew and helm sporting full tartans, complete with low slung sporran and tape recorder giving us all the "thrill" of the pipes.

The onlookers had a choice of vantage points, from the canal side at Heybridge Basin, then after a quick drive up the road to Langford Water Works, one had a pleasant view from the bridge just below Beeleigh Wein, watching the boats being carried from the canal across to the river. MLSC supplied the porterage, which seemed to run chiefly on rum. Then back in the car again to see if you could beat the boats back into Maldon and alongside the quay to celebrate their arrival in traditional style, in the pube A very worthwhile exercise, which deserves more public attention and raises a considerable sum each year for the life boats and life boat men, Make a note in your diary, the next race is on Boxing Day 26th December, 1981.

Brenda Tate,

COMMODORE'S NOTES

The River Blackwater being an important area of natural beauty, is used extensively for varied recreational purposes during summer weekends, and additionally having other commercial pressures it is inevitable there could be conflicting interests. To protect these interests there are a number of organisations and authorities acting as advisory or in executive capacities.

The Essex County Council are currently publishing a report "Coastal Water Recreation in Essex", and this will be studied with interest by the Club
committee.

Maldon District Council who has immediate authority over the majority of the Slackwater has recently initiated occasional regular meetings to bring together representatives of all the river organisations to discuss matters of mutual interest, and Dennis Byatt will be our representative at the inaugural
meetings

An organisation formed some years’ ago, to act mainly in an advisory capacity towards preserving the environment of the river consistent with the interests of sailino, is 8.A.C.S.P.A. (Blackwater & Colne Sailing Protection Association). The local Sailing Clubs, Power 8Boat Clubs and the are all gathered twice a year in discussione A recent topic has been concerned with the Stone Water Ski and Power Boat Club activities on the river. The Stone Sailing Club, particularly, were very concerned with increasing use of the river by fast power boats including organised races in an area already used by racing and cruising yachts. After negotiation the Ski Club agreed to limit their practice and racing to a stretch of the river between Thirslet Spit and Tollesbury Creek on the north side of the fairway. Their race dates this year
are programmed for May 10, 24, & 25, June 7 & 21, July 5, August 16 & 31 4
September 13, between 1 = 2 pm, except May 24 which is all day. Therefore it
may be sensible to avoid this area if peace and quiet relaxation is desired at these times,

John Weedon,

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

Our next programme at The Generals Arms will be presented by John Todds. John spent a considerable time on business in the Caribbean recently and took the opportunity of doing some travelling and photography. We can look forward to an interesting evening.

Last month P.C.Winter, a member of the crew of Alert visited us and Qave a very humorous account of the history and work of the Marine Police. He was also interested to hear of our relationships with other users of the river. Concerning the saffety aspect of our moored boats, P.C. Winter endorsed our club recommendation of using mooring lights on all the outer and end boats, as bright as possible on the end positions. He also emphasized that permanent use of a radar reflector was to be encouraged,

Since these recommendations come from the River Police we would do well to attempt to observe them. It was pleasing to hear, on the other hand, that, at least at present, the new lighting regulations are not the subject of any great interest to them. However, in the event of any insurance claim I'm sure that importance would be attached to compliance with the rules so it is still wise to have approved lights, which must be fitted by July.

On Saturday March 14th the cruising fraternity downed tools, left their paintbrushes to soak, discarded their dungarees and wellies, and repaired to the Clubhouse for an informal fleet dinner. And what a dinner!

The flowerebedecked tables were decorated in a suitably nautical theme with little boats of flowers each with a candle mast, blue sail and minuscule M.S.C. burgee. All these were concocted by Sylvia Crisp and won "oohs" and "ahs" of admiration.

Spring Vegetable Soup with Roll and Butter,

Chocolate Gateau,

Good Friday came with winds of about force 4 = 5 with occasional gusts of 6+ 3 This year the Hornet has a new larger rig and many of the competitors were worried about trying out the new ‘set up* in such conditions and subsequently the number of starters was only about 10 out of a fleet of 19,

Soon after 3 more boats retired leaving just Malcolm Goodwin from Brightlingsea and our own Graham Mead and Danny Lumley sailing Ultimate to fight it out. boatse

Dear Sin,
We are writing to seek the support of your club in inviting your members to participate in a new phase of research at Loch Ness.

Shore based surface surveillance has been discontinued owing to the very small proportion of body revealed by the films shot during the sixties. Underwater photography, on the other hand, is largely thwarted by peaty water and the fact that we simply do not have enough behavioural information to place cameras in such a vast body of water. It should be borne in mind that Loch Ness is scarcely explored biologically and would be capable of comfortably immersing every man, woman and child on earth; and the Post Office Tower for that matter.

The only search method producing repeatable results is sonar. All adequately equipped sonar expeditions have so far recorded targets larger than salmon and having behaviour very different to fish shoals. These include Oxford and Cambridge, Birmingham University and Vickers Oceanics. The problem lies in interpreting the results since a sonar record alone can only indicate the presence, strength and behaviour of the target.

The Project is now undertaking a major sonar monitoring programme in order to resolve the ambiguities of sonar contacts made at Loch Ness. We now need to know what they are. We have been fortunate in acquiring sonar equipment with greatly superior detection, assessment, tracking and recording ability to any so far used, We should now be able to hold contact for long enough to glean real hints as to a target's identity from its speeds and diving rates. A methodical study of the times, places and depths of contacts will also allow us to place underwater photography on a truly active basis.

But if our results are to mean anything, we shall need more than the equipment. In order to bring back valid results, a very protracted operation will be necessary. The search must be pressed at different times of year, day and night until a pattern emerges. This is far beyond the capacity of a single volunteer crew. We shall need manpower and seamanship.

/continued.

The work will be conducted from a specially constructed 40ft. inflatable catamaran with cabin requiring a crew of six. The vessel is powered by a combination of engine and square sail for silent patrol, A staff is responsible for administration, training and maintenance, but the main work of the expedition is to be carried out by volunteer crews of six including a suitably experienced skipper. It is hoped that three crews shall be maintained at any one time in order to allow the following cycles: One day will be spent as crew of the sonar search vessel which includes night patrols, one day running the base camp and one day shall be left free, during which members may stay on camp or visit the surrounding area. The Project has a base camp at Ballachladaich Farm near Dores off the B 852 on the south shore of the loch.

The Project is therefore in need of volunteer crews of six including a competent skipper and preferably already known to each other, For this reason we hope our proposal may be of interest in a club context. we emphasize that such a group would be treated as an entity within the expedition. After training, the crew would be entirely responsible for the conduct of the work and would naturally merit a great proportion of the credit for success.

Individual applicants contribute £32/wk. towards tentage, food, fuel and other running costs but in the case of a complete crew, this is reduced to £25/person/uk.

Volunteers should provide themselves with a sleeping bag, waterproof gear and are advised to bring warm clothing. They may also wish to bring their own tent. There is a minimum age limit of 18 years and from 16 years if accompanied by an adult.

Individuals and potential crews should write to the above address
stating preferred dates (20/7/J%e- 344/Yiu,—).
Skippers of crews should have at least inland cruising experience.

For the first time ever, we are in possession of the means to do a good job at Loch Ness. Now we need the men (and women). we hope that you may be able to find room for this invitation on your notice board.

Yours faithfully,

CLUBHOUSE

Days spent at Stansgate are times enjoyed by the whole family. The sailing facilities, the comfort of the Clubhouse and the uncrowded grounds provide the freedom for all the family to relax and follow their own interests. The sailing and the Club facilities are organised and maintained by the small band of hard-working Officers and Committee Members who put in a large amount of voluntary time for the benefit of a membership of about 400 families. To keep the Club operating smoothly and to ensure that all the facilities are available, it is essential that the responsibilities for various activities within the Club are spread as widely as possible if the voluntary basis on which the Club operates is not to break down. These arrangements have worked well in the past, but this year the Committee is experiencing a particular problem, in that it has so far not been possible to find a volunteer to take on the job of Clubhouse Secretary. This is an extremely important post on the Committee and one which it is very necessary to have filled, if we are all to continue to enjoy the facilities at Stansgate, and to ensure that everything continues to work. For the last three years this position has been filled by Cyril Draleford who is now taking a well deserved rest after ensuring that the Club operated smoothly durinag his term.

We feel sure that from our membership there must be someone who could be and would be willing to undertake this role, and so that the requirements of the job can be better understood here is an outline of the main responsibilitie,

1. Provision of all consumable supplies, i.e. soap, disinfectant, paper
towels etc.

2e Monitor the working of the Clubhouse services, and arrange for repairs and replacements, ieee light bulbs, tap washers, hoses, gas appliances etc,

30 Arrange for maintenance of the fabric of the building and the furnishings, ieG@e Painting and decorating, window repairs etc.

4, Arrange for maintenance of the grounds.

The job of the Clubhouse Secretary is not so much doing the work, but organising it and arranging for tasks to be undertaken by other members who have the relevant skills. Much of the work is undertaken by Claude Emerson our hard= working Caretaker.

The old proverb "Many hands make light work" is particularly true in respect of the tasks associated with the Clubhouse, and to enable the work to be spread more widely the Committee is going to experiment with a scheme to attract more volunteers.

The basis of this experiment is that a jobs register will be created and a copy will be available at all times to the Officer of the Day. It is then hoped that anyone at Stansgate who is for any reason at a loose end will approach the 0.0.0. to see if there is anything that can be done to assist the Club. It is surprising how many times people come to Stansgate, and, for various reasons outside their control, are unable to pursue their intended activity, and if people finding themselves in this position could use the time profitably to the benefit of the Club a great deal could be achieved towards maintainino the facilities. This is not intended as a substitute for volunteers, who are always welcome and for whom there are always tasks.

From this it may be seen that the role of Clubhouse Secretary is primarily one of determining the needs of the Club and co-ordinating the activity. The job is made easier if the post is filled by a practical person who can undertake some of the tasks and show others what is required.

ALTERNATIVE SCORING SYSTEMS

(or "The Best Man May Win").

The Sailing Sub=Committee are sometimes asked to consider, or suggest, an alternative scoring system for a Class Points series, or the special series such as Ladies, Cadets, and Helmsmen of the Year. Behind such a request often lies the desire to encourage larger turnouts or give more incentive to less expert helmse With small fleets e particular problem is the ever present threat of a class race being abandoned because fewer than three boats sail. t temporary bolt hole of the Handicap Fleet will be less than satisfactory unless the whole series is sailed. Even then we have the problem of how best to extract Class results from Handicap points.

Having set out some possible problems with the established system of scoring we reach the difficult part of suggesting a viable alternative. A major problem with many alternative systems is that they require times to be recorded. Possible in the Handicap Fleet, but do we wish to burden our Race Officers and Results Secretary with more number crunching?

In recent years we have combined Ladies and Cadet Fleets to avoid the ‘less than three boats sailing' problem, and by moving the Enterprise Class into the Handicap Fleet we have given the Class breathing space to regain its former glory. Soth the actions have worked with some limited success, but we may be
able to do more in these and other directions. Looking back over the Club's history one can see the evolution of new Dinghy Classes and the disappearance of others. A Fleet may rise out of the Handicap dinghies and fall back in over a period of years, or we may suddenly find ourselves with a new class. (Either way we should accept change and frame our scoring system to allow for it.

A points scoring system inevitably produces a winner, the prize sometimes going to the "best" helm. No system can guarantee that the "best" helm will win, some indeed are designed to make this more difficult by personal handicapping, by creating a "second class division" or by givino extra points for performance above normal standard. The Sole Fleet are this year playing with a personal handicap system suggested by John Rutherford which gives the lesser mortals a chance to catch him up. A nice thought here is that if they used their personal handicap in pursuit fashion J.R. would have to sail through the rabbits dirty wind. Not so far fetched, this suggestion, it is used regularly by IeP.C. Yacht Club.

A particular example of a scoring system designed to make your Fleet champion sweat blood for his points series cup is "The Ostroboqulous Leaque" as described by Eric Twiname. It attempts to hold interest in a points series to the very end by counting all races for the helms who compete in them, and awerding points to each helm only for beating helmsmen of similar standard to, or better standard than, himself.

It works like this = you get one point for starting and not subsequently being disqualified, so if you retire you get one point. In the first race of the series you get a point for every boat you beat, so that if you won the first race when the turnout was ten boats you'd get your starting point

/continued.

- ll -

plus 9 = 10. All very straightforward so far, but then what happens is that if you win the next race you score only your starting point plus a point for every boat you beat which was within a fixed, critical number of points of you before that race. For example, if the critical number (which is the same for everybody and decided before the start of the series) was 6 then you'd only score points for boats that had 4 points or more (the 10 points you had before the race minus
the critical number, 6, equals 4).

In practice this means that no-one can streak away into an unassailable points lead by the middle of the series, for as soon as they get more than 6 points clear of the second boat they can only score their startino point, though anyone beating them will score a point. The scheme works a little like a squash ladder, in that merely by looking at the scoring sheet you can see where you are lying at any time during the season, but it has the merit that to build up a good position you have to sail well in a fair number of races,

The beauty of this system is that a Club, or even a Class within a Club, can decide exactly where it wants to strike the balance between Harry Flyer who pops in occasionally and wins and Plodwyn Round who is almost part of the furniture and doesn't — except when the experts are away. A biog Critical Number emphasises success, while a low Critical Number emphasises frequent
attendance.

In the light of experience gained from Clubs using the system a Critical Factor of about 14 to 2 times the expected average turnout for a series of 10 to 30 races is recommended.

As an example of how the system would work, the 1980 Sole Summer Points are reproduced with our standard scoring system and as an Ostrobogulous League. It is interesting to note that despite nine wins out of fifteen races sailed S.2862 fails to win the League using a Critical Number of 10, However in practice had we been operating the League and displaying accumulated points each
week on the notice board our S.2862 may have put aside his dreams of H.e2100 and
won both Cup and League.

Finally, please don't take this too seriously — I'm not all that good at adding up.

Malcolm Stuart,

JUST LOOKING SV
I do not often get the opportunity of racing in close company with other boats and consequently rarely have to bother about applying the racing rules. I suppose the most often used rule at the Club is Rule 36, Opposite Tack = Sasic Rule, which tells me that port tack gives way to starboard. Even the start of our races do not offer too many opportunities since, by the time it is the turn of the Mirror Fleet, there is so much room and so few Doats that the rules are just never invoked. Therefore, whenever I'm watching other boats racina, I ‘practise’ the rules on the situations that occur. It was whilst watching from the rescue boat that I observed the following event.

Two boats P (on port) and (on starboard) were converging on the beat from A mark to Noe le I glanced away and looked back in time to see what appeared to be a very hurried tack by P from port to starboard and an equally rapid luff by 5 to avoid a collision. This made the boats overlap with P just ahead butto leeward of S.

Hai Hag I says to myself, says I, this ought to be good for a protest — but to my surprise both boats appeared to be sailing happily onwards (at least I did'nt hear anythingsS). I thought it was a clear case of Rule 41 in which the tacking boat P had failed to keep clear of right-of-way boat S and forced S to alter course before P had completed her tack. After all, at the time S was luffing, the crew of P were not in their 'normal' position for a beat and looked to be in a bit of a shambles. Since nothing came of the incident, I looked up the rules and their interpretation when I got home.

It seems to me that P%s obligations to keep clear of S under Rule 41, and S's obligations as windward boat to keep clear of P under Rule 37 once the tack is completed, depends upon how you define the ‘completion of the tack’. For this beating situation, the definition of tacking is that P is tacking from the time she is "beyond headetoewind' until she has ‘borne away to a close=hauled course’, I read in a yachting magazine that it is an established principle that when beating to windward, a boat is considered to have ‘completed her tack' when she is heading on a close=hauled course irrespective of her movement through the water or the sheeting of her sails, Although in my eyes P was not sailing ?mormally' and her crew were not in their 'normal' position for beating, she was "heading* on a close=hauled course parallel to that of S and had therefore completed her tack = hence S's sudden luff to keep clear.

Perhaps the acid test of whether P has completed her tack isse

(a) if S hits P"s transom, then this proves P has completed her tack, and

(b) if S hits P*s side, this proves P had not completed her tack.

Maybe those with more experience of applying the rules would like to comment on this = in the meantime I'1l carry on just looking.

Mike Boreham.

CRUISING WITH THE OQCEAN YOUTH CLUB.

l6the23rd flay, 8l.

The Ocean Youth Club maintains a fleet of seven 72ft ketches at various points around the coast. Whilst they are mainly for the use of 15=21 year olds, during term time adults have the opportunity to sail aboard
them.

On 16th May I arrived at the Old Customs' House at 8rightlingsea and, finding no-one around, I went to the nearest pub. In one corner was a group of people who turned out to be the Skipper, lst and 2nd mate, and Bosun of "Master Suilder". B8y about 2100 hrs a total of 14 people were assembled and we left for the tender and the trip out to the boat.

During Sunday morning with typical British sailing weather of rain and too much wind, we provisioned the boat with water and fuel, despite the various thick heads.

By lunch time the wind had begun to moderate, and the mooring was dropped at 1400 hrs with the intention of heading for Harwich. However by 1600 hrs the weather had improved sufficiently that course was set for Ijmuiden and Amsterdam. Four hour watches were set and by 1200 hrs on Monday with no wind, the more hardy types (all female) went for a swim over the side before the engine was started, Sy 1600 hrs the lock at Ijmuiden was entered and we travelled up the Noordzeekanaal to Amsterdam,

Monday evening and Tuesday morning were spent exploring the city and
avoiding the cyclists. We left at 1630 hrs to go through the lock into the Ijsselmeer (Zuider Zee). As the average depth here is only 8 feet and the draught of the boat was 7.5 feet there were a few interesting bumps accompanied by the skipper's cry “i'ts a bit thin here". Sy 1900 hrs. we were moored alongside a Dutch barge in Muiden on the Southern edge of the Ijsselmeer. After a visit to the local pub, some people decided to sleep on deck as the weather was very warm.

On Wednesday we motored to Enkhuizen to visit the Zuider Zee Museum and also to watch the U.eE.F.A. Cup Final in the local with a number of Dutch supporters, Again the weather was hot and clear enough to sleep on deck which helped relieve the "snoring" problem.

An early (relatively) start was made on Thursday for Den the locks and open sea so that we arrived at Qudeschild on the Friesian Island of Texel at 1530 hrs. After showers in the local yacht club we all visited a restaurant for a meal of eels, mussels, fish or steak before setting sail for England at 2330 hrs.

This crossing is 140 miles but due to S.W. winds the best that was achieved initially was a course down the Dutch coast. By 1200 hrs on Friday the wind had started to turn southerly and freshen so that we could head for
Harwiche During the 2400 — 0400 watch we passed the sunken lLightvessel at about

10 knots with No. 2 jib, mainsail and mizzen set. However the weather was now becoming Enalish again and at 0400 hrs. we handed over to the other watch as the rain started.

By 0630 hrs. on Saturday anchor fad been dropped at Srightlingsea after a sail of 190 miles in 31 hrs.

All in all it was a marvellous week of sailing and cruising with that memorable night sail on the return journey.

TREATMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA

Reported deaths due to Hypothermia regularly make the headlines in our National Press every winter, Victims include elderly people dying of the cold in their own homes and healthy younosters unexpectedly overtaken by bad weather whilst tracking in organised parties across exposed country within normally easy reach of urban communities. All this happens in a temperate
climate.

' Now you sailors are going to ask what the above paragraph has to do with us! It has an awful lot to do with us. Just a few minutes in the Blackwater doesn't do some people much good, so imagine what half an hour would do to a sailor (not properly protected) after capsizing = the rescue boat could be unaware of your trouble because he is helping another sailor elsewhere on the
river?!

If you are called to a hypothermic casualty this is what you are likely to find.

The patient will bes

1, Blue with the cold.

2e Stiff with the cold.

3. Immobilised with the cold.

4. Unconscious or semi=conscious with the cold. Possibly able to nod
his head weakly in the affirmative to the question "Can you understand what I am saying to you?" He is likely to be irrational.

Se His respirations will be shallow, slow and irregular.

6. His pulse will be weak, slow and difficult to feel.

7. His rectal temperature is likely to be below 31°C.
8. His blood pressure, if you could record it, would be very low.

9. Since he is exposed to the cold and long past the staqe of
shivering his deep core temperature is likely to be below 31 CC. I am not suggesting that you should stick a thermometer up his anus to find oute In any event, unless you take immediate action his temperature will accelerate downwards to death by heart failure,

What you should dos

l. Treat him very gently. Rough handling may precipitate heart failure in a dangerously cold man.

2. Get him into the warm, out of the cold and away from the wind.

3e Keep him horizontal. His heart is weak and his blood pressure is low. Blood supply to the brain must be maintained at all costs to avoid irreversible brain damaoce,.

4- If local conditions permit, get him to the nearest shelter and stop his heat loss. Remove his wet clothes = dry him — put on warm clothes
- wrap him up in warm blankets with a warm human being beside him.

5- Do not waste time giving him hot drinks unless you are sure he can swallow. If he cannot swallow you may drown hime Unless he is getting warm and beginning to shiver do not give him alcohol. Alcohol dilates surface blood vessels and increases heat loss.

Trained mountain rescue teams carry special breathing apparatus capable of administering heated, oxyaen enriched, air.

/continued.

7. Take him to the nearest available HOT BATH.

8. The water should be at 42—44°C, Test it oy putting in your slbou,
If your elbow will accept it — so will the patient.

9. Lower the patient gently ine If sufficient help is available
attempt to keep his upper and low limbs out of the water, It is his trunk that needs reheating. The limbs have a larger surface area in relation to their mass than does the trunk. If immersed, it is possible to reduce markedly an already low blood pressure by inducing vasodilatation over the skin of the limbs and to make matters worse excite the return to the heart of a pool of very cold blood in the extremities. This could prove to be the last straw that broke the camel's back and arrest cardiac function by lowering still further Deep Core temperature.

10. Do not foroet to_top the bath up with hot water to maintain the
temperature at C,

ll. The first sign of positive recovery to look for is the onset of shivering. At that moment, the patient will start dynamically to reeheat his own body. Continue to reheat him passively with the bath treatment. His bodily functions will begin to return. wWhen you are sure he can swallow in spite of severe shivering, this is the time to give him hot groge Alcohol is good fuel and quickly absorbed from the stomach.

12. You have now saved a man's life. Hopefully, by this stags, the
patient is in hospital or medical help has arrived. Hand over, for the patient is not out of the wood yet. Lots of complications could occur = for instance, a common one is pneumonia. Yourpatient is ooina to need expert medical care and devoted nursing.

The practical aspects of survival training will now be considered under the Following headings in decreasing order of importance.

l. Protection.

2 Location.

3. Watere

4, Food.

THE HANOLING OF 30AT TROLLEYS.

As we now have a large number of boat trolleys of the four wheel steerable type, I think it is appropriate to give some quidelines on their handlinge For moving in the forwards direction the automatic steering works well provided care is taken not to try to steer too tight a circle. wheels can in some cases go "over centre" and require manhandling to get them back, so always restrict the steering angle as much as possible. Manual steering will limit this and the possibility of bent steering arms, but pedestrians must be very aware of the weight of the tow and avoid finger accidents. A supply of wheel chocks is advisable,

For reversing a different set of problems arise. It is not generally recognised that it is impossible to reverse any great distance with the draw bar coupled in any way to the towing line. Trolleys being reversed down the hard must be steered entirely by hand until the trolley reaches the water; the draw bar may then be secured to the tow: line to assist removal from the water,

It is always preferable to secure the winch wire or towing rope directly to a strong part of the trailer chassis. Steering bars are not normally as strong for taking the pull of the heavy load.

It is strongly recommended, and at club sailing times essential, that a recognised tractor driver or winch supervisor be called in to help. The list of these names is displayed on the Club noticeboard. It is not the duty of an 0.0.0. to help here = he is too busy with other duties and may not be qualified to do the job anyway, so, out of season, please make prior arrangements. No other person may drive the tractor, it is not the same as a car and needs to be properly understood.

The qualified operator will satisfy himself that the load appears safe, the gear appears fit for the job, and that the working team is sufficient for the job in hand. Onlookers are normally willing to help if asked but if not involved may become critical observers,

All persons concerned with launching boats must be sure that no-one is infon the water in the immediate vicinity. Dinghy owners approaching the shore don't like to see lifeboats approaching from the shore!

Less seriously but worth a thought, it would help if steerable wheels could be locked in the straight ahead position, just for when the trolley is in the water — they always slew round a bit otherwise. Trolley wheels should be as large as possible to assist rolling and as for conventional jockey wheels, they Frequently jam in the gaps between the blocks on our hard. How about engineering up a Mini wheel, non steerable, to replace it,

/continued.

a 6 =

Finally, concerning all trolleys, please try to arrange for the boat to be floated to its correct position without the need for either looking or feeling — these may be acceptable for light day boats but not for cruisers. A 'V* shaped frameework in the vertical plane will often do the trick, so will a flat platform in conjunction with a pair of verticals which the starboard side of the boat may be secured to.

420 NEWS

Although August is a difficult month for fleet sailing I am happy to report that the number of boats competing has remained constant during the month. This can be attributed in part to the summerelike weather we've had.

On a personal note, the camping week was undoubtedly the highlight of the year and although there was little wind for sailing I believe we all benefited from living in close quarters for a week (sorry about the noise, Lou!). The main event of the week started in what can only be described as unbelievable weather, with the Blackwater resembling the Meditteranean. The central theme was to have a 'tuneeup! session starting with some basic measurements on the boats, followed by a number of short races where helm and crew by a rota system sailed each participating boat in turn. The boat measuring aspect of the afternoon was intended primarily to establish a data base against which rig alterations and performance can be measured in the future. Oue to the difficult nature of some of these measurements (e.9. spreader deflections) some time was taken over them, and due to the high ambient temperatures it was noticeable that everyone except the fleet captain and John Chisnall disappeared for a swime However, the exercise was worthwhile and the details will be kept in a book which we can hopefully add to and upedate. Those not present at the session can have their own boats measured by prior arrangement.

Six boats were raced in very light airs, in what turned out to be a mammoth racing session of about 34 hours duration. In fact, after the fourth race, several helms and crew were seen disappearing over the sea wall by the race box presumably to irrigate the cruiser park! The lady crews tightened their harnesses and managed to "hang ont (sorry about that Pete!) until the end of the session. All the race results were duly recorded by Robert Weedon (now affectionately known as Robitehead) in the race box for later analysis in the bar.

The one thing that the session produced was a lively discussion of the results and the way in which future sessions could be organised. Several useful points emerged from the discussion:=

1. Since the aim was to quantify boats and helm/crew combinations, spinnakers
were not used since they represented yet another variable in the analysis. Although this was falt to be reasonable at the time the consensus of opinion was to include them next time.

2e Since all racing was conducted in light airs the results are only applicable to those conditions.

3e Some participants infringed the sailing rules at times during the races without recourse to alternative penalties, (sorry about the green stripes, John and Murray!) and although these were overlooked at the time, future sessions will have to be more strictly controlled.

4e Awkwardly placed or dangerous fittings were pointed out by helms and improvements to centre board and kicker fittings suggested. To my knowledge these aspects were acted upon the following day = (yes, my boat is safe now!).

Se 8y discarding the worst result the analysis showed that the best helm/crew partnership on the day was that of Janet Chisnall and John Weedon. The best tuned boat was found to be 41106
= "Wishful Thinking" (shortly to be renamed$),
followed closely by 36372 = "Zoot", 29379 = "Boobs", and 27858 = "Blackbird",

After further discussions it was felt that the next session should be held on a course that embraces all the aspects of sailing — due to the conditions, available time and courses, little or ma tacking took place. Finally the overriding observation and admission by some helms was their inability to start

well and get clear wind. The only answer to this problem is to get out and practise, watch those who do it well and try reading Chapter 6 of "Start to Win" by Eric Twiname (I have a copy for loan).

It started with a casual remark after dinner one night, as these things often do.

"Darling, there's an article in the local rag about the Maldon Little Ship Club running a Radio course for Yachtsman",

"You should do that", replied the skipper.

"Why me?", said I, thinking of the sails and the anchor, the galley and all the rest.

"Well, I*m too busy holding the bit of wood, and in an emergency, it would be you using the radio, and, anyway, it's all good experience",

The result of this profound logic was that I attended the six week course and am now certified by the Home Office, to be competent in the use of a VeHeF.e Radio, I hasten to add.

The course was held in the M.L.S.C. Clubhouse on Maldon Quay for two hours on Wednesday evenings starting at 7.30 pm. Our tutor, Cyril Mansfield, a college lecturer and member of the Slackwater Sailing Club was the instigator of these short courses, an off shoot from when he was lecturing for Yacht Master Courses and had been asked on many occasions to go into V.H.F. Radio procedure in more detail. The outcome is that over 300 people have attended the lectures, many taking and passing the Home Office examination for the Certificate of
Competence.

The six lectures cover basic standard procedures, which channels are used for what etc., how to make a link call through a coastal radio statisn and how to contact your friendly neighbourhood Coastquard. Ample opportunity is given to practise as Mansbrite Electronics of Maldon provide two radio telephone sets, which are placed at gach end of the lecture room and calls can be made and
received.

Each week, Cyril asked for a script concerning the procedure on making a certain type of call, Mayday, Pan, Pan, stc. The following session we would present our scripts using the radios and trying to be as realistic as possible. Imaginations ran riot and some hilarious situations were invented. At the end of six weeks we attended ane sunny Friday afternoon for the examination. The course is cheap, cost £5., the exam isn't, the fee being £17.50p, but if you pass the Home Office send you a pretty certificate with your picture on it, that you can keep. The paper was a written one, there was no verbal test, and consisted of a selection of 20 questions from a possible 60. It took. about an hour, and as we finished, the man from the Home Office sat down and marked them, there and thens; not normal procedure, so I have been told. Twelve people out of sixteen passed, several being Marconi Sailing Club members.

If you are interested in taking a Radio Course, the man to contact is Derek Steel, Commodore of M.L.S.C. Telephone Maldon [redacted] as they will be organising another series of lectures in the near future. If you would like to know more about Marine Radio, what is available on the market, how difficult they are to install etc., then come along to the November Cruiser Meeting at the General's Arms, Little Baddow, when 8rian Ash and 800 Donaldson from Mansbrite Electronics will be there to show us their range of equipment, give advice and answer any questions you may nave for them.

Srenda Tate. 3/9/81.

What a lovely week my family and I had camping at the Club during the August Sailing Week. In contrast to last year's excess of wind, this year had wind just right for experiencing the joys of meandering around by the simple means of wind upon sail = not going anywhere particularly = just sailing. I enjoy cruising in the Mirror just as much as I enjoy racing and I hope I'm never tempted to become so devoted to one that I forget the other, Now, you might ask what all this has got to do with Mirror news, and [I must admit = not a lot. However, during the week the mideweek handicap race saw six (yes =— SIX) Mirrors taking part. Our regular mideweekers of Alf Cottam and P.Collis were joined by Robert Coy, John Stringer, myself and David Green in his new Mirror which looked to be quite fast. It proved to be an interesting race and, for me at least, provided a number of lessons on how NOT to deal with the tides. BP, Collis had the right answers and
I'm told by those watching on shore that he made up at least 150 yards on the leading boat between No. 1 and A mark by intelligent use of the tide. However, although first Mirror over the line, he came second of the Mirrors to Robert Coy on handicap since he was single handed.

The Summer Points racing was resumed on Sunday 6th September and although the morning race was a bit of a drift (Vic Sraybrooke won after sailing for almost three hours — whilst I got fed up and retired for an early lunch), the afternoon race was very enjoyable with Vic and myself swopping the lead until the last beat when Vic pulled ahead to win by a few yards, You may get the impression that Vic and myself were the- only Mirrors racing and this is almost true. The third Mirror in the races contained my wife Margaret trying her novice hand at helming with Marie Dear as crewe The morning race saw them towed back from Osea having run out of wind, whilst the second race saw them sail throuch the moored cruisers and finally retire (in embarrassment for fear of hitting one. They needn't have worried since L manaoed to run full-tilt into a mooring buoy (cruiser attached) and come to a surprised halt. My crew innocently asked why I'd done that and I replied I didn't know — or words to that effect. The lesson is = don't be afraid of making mistakes = we all do it sometimes and we can only improve. Anyway, let's hope Margaret and Marie have another qo.

I referred earlier to the very enjoyable August Sailing Week and was most impressed by the 420 fleet who organised a "tuning! session for S or 6 of their boats and then raced them in a series of short races with the helm and crew swopping boats for each race. Their aim was to determine the effects of tuning on boat performance. I don't know what their conclusions were but the effort was impressive and I would love to see the Mirrors adopt a similar fun=sailing session next year. I propose to call a meating of members of the Mirror fleet, say in November, so that they can discuss what they would like to see happening with the Mirrors. For example, we could encourage each other to race and so improve our boat handling skills. We could hold a "racing rules session" before the start of the 1982 racing calender and perhaps try to arrange for a quest speaker to tell us the secrets of "go faster" Mirror handling. Perhaps we could arrange for a Mirror fleet "gathering" one day during next year's August Sailing Week. With these possibilities in mind I invite ALL Mirror owners in the Club to phone and tell me specifically that they would/would not attend such a meeting in November. It doesn't matter if you haven't sailed this year or are simply not interested in racing, I would very much like to hear your view. If there are enough people (say 6 or more) then I'll call a meeting. Please accept my invitation to phone me and tell me YES or NO.

Finally, a warm welcome to the Mirror Fleet for my daughter Lucinda (aged 7) who has now taken part in her first two Mirror races. My thanks to Vic and Kim Braybrooke who have volunteered for rescue boat crew duty for 18th October,

The final "finally" =— most of the Mirror Fleet News is mine. Why not let me know your Mirror Fleet news, e.g. you are buildino a new boat, have taken

part in an open meeting, caught a fish in your spinnaker whilst capsizing off Osea Island or have introduced your husband/wife/son/daughter/girlfriend/ boyfriend to the delights of Mirror sailing.

MAMGU = DECEASED !

Older members of the Club who enjoyed happy times at Heybridge when the barge=yacht Mamgqu was our headquarters will be sad to hear that she has finally reached the end of her useful life and lies derelict at the end of the Maldon promenade adjoining The Maldon Yacht Club.

In 1957 our Clubhouse was a shed on the seawall at Heybridge Sasin and we were seeking more adequate accommodation when we heard that Mamgu was up for sale, the asking price being £2,000 which, at that time, was far beyond our means. However, the owner who had been living aboard whilst she was moored alongside the quay at Maldon, had taken up residence ashore, was anxious to sell the barge and we heard the whisper that an offer of around £500 would be accestable, After prolonged negotiation, towards the end of 1957 we finally bought her and started Fitting her out as our new Clubhouse,

During this time we laid moorings at Heybridge Basin outside our shed on the seawall,

/continued.

as

On April 20th we arranged with Cecil Stebbens Senior, the Pilot and River Bailiff, to tow her round from Maldon quay to Heybridge, some of us taking the wheel during the voyage. Sy choosing suitable states of wind and tide, we managed to manoeuvre her bows=<on to the beach outside our shed, adjusting the Bow moorings on the seawall and the stern moorings which we had already laid.

Access to the barae from the seawall proved to be quite a problem and we Finally constructed a pier at seawall height extending to the bows of Mamou, the final section being hinged to allow for the rise and fall of the tide, a matter of some 4 metres. We then proceeded to fit her out to suit our requirements as a Clubhouse, with changing rooms, saloon and galley, not forgetting the motor pump which was essential for keeping her bilges reasonably dry, and from time to time, caused us some anxiety.

The barge served us very well for some five years but our main limitation was that we could sail for about only two hours on either side of high water, so we scoured the river for a more suitable site, After a considerable search, we finally decided on a site adjoining the summer residence of Tony Senn at Stansgate Abbey where there was a concrete hard which extended right down to the water's edge at low tide, thus permitting sailing at all states of the tide.

A lease for the site was obtained and we bought a hut which we found right in the centre of Braintree, which we dismantled and transported to Stansgate, where it was reassembled and made into a very nice clubhouse. This was in
April 1963 and it served us very well until we were treated to a permanent bricke
built premises which we now enjoy.

In the meantime, Mamgu was sold to the London borough of Newham for the same price we had given for her,and after a refit, it was used for training young people from that borough in the ways of the sea,

However, the condition of Mamgu deteriorated to the extent that she had to be abandoned and another barge substituted, which is still giving excellent service and giving London youths a taste of the sea.

Eric Payne.

COXSWAINS REPORT 1981

As I write this, there are just two weeks to go to the last race and

I'm glad I invested in a Thermotic suit:

Looking back, it's been a season of ups and downs. The new 55 Hp

Yamaha engine has been a delight to use but we were very unfortunate

to have a major breakdown at the same time that the work boat was having

its overhaul.

A lot of nice things were said about our coverage of the Regatta and a

lot of this good work was the result of cooperation with other clubs.

Having just a few regular drivers means we've come to know the other

drivers and recognise their voices over the Radio. Our Regatta has

become a sort of club for us all to meet.

We also had the help of the Police this year (at last they now have our

Radio Channel) and they turned up in their new Even inflatable (still

wearing peak caps!)

Rescue crews get a lot of thanks when the weather is bad but I would

like to thank all my drivers for turning up and for their patience during

all the quiet days of July, August and September. Waiting for that last

Mirror in a Force 2 when everyone else is in the bar is no fun.

We did have one or two critisisms and these were discussed fully at

Sailing Sub-Committee meetings and hopefully we learned from the episode.

One example is that we now carry two 20 Metre floating lines to cut out

the need to approach fragile dinghies in rough weather.

In conclusion we are fortunate in having our small band of non-sailing

drivers and I hope they will carry on being available.

NORMAN KERRIDGE
COXSWAIN

P.S. The Commodore recently asked how we could quieten the enthusiasm

of the Saturday night Regatta. Ray Harvey tells me that at the

last Maylandsea Bay open meeting, they showed the film "Jaws 2"

COXSWAINS VIEW OF THE PILOTS CUP

The sailing sub-committee's decision to run the postponed Pilots Cup race to Mersea No. 5 in October was rewarded with ideal conditions with a Force 3-4 N.E. wind on a flowing tide.

No problems for anyone of course but I know from comments from one anxious wife on the shore that they do worry when you leave the haven of club waters and I was out of sight of most of you for the day so here's how it was covered.

The course was Mersea No. 5 to port, Marconi No. 4 to port. Entries varied from the fast Dart to the comparatively slow Solos and we weren't even sure if West Mersea No. 5 was still there.

So, the-0.0.D. agreed to cover up river from the club when the faster
boats returned and we proceeded down river - needing half speed to
keep up with the Dart : Problem No. 1] the Solos will soon be out of
Sight.

"Stone Rescue 2 - this is Marconi Rescue - over "

"Marconi Rescue from Stone 2 - Good Morning Norman - over"

So contact had been made with Derek on Stone Rescue 2 and their two boats kept an eye on you through their section to Bradwell.

We proceeded to the buoy half hidden amongst the dozens of participants in the Golden Cod contest and dropped anchor. My high visibility orange suit came into its own and was seen by competitors long before the buoy!!

The Dart rounded 10 minutes before the Hornets and by the time the 420s arrived Stone were reporting the Dart back in their waters and the Solos were only just in sight at Bradwell.

We then had a bit of luck. I spotted Steve in the Dabchicks No. 1 Rescue Boat at anchor fishing ! (They weren't racing until 2.30 PM). He agreed to watch the Solos and kept in Radio contact. We caught up the 420s and by this time the fleet was back in visual contact. All in all a good day out and for me at least a pleasant change from the usual
triangles.

A final message to shore based relatives.

If you are at all anxious - get the 0.0.D. to call us on the Radio. We
can usually put your mind at rest even if we don't appear to be in the right position.

NORMAN KERRIDGE
COXSWAIN

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT -— 1981

The 1981 season started on the first weekend in April, with 10 crews competing for the first of the Spring Points, The series, 12 races in all, turned out to be very wet and windy, and provided plenty of work for the rescue boat. The Summer Points, by way of contrast, were sailed in mainly light conditions. Soth the Spring and Summer Series had increased support this year, with average entries up in most fleets. The Enterprise fleet has recovered some of its lost support and managed to compete in both series, but the Mirror fleet only managed to race a Summer series with an average entry of 3.18.

The Cadet Series entry showed a small increase this year, with 5 races sailed, and the average entry was 5.8, Whilst on the subject of cadets I think it worth noting that for the second year running the Helmsman of the Year has been won by a cadet.

The Ladies Cup had very poor support this year with only 3 of the 6 races sailed. The major event in the Clubs sailing calendar is the Regatta. This year it attracted 206 entries, which was very good considering how wet and windy the weekend was. The Clubs two open trophy races, the Dinghy Challenge Cup and the Cruiser Cup were both won by competitors from outside the Club, with the Dinghy Cup going to G. Palmer of Stone Sailing Club, and the Cruiser Cup to J. Littlewood of Maldon Little Ship Club.

With an average entry of 19 the MideWeek race has proved to be as popular as ever. Indeed, one race had 33 entries, which is better than some
SundaySe

The Solo, 420, Hornet Open Meeting, held in September, again attracted a good entry, particularly the Hornets.

As for open meetings outside the Club, we had no major successes this year, but a party from our Hornet Fleet did travel to Holland for the World Championships. The best placed Marconi Boat being that of Graham Mead and Mike Turner, who finished in 15th place.

Finally, my thanks to the members of the Sailing Committee, Rescue Boat crews, Race Officer and all Club Members who have given up their time to help during the past year.

Murray Bates,

2. Useful discussions wave held on the arrangement and scheduling of points
series. The concensus of opinion was that most fleet members would welcome a third points series as it is felt that at present there is a six week spell around August uwtere points series are dropped. It was proposed that these series could be called Spring, Summer and Autumn, with probably more emphasis on the Summer Points (i.e. more races). Since at present the end of Spring points occurs at a nature! break in the racing calendar (the week before the Regatta), this series is best left as it is. If the proposals are adopted then the end of the Summer Points could conveniently be arranged for the week before the August Bank Holiday.

The meeting also supported a move towards scheduling the afternoon races for 1400 hrs. The main justification for this move was that less time would be spent sitting around getting cold (or drunk!) between the morning and afternoon races. One problem with the proposal is that race officers might set very short courses in the morning to make sure of starting the afternoon races on time. The meeting then launched upon discussions concerning the abilities or otherwise of race officers to which various points emerged. Firstly, since not all race officers sail 420's it was proposed that more fleet representation be made when courses are being set. It was felt that this could best be achieved through ~he fleet captain. Secondly, concern was voiced that perhaps more course guide!ines could be issued to novice race officers, these guidelines to be based on existing race records. This information, however, could be difficult to coliate and may well be a complex task since the time to cover a given course is a function of tides, wind strength and wind direction. Furthermore it was not known how well the race officers sheets are filled in} (I expect Malcolm can tell As an aside, Ron Greygoose is organising race officer instruction for those interested, as part of the winter meetings.

Finally on this point there appeared no resistance to the proposal that the order of class starts be reversed in order to reduce the time on the water for the rescue crews.
/continued.

3. It was proposed that next season the fleet should hold two or three team
racing sessions. It was felt that our team racing tactics and skills are non- existent at present and that if we are ever to win the Boothby Cup we must do something about it. The format of these meetings is at yet undecided, but they will almost certainly be held on a Saturday since the normal sailing programme is usually full. On a personal note I think that these sessions could be a boost to getting a firm commitment to team racing from the more active crews. Remember that being a good team racer does not necessarily mean having the fastest boat —- so those of you that are interested in joining these sessions please let me know.

4. The holding of a 420 Open Day was briefly discussed. It was decided that
having a single specified day would not necessarily reach the largest number of possible converts and could wastefully occupy crew's time and boats unnecessarily. A better solution would be to advertise through Navigans, that anyone interested in sailing a 420 could do so by contacting the fleet captain, who would arrange a suitable time and helmsman. Several boat owners at the meeting pledged their support (thank you Pete and Anna!).

5. Finally, the meeting discussed tuning sessions for next season. This year's
session was held during the August camping week and although the benefits were difficult to quantify, it was felt that much experience in the running of the event was gained which could be used to produce a better organised and more beneficial (and more fun of course!) session next season. To summarise the discussions it was felt that perhaps two days were needed and that time should be given to boat tuning adjustments. This would necessitate two or more boats for instance, sailing parallel courses (but each in clear wind), at the end of which the slower boat alters boat tuning in a attempt to increase boat speed. If this is successful, then the initial fast boat may well have to alter her rig if she is now the slower. To obtain any reasonable conclusions from this approach, all points of sailing will require covering. This of course will require considerable organisation and monitoring! Some of these points have already been discussed in the September .Navigans so will not be laboured further. There will be a "weightlifting" sessionWJanuary at some suitable hostelry so we can formulate some ideas then.

Well it's been a memorable year and I will be sorry to see John and Murray and Dave Harper leave the 420 fleet to join the Hornets, It would seem that the main qualifications required for joining the Hornet Fleet (apart from a Hornet that is) are that you are ‘slightly overweight, can drink enormous quantities of beer, know the words to countless rugby songs (if not be able to hum in a deep tone) and, as Kate Nicholson puts it, be 'mental', Of the first two qualities John and Murray rate highly and of the latter two only time will tell! Dave, I think, will have no problem in making the transition. Kate and I will miss John and Murray whose victories on the water are only surpassed by their repartee before and after races,

I*m happy to report however that John and Murray's boat will still be seen on the water as it has been bought by Russell Jeffries who, through the Marconi Grapevine and thin office walls, is prophesying spectacular victories next season. Well, good luck John, Murray, Dave and Russell.
Russell's boat has been bought by Nick Pavitt, so I hope we shall see him racing next season, and I wish him the best,

Phil Gray.

GUR TROPHIES

For a Club which has been running for some thirty years, members must have looked with pride on the handsome trophies arrayed at the Laying- Up Supper and some of them may have been intrigued at the names given to
theme

The President's Cup was presented by one of our founder members, and first President, the late Sir Eric Eastwood, who intended it for Fleetwinds, a class originally favoured by us. We adopted this class because of its ease of construction and good all-round performance 3; also we knew its designer, Alan Eckford from Stanstead Abbotts who helped us and gave lectures at the Clubts winter evenings, which, at that time were held at The White Hart in New Street, before we had the use of our present fine premises at Beshive Lane. The Fleetwind was popular at the time and some of them found their way to Ceylon and are still sailing today.

The Pilot's Cup was presented by the late Cecil Stebbens of Heybridge Basin, who was pilot and River Bailiff, and was intended to be awarded for an all- in long-distance race. He was very helpful to the Club and towed Mamgu from Maldon to its moorings and he constructed the access ganqway from the top of the seawall to the bargée

Mona's Cup was also presented to us for an all-in long-distance race by Mona Clark, who with her sister, Reena, ran the Jolly Sailor, which was handy for the barge and was much patronised by our members. for the first race we asked her to come aboard Mamgu and fire the starting gun and we also invited them both to our Laying=Up Supper,

The Garrett Memorial Cup was presented to us for cadets by the wife of the late Fred Garrett who was our Secretary and because he attended to Mamqu, he was known as the ship's husband. He did a tremendous amount of work for the Club and he owned a cruiser named "Melody". He cycled to Heybridge from his home at Great Baddow each weekend and some evenings but unfortunately he suffered a heart attack and was unable to cycle, but, undaunted, he acquired a scooter so was still able to reach the barge until his heart finally failed. His daughter still works in the canteen at Great Baddow.

The Boothby Cup was preented by Bob Boothby, Commodore of the Osea Sailing Club when they built a clubhouse on the seawall at Millbeach and were and still are keen sailors, turning out in good numbers, in all weathers. In their early days their members joined our Laying=Up Supper which was held in the New Street canteen, when some 60 of them occupied one complete spur of the top table, making an attendance of some 450 = an all-time record!

The Mamgu Trophy is awarded annually for the best log or account of a member's cruise or adventures during the past season. It is a beautiful model of the sailing barge in her heyday and is correct down to the smallest detail, It was constructed by one of our founder members, Arthur Adam and there is a similar model in the Science Museum at Kensington.

The Triple K may be something of a mystery to somes; it was presented by Nic Tovey and Brian Partridge for Enterprises of which they were exponents. Their boats were named Kiora and Keel Kat respectively, and they were all spelt with Ks, hence the triple Ke They seem to have taken it in turns in the early days to win their own cups.

Eric Payne.

This can only mean one of two things I thought, either I have “= left work before time, or the shortest day is well behind us} Those of you with an astronomical bent will know the answer. It is about this time of year that a young mans (or womans) fancy turns to other things = yes, you've guessed it, the sailing season is almost upon us. By the time you read this there will only be about 6 weeks and one more 420 News before the start of the season. With this in mind I shall forwarn you of the seasons earliest activities.

This year the fleet are moving to a different position in the dinghy parke The new position is Row A which is the row nearest the sea wall. The reason for this move is to help the older men of the Hornet fleet who were complaining of having to pull their boats from the cruiser park. Our new position is very favourable and certainly has more grass underfoot than the previous spot. As an aid to boat positioning within the row, I shall drive some wooden stakes into the ground to mark the centre of each transom and shall space the stakes to allow adequate room around each boat for rigging etce We will then operate on a "first come — first served" principal with the first boat being nearest to the Clubhouse (sorry lads, my boat is already down there!).
