Another planned activity and the one I'm sure you've all been dying to hear about is the early season working party! This year our fleet is charged with preparing the rescue boat for the water and launching it. This job normally occupies two weekends since it involves anti—fouling the hull. This first activity does not require many people so the fleet will be split into two groupse Since the March Navigans will appear too late to advertise the final dates I shall contact those involved personally. As usual of course, your hard working fleet captain will be there both weekends$

At the last Pleet social gathering in the General's Arms the topic of dinghy insurance was raised, and it was felt that an insurance survey could be useful and that if any one Company/Broker was found to be universally preferred, then perhaps they could be approached with a view to obtaining cheaper insurance for a larger number of boats on their books. At the end of this month's news there follows a simple questionaire which I ask you to fill in and post to me. I notice, from last month's Navigans that the Mirror fleet also have cheaper insurance in mind, so if they feel so inclined I would be pleased to receive completed forms from them and indeed from any other fleet/ dinghy owner, who may be reading these In fact, the more replies received the better since a more accurate view of the market can then be achieved — so please take a minute off to complete the questionaire — it may save you money in the long term!

IDEAS _ SECTION.

As promised last month I will open this section with a description of how to mount the kicker lever under the thwart with little loss in
efficiency.

The figure (on Page 6) shows how the wires, pulley and lever are positioned. The two wires should be of substantial thickness (2 mm suggested) since the lever generates impressive forces. The upper half of the longer wire, above thwart height should be plastic sheathed to minimise damage to the crew (actually this system improves crew mobility during tacking). The main anchorage point for the system is at the aft end of the centreboard casing. This should be achieved by drilling a vertical hole through the casing and attaching a substantial eye bolt. Ensure that a washer is employed to distribute the load on the casinge Attachment of the wire to the eye bolt can be by shackle or by direct attachment with a thimbled eye in the wire.

Sincs the rules allow only two pulleys with a lever, and since one of these pulleys is required on the mast, the second cannot be used to any
mechanical advantage. However the length of the lever is not restricted and it is possible to employ a longer lever than is conventionally carried in the classic kicker arrangement. I have not found this to be necessary but for younger helms/crew this is worth considering.

All dimensions shown in the figure can be varied by plus or minus one inch without any problems if the boom fixing is variable. If this is not the case the long wire length must be determined to suit your own boom setting. The modern 420 has a fixed gooseneck with sail luff tension controlled by the cunningham. If you have an older boat (eog- Snapir) the gooseneck can be permanently fixed and the same principals of mainsail tuning applied,

To prevent the lever slapping the centreboard casing it: is possible to loosely mount the lever to the casing with a rubber bush. The mounting

/continued.

must allow enough movement for the rotation of the lever and should be placed as close to the centre of rotation as possible. Finally the kicker control rape is led out through a cleat on the top edge of the centreboard casing, and here the spare pulley can be used to provide directional variations for the linee If you wish to know more about these last two aspects have a look at K38346 when she's next out.

Phil Gray.
Fleet Captain.

OUR TROPHTLES

Continued from previous Navigans.

The Jackpot. Cup was presented by Jack Bigden for a race for the over=forties. Jack did a tremendous amount of work for the Club and was largely responsible for the construction of our original wooden clubhouse at Stansgates he also presented the Commodore Cupe

The Costain. Cup was presented by the late Sir Richard Costain whose firm constructed the M.A.S.C. clubhouse in Beehive Lane; he was told about our sailing activities in which he took a great interest and offered to present us with the said trophye

The Hornet Challenge Cup was presented by The Saltcote Sailing Club, in the ballast hole at Heybridge and has been won alternately by them and us. They are to be congratulated on their new floating clubhouse and their enthusiasm in turning out in good numbers in all conditions. We were pleased to welcome their then Commodore, Derek Gerkin and his wife Mollie at our last laying—up supper, in fact Derek proposed the health of our Club.

The Twin=Flags Trophy was presented by the 8.8.C's club known as The Ariel Sailing Club, whose clubhouse is at Teddington on the River Thames, and was won alternately by us and them. Sailing for these races was an interesting experience because, in their case, it involved dealing with flukey winds caused by buildings and trees,and when they sailed with us their experience of having to contend with choppy salt water!

The Jonathan David Craig Cup was presented by Jack Sigden and is called after the name of his grandson.

We are indebted to Vic Tate for producing the pictures of these trophies in the issues of Navigans for March and April 1974 when his wife Brenda was Editoress, and to Vice=President Nick Tovey for his painstaking research in supplying the names of the early winners, — his name being seen frequently amongst them.

THAT WAS THE YEAR THAT WAS

Well, my ears have only just stopped ringing from the calls of STARBOARD!, WATER!, and UWP UP UP!, it seems that if nothing else, Hornet sailors can outeshout anybody on the river or in the barJ But despite my temporary deafness, "mine's a pint of lager", I have survived a very enjoyable year with a new boat in the Hornet Fleet and it's not called Stimulation for nothing, being a largermainedstiffriggedgybing= boardgofastershapedgoodwinhornet$ Steering me round the buoys has been Simon Kenworthy, who has perfected his Jacque Cousteau impersonation despite ‘all sorts of problems depending on the wind(pardon). But as if to confound our sometimes brutal treatment of the boat, due to our unusual sailing techniques, it has proved to be very strong and resiliant.

The fleet at Marconi is looking very healthy (boat numbers that is}) under the careful guidance of Murray Todd our Fleet Captain. The Tacing at the club has been excellent and Marconi boats have also done very well in other clubs! open meetings.

Along with Colin Harper we competed in the Junior Nationals at Medway Sailing Club. The sailing was good but the social life(?) left something to be desired. The event was won by the Newman brothers with Div Mellor second, we finished Sth. and Colin 8th. We also competed in the Stone open meeting and finished 10th out of 38 boats, This together with a 7th in our own Regatta and a 4th in the Summer Points are good results, we feel, for the first year.

We also competed in the Brightlingsea winter series, and although this is a closed event, Colin and ourselves were given temporary membership of the club. In spite of not managing any major success we enjoyed the sailing and our thanks go to the Commodore, Roger Robinson, and everyones at the club for making us so very welcome.

The social life has been, and still is, the best of any fleet with great friendship extended by other clubs* fleets, much entertainment being enjoyed both organised and impromptu< "nice one moonie and steady. dickie". So, eagerly looking forward to the new season, which starts for us with the Easter Egg at the Royal Corinthian Club, Surnham, on the 9thel2th April, we hope to see you there and we'll go ffor it in a really big waye

Congratulations must be extended to Dave Harper, Murray Bates and John Chisnall for their excellent taste in joining the Hornet Fleet.

MIRROR FLEET NEWS

FIRST, THE GOOD NEWS = the Mirror Fleet meeting at my home in Sillericay was well attended by eleven members, with another four members sending their apologies for absence due to illness or other unavoidable commitments. Since the four absentees have all raced and helped with Mirror duties in 1981, then I am encouraged by the response to this meeting and hope the fleet can carry it through to the racing programme
in 1982,

The meeting was arranged to hear a talk by Dennis Sristowe on Sailing the Mirror. Dennis is a well-known Mirror helmsman of national standard and (to borrow a theme from a well-known advertisement) his talk reached those theoretical parts that the text books cannot. reach. In other words, Dennis avoided the pitfall of merely repeating the standard text—book theory of sailing and instead gave us a more practical approach to solving the problems of mast rake, lee and weather helm, rigging, sail setting,
spinnaker systems, hull painting etc. - in fact, all those subjects falling
under the more general heading of "boat tuning". The meeting soon took the form of "question and answer" and I personally found the talk just right in:

NOW FOR THE GAD NEWS = the Mirror Fleet has unfortunately lost half of its prime dinghy parking space in the Dinghy Park (West) to the 420 Fleet. This has occurred due to the Hornet Fleet not unnaturally feeling a little aggrieved at having to drag their boats a considerable way on race days whilst many Mirrors never move from the park from the beginning of the season to the end, or, if they do move, do so on relatively rare occasions and not as part of the racing programme. The consequent rearrangement of dinghy parking means that part of the Mirror Fleet will be in Dinghy Park
(West) and the remainder in the space vacated by the Hornet Fleet in the
Dinghy Park (East) i.e. the cruiser park, In order to keep the Mirror Fleet alive as an active group and to encourage a Mirror "awareness" both amongst ourselves and the other fleets, I have asked that the known racing Mirrors be kept together with the other racing fleets in Dinghy Park (West). I would be grateful for the co-operation of all Mirror owners in ensuring that their Mirror is correctly parked in their alloted space and not in any other space. This may mean that you do not have the same space as last year.
/continued.

NOW SOME MORE GOOD NEWS —=— I've now bought a second Mirror dinghy and hope to have all the Boreham family sailing this season = subject to suitable weather conditions. EVEN BETTER NEWS -— Phil Gray has very quickly organised a Cadet:
training programme with the assistance of Colin Leveridge and I hope all you Mirror Cadets will take advantage of it. If you take your youngsters to attend the meetings, you can enjoy a drink in the bar safe in the knowledge that you're only there for the benefit of the kids,

BEST NEWS YET = the sailing programme starts on Sunday 4th April and is only five weeks away at the time of writing this article. By the time you read this, the first race may well be over. If you haven't got your boat down at the club yet then hurry 'cos it'll be the Laying=—Up Supper before you know what's happening and yet another sailing season will have been wasted.

FOOTNOTE = I'll endeavour to introduce myself to as many Mirrormen, Mirrorwomen and Mirrorcadets as possible, but remember such introductions are a two-way affair. why not introduce yourself to me = I'll be pleased to meet you since it shows you have an interest in the Mirror Fleet. IF I DON'T CALL ON YOU = WHY DON'T YOU CALL ON ME INSTEAD.

DINGHY PARKING

On reading the March issue ef NAVIGANS I was concerned to find items which indicate a trend of opinion which cannot be allowed to go unchallenged. The contributions in question refer to the re-allocation of space in. the dinghy park and clearly imply that racing helmsman should be given prioity over those who do not race.

I have no axe to grind as to how people make use of their sailing time whether it is to race, cruise or potter but it has always been recognised that, unlike some other clubs, the M.S.C. is not a purely racing club.

It should also be remembered that those dinghy owners who do not appear to sail. very often are still contributing to club funds and are therefore making it possible for the more enthusiastic to organise their racinge Those who spend little time at the club are the losers as they are not making the use of the facilities to which their subscription entitles them.

It may be a sad fact to the racing committee but an examination of the club's statistics leads one to the conclusion that the racing members are in fact a minority of the membership. Under these circumstances why should a Tacing helmsman have priority regarding parking position over the next?

I have always in the past been reluctant to make criticisms of the club's management as I am only too aware of the valiant work they do and what little contribution I make to their work (also some are my friends?). On this occasion, however, I must point out that such a move constitutes a change in club policy which to my knowledge has not been referred to the membership. All dinghy owners who pay the same subscription must have equal access to the club's facilities.

Douge Paynter.

The following article came into the hands of our President, Mr. Jack Pateman, from an unknown source:=

"MARINE CASUALTY = A report sighted by Captain G.P. Byth (1940).

Dear Sir,

I write in haste in order that you will get this report before you form your preconceived opinions from reports in the world press, for I am sure that. they will tend to over=dramatise the affair.

We had just picked up the pilot, and the apprentice had returned from changing the 'G* flag for the *H', and being his first trip was having difficulty in rolling the 'G* flag up, I therefore proceeded to show him how, coming to the last part I told him to ‘let go', the lad, although willing is not too bright, necessitating my having to repeat the order in a sharper tone.

The Chief Officer overhearing from the Chart room, and thinking that it was the anchors that were being referred to repeated the ‘let go' to the Third Officer on the forecastle. The effect of letting from the the port anchor drop ‘pipe’ while the vessel was proceeding at full harbour speed proved too much for the windlass brake, and the entire length of the cable was pulled out ‘by the roots? I fear that the damage to the chain locker may be extensive. The braking effect naturally caused the vessel to sheer in that direction, right towards the swing bridge that spans a tributary to the river up which we were proceeding.

The swing bridge operator showed great presence of mind by opening the bridge for my vessel, unfortunately he did not think to stop the vehicular traffic. The result being that the bridge partly opened and deposited a Volkswagen, two cyclists and a cattle truck on the foredeck. In his efforts to stop the progress of the vessel the Third Officer dropped the starboard anchor, too late to be of practical use for it fell on the swing bridge operator's control cabin.

Up to now I have confined my report to the activities at the forward end of my vessel, aft they were having their own problems. At the moment the port anchor was let go, the Second Officer was supervising the making fast of the after tug, and was lowering the ship's towing spring down onto the tug.

The sudden braking effect on the port anchor caused the tug to 'run in under! the stern of my vessel, just at the moment when the propellor was answering my double ring Full Astern. The prompt action of the Second Officer in securing the inboard end of the towing spring delayed the sinking of the tug by some minutes thereby allowing the safe abandoning of that vessel,

It never fails to amaze me, the actions and behaviour of foreigners during moments of minor crisis. The pilot for instance, is at this moment huddled in the corner of my day cabin, alternately crooning to himself and crying after having consumed a bottle of gin in a time that is worthy of inclusion in the Guinness Book of Records, The tug captain on the other hand reacted violently and had to forcibly be restrained by the Steward, who has him handcuffed in the ship's
hospital.

I enclose the names and addresses of the drivers and insurance companies of the vehicles on my foredeck, which the Third Officer collected after his somewhat hurried evacuation of the forecastle, these particulars will enable you to claim for the damage that they did to the railings of number one hold.

I am closing this preliminary report for I am finding it difficult to concentrate with the sound of police sirens and their flashing lights. Had the apprentice realized that there is no need to fly pilot flags after dark, none of this would have happened.
I am Sir, Yours faithfully, MASTER.”

REMEMBER = COLD CAN KILL

Extract from R.Y.A. Publication = G 16,

Hypothermia is the most dangerous of conditions caused by exposure to cold, and is a condition best avoided} Indeed, cold is probably. the main threat to life during prolonged immersion in any waters other than trapical ones. It is therefore sensible to assess the risks before sailing on cold water and take all possible precautions to avoid becoming chilled. when the water is very cold, say around 5 C (41 F) a man of ordinary build would be hypothermic and helpless in half=-an—hour or less. He would be reduced to the same state within one or two hours if the water were 15°C (59°F) although these times may be doubled by the wearing of conventional clothing and even more if special clothing is worn. Some sailing clubs insist on their members wearing
"wet-suits"
when water temperatures are below 5°C(41°F) and this is a very wise rule because, quite apart from hypothermia, immersion in cold water can cause sudden death and because the shock of immersion makes it difficult to breathe:
normally.

Avoidance — Avoiding hypothermia therefore resolves itself into a matter of wearing a sufficiency of warm clothing with a wind=proof and waterprooff outer layer. When in the water it is preferable to float quietly and wear gloves or mittens whenever possible to minimise the chance of cold injury to the fingers.

Ignorance — There seems to exist a considerable ignorance about the dangers of immersion in cold water, or alternatively, there is a reluctance to accept that the hazard is important. Measures are taken to avoid ordinary physical injury and drowning and, indeed, most sportsmen and others are familar with the first aid treatment of these conditions. Oddly enough, the universal acceptance of approved life-jackets has probably increased the danger of death from hypothermia, though only because drowning is delayed long enough for cooling to take place. Drowning occurs very rapidly after immersion in cold water because of certain respiratory reflexes and the fact that very few people can swim for more than a few minutes in very cold water,

More and more enthusiastic sailors, canoeists and others use their boats all the year round, even when conditions are extremely cold. In general, such activity should be encouraged, but with reservations, because there is no doubt that there is an appreciable hazard, although the risks can be reduced to an acceptable level by sensible appreciation of the simple actions necessary to reduce the possibility of injury by cold, and the reasons for them.

Your committee strongly advise all dinghy sailors to wear wetsuits when sailing particularly in the Spring and Autumn Series.

I am writing this with sticking plasters on certain fingers — this being a sign that the season is well under way and that excellent winds have prevailed (except for one Sunday that is).

Russell Jeffries was out with his newly acquired boat and he rapidly discovered new found power that led to a few encounters of the fishy kind$ The race finished with Heather Stuart and myself taking first place with Pete and Dave Sayer a close second. However, by the time the boat was righted Pete and Dave Sayer had taken the initiative and had sped past to win the race.

So it was all down to the last race with lots of sailing psychology being applied in the bar at lunchtime. The race proved to be very exciting with Pete and Dave getting away to a good start leaving Malcolm and myself to restart after crossing the line before the start signal. Some lost ground was made up on the leading 420 but no amount of effort could prevent Pete and Dave coming home first and winning the series. Seventeen Cadets travelled to Musto and Hyde sailing loft at South Benfleet on Thursday 22nd April. The First Time

A Nearly True Story.

Well, there was I, the owner of a motor cruiser, and suddenly the cost of my trips poodling up and down the river were beginning to get quite frighteningly high. It was then that a friend suggested that what I was doing was not real boating, and offered to introduce me to sailing. He took me sailing in a Wayfarer on an idyllic summer Sunday evening with a puff of wind blowing now and then, and we cruised down to the local hostillery and drifted back somewhat more ballasted than when we went. That was the moment I decided that this sailing was for me. [I decided that I would like to build a popular fibre=-glass dinghy because the local dealer was very close, and I was sure he could advise me if I got into trouble, but to cut a very long story short that was an absolute disaster, because, not only was the dealer an incompetent fool, who eventually delivered to my home enough resin and matt to build two Morning Clouds (the gel of which was the wrong colour anyway), but as the moulds (hired from the imcompetent fool) were being delivered, one half fell off the trailer and was last seen apparently trying to overtake a police car on Blue Bell Hill.

After that I decided to look through the magazines, try to find a second= hand boat, and suddenly there she was, an Enterprise, called Wild Times, trolley, trailer, cover, and all go fast gear. What else could I ask for (I didn't even know what size an Enterprise was$) but the owner proudly told me of the races she has won and the thought of getting to the hostillery somewhat quicker than the Wayfarer spurred me one I took delivery on a day that was to be somewhat of an omen. A ; tremendous thunderstorm was in progress, complete with lightning, hail and torrential raine A bedraggled man rang the door bell and asked if this was Mr. Noah's house, handed me a soggy envelope with a "certificate" in it and disappeared into the wettness forever. So Wild Times was mine.

That weekend I thought I'd sort out all the ropes and wires and funny looking gear and it took several lengthy phone calls to my friend with the Wayfarer to rig the mast, but finally we made it and decided to hoist the sails — whereupon the boat promptly blew over, and looked most undignified lying on the next doorneighbours car, so we very hurriedly righted her before it was noticed (my neighbour is a very big bloke, and has no sense of humour?).

I think it was then that I noticed these silver things in the bottom of the boat. I rang my friend and again "it's okay, those are the elevstrom bailers", "just part of the sophisticated bailing system". Then I noticed two perspex flaps in the flat end, I rang my friend again “what are the windows for", I asked, "just part of the sophisticated bailing system", he said, and this time I detected a touch of impatience in his voice, I then noticed something else which I didn't understand, but decided not to ring my friend as maybe I was straining relationships a bit far.

So the big day arrived. Michael Fish said it would be force 3/4 and sunny and warm — and so it was. My wife and son rigged the boat while I took one more glance at my "teach yourself" sailing book. It is at this stage I should explain that the better half of my marriage was not relishing the maiden voyage of Wild Times, and with life jacket, water wings and Rosary at the ready climbed aboard. A good shove from me and we were sailing."Beautiful — now I think the pub is that way", It was then I wished I had strained my relationship with my friend to one phone call more, because there were these two holes in the transom letting in water like the Murda Dam after 603 Squadron had finished.

The crew drew my attention to the fact and I informed the crew that it was all right — probably just part of the sophisticated bailing system and when we really got going the stern will lift and the Elevstroms would take the water away", Well, it didn't happen quite like that. In fact the water got deeper and deeper and crew got more and more agitated until I wasn't sure whether it was my blood pressure causing the screaming in my ears or the crew requesting — no demanding = that I do

/continuede

mt kk =

somethinge Fortunately, just across the river to where we had launched is an island, and we headed like a wounded wallowing water buffalo towards the beach with the finger of the crews glove in one drain: hole and my bobble hat jammed in the other. We landed, and with the crew standing with arms akimbo (the classic mother-in-law pose) demanded I empty the Medway back into the Medway. “What with?", I asked, meekly. "You work it out — you're the skipper", came the acid reply. I looked around for something to bail with — nothing — not a thinge There was only one thing to do — I took off one of my wellies and started to bail. This was too much for the crew who broke into uncontrollable hysterical laughter. Somebody said that being a skipper is a lonely business so I took. no notice. I got the boat relaunched with my hankie ripped in half, and, with a big knot tied in each, rammed into the drain holes. We sailed back to the slip whereupon the crew ran to the parked car, screaming oaths about male chauvenists, incompetent helmsman, and mumbling "that's it, that's it, never again{". So it was that the crew of Wild Times hurled themselves at the delights of sailing.

A short time after this we found, and joined, the local sailing club - with all the advice and help one could ever wish for (plus a safety boat on hand). There, Wild Times and both of her crew learned how to sail safely and properly, and the true reason for their existence, which is to continually cut down the amount.of — time that it: takes to reach the pub on the river, ,

Rule 50 states that a yacht whose entry has been accepted and which sails about in the vicinity of the starting line between her preparatory (i.e. 5=minute) signal and the starting signal shall rank as a starter whether she starts or not. I've always understood that this requirement is satisfied if a yacht is actually in the water at the 5eminute signal, even if merely being held stationary by a member of the crew, and still ranks as a starter even if held after the starting signal or indeed never actually crosses the start line at all.

In one race this year, it appeared from the race box that one yacht was still on the hard at the Seminute signal and, in accordance with the rule, did not rank as a starter, In fact the yacht was still on the hard at the start signale The yacht in question then got afloat, sailed up to and crossed onto the pre—course side of the line, and started "correctly" (if that is possible for a yacht not ranking as a starter!}). SAILING TECHNIQUES FOR TIROS

We have members in our Club who have a wealth of knowledge which I feel sure would be of real interest and value to novice or less experienced sailors. Why not use Navigans as the medium to impart your pearls of wisdom! Unfortunately most potential contributors are too busy sailing to put pen to paper but somebody has to make a start = so here goes}

There are many excellent books available on boat tuning and the sailing techniques and tactics necessary to win races, but the Tiro can easily become confused by the detail and get his priorities all wrong, e.g. the finer points of tuning and having the best equipment only marginally effect performance whereas what really matters is Helming Ability, or as it is sometimes said, the nut on the end of the tiller. How does one obtain this Helming Ability? Obviously there is no substitute for hours spent on the water, nevertheless there are bad practises which need to be unlearned and good practises which must be followed at all times if you are to get amongst the race leaders. Probably the most difficult skill to master is the ability to sail to windward. It is here that most races are won or lost.

Sailing
to Windward

Getting to the windward mark first depends on a combination of speed and directiane Direction is a matter of choosing the shortest route by making use of
/continuede

the wind and tide but it is no good going in the right direction if you are not getting there fast enough.

Real improvements in speed to windward may be obtained if certain basic points are understood and mastered. It is the relative trim of the sail and centreboard which determine how well you sail to windward. If the boat is not to slide sideways through the water the centreboard must generate a sideways force equal to that exerted by the sail.

NeB. In order to generate drive and sideways force it is necessary for both the sail and the centreboard to be set at a small angle of incidence to the wind and water respectively.

Priority 1 — Keep the boat Upright.

Both the sail and the centreboard operate at maximum efficiency when the boat is absolutely level and the mast and centreboard are vertical.

Centreboard theory.

The force generated by the centreboard (F C.) is proportional to the square of the speed of the boat through the water (S) and the angle of incidence to the water (A), 00 A.S*, The angle of incidence is in fact the angle at which the boat is slipping away to leeward. Every effort must be made therefore to keep this angle to a minimum. Remember Aoof C. and 1/82, If the boat is to be kept upright all the heeling forces must balance. Let us consider a typical situation. (Any resemblance to a SOLO is purely intentional).

TAKING YOUR MOORING

To the single=handed yachtsman taking his mooring, every second counts.
Having grasped the buoy it still takes several seconds to belay the mooring rope round the bitts, while to haul in the chain to the required length and flick it vigourously to remove most of the mud, may take minutes and a lot could happen in this time.

The operation can be facilitated by splicing a loop of strong line into the main mooring rope at about one metre from the buoy. It is then an easy matter to haul in the buoy over the anchor chain rollers just far enough to secure this loop round the bitts.

The skipper can then relax and return at leisure to the cockpit to stop the engine or release the sheets, which have an uncanny habit of fouling on these
occasions.

But don't forget to haul in the chain and secure it before going ashore Incidentally, it is much easier for the boat hook to take the loop rather than the thick strop or the buoy itself.

As announced previously in Navigans our colleagues at Rochester now have a Clubhouse with sailing facilities and they have invited us to visit them on the August Bank Holiday weekend 28th — 30th August.

To encourage as many participants as possible we intend to sail as a fleet. Some boats have radio but we shall intend to keep within hailing distance throughout.
/continued.

oO 3 =

The distance involved is about 40 miles each way which will be sailed entirely with favourable neap tidese This means the fleet will leave Stansgate at 10 am on the
Saturday morning. The return trip on Monday will leave at high tide = about 10.30 am.

On each of these trips it will be essential to maintain a speed of 4% knots, which will mean use of the motor if the wind is unfavourable. From a comfort point of view the trip as a fleet would be called off if winds were expected to be above force 4. From a safety viewpoint the expectation of fog would also mean cancellation.

I did this trip in Kalinka at Regatta time this year and found it an easy one in the conditions we then had. It worked out that I did 50/50 sailing and motoring as breezes came and went. I had about 1 mile of visibility which presented no problem and we completed the trip with time to spare before the tide changed.

Please let me know if you hope to come then I will give out any final details as necessary.

Anyone who would like to come as a crew should also contact me as there may be boats looking for crews. Given fair weather this will make an enjoyable trip and I hope we can get a good turnout. Remember Rochester have been visiting us regularly for several yearse

One small detail is worth giving at present. Do not bring rigid dinghies, but inflatables. In my experience these are best towed stern first hauled in tightly to the transom by two warps attached to the outboard mounting points of the inflatable. This prevents flipping in a strong breeze, and if you get something round your prop you have a stable platform from which to work to remove ite In my case recently it was a large piece of polythene that came off easily with the boat hook.

Remember — August Bank Holiday is Rochester weekend.

SUMMER CRUISE I98I

S. Crisp. BEEHIVE

Sat. Aug. Ist.
Beehive and Tijo left Stansgate for Levington Marina with Margaret Cambell from Tijo stating that as she had six people on board, namely Tan Campbell and his fiancee Kim and Jimmy Campbell and Jackie Hall as well as themselves plus all the extra food stacked quite high, they were going to have a steady sail and were not going to push it too hard.

The wind was a northerly force 4 gusting 5, right on the nose and while sailing with wind over tide in the wallet I watched Tijo being thrown all over the place and realised, not just from the Way my stomach was trying to escape from my mouth, that we were doing exactly the same thing. While keeping my back to the bow of the boat and trying to concentrate on what the first thing was that I would do when discarding with my wet oilies Vic kept me informed of the state of each wave in short form, MY. (medium wave) L.W. (long wave) and F.W. ( which he assured me was a freak wave)

With wind over tide it took 9 hours to reach Levington Marina where we met up with Brenda, Vic and Mary Tate of Copernicus and Sandra and Peter Claydon of Peace who should have been in Holland but were held up by unfavourable weather. The following day (Sunday) we were all held up by very favourable weather when the sun beat down on us and the only relief had to be the nearest watering hole at Levington, so there we were outside the local pub, taking up most of the seats and tables lunchtime and again the evening and what an enjoyable day that was.

Mon. Aug. 3rd.
Still glorious sun but winds barely force 2. Copernicus and Peace had left very early that morning for their destination in Holland and we set motor for Southwold. According to Mr Trigg, the harbour master, our boats would be able to enter the Southwold entrance at any state of the tide. We approached the entrance at about 7.15 pem. and low tide was about 8 p.m. We saw Tijo who was just ahead of us looking slightly stationary for just a few seconds and when we followed we realised why, we bumped a few times but made it in okay. At least we know now just where the bar lies.

On tying up at the quayside we were delighted to find that
the pub there was serving fresh fried fish and chips bonus - especially for
me who had ran out of calor gas that day and had been looking forward to a mere sandwich that evening. It was the freshest fish and chips we'd tasted for a long time. Whilst in the town the following day (Tuesday), Tijo's scouts spotted a fellow member, Bill Penkham of Sirius but although we made our way to where the sighting had taken place, he had obviously gone to ground or perhaps we'd passed him on the way, anyway we returned to our boats in readiness for our sail? to Lowestoft the next day. At this point, Margaret discovered that Tijo's loo was completely blocked to which we all discussed the possibilities of the cause of such a thing while Stan, looking a bit down in the mouth knew that he was going to have to do the curing of it.

Weds. Aug. 5th.
Still hardly a puff of wind, plenty of sun and some fog banks.
Vic and I were sitting having our breakfast in the cockpit, marvelling at the still glorious morning when other sounds caught our care coming from Tijo -

It was Stan, banging and retching whilst clearing his blocked loo = suddenly, up came the forehatch cover and one at a time out jumped the four inhabitants who had been sleeping only seconds beforehand, gasping for air as they came. The job done and up came stan, bucket in hand and proceeded to throw the
contents overboard - on our side = oh well, we werent that hungry anyway.

Before leaving Southwold we met up with another Macwester called Penelope Jane, the owners were schoolteachers on holiday and had sailed down from Humberside, so before leaving there were hurried inspections of each others boats. The weather conditions were so calm en-route to Lowestoft it was hard to believe that this was the north sea, and it seemed Jimmy Campbell didn't believe it either and leapt overboard to investigate, attached to a warp and a
buoy - although we rather suspected that Margaret and Stan had that many on board
they'd been eaten out of a boat and a dinghy so they'd cast Jimmy overboard as
live bait - but the fish didn't want to know.

Reaching Lowestoft, was for me, absolutely wonderful - although
our main intention for this holiday was to go to Lowestoft I somehow had the thought in the back of my mind that weather conditions would not allow it in the
two short weeks that we had - me of little faith.

We had been forewarned that the mooring charges would be £6. a night for our boats in the outer harbour, but if we had chosen to wait until the road bridge was lifted we could have gone up river for a mile or so and the sailing club there would have let us use their moorings for £1.50 a night, but as we did not want to be dependant on waiting for the bridge to be opened for coming out we rafted up in the outer harbour where, with quite a lot of other boats, especially Dutch, spent a few not too comfortable days of snubbing and not too easy times getting onto the ladder up onto the quayside.

The Royal Norfolk and Suffolk Yacht Club however was very welcoming and very comfortable, we proudly left a Marconi burgee to be hung amongst the other club burgees in one of the lounges.

Fri. Aug. -7the
Left Lowestoft for the Butley River, once again hardly any wind but the sea had some nice rollers coming in and when Tijo and Beehive were both in a ‘downer’ we could only see each others masts, In spite of the fact that we were having to motor again it was a very pleasant trip. On passing Southwold the Macwester we had previously met there called Penelope Jane re-joined us and stayed in our company for the following week.

—
Sat Aug 8th.
Left the Ore making for the Deben and Woodbridge Marina. Passed Ron Phillips of Vanellus making for Lowestoft and Ann and John Smith of Freya making for the Ore. We were to meet up with Wendy, Jean and Peter Hall (and one plastered leg) of Jappa in Woodbridge and their guests for the weekend, John and Shiela of Two's Company, where we spent a very pleasant weekend. A very reluctant John and Shiela had to leave Woodbridge by train to go home on the
Monday and I Don't think that the rest of us waving them off and jumping up and
down at the station made them feel any better. Monday night the men had our five gallon water container half filled with real ale in readiness for the bar-b-que the following night.

Tues. Aug. IIth.
Prepared to leave Woodbridge Marina for the Rocks, weather glorious again and a calm day. Vic had rather a long walk into town to get petrol before we could leave as only diesel fuel is available in the Marina. On reaching the Rocks we walked to Ramsholt and collected wood on the way back in readiness for the much awaited bar=-b=que that night. It was Kims birthday as well so it was to be a celebration, and we certainly had a terrific celebration
the singing round the fire that night was pure harmony - well it sounded so at
the time although we did start a few wolves howling somewhere in the distance.

Five Marconi boats entered the World Championships this year at Highcliff Sailing Club. Dave Harper crewed by Murray Todd, Colin Harper crewed by Danny Lumley, Simon Kenworthy crewed by Ian Stott, Graham Mead crewed by Mike Turner and Pat Black crewed by Caron Stuart.

After a good journey down to Highcliff, the boats were unpacked, measured, weighed and then entered, this taking all of the Saturday. However, with 70 boats to be done and with nice sunny warm conditions, the wait did'nt seem all that longe All the boats were passed fit, but a little on the heavy side, and we all looked forward to an eventful series on large Olympic courses.

Sunday Practice

Winds light, Westerly, Variable.

The fleet started first time and on time on a very long line start.
Colin Harper 2100 sorted out the wind shifts on the first beat to arrive 7th at the windward marke Simon Kenworthy 2093 started late, after being line shy, to reach the mark in the pack with Dave Harper 2078 not far behind.

The first reach developed into a run allowing the back of the fleet to
overtake the middle of the fleet. Many place changes took place with 2093 and 2070
moving up through the fleet during the following legs.

I have just calculated that I have spent twenty days under canvas during August. There was a marked absence of wind during the week (apart from that coming from Kate’s tent that is) and although this curtailed some of the planned sailing activities it appeared at times that we had forsaken sailing for canoeing! My only memory of the canoeing races is that of suffering pains in places where I didn't even know I had places!

If the Obstacle Race is ever held again the rules will be changed so that I can win something’ It showed me two things = firstly I do not sail backwards well and secondly that for those intrepid single handed sailors in a two man dinghy who do in fact raise the spinnaker (well done John in the Hornet and me in the 420) - these should be rewarded with a longer spinnaker leg (weather permitting that is!). I observed several things during this epic event. Firstly during the capsize exercise, on leaping over the side I found that Kate had not put the centreboard down$!$ (what are crews coming to these days). Secondly two man (or one man, one girl or one boy, one girl, etc.) lasers came first and second, and thirdly we appear to have an olympic swimmer in the club who can swim from A mark to Osea faster that a dinghy can sail the same distance Anyway, everyone joined in the spirit of the event and I'm thinking of joining the Hornet Fleet to learn how to sail backwards.

The innumerable games of volleyball, rounders and football once again brought out the competitive spirit in everyone. The volleyball produced a superstar in Janet Chisnall whose spatial awareness and her dexterity close in to the net was sheer poetry. (Janet — I was a little disappointed that you didn't keep falling on me this year$) The mixed football proved to be very physically demanding with some impressive tackling and dribbling (I had forgotten my handerchief!). Power struggles eventually started between the Gray Brothers and a duo of Robert Weedon/Little John Chisnall and the game was only finished when Lucy Boreham stopped an almost certain winning shot from Bob Gray, with the back of her head. Well done Lucy, and keep taking the pills luv. What a great game rounders is when you have a left hander on your team who can whack the ball. into the ditch and then stroll round for one rounder. Even with this advantage, the final outcome was very close and apart from a few obvious cases of obstruction, (worth half a rounder I believe) very little rule=bending was evident (shame$).

Man overboard drill for the Cadets went with a splash with scenes reminiscent of the Marie Celeste. Some cadets were seen re=entering the boat over the stern and this is to be discouraged as even a big cadet like myself can get over the side! (enough of the serious stuff).

To those of you: who enjoyed the week, on your behalf I would like to thank the followinge Cheers John and Murray for the support and something like ten man= hours of work (hard work) in constructing the deathslide. Thanks to Bob and Russell for their help on the Sunday and to Bob for all the canoeing instruction and the nightcapse Thanks to the Sailing Sub-committee for their finalcial support and the authorisation of the splashing out on prizes (they haven't had the bill yet!). Thanks to Mike Boreham for the prize=giving ceremony (see list of prize winners at the end) = you lucky devil Mike, I hear you got two kisses from Kate. Special thanks from Bob and myself to all those that so generously contributed towards our second favourite pastime. Finally thanks to all those that joined in the spirit of things and for anyone that may have been bored for the odd hour or two — you had better watch out next year$

Code of Practice for Launching and

Recovery of Cruisers

Large Boats = Boats above 27 ft length will NOT be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress, At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight. The tractor is more suitable than winches for heavy boats but see below concerning ropes.

Tractor - Only to be operated by authorised drivers. It is extremely dangerous
for non key holders to operate the tractor.

Winches - When Club organised dinghy events are in progress the winches must be
under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies.

The OOD will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for information of dinghy sailors,

At other times the following code should be observed:=

When winding up the slope always use the ratchet.

Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed.

Avoid sharp bends in winch cables = shackles should be used for attachment to trolleys.

It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strom team of helpers,

If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain on level and always clear of loose shingle.

Boat If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to Trolleys = other boats,

Work Boat - This may be operated by any club member after obtaining permission
from Peter Clayton who will advise upon its use. A team of at least two people is necessary for work on moorings.

OUR COMMODORE'S NOTES

Having recovered from the annual withdrawal symptoms once again it is time for the autumn activities. The Laying-Up Supper (which we hope is successful) at the Chancellor Hall, and the A.GeM. which is usually well supported, come close
together.

The committee are very reluctant to put up members! costs but our expenditure over the last few years has been rising and there is no choice but to increase members! contributions. There were no increases in fees last year when the Club made a loss of a few hundred pounds, thus reducing our reserve to just
over £2,000. This year we expect this to fall to around £1,000 which is considered
to be the lowest acceptable level. With projected increased expenditure we have to look for extra income next year. Increases in our running costs which are mainly rates, rent, fuel and maintenance are continually rising and unavoidable. Unfortunately membership has fallen over the last few years, but this is the trend nationally so we are no exception, which all means increased fees but we hope you will be aware of the reasons and support the resolution.

Weds. Aug. I2th.
Yet another sunny day. We spent the morning re-cooperating Stan organised the cleaning up of the debris from the night before, heard the news that Peggy and Jimmy James of ‘Sonya had sailed past our boats earlier that day while we were all out for the count and only Peter Hall was up and about to hear them..Now as Peter had his leg encased in plaster, the best way for him to get ashore the night before was to put insulating tape round the foot of his plaster and then put his leg into a plastic bag to keep the plaster dry while rowing ashore. The trouble came very early that morning when Peter woke Jean to say he was in agony because they'd bound the tape too tightly, so while Jean fumbled for the light switch she also unwittlingly put their clock forward one hour, and when later that day we sailed up to the river Ore, Peter was entering one hour earlier than the rest of us, saying to Jean that he was convinced we'd worked the tide tables wrongly, why else was he taking so long to clear the entrance, We made for a mooring at Aldeburgh that evening but being Wednesday it was early closing so we were disappointed about not being able to get fish and chips for supper,

Thurs. Aug. I3th.
We made our way for Orford where we spent a few leisurely hours looking round the castle before going back to the Butley river. The castle has an old well covered by an iron grid, and with Stan Campbells natural charm with children he obliged them by letting them know how deep it was by daintily spitting into the well and the kids listened intently with their heads on one side waiting for it to land. By evening we were back in the Butley and once more found our feet taking us in the direction of the Boyton Bell and spending another happy evening in good company, besides, Stan was quite dry after all that
spitting,

Fri. Aug. T4th.
Left the Butley for levington Marina, Winters Maid and Myth of Mynto were already there after returning from their holidays in Holland. Now I like to think that coming into a marina presents no problem for me as long as I'm not helming, so I didn't foresee any difficulty this time until on reaching the rest of our boats in Levington, in readiness to go alongside I suddenly realised that we were going to have to back Beehive in and she does do some odd things when in astern, anyway there were lots of hands there to help us and I think that most of us were to our sleeping bags early that night ready for our first very early start the next morning at 5 a.m. The operation by our Marconi fleet, casting off whilst our eyeballs were still protesting at being woken so early was
probably done with great skill - I never noticed - it was all done so quickly
but I wont mention the boat who was trying to take the pontoon with him with his stern rope still tied onto it = no better not = he might mention the fact that he was too busy noticing that Tijo was trying to motor off and we still had her tied to our bows.

Well for Beehive it was back to the mooring at Stansgate and after such a lovely holiday we were quite sad to leave her = I wonder where we will be going next year?

1983 YEAR BOOK

I should be grateful to receive any comments you may have on the format of our Year Book. Some of the changes this year are obvious and will I hope make it easier for new members to understand. Other detailed changes I should like to bring to your attention are:=

PRIZES: Recently 2nd and 3rd prizes have been awarded for all races on the same basis so the special arrangement for open and closed races is deleted.

COURSE INSTRUCTIONS: Following a Protest last season the instruction has been clarified so that Race Officers are free to change courses for standard fixed club line starts if weather conditions change after the course has been displayed at the signing on point. The Course displayed on the front of the race=box at the Class Warning (10 minute) Signal is the one that counts.

FINISHING LINE: A clear statement is now made that there is no ‘long line’ finish except for the Marconi Cruises Cup which is sailed to BIRD course instructions.

/continued.

PERSONAL SAFETY: For all races sailed before the Whit Regatta Wet/Dry suits must be worn by all competitors. Failure to do so will result in disqualification.

SIGNING ON AND OFF: Much confusion exists between clubs on what to call race sheets. A declaration sheet can be for signing on or off or both. This year you will have new race sheets and all references are standardised on the most direct description, i.e. Signing On Sheet = Signing Off Sheet.

COURSES: Although space did not allow inclusion of a map covering the whole of the river the Year Book does now make reference to the long distance courses traditionally used for All-In and Cruiser races, Details of these courses are available on a new "4 double sided map which will be available at the signing-on point in the club house.

DESCRIPTION OF MARKS: The new mark at the East end of the outer cruiser moorings is included as Mark Fe Responsibility for this mark may be taken over by the Fisheries Protection in which case its description will change.

E Mark is traditionally off Osea to the East of the Pier, The Speed Limit buoys are often used or alternatively our Orange Inflatable Buoy. Or sometimes as happened last year, we caused confusion by using both,

Consideration is being given this year to sailing a triangular course for one or more races in which case E buoy may be positioned anywhere with respect to two other fixed River or Club marks.

To avoid last year's confusion and to allow for new courses the description of E mark this year has not specified it by type or position. Therefore any courses using E mark must add the description on the board at the signing on point.

LADY PERSONS: Finally I have set out to remove the last vestiges of chauvenism from the Year Book — now we are all helms together.

Malcolm Stuart,
Husband of the Sailing
Secretary's Wife.

Anyway well done all those who supported the Hornet stand.

I contented myself with evening runs round the estate to build up my stamina and Sue got cracking on the sausage rolls, eventually producing a round one hundred. Kate and I are very disappointed in the Hornet Fleet. We were under the impression that it was a very competitive, lively and go-ahead fleet famed for its massive turn=—outs and bawdy socials. Well readers, I can reveal that this is not the case and I may have to change class (maybe to the Mirrors) if things don't improve. Come on lads, I can assure you the estuary is nice and warm now}

Six intrepid sailors made Spring Points 3 and 4, the first Hornet class race of the season. They were Graham/Mike, Graham/Murray (F.C.), and Phil/Kate. The first race was held in wind strengths of 0 to force 1 from a N./NeW. direction. The two Grahams made good starts with "Stimulation" fighting the current armed with the knowledge that all those sheets must do something and eventually making the start line about one minute later. Mike/Graham in "Ultimatum" immediately stamped their authority on the race rounding 'E' mark with the Mirrors and a substantial lead. This lead was maintained throughout even though "Stimulation" forsook the northern route from C to Breezy (very slow run against the flood tide) and opted for a reach to the race box and then a course out of the tide to Breezye This course to be a mistake on the crews part]

After a pint and a sandwich, Spring Points 4 was started in even lower wind strengths. The start was with the tide and the first mark = A to port. "Ultimatum" arrived there first only to find the leg back over the start line and then on to Breezy was to be a very protracted affair. All three Hornets were soon involved in a tussle for windward position (albeit out in the wicked tide), but "Stimulation" opted for a shore hugging position and with the help of a foot over the side to avoid a breakwater soon established a small lead. The other boats soon followed this example and an orderly progression made its way to Breezy. Graham/Murray rounded first and established a good lead to Noe 1 with "Ultimatum" moving into second place. After gybing in order to lay "A" mark Graham/Murray Overstood and immediately made a bee line to the shore and out of the current. "Ultimatum" and "Stimulation" stayed out in the current and at 10 yards from the finish all three boats were in line abreast, and despite all the pumping and Flatulence aboard the other boats "Stimulation" creamed over the line followed fractionally later by Graham/Mike and Graham/Murray.

The same three boats mustered for Spring Points 5 in bright and windy conditions. The course was reasonably long with an easterly start in a southerly

a

1 to No. 4 proved to be a very exciting broad reache This lead was maintained throughout with Graham/Murray finishing second. THORPE BAY YACHT CLUB -— 30th April = lst May, 1983.

Thorpe Bay Yacht Club hosted the annual Two—Pint—Pot meeting for Hornets. The entry of twenty four boats included three Marconi teams.

Saturday's race was sailed in medium winds and sunshine and the olympic
course was set very accurately which made for some very close racing.

Nick and Tony Smither (winners of the faster Eqg meeting) and Sally Allyard dominated the race and soon got well clear of Chris and Andy Bines who were unchallenged for third place,

The following oroup of four boats contained two from Marconi; "Ultimatum" (Graham Mead and Mike Turner) and "Renaissance" (Colin Harper and Ian Stott). This group remained close together for the whole race (about 2 hours), with Graham making up for his poor upwind performances with very fast downwind legs. Eventually however, both Marconi Boats lost out to the other two in the group and Graham and Colin finished 6th and 7th respectively.

The race was won by Sally Allyard who was sailing her last hornet event Since she intends entering the ladies World Championships in which she will sail a laser.

After the race most of the younger competitors went down to Southend to the Kursal where great amounts of time were spent arranging group discounts

/continued.

on the various rides.

We all returned to the club for a ‘Chicken and Chips! supper which some people ate and others ended up wearing. The disco which followed was enjoyed by all who stayed and finished with a rapturous chorus of a few well known songs!

Sunday Morning's weather was dismal with torrential rain and very little
wind. There was an encouraging forcast however and by the time the race started the rain had stopped, but the wind was still very light. (IDEAL FOR PHIL).

Colin and Ian made a poor start and tacked out on port to gain clear winde In doing so they picked up a good wind shift which allowed them to lee=bow the tide on the starboard tack and the whole fleet crossed behind them. SAFETY

CAPSIZE DRILL — THE R.Y.A. METHOD — (LEEWARD CAPSIZE),

Stage 1 = Crew (c) and Helm (H) fall into the water, each checks that the other is 0.Ke and then they both move towards the transom (Fig.A).

Stage 2 = Helm checks that rudder is secure, crew frees the mainsheet.

Stage 3 - Helm moves to the back edge of the centreboard using the mainsheet
as a safety line (Fig. B).e If the centreboard is not down crew moves into the boat and lowers it. CAUTION = crew should make sure that the helm is not struck by the centreboard!

Stage 4 = Crew throws jibsheet to helm who acknowledges its receipt (Fig C).

Stage 5 =— Crew lies in the boat facing downward supported by the water (NOT the boat) Fig D).

Stage 6 =- Crew informs helm that everything is ready. The helm climbs onto the centreboard using the jibsheet and leans back (Fige The boat will come up slowly (Fig. F) and in doing so scoops up the
CTeW.

Stage 7 = The boat is upright and the crew uses his/her weight to balance the boat.

Stage 8 = Getting the helmsman aboard is achieved in several ways:=

(A) The helm might be able to climb in unaided as the boat comes
upright,

(B) In boats with high freeboard (i.e. 420's) the crew rocks the
boat boat towards helm, grabs his/her hands, and rocks back pulling him aboard.

(C) In boats with little freeboard it may be necessary to bail
out some water before the helm comes aboard,

REMEMBER: Do not enter the boat over the transom,

Stage 9 = Open self bailer, transom flaps or bail out the water and sail
awaye

Dear Mary,

In the 'Navigans' - anf excellent publication, I think; - and for which
many thanks to you all the effort you must put in each month - there is one

particular point with which I feel I'd like to take issue. May I refer to

the article in the March Issue entitled 'Calling Willing Ladies'?

As a mere male I have many times been grateful for the care and concern

shown by ladies, and it is always very nice to be on the receiving end of such ministrations, — but why is it always considered the 'normal' for men to have

their ladies prepare and serve their refreshments, - and wash up afterwards!

Surely nowadays there is no discrimination in the kitchen, galley, or what you

will - or if there is, what are the ladies doing about it? More to the point,

perhaps, what are the men doing about it? Are we incapable of cutting sandwiches,

or making tea or coffee - and of washing up afterwards? — Fuex poke ahead?

Many ladies nowadays sail with a great deal of expertise, and no one

thinks it is strange that they do. No one apparently finds it strange to

see a man behind the licenced bar. Would it be too strange to have men working

in the refreshment bar? — and notice the word 'working'. That's what happens

there - from start to finish with very little respite, respect, or even

appreciation, especially at Regatta Time.

I would like to suggest that one member of eeth fleet in turn wee- bo made responsible for refreshments = to be aided by a cadet. After all they

get all the benefit of tuition and experience from the Club, and they should

be prepared to give something back - No doubt they are. If the idea is

acceptable, perhaps we shall not again have such notices as ‘Ladies — Don't

Forget to Volunteer to Work in the Galley, Will You?' - Why should you?

After all, isn't your leisure as precious to you as your male's is to him?

Of course, if doing your thing is serving, etc., ... That's great!

Best Wishes & Tiianks — Yours,

SADLER SHAKEDOWN

There we were, George and I, in the middle of the main shipping channel at Harwich/Felixstowe harbour, We were motor sailing intending to clear the harbour entrance as quickly as possible.

I had already noticed a floating block of flats being towed by three tugs bearing down on us from our stern. Looking ahead I saw a Townsend Thoresen ferry start to leave Felixstowe, soon a huge white bow wave grew in front of it and was heading our way, then out of the blue, the engine's warning bleeper started, setting my heart racing. Was it the oil pressure?, was it the temperature? was it I called to George to helm whilst I started to check. There were no warning lights illuminated on the console, but not having any gauges I could not check whether it was a malfunction of the bleeper, a malfunction of the warning lights, or prelude to engine seizure. The engine did not smell hot and kept a steady beat.

To stop the engine would have been suicidal as the light wind was blowing directly towards the Felixstowe harbour, the very direction that the Floating block of flats was heading. The Townsend Thoresen Ferry kept forging OUr Waye

George called to me that a Sealink ferry was just rounding the corner and heading towards us. There was nothing for it but to turn out of the channel and hope the engine would take us out of trouble. With the warning bleeper becoming louder I increased the throttle. The engine responded and we were soon surging out of the main channel and away from being run down by the two ferries.

We stopped the engine and sailed on. The floating block of flats was in reality 15,000 tonnes container ship — it was enormous, or seemed to be in those confined waters. Once clear of imminent danger and with the tide under us we sailed up the Orwell towards Pin Mill, JI checked the oil lever, it was correct and the oil was not burnt, I checked the water inlet, it was not blocked. I gingerly started the engine, no warning came from the bleeper, it ran smoothly. I then checked the water flow, the delivery pipes were running full bore, nothing wrong there. In fact there did not seem to be anything wrong with the engine at all, Of course there should not have been, the engine was almost brand neu, having only run approximately 10 hours. We were on the first cruise of my new Sadler 29 = I had just spent the last year building it and did not expect any troubles apart from minor adjustments. I had tested the engine on short trips previous to this cruise,

We fetched up at Pin Mill, picking up a mooring buoy. The tranquility of the mooring soon made me forget the near panic situation just a short time ago. We cracked open a couple of cans of beer, I was at peace with the world once again.

That evening we were cordially entertained at the Pin Mill Yacht Club, by some of the members of that club. On returning to our dinghy we found it to be a very long way from the water's edge! We had arrived at high tide earlier that evening and now it was low tide. The hard at Pin Mill has a very small rise from top to bottom, consequently the tide recedes very quickly leaving a long hard.

We staggered back to the water carrying the dinghy. George stepped off the side of the hard into the mud. We both started to laugh as neither of us could see where we were, (It's very difficult to direct a torch when carrying a dinghy!) covered in mud we rowed back to the boat,

Next day we sailed back to Tollesbury, having a very pleasant sail without any drama.

Next day I telephoned the engine's main agents. “what age is your engine", the engineer enquired, "When did you buy it"? My reply was that it was

/continuede

- Fw

new and came with the boat. "Oh yes", he said "your engine is in the series that needs a modification, I will send you one in the post",

To my surprise and delight the modification turned up by return of post. It consisted of a new terminal strip with two resistors and a diode soldered on to it. This was easily fitted and the old terminal strip returned to the agents.

The fault that had occurred in my installation was that the diode had been leaking a voltage across the terminals and this had operated the bleeper. The fact that this only happened when the engine had run for some time was due to the diode warming upe When cold the installation was perfect, but on running for a period the bleeper would operate,

The moral to this tale is that although warning lights and bleepers bring one's attention to a fault in the engine, they do not tell the full story and only a set of engine gauges can be used to actually know what is happening inside the engine.

Needless to say, I am now fully instrumented, the little bleeper will not worry me again! :

D. Field.

THIS IS THE 420 NEWS

In the absence of Peter and Anna (you remember them, they are the ones always seen low down on the horizon) who have temporarily deported (sorry departed) to Australia in search of didgeridoos, I thought I might emulate Phil Gray's inimical prose and write a load of old rubbish on the 420 sailing events.

First, the Summer Points - John Weedon immediately stamped his authority
on the series and left no chance for anyone else to win the series. We had him worried at times though as occasionally we were almost close enough to see his sail number. This left second place to be contended between myself and the indomitable duo of Alan Mack and his ace crew Julian Brown. With equal points and one more race to go I used my secret weapon (my wife as crew, not wings on the centre board) and had a really exciting race with Alan, narrowly beating him by a mile at the last mark (sorry Alan). Julian was seen to be heavily bandaged after the race.

Seriously though, Alan and Julian had an excellent mid-week win, storming ahead of the fleet and intimidating Phil Gray into retiring.

The Mona's cup was won by John Weedon and Damian Boreham. Damian also crewed for John in some of the Summer Points races. Are these two really invincible? Phil Gray ex=420 only came second!

Those 420 sailors who have not sailed lately will not have experienced the new hazard to blissful 420 sailing. It's called the blue peril. A certain type of boat seems suddenly to ap;ear to windward creating massive holes in the wind leaving the poor hapless 420 sailor bemused, sails flapping, spinnaker collapsed, speed zero and spray kicked in ones face, (enterprising sailors will have guessed the class by now)e The only known cure for this malady is for more 420s to sail and regain our oun fleet start,

The real highlight of the season was David Hall's visit. 420 sailors who missed this really must kick themselves. David instructed us on the theoretical and practical handling of the 420 and imparted many useful ideas and tips on topics such as rig setting, spinnaker handling, barbar hauling and tacking. I will not go into further details as I feel sure that Peter on his return from holiday will want to write a separate report on David's visit. I would like to thank David on behalf of the 420 fleet for sharing his valuable time, knowledge, and experience with us.

As I work in the same office as Phil Gray — no violins please - I have
instructed him on some of the techniques learnt from above, so the next time you see him on the water, keep clear, he's still learning.

I apologise for numberous references to Phil (who is this guy anyway) and assure you that it won't happen again as the next 420 news will be in the erudite hand of our intrepid pommy fleet captain ably assisted by his Sheila.. (you remember, she's one of the prettier 420 crew/helms).

CADET WEEK 1983

Now that the cuts, bruises and scars have healed (all except Neil Pembleton's that is!) we can look back and reflect on this years' cadet week.

The Sunday evening treasure hunt supplied the usual surprises, one of which was that a live crab can survive ina pint of beer! I was disappointed that no-one produced an octopus (although one was seen alive and well later in the week?), although there were a lot of poor imitations. By the way, the answer to the last question was any number between 20 and 25. It's unbelievable but one team wrote 35 and another wrote "very ancient",

To reduce the fire risk due to long dry grass the cadet skipper arranged for a moderate fall of rain during Sunday night! Monday dawned with more rain and high winds which proved to be a realistic background for capsize drill, Malcolm Stuart kindly offered his services as a proving ground for potential 420 crews wishing to learn the art of trapezing. I use the word ‘art' loosely as many aspiring crews appeared to spend a large amount of time under the water. These crews I should add were mainly parents and the mirth they caused was only topped by Malcolm's demonic laugh as he dunked one after the other in the soup — well done
Malcolm!

Tuesday saw an improvement in the temperature and a lessening in the wind
strength. The morning was well spent in learning and practising how to start a race, Four practice starts were made and each one was video-taped from the racebox by Pat Stuart. The tapes were later played back in the lounge and proved to be very constructive. It was plain from the tapes that most boats got a good start once but no-one got it right all of the time. However, it was noticeable that the three Mirrors taking part showed considerable and sustained improvement throughout, In fact, so good was the general improvement that when the Cadet Skipper made his final run for the start line in the Wednesday evening race he found the line blocked with
Mirrors$
Race 1 for the Cadet Series was held on Tuesday afternoon in fairly light winds. Ten (yes, 10) cadets took part which in itself must be a record judging from the last few years' performances, The race was won convincingly by Damian with Kate second.

Race 2 was sailed on Wednesday morning in very light airs and with the
/continued.

crew of 420, K.41106 looking slightly the worse for wear. Conditions were difficult
because of a tight leg to No. 1 against an ebb tide. The faster boats made agonisingly slow progress whilst the Mirrors were slowly drifting seaward. 41106 retired with sun-stroke and hangover (the boat was also sinking — yes, honestly!) and the race was abandoned after 1 hour 55 minutes to allow Bob in the fisherman to rescue the tailenders. As the abandon flag was being raised a zephyr of wind appeared and Penny (crewed by daddy) who was by now virtually on the northern shore of the estuary began to move and eventually finished the course. Well done, Penny - hope you enjoyed the "After-Eights" luv.

As a bit of light relief and because of the rapidly rising temperatures, on Wednesday afternoon a Super Teams competition was held. This involved the various skills of cycling, dribbling (with a football that is!), running, tug-of-war, throwing the welly, throwing the ball, cartwheels and canoeing. The dribbling produced a play-off that resulted in a draw between Robert Weedon and Robert Gray. The cartwheels were included when it was found that there were so many budding gymnasts on site and Damian showed us that he can do other things besides sailing. The cycling race required stopwatch timing to 1/100th second and it was during this event that Adam Bloomfield decided to audition for the next James Bond film by arresting the motion of a bike and rider doing Mach 2 by merely placing his body
in the path of the machine. Well done, Adam - hope the hand, arm, leg etc. are
better. The canoeing event provided its usual thrills and spills with something like a span of eight years separating youngest and oldest. The event was won by Steven Gray (youngest) whilst Andrew Sharp (oldest) canoed three quarters of the course and then decided to swim the remainder. If you can remember whose team you were in then the final winners were team C captained by Robert Weedon.

Cadet Race 3 was sailed Thursday morning and this time a fairly old looking cadet called Frank (or Uncle Frank as he is now known) sailing a Solo (sail number withheld!) joined in, and in fact managed to win} Now seriously the winner was Keith Boyles followed 34 seconds later by Alec Pembleton. Alec by this stage in the week had ditched Dad and his "Graduate" for a slightly up-market boat and a younger crew (that will cost you a pint Malcolm!).

The final Cadet race was sailed on the Friday morning and once again the wind was very light. The windward mark (S8reezy) was reached quite quickly by virtue of a strong ebb tide but the beat to C was to leave only three boats in contention. They were Keith, Kate and Alec. Alec showed very good boat speed (and sailing skill) and when he rounded C mark the other two boats were 400/500 yards ‘yw behind in lightening winds. The duel for second place raged over the next two legs with Kate easing past Keith on the Osea shore and then making a late break for A mark with the tide. Alec was first home with a 22 minute gap before Kate with Keith a close third.
In the final reckoning Alec won the series with Keith second.
Uncle Malcolm can now boast that he has crewed a winning boat in a series (give me a call sometime Malcolm).

About 20 participants tried Phils walk along the seawall on Thursday evening and made it to Steeple Bay sailing club where they were picked up by the Mariner, a Leader and a cruiser for the return journey. Those lucky enough to join Lynn (I hope that's how it's spelt!) in the Mariner experienced a brisk and damp sea passage home with the golden orb of the setting sun kissing the world goodnight (good stuff eh!).

Well, what a change Saturday was! Winds force 4 and where had the sun gone? The plan had been to cruise up to the "Jolly Sailor" at Heybridge, get outside of a few Cokes, have a spot of lunch and cruise back — but it was not to be. However, a few intrepid souls did manage a picnic on the lee shore of Osea Island with a little help from Malcolm and Lynn in the Mariner.

One final event (I used this word loosely) was the paper chase held .in. an attempt to clean our site of rubbish. If there were any rules at the start then

/continued.

they disappeared as soon as the bin-liners were handed out. At one time I saw Claude looking resignedly skyward as bag after bag of rubbish turned up. Some of these bags had been stuffed full with inflatable dinghies, tenders and for all I know, dinghies out of the park’ To all those that took part you can rest assured that you have performed a civic function for the good of your club.

Well, that's about it for this year except of course for the list of prize winners, Well, throw me to the sharks I nearly forgot to mention the Friday evening fancy dress party. I was most impressed by the turnout and enthusiasm shown by the younger cadets for this event. I was less impressed by the older cadets who spent most of the evening sitting anti-socially on the sea-wall. Well, all I can say is that you missed a good evening. It appeared that some of the costumes had been scraped off the sea—bed and this was confirmed by the pervading smell of rotting vegetation in the lounge. Many thanks to the Octopus, the Thing from the Deep, the Caterpillar, the Hawaiian Girl, the Chinaman, the two young Arabs and many others who made it such an enjoyable evening.

Before listing the prizewinners I would like to thank the Following people (not an exclusive list, I might add) for their help during the week. My brother Bob for supplying the canoes and canoeing instruction. Bob and Lynn for excellent rescue services throughout the week, Uncle Malcolm for trapeze lessons 2 the picnic and ideas, Auntie Pat (Spielberg) Stuart for video=tapping and race= officering and Uncle(I won a Cadet race) Frank for being himself. Oh, by the way, thanks for the grog chaps.
