CRUISER FLEET NEWS

There will be a Fleet Meeting at the General's Arms, Little Baddow on Wednesday 5th October, at 8.30 pm. The main business will be to elect a new Fleet Captain as I have decided it is time to stand down and let someone else bring in some new ideas. John Wade has kindly agreed to take over but other suggestions or offers are welcome up to the time of the meeting.

The business should be quickly over when we will continue with a slide show, so whatever you may have taken recently, please bring it along.

It has been necessary to re-arrange the winter lay-up plan for cruisers in order to reduce the risk of heavy boats damaging the boat park. The new plan is shown in the Clubhouse.

It is not easy to be precise in planning a major change so members are asked
(a) to park as economically of space as possible
(b) to follow the spirit of the plan rather than the letter if necessary.
(c) if anyone gets squeezed out of their allocated space to use the marked overspill area.

Please note it is essential that neither boats nor lowered masts obstruct the access area which will be used initially by the tractor and possibly later by the river board for sea wall maintenance. Remember - if the wall is breached urgent action will be needed.

Finally, I would like to thank everyone who has helped me during my term as Fleet Captain whether they be fleet members or other club members and especially Mary, Anne, Shirley and Brenda who have put me into Navigans quite a few times. - Thank you all.

Russ Fuller.
Fleet Captain.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

You may have been surprised to find a raft race starting from the club on Sunday October 9th. The request for the use of our premises was made at short notice, but since the event was organised in aid of the R.N.L.I. the committee agreed that it should go ahead.

Maintenance costs have continued to rise. This year maintenance for our tractor and rescue boat engine has been particularly expensive and next year we are predicting significant costs for clubhouse maintenance. In addition, as the size and number of boats in our cruiser fleet increases, we shall need extra equipment for mooring maintenance. For these reasons, as well as normal inflation, it has been decided that an increase of approximately 10% is required in our subscription rate for 1984, Final details will be published next month, however, it is intended to place the major burden for the increase with boat owners since they will see most direct benefit.

Only minor changes are required for next year's committee since most members have agreed to stand for re-election. However we will require one or two ordinary committee members. It is important that we continue to inject new blood in order to provide a strong committee in the future. One post that has not been filled for two years is that of Clubhouse Secretary. This puts an additional burden on club officers with the inevitable result that standards reduce. Please help Find someone to fill this post.

See you at the Laying—Up Supper.

Frank Savill

1983 MIRROR NATIONALS AND WORLDS

I was fortunate enough to be offered a crewing job with ex=National Champion, Dave Sherwin, at the beginning of this season. I jumped at the opportunity and started training at some open meetings. The Marconi Regatta was one of them.

This was all easy going with not too much wind at any of them, but it was a different story when we arrived at Mounts Bay for the Nationals,

At the beginning of the week it wasn't blowing all that much so I just had to sit around and watch the kite and all those other things crews have to do. By the middle of the week the wind was up to a S gusting 6 and I was getting a bit worn out hiking all daye At some points of the race you could see more centre plates than sails. Our turn for a swim didn't come until the last gybe mark, when I am sure there was an extra strong gust of wind. But there was only time to catch the spinnaker pole before the boat was up and off again, even though we had to chew through the painter to free the gib sheets.

At the end of the week Dave Derby was the winner, winning all but two races.

2. Dave Sherwin (and ME)

4. Mark Sherwin

After a long haul round in the car everyone was at Mumbles for the Worlds. The place was full of foreigners. There were Australians, Swedes, Danish, Welsh, (well that's understandable in Wales), Americans, some very British looking Maltese and lots of others.

The first race was really boring. There was barely enough wind to get us all to the start and then we just drifted about for an hour, waiting for a ten minute gun. We all tied ourselves to the committee boat for another two hours until finally they postponed till a later date.

Well, on that later date it was blowing a 4—5 and we had to do two races back-to-back. I washiking out hard, freezing cold and the only thing keeping me awake was the agonising pain in my legs. We were almost blown over on some of the reaches and had to let out our sails, but the heavier Australians could hold it and managed to win both races.

The next three races weren't so bad and we worked our way from about 20th in one race to win it by 7 minutes. We managed to win the other 2 as well, going really fast in the 2—3 wind force. At the end of that week we had won 4 of the 6 TaceS.e

420 FLEET NEWS

First of all I would like to say a big "thank you" to the Hornet Fleet for the way they organised the 420 Open Meeting. Everything went very smoothly - apart from some completely unfounded mutterings about the competence of the Race Officer (thanks Phil, moving E mark to the opposite side of the river was a really good idea, we should do it more often). Thanks to Ann Bates for chasing up those notorious entry fee dodgers as receptionist and to the ladies who organised and ran the galley. Luckily somebody volunteered for the arduous task of running the bar =— thanks Colin.

The Open Meeting itself was very well attended, attracting 18 competitors (six from M.S.C.). Saturday dawned Foggy, grey and drizzly with practically no wind at all. However, it soon improved to be foggy, grey and drizzly with some wind. As the wind was southerly it was very difficult for the R.O. to arrange a beat, and, in fact, by the time we had reached what should have been the windward leg the wind had shifted and it was a reache The visitors soon showed the Marconi Fleet their heels reflecting our lack of practice against good opposition, and this is shown in the positions of the Marconi entry of llth, 12th, 13th, 14th, and 16th out of 16 entries, Paul Springett won this race closely followed by Dave Hall after the lead had changed several times during the race,

Sunday was much better from the point of view of the onlookers (in that
the sun was out, the water was blue and visibility was well over the 100 yards of the previous day). However, the wind strength was less and dropped gradually throughout the course of the first race. The wind was now straight out of the west and so the first leg was a beat with everyone trying to keep close to the shore to be out of the tide. This made for an exciting beat up to the corner off the Club with the air ringing with shouts for water at the shore, at cruisers and for starboard boats. Much to my surprise we didn't hit anything! After the point, however, things eased off as the visitors pulled away again. Springett and Hall again tussling for lst and 2nd places. Unfortunately they were both disqualified for being over the start line and so first place went to Geoff Lynch from Hickling Broard. Marconi men again bringing up the rear,

The final race started in very light airs and was really a repeat of the morning race as far as positions went, with Paul Springett and Dave Hall monopolising the lead between them. Despite the fact that Paul spotted the new position of 'E! mark first and made a long leg on starboard tack to reach it first (we thought he must be on a really good wind shift) at the finish line Dave Hall took first cannon with Paul taking the second. Again the Marconi entry maintained their positions. These results meant that there was a tie for lst place between Paul and Dave as they both had identical results (one lst, one 2nd and 1 disqualification) and Geoff Lynch was 3rd. SIAN 11 GOES FOREIGN

Introduction
The following is an account written in 1983, of the cruise of Sian 11 to
Holland. Modern technology has provided the means to copy the log, the text has
been rearranged so that the photographs taken on the trip could be included.

The Log
Our plan for the 1983 Summer Cruise was to take our boat Sian 11 to
Holland. The skipper had done the crossing before, but only as crew on other boats,
but it would be the first crossing for Carys (mate, deck hand, cook and all other tasks
allocated by the skipper).
Sian 11 is a 28ft. Twister, which was bought as a hull and deck in 1980
and fitted out by ourselves in the back garden, she was launched in 1981. Due to
domestic complications of having to find ‘cat sitters’ for our 23 year old cat
(eventually solved by bringing my mother and aunt from North Wales to perform the
task, however they could only stay two weeks ) we decided to take two weeks holiday
from July the 9th to the 24th inclusive, and attempt to sail the boat to Holland in the
first week and spend the second week relaxing and cruising Holland, and then leave
the boat in Holland and take another week later on to fetch the boat and sail home
---- the plans of mice and men.
Since our experience of night sailing was limited, Carys having not done
a night passage before, it was decided to start from Lavington, and so at midday on
July 9th we set off from Bradwell, our home port. Out in the river visibility was not
good, and we were beating against an Easterly wind towards the Bench Head Buoy,
visibility became worse, we never did find the Bench Head that day, the trip to
Lavington was abandoned and we headed for Pyfleet to anchor for the night. There
we met Stan and Margaret off Maldon Aries, Jack and Jackie Off Winters Maid and
Albert Shirley, Jeff and Lesley off Myth of Mynto, all from the Marconi Sailing Club,
they were heading for Ramsgate enroute to Normandy and had aborted the journey
for the same reason as ourselves.
Sunday morning (July 10th )was even worse, visibility was less than the
day before, so we decided to sail to Rowhedge for a pint, we left Maldon Aries and
Myth of Mynto at Pyfleet and took Winters Maid and Sian to Rowhedge. We sailed
back in brilliant sunshine and tied up at Brightlingsea, later to be joined by Maldon
Aries and Myth of Mynto. Walking back from the pub that evening saw us all very
exited since all the fog had gone and all the stars were clearly visible.
On Monday (July 11th ) we said goodbye to the ° Marconi ’ fleet they
were heading for the Spitway and we were heading for Lavington, the wind had
backed Northeast and we had to beat up the Wallet. We always seem to be beating in
the Wallet, Carys remarked that she should have married a gentleman, since
according to Russ Fuller gentlemen never beat to windward. We arrived at Lavington
about an hour before low water and ran aground about 50 feet from the visitors
pontoon. We had our evening meal on the mud and eventually tied up against a boat
called Storyville, from the Deben, for a few hours sleep.

1

Tuesday ( July 12th ) quarter past midnight weather forecast was wind
NE force 4 with fog patches, this was good enough for a start and at half past
midnight we left Lavington, wind speed was 3 knots and variable. The main was
hoisted and we motored towards Harwich, we noticed a sailing boat, also under
engine, coming up behind us, they caught up to ask where we were bound for, it
turned out that they were heading for Oostende, the boat was called Mach Fluff and
we promised to keep in touch by radio throughout the journey.
At 1.40 a.m. we hoisted the jib and switched off the engine, the wind
had picked up slightly and the log was streamed, log 00.00. By 3.00a.m. Sian was
putting her shoulder in and speed had increased to 6 knots. We were surprised that
we could not see the Sunk Light Vessel, but we could see Mach Fluftf’s stern light
about half a mile ahead. At 3.30 a.m. Sian was beginning to surf, we were by the
yellow No. 2 buoy, when there was a loud crash from below, on investigating we
found six broken eggs on the floor, the cabin sole was like a skating rink, the
cupboard door could not have been clipped properly, anyway we should have stored
the eggs in one of the lower lockers where they could not fly across the boat.
Cleaning the mess took a good ten minutes and the result could only be described as
barely adequate. Back in the cockpit we noticed that Mach Fluffs stern light had
disappeared, but where on earth was the Sunk?. At 3.45 a.m. we heard the Sunk and
suddenly we were in fog, we assumed that this was one of the fog patches mentioned
in the weather forecast. By 4.05 a.m. we were by the Sunk altering course towards the
Galloper, wind speed was 20 knots and we were making 6 knots. Because the surfing
was making steering a compass course difficult we decided to take it in turns to steer,
half an hour on and half an hour off. I decided against using the Autohelm as the
seas were terribly confused and it was difficult to imagine how the Autohelm could
cope. At 6.00 a.m., we had just finished breakfast, hot chocolate and marmalade
sandwiches, when we made radio contact with Mach Fluff but when I mentioned
breakfast he signed off rather abruptly. While we breakfasted the Autohelm was
switched on and it coped very well so it was left on, it did make life easier.
The weather forecast at 6.25 a.m. was wind Force 4 NNE with fog
banks, big these fog banks, we had been in one for the last 25 miles!.
At 7.00 a.m. we found the Galloper, we heard it first, and had to alter
course to get to it, we were a bit South of our dead reckoning position but only by
about half a mile. We again made radio contact with Mach Fluff, it turned out that
when I mentioned breakfast he had to call off to be sick, the three men on board
were all sick with the one female member on board left in charge. Course was
changed for Oostende and Sian was really surfing making more than 7 knots, with the
wind speed exceeding 20 knots but still in fog, visibility was less than half a mile. I
tried to get bearings from the RDF, a Hitachi combined RDF and radio, the radio
worked but not the RDF-----what a fine time to find out!. At 8.00 a.m. we saw a
rather watery sun but it soon disappeared, we made contact again with Mach Fluff
they had managed to get a good RDF cocked hat position, we estimated that they
were North of us. We calculated our position to be three miles from the South bound
shipping lane.
At 8.30 a.m. we estimated that we were just entering the shipping lanes,
visibility was bad, we did not see any ships but we could hear their fog horns, it was
not very pleasant, there was one of them very close. The next two hours kept us on
full alert, we kept on seeing shapes that were not there. I think the shapes were due

2

to the fact that we kept on looking at the pulpit and when we looked away an image
left on the eye was carried when we turned our heads.
The confused seas and the surfing continued, and at 11.00 a.m. the log
read 50.29 miles and the visibility was still very bad.
At 12.25 a.m. we heard the West Hinder Light Vessel but it was North
of our dead reckoning position. This was puzzling but there was no doubt that the
signal was the West Hinder, the next minute a large container ship came towards us
from the fog, she was called “Gertrude H’ travelling eastward, I tried to call her on
channel 16 to ask for a position, but they did not reply. We deduced that if the ship
was in the shipping lane and the West Hinder was to the North of us, we were also in
the shipping lane, no place to be in the fog. I did a running fix by taking bearings off
the horn of the West Hinder and plotted a course to arrive 5 miles off Oostende.
The theory was that we ought to see the traffic or the buoys off Oostende, we would
be unlikely to miss everything.
At 2.00 p.m. I estimated our position to be about 10 miles off Oostende
and visibility if anything was getting worse. Carys was getting a bit anxious but the
skipper assured her that we were definitely in the Southern North Sea. It was decided
to call Oostende radio to have a visibility check, the theory being that if the visibility
was three miles from the shore we could close in, if not we could carry on hoping to
see a buoy or some traffic. Contact was made with Oostende, and when I asked what
the visibility was like?, they replied "We haven’t that information sir". At this point I
would have swopped the VHF radio for any crude RDF that worked. Whilst I was
below cursing the VHF as a safety aid, Carys said "I can see a yacht ahead" and when
we were about to change course to ask for a fix she said " I can see a green buoy" I
said "You little darling" and gave her a wet salty kiss on the cheek. Twice the green
buoy disappeared in the fog but at 2.15 p.m. we knew we were at the Middelkerk BK
green buoy, log reading 67.85. Course was changed for Oostende and at 3.03 p.m. we
identified the Brittenstroombank North Cardinal but still no sign of Oostende At 3.35
p-m. we saw land about a mile away, but where were the block of flats that you
should be able to see 15 miles away?. Suddenly we saw yachts and fishing boats all
gilling about outside the pier, we were there!. The problem was that we were still
surfing at 6 knots towards the lot of them, it was time to slow down, the jib was
dropped but the speed did not drop significantly. Lights were flashing on the pier so
the engine was switched on, and the log pulled in recording 76.4 miles. Taking the
main down was another problem, the seas were huge, Carys remarked afterwards that
she had not seen a wall of water before, the boat was rolling +30°. I found the only
way was to take in the main on the roll to port and hang on for grim death whilst the
boat rolled to starboard, Sian’s sail was never stowed so untidily. Suddenly everybody
was making a dash for the entrance, the flashing lights had gone off, we followed and
noticed that the locals had the main sails hoisted and took them down in between the
piers. We were showing our inexperience!. Inside the harbour we turned right just
before the ferry terminal and saw that the green light was showing that we could
enter the Macator dock, we had already decided on a day’s rest at Oostende and the
Macator is much quieter than the North Sea Yacht Club. The wind was blowing right
behind us into the lock and Sian was sailing in under bear poles. On reaching the lock
applying reverse power produced the inevitable result, Sian went right across the lock.
The lock keeper remarked "First time in the Macator Sian 11" and I replied " Yes,
isn’t rather obvious". Two Dutchman helped us out and one remarked "Long keel

3

yah!", it said it all. We were berthed and tidied up by 5.30 p.m. and the sense of
achievement is almost impossible to describe. There is nothing like taking your own
boat foreign for the first time. The problem of being too far South of our course
bothered me a great deal, the only explanation I can think of is that due to the
surfing the Autohelm only tried to correct at the end of the surf and not when the
surf starts as when the helm is operated manually. As a result we were being set
South by the continuous surfing.

MECATOR DOCK

SIAN II IN THE MECATOR

Wednesday (July 12th) saw us in a rather foggy Oostende, at ieast we
could see the top of the block of flats, we had a Vivacity called Opus 111 in the berth
next to us owned by a friendly Belgian couple called Pete and Fenandel, they gave us
some very good advice not least to recommend a little restaurant called Petit Paris,
the fish was delicious.
Whilst walking to the pier we saw Mach Flutf moored in the North Sea
Yacht Club and we went to see them, for up to now they had only been voices at the
end of the radio. It turned out that the skipper ( John ) was a Concorde pilot, which
accounted for the boat’s name, Mach being the speed of sound and Fluff being a Fat
Little Ugly F--Flyer, his crew was his wife Sue, a German called Friedle and another
pilot who had left for the UK to fly Prince Andrew to the OSC. Friedle’s wife Erica
was joining them in Oostende for the rest of the cruise. When they entered Oostende,
on reaching the inner harbour the lights started flashing so they turned to go out
again, only to find a ferry coming in, so they turned to go in again. At this point a
voice from a loud hailer said " English yacht | do not care where you go but get
bloody lost ". Like us they planned to go to Flushing the following day and we agreed
to keep in touch on the way.
We had a drink at the North Sea Yacht Club and talked to Ron and
Ness and their son Martin on a boat called Indecision from Lawling Creek, they were
leaving for home the following day. On the way back to Sian we noticed Storyville in
the harbour. It turned out that they had left Lavington four hours after us but
abandoned their trip outside Harwich harbour because the fog was too thick, they had
a relatively good passage that day visibility being no less than two miles. That night we
got to bed at two o’clock in the morning convincing ourselves that it did not matter as
we did not need to make an early start that day.
Thursday July 14th, weather forecast was winds West 3 to 4 , visibility
moderate, ideal for our trip to Flushing, our start was a mad rush. contrary to all
other advice received, the harbour master at the Mecator would not take English
money and we had to make a dash to the railway station to get some change. By 3.00
p.m. we were outside Oostende sailing a course of 060° magnetic with the wind from
the North North East, so much for the weather forecast.

5

At 3.30 p.m. we changed to the No 1 genoa and by 4.00 p.m. the wind
had dropped off altogether and the engine was started, we also made contact with
Mach Fluff who had left Oostende before us. At 5.20 p.m. we were off Zebrugge and
the seas were very confused in spite of the light winds. At 5.35 p.m. we were by the
Wilengen Buoy changing course to 085°M heading for Flushing, the wind picked up
and we had a super sail along the coast. ( Sailing from Oostende to Flushing is easier
than sailing from the Blackwater to Harwich, plenty of buoys and no sandbanks.) At
7.00 p.m. we again made contact with Mach Fluff and we told them our position they
said that they could see us, we altered course towards them and we sailed in company
into Flushing harbour.

Our log was switched off and we noticed that the reading was
considerably less than the distance on the chart, showing the importance of working
the tides along this coast. It is also important to remember to fit your fenders at water
level in the lock as the wooden surround is at water level. We tied up at the marina
at Flushing at 9.05 p.m. and felt that our holiday had now really started. Mach Fluff
invited us on board for supper, and several glasses of wine later we collapsed into our
bunks at 1.00 a.m. in the morning.
Friday July 15th, and we did not bother with the early morning shipping
forecast, sheer bliss, came to about 10.00 a.m. and left for Middelburg at 11.30 a.m.
encountering lifting bridges for the first time, these presented no real problem, but in
planning a passage ample time should be allowed to pass through the bridges, the one
outside Middelburg kept us waiting three quarter of an hour.

LIFTING BRIDGE AT FLUSHING
APPROACHING MIDDELBURG

We planned to stay at Middelburg that night so that we could visit
friends, and sail to Were the following day. Mach Fluff decided to only stop long
enough to do some shopping and move on to Were that day, so we said our goodbyes
and agreed to keep radio contact at 11.0 a.m. the following morning. Middelburg is a
delightful town and the day was spent sightseeing. After supper we went to see our
friends, but they were out, we would try again in the morning. We had one or two, or
was it three or four or five or ----------- ? drinks at the Yacht Club, we returned to our
berth and when we saw Sian we both had the same thoughts. " How could we have set
out with a plan that ment leaving her in some foreign country ?." We decided that if it
was at all possible Sian would be bought home at the end of the fortnight ------ the
plans of mice and men!.
Saturday July 16th, we were woken up in the middle of the night,
actually it was 8.15 a.m., by someone singing the Max Boyce song "Hymns and Arias".
I remember thinking I must be at the Arms Park in Cardiff. It was John and Cath
Morle in their boat Tea Tetua from Bradwell, we helped them tie up. Our friends
from Middelburg also turned up, they are also friends of John and Cath, and invited
the four of us to supper that evening, how could we refuse?. We had a smashing time.

TOURIST TRANSPORT IN MIDDELBURG

The following day, with Tea Tetua in company we motored to Were and
sailed on the Veersmere, they say that there are a million surfboards in Holland,
ninety thousand nine hundred and ninty-nine must have been on the Veersmere that
day, they were everywhere.

WERE HARBOUR

li

DUTCH BARGE UNDER SAIL

We made radio contact with Mach Fluff they were on their way to
Goes. It was decided that avoiding surfboarders was not a good pastime and we tied
up to the landing stage on one of the islands in the Veersmere called the
Haringvreter Island. It is very pleasant walking on the island, with horses, cattle and
deer as company.

Monday July 18th, we all sailed in Sian to Were and phoned our friends
in Middelburg inviting them to the barbecue, they accepted, and said that they would
sail up in their boat to join us.
One must be careful at Were, because if you decide to tie up along the
town pontoon there is very little water on the east side of the pontoon. Although we
managed to tie up, we found that in the swell of passing boats we were touching the
bottom, and it is very hard.
Whilst the ladies were preparing the barbecue, the men did a bit of boat
maintenance, and John notices that he had more water in the bilge than normal and
found to his dismay that one of the engine mounts had sheered.
We had a discussion and decided, that rather than go to the Ouster
Schelde the following day, we would sail back to Middelburg with John, in case he
would need a tow and see if we could get some engine mounts in Holland. If we
could not John would sail back to England with us, where he knew he could get the
mounts and go back to Holland by ferry.
Having decided on our plan we enjoyed a superb barbecue.

JOHN MORL
PREPARING SUPPER

LEAVING THE
VEERSMERE
Note length of bargai

Tuesday July 19th, saw us back in Middelburg. John managed to locate
engine mounts and our friend took him by car to collect them, they were back by 3.00
p.m. John with myself as handyman, had the engine lifted, engine mounts fitted and
the engine running by 8.00 p.m. We enjoyed our supper that evening and decided to
return to Flushing the following day.
Wednesday July 20th, we made radio contact with Mach Fluff at Goes,
they were off to Zierikzee that day ready to sail home the following day, we wished
them a safe journey home and signed off for the last time on this holiday.
We got our shopping done and when we returned we saw Storyville in
the harbour, they were also going to Flushing that day. We agreed a time of
departure of 2.30 p.m. We said our goodbyes and got under way.
The weather forecast at 5.55 p.m. was variable 3 becoming NE 3,
visibility moderate to good. That evening we spent having a drink on Storyville, she is
a Colvic Countess 33, compared to our Sian she is enormous, and fitted with a Decca
navigator, most impressive.
Thursday 21st, we motored into the lock at Flushing at midday, the lock
was full of sailing and motor boats, this gave us confidence that we had worked the
tides correctly. With the tides running as strong as they do along the coast, everybody
tends to leave at the same time, if you find your in the lock alone, it is worth your
while to check your tide calculations.
We locked out at 1.00 p.m. and heard somebody shouting "Sian II,
Arthur ", it was Dave and Joan Thomas on Marinero, they were just going into the
lock; we heard later that they had a big piece of tarpaulin around their prop.

It was nice and sunny with the wind NE about 12 knots and under No 1
genoa and full main we enjoyed a soldiers wind towards Zeebrugge. At 4.30 p.m. we
were off Zeebrugge and changed course for Oostende we could clearly see the block
of flats some 15 miles away. When we arrived off Oostende the light was flashing and
we had half an hour wait, rolling about outside the entrance, it was surprising how

16

strong the wind and tide were when we eventually were allowed to go in.
This time we moored at the North Sea Yacht Club as it was our
intention to leave for home the following day. It was very crowded in the harbour,
with boats rafted nine deep. Because of our narrow beam we were given a fore and
aft mooring which made life a little easier. Whilst we were mooring we missed the
weather forecast at five to six, everybody we asked said that it was not good. We
decided to leave at 6.30 a.m. the following morning provided the forecast was
favourable.

Friday 22nd July, we were up at six preparing for the off,the 6.15 a.m.
weather forecast was wind East 5 or 6 locally 7, with fog banks, we went back to bed.
We spent the day waiting for weather forecasts and walking. The 1.55 p.m. forecast
was wind East 3 or 4 locally 5, thundery showers, visibility moderate becoming poor.
The 5.55 p.m. forecast was East 5 locally 6 becoming cyclonic 4, thundery showers
>

visibility moderate to poor. We decided on a 4.00 a.m. start.
In between weather forecasts we went to listen to a jazz concert in the
open air. The band was the one that played in the funeral scene in the James Bond
film "Live and Let Live", they were very good. Nick the skipper of Storyville was a
keen jazz fan, hence the name Storyville, and was anxious to have his photograph
taken with the leader of the band. Carys went and asked if this was possible and the
leader said "Let me meet this guy", he seemed very old to me but it made Nick’s day.

Saturday 23rd, what a grotty place Oostende is at 4 o'clock in the
morning!, especially when we realised that there was a Dutch sailing boat tied up to
our aft mooring and we could not get out. A knock on the hull brought a quick
response and he soon moved and was very grateful as he could occupy the slot we
had just vacated. Our problems however were not over as there was a raft of boats
across the entrance to the North Sea Yacht Club blocking it completely. On the
outside was a large British motor cruiser with four men sitting in the cockpit. When
we asked them to move we realised that they had been sitting there all night drinking.
What followed could have been a scene from a Carry-On film, the motor cruiser
under full power moved off but was still attached to the raft. When it was eventually
sorted out, we apologised to the boat immediately attached to the motor cruiser, and
with typical Dutch diplomacy he said "Perhaps it is not your fault".
By 5 o'clock we had cleared Oostende harbour, the wind was right

18

behind us and we were rolling from side to side unmercifully, it was terribly
uncomfortable. and no combination of sail setting seemed to help, we left the engine
on. The weather was dry, and visibility was moderate, we could see a thunder storm to
the North East of us, the lightening was quite spectacular.
The rolling continued, but as we were approaching the Middrlikerk Bank
Green buoy the wind veered South, the rolling stopped, and we were sailing. As we
were approaching the East Dyck buoy, at the edge of the east bound shipping lane I
went below to check the chart, Carys remarked that the wind speed was increasing
and the next minute we were flattened as a squall hit us. Carys did her best to get
Sian’s nose to the wind but not before she saw the dodgers being covered in sea
water. The next few minutes were taken up in getting safety harnesses on and putting
a reef in the main. I went forward to put a reef, wearing a track suit over my shorts,
and got saturated by the spray and the waves, the elastic in my track suit could not
hold the weight and I arrived back in the cockpit with a sodden track suit around my
ankles, not looking at all as your well dressed yachtsman should. The wind speed was
35 knots and we were close hauled. Sian is a wet boat at this point of sailing, we had
waterproof tops on but the rest of us was saturated. There were breaking seas
everywhere, and we were in the shipping lanes, but the visibility was good, we had to
tack twice to avoid shipping, by the time we reached the West Hinder the wind speed
had dropped to 25 knots and veered South again. We were sailing comfortably in
confused seas. Carys went below to change and I shall never forget the sight of a bear
bottom in a red jacket being thrown about below trying to get her trousers on. we
were doing a comfortable 6 knots under a reefed main, heading for the North and
South bound shipping lanes. By the time we had reached the North bound shipping
lane we had the reef out, the fog was closing in and it was raining hard, but the
visibility was not too bad, we could at least identify ship shapes a mile away. Half way
across the shipping lane the wind died away completely and the rain was torrential,
the engine was switched on and was left on to clear the shipping lanes. From the
shipping lanes to the Galloper was the most frustrating two hours of the whole trip, it
consisted of jib down genoa up, genoa down jib up, reef main shake out reef, jib
down genoa up and by the time we were approaching the Galloper we were under jib
and full main sailing comfortably in fog, visibility was less than a quarter of a mile. It
took some time to find the Galloper we had sailed passed it, we could not believe
that it was North East of us, but it was. The sail from the Galloper to the Sunk was
uneventful, the weather improving all the time, we could hear the Sunk ahead of us
but could not see it as we were looking directly into the sun. At 5.35 p.m., log 66.6 we
had the Sunk on our port side and we were steering a course of 260° magnetic
heading for Clacton. We were under genoa and full main, Sian had her shoulder in
and we were sailing at 6 knots in a calm sea, and at 6.45 p.m. we spotted the Wallet
No 2 buoy and we could see land.

19

THE SUNK LIGHT VESSEL

It was interesting to note that
looking at the Sunk with the sun
behind us, we could see it 7 miles
away. At 8.15 p.m. we were off
Clacton, changing course for the
Knoll, the red sunset was well worth
coming home to see, the wind
however was right in the nose, we
dropped the genoa and switched on
the engine, this cruising is making a
gentleman out of me!. At the Knoll
the engine was switched off and the
jib set, the wind speed increased
again, we were on our last leg home.
Off Bradwell we unshiped the log
reading 93.51, and by 10.45 p.m. we
were having a drink at the bar in the
Club. We were glad of our bed that
night, and remembered in the
morning that we had not phoned the
customs before going to bed, one
should phone within two hours of
arrival.
Looking at Sian II in her berth
the following day we could not help
but feel that she had done everything
asked of her and could no doubt do
SIAN II IN DUTCH WATERS much more. Unfortunately the joy of
having made the trip and gone
foreign for the first time, was dimmed by the fact that when we phoned home to say

20

that we had arrived, we learnt that our old cat had died, anyway that’s life 1 suppose
up one minute down the next.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

I should like to thank all members who attended the working party in October, We got a lot of work done and the club is now reasonably tidy for the winter.

The good turnout was helped by the marvellous weather, but might have been even better had we been able to advertise the day's entertainment. For those not present the entertainment was caused by us when we decided to burn rubbish on the foreshore, including a fibreglass hulk from the dinghy park. Before we knew what was happening we were invaded by the coastquard, two fire appliances, the police launch, and finally a police car = all this triggered by radio calls to the coastguard from boats on the river. I suppose, had it been the stubble burning season no-one would have taken any notice.

Elsewhere in Navigans you will find the A.G.M. Agendae Please come — it is probably the best op:ortunity you have in the year for giving your view on how the club is run.

Mary Greygoose has now finished her second three year stint as Editor of
Navigans, the first being from 1969 to 1972. She leaves the post having set a high
standard for Sue Gray to follow. My sincere thanks go to Mary for the effort she has put into the production and my best wishes go to Sue in anticipation of effort to come.

Frank Savill

THE GLITTERING PRIZES

Another season is over, and by the time this is printed and read we will have enjoyed the gourmet delights of the Laying—Up Supper and the presentation of the annual club prizes. In preparation for the big night I was scrabbling around in my wardrobe the other day, when I came across ‘a rather tatty evening bag, and an even tattier prize list for last year. Idly glancing through the titles I noticed that many could be interpreted more literally, particularly if the emphasis is put on cruising rather than dinghy sailing. Enlarging on this theme, I would like to present the "Alternative Prize Winner's List for 1983, Cruiser Fleet Style",

PILOTS CUP - a pilot is defined as one who shows the way, and this year this
award must be given to John Todds in "Chimo", who, during the summer holidays, sailed from the Blackwater via the Kiel Canal to the Baltic Sea, a first for John and the first time a Marconi boat has cruised this area.

MUD RACE = was heavily contested this year, (well, we all went up the Alde, didn't we). Quasar, Aces and Eights, Copernicus and Maldon Aries were all strong contenders, however, the undisputed winner, without doubt is Albert and Shirley Pearce in "Myth of Minto", They really explored the depths of Abraham's Boson (look it up in Cootes), it took half an hour to tow them off!

MARCONI CRUISER CUP = Joan and David Thomas in "Marinero" who cruised France, Belguim, Holland and the Channel Islands this season in one trip that lasted 34 weeks and covered over 800 miles.

BARNACLE POINTS — too many entrants for this event, the winner Nick Tovey in "Tirzar" for giving his boat the opportunity to collect the most barnacles on her hulle Did Nick leave the mooring this year? Answers on a plain postcard please.

MUG'S MUG = for the crew of the year, Mug's Mug is just the thing for that evening cup of tea and toast, Joyce! (Ann Bates! Mum).

JACKPOT — an award for the over forties, and proving that you can still cruise well over forty is Bill Buchanan, still sailing regularly from Stansgate,.

MOANER*S CUP -— the junior crew of Clara Anne, they can and they do!

HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR = one skipper with some health problems has been determined to enjoy his boat to the full and has done so with great success, Cruising Helmsman of the Year — Jimmy James.

DAY TRIP JO FRANCE

After getting up at 5.30 am, we managed to be ready at 6.30 am and were
waiting for Ron and Mary Greygoose who arrived about 6.45 am. Our coats and bags were put in the car boot and we were off.

Less than two hours later we arrived at Dover's booking hall and bought five tickets to Boulogne. Mum and Mary got their Identity Cards — they both hated their photographs. We got back into the car and drove to the dock entrance, where we gave the officer our tickets. He tore a bit out and gave them back, then we drove along to the passport office.

The officer was reading a book, and when she saw our car arrive she opened the window of her office, took our passports, looked inside them and gave them back, without looking at us at all. She just closed her window and carried on reading. We then drove off again towards the ferry, where another officer told us to park next to the two coaches. We had plenty of time to go to the cafe to have a drink, returning to the car at 9.30 am to find more cars in the queue. A few minutes later we drove onto the M.V. Tiger, a P & O ferry.

We were one of the first cars on the boat, and, having parked close to the exit, went upstairs where we found five seats in the lounge before looking around the ferry. At just after 10.00 am we left for Boulogne. After reading for awhile Dad and I went for another walk and had a look at the radar. It was fairly rough and when I sat down again I began to feel travel sick. I had one of Mary's tablets and went with Dad to stand on deck and look at the horizon, which by now was the French coast. Half an hour later we were told to go to the car, and after about ten minutes the front of the ferry opened and we were let out.

Before we left the dock we had our passports checked again. Leaving the dock we turned onto the road (on the right-hand side). The second car we saw we all thought was a mad driver. We drove through the town to the old part of Soulogne, and had a look in a small shop. Then we found a nice restaurant. We were taken upstairs and saw at least a dozen people all eating at one big table, but they were English. I think we hoped they would be French. It took two hours to eat our meal. The ice cream at the end was the nicest part. On the way back to the car I bought a Boulogne doll from the small shop we had looked in before,

Leaving Boulogne we drove to Calais, and from the road we could see the white cliffs of Dover. When we got to Calais we went to a hypermarket. Dad, Mum, Ron and Mary bought all the wine they were allowed and I bought chocolate, chewing gum and some other sweets. At about 6.00 pm we drove back to Boulogne.

We were just in time to catch the ferry, and were the last car on. It was a 7.00 pm sailing and as soon as we drove on the boat we started moving. lt was dark, so we could see both sides of the channel because of the lights.

We arrived at Dover just before 8.30 pm and were let through customs. wWe all slept a little in the car on the way home, except Ron, of course, who was driving.

SAILING ETIQUETTE

It was one of those rare hot, sunny Sunday afternoons and we were having a lovely run-back up the Blackwater with the tide under us. We had anchored for lunch in a sheltered spot in the mouth of the estuary and, with a fresh NE blowing there was no
point
in hoisting more than the working jib for the return trip.
It would also give a chance for my non-sailing friends to take a turn on the helm since, in the morning it had meant hard tacking down river into very short lumpy seas.

My MacWester 27 didn't quite look like a carnival float but with two families plus a friend on board, Blucette's foredeck and cockpit were groaning under the weight of 5 adults, 3 growing children and good lunches. Hardly in racing trim!

We had manoeuvred safely through two legs of a dinghy race and:
were managing to leave plenty of room for a stream of racing cruisers to pass with spinnakers flying when, uh-ho! The upwind leg of that race?

Here he comes, hard on the wind, crew way out on the trapeze, going like the wind and he has us on starboard! I'm standing on the companion steps and my wife calls from her reclining position on the foredeck.

"See the one to Port?" "Yes" I say.
He'll pass ahead of us I had decided, so best leave the hehksman alone as he had been steering a good steady course. Now what's happening? The approaching craft had altered course and was now aiming to go clear under my stern. I was secretly glad I hadn't gone to port to cross under but I still came back into the cockpit, stepping over the maze of legs, and reached behind me for the tiller.
That was the best move I had done all day as - you guessed it -
he altered course yet again and, with a very few yards now separating us was obviously aiming at my sink outlet 6 inches or so above the waterline just abaft the after chain plate! At that moment he called "STARBOARD" and I hauled the helm hard over and 4 tons at 4 knots did a reasonable impression of turning on a sixpence.

"Not that way, you stupid B----r!}"; "Oh, B------ y hells"; "Who taught you to B------ y saili"; "Oh, They went down my starboard side with 6 to 8 feet to spare shouting all sorts of abuse, something about rules and parentage and the number of arms
and legs I didn't have, which continued way into the distance...

Now, turning as I did to Port mean't I only had to turn 45° or SO; reduced the time to pass; kept the jib flying (it was out to starboard) and didn't knock my helmsman overboard (he was standing to port of the tiller).

Turning to starboard - I suppose that was what he mean't, or was
it reverse - would have mean't 135° of turn; an increase in the
time to pass, thus allowing the tide to set me across him; backing the jib, reducing directional control, and would have given my helmsman indigestion, with a stout tiller in his stomach so goon after lunch. Maybe I could have argued that the almost inevitable.

420 *LEET NEWS

In the absence of the usual crop of earth shattering events, I have decided to commit to paper some of the hints and setting-up procedures for getting the best
out of a 420. Those that attended the race training session this year will know most of it as it is basically going to be a summary of what Dave Hall told us. (Not necessarily in order of importance).

The first item concerns the jib sheets. I expect this is old hat to a lot of people but it was new to me this season and, having tried it, I've found it an improvement. The basic idea is that, instead of fixing the centre of the rope that forms the jib sheets to the jib, both ends of the same rope are attached, so forming a continuous
system.

When I was shown this my initial reaction was that the rope would not now be long enough for the crew to go out on the trapeze. In fact, this is not the case. Using this system means that the crew always has the jib sheet to hand instead of having to reach across the boat. This is particularly useful should the jib need adjustment when the spinaker is being flown.

Most of us are stuck with our crews but it is still worth pointing out the necessary qualities (according to Eric Twineme) that all crews should aspire to??;:— Ts Unquestioning obedience;

COMMODORE'S REPORT 1983

This report for the 1983 season is my first as Commodore and I start by thanking my Committee for the support given to me during the year.

Our Sailing Secretary, Malcolm Stuart, will report on the year's sailing activities; however, I must make some comment about our Regatta and Open Meetings. Although we will remember 1983 for the glorious summer, you may need reminding that the weather prior to the Regatta was generally wet and cold. This resulted in a lower than average turnout of boats and an even lower than average turnout of camperse
Income
was down and this was particularly noticeable in the Regatta bar. In an effort to overcome the problems caused by bad behaviour, it was decided to cancel the
disco
and in addition arrange for the Police to be on site for the Saturday evening. Unfortunately, plans for an alternative entertainment fell through, with the result that we still had a minority causing problems. However, we believe that we must find a way to combat these problems, because there is no doubt that the majority attending events like our Regatta are well behaved and we cannot allow a minority to spoil this great event.

We also had a behaviour problem at the Disco evening held during our September Open Meeting, but, again, it is our intention to continue with these events. For our Barbeque we also provided additional security cover following a threat of trouble, but, in the event, there were no problems and I hope everyone enjoyed the evening.

My own sailing activities were over very quickly this year. Having made a late start, within a few weeks I managed to trap a nerve in my neck, which put paid to my activity.

Qur colleagues from Rochester visited us as usual this year and two of them returned with their families to camp with us later in the season. For once we planned a return visit. 1 went along as one of Dennis Byatt's crew, enjoying my first cruise out of the Blackwater.

Later you will be asked to vote on a proposal to increase subscriptions. ‘The aim of the suggested subscription increase is to increase our income by approximately 10% in order to keep our income end expenditure account in the black and increase our reserve to cover future replacement of capital equipment, (radio, tractor, rescue boat, etc.) as well as provide the large sum that is needed every few years to cover road maintenance. The proposed increase has been added in such a way that members making the most use of the Club, i.e. the sailors, will bear the major share of the increase. Your Committee feel that this is not only fair but necessary in order to encourage new non=-sailing members. I do hope you will support this Committee
proposal.

We started the season with no one nominated to organise the Galley. My thanks go to those involved in keeping it going during the early part of the season and, of course, to Maureen Ball for later accepting the post of Galley Organiser.

I am glad to see that most of the team have accepted nomination for the coming year, and at the same time I thank the retiring members: Vic Crisp, our Treasurer, Mike Cerey and Tony Cockrell, for their past effort. Two junior Officers retire this year: Phil Gray, our Cadet Captain, who has done a magnificent job motivating our youngsters, and Mary Greygoose, who ends her second term as Editor of Navigans. Sue Gray (Phil's wife) has offered to take on this job and I wish her every success.

Finally, may I say to all who have in some way helped the Club run smoothly during this year, thank you.

Frank Savill
Commodore

SAILING SECRETARY's REPORT 1983

INTRODUCTION I will outline this years sailing activity drawing special attention to a significant reduction in the numbers of boats sailing. But first I will take you back to this time last year when we started to put together the 1983 sailing programme.

SAILING PROGRAMME

The sailing year starts with the appointment of officers at the AGM. By that time details will have been collected on tide times and dates agreed through the BJRC on the major sailing events for the following year. The December Committee meetings then put together the basic sailing programme, allocating duties and trying to avoid conflicts with other sailing events and social activities. Inevitably it proves impossible to avoid all conflicts but the aim is to produce a balanced programme from the beginning of April to the end of October.

The 1982 season had seen the successful introduction of an Autumn Points series for dinghy racing but a lack of support for the Ladies and Cadets series of six races spread throughout the year. It was decided therefore to perpetuate the Autumn Points series and replace the Cadet races by a series to be run during Cadet Week. The Ladies series reverted to the original formula of a single race and it was planned to extract results from a new Figure of Eight race to be sailed round Osea and Northey.

The basic sailing programme for 1983 was therefore constructed round the three points series taking notice of suggestions made in previous years that racing should continue through the summer since not everybody took their holiday during August. Also all points races were programmed as morning and afternoon pairs since complaints had been received when only one points race was scheduled.

Although a Spring Points series was introduced as far back as 1969 it was not until this year that the change from one premier series was fully recognised in the Year Book. It was anticipated that the new format for displaying the Clubs awards would encourage fleets to present new trophies to fill the now obvious gaps on page 2 of the Year Book.

Did you all notice that this year saw the last postage of male chauvenism removed from the Year Book. Now we are all Helms together in eager anticipation of one of our ladies carrying off the Costain Cup.

DINGHY POINTS SERIES

The season has been an unmitigated disaster for the three dinghy points series. An overall reduction in points racing of 36% compared with 1982 affected all fleets as the statistics show:-

The basic sailing programme changed very little and in both 1982 and 1983 there
were 34 points races scheduled. A superficial examination of the number of races sailed in each month appears to show a difference in the distribution of races in the Summer months until one remembers that a month can have either
4 or 5 weekends.

At this point the exercise becomes too difficult and one is tempted to say that comparison of statistics from only two consecutive years is a mathamatical nonsense. Afterall we know what a difference weather conditions can make to our sailing. 1983 one argues was a classic balmy English summer and we all opted for a lazy year. Whether or not this is true, and who is hoping for bad weather next year to prove it, the fact remains that the average entry for a points race was only 15 dinghies. (By conincidence entries for Wednesday evening races also averaged 15)

Fleet as opposed to handicap racing remains remarkably popular at our club and runs against the trend at other local clubs. However when you consider that we currently try to support 7 fleets each needing at least 3 boats on the water to make a race, then our average entry of 15 dinghies doesn't indicate a healthy state of affairs.

To support this mini-armada of 15 dinghies on race days we have to organise about a dozen volunteers acting as duty officers looking after the clubhouse, the race box and the rescue launch as well as assisting with the Galley and Bar and totting up the results. Then there is Claude Emerson who clears up behind us. We have often debated the organisation required to run our Regatta, but this, for some 200 dinghies, seems well worthwhile compared with the effort we put in each weekend for a meagre 15 boats.

One aspect not considered above is the National trend in dinghy racing. It is claimed that the advent of Sailboards has reduced the number of dinghy sailors and there is some evidence from attendances at National events that this is true. More optimistic forcasters reckon that the total sailing activity will increase with Sailboarders turning to dinghies as they get older or wiser. There are few sailboards registered at our Club and there has been no demand for organised racing, but we may have an artificial barrier to sailboard membership in the way in which we make up our fees when one considers the minimum facilities required to launch a sailboard.

REGATTA

Although the total entry was 30% down this year, this was largely due to the atrocious weather preceeding the weekend, which discouraged camping. Marconi entries remained steady at 24 dinghies but we didn't get any nearer to the prizes.

The event remains remarkably popular with our visitors who this year had to put up with light and variable winds which played havoc with our starting and finishing procedures. As a result the Regatta Sailing instructions were altered after the second race to allow for a committee boat finish, and this facility was used in the final race to stop the Mirrors and Toppers at Breezy. The detailed procedure will have to be refined somewhat for 1984 because the assistant race officer who was hastily conveyed to Breezy got her wellies full of water.

OPEN MEETINGS

The three Autumn open meetings were well supported and actually showed a small overall increase on last year.

The only successful match of the year was the Rochester visit when the BP/MAV contingent brought six dinghies and took away both the individual Colwyn Stone

CLOSED RACES Contd

Jackpot was as enjoyable as ever this year. The racing up to the Jolly Sailor at Heybridge and back with the tide is always interesting, but the added spice comes at lunchtime. It is invariably sunny and one sits on the sea wall quaffing ale, trying to give the leader of the morning race a special handicap for the return leg, but basically just sitting around and waiting for someone to provide the entertainment. This year the prize went to a lady who appeared out of nowhere to create havoc in our moorings. The poor innocent lady, who owned the large wreck that our geriatrics had tied their dinghies to, was overwhelmed with male helpers, one of whom managed to capsize his Solo in his eagerness to display his gallantry. In the best Jackpot traditions said gallant helm was awarded the trophy, despite the fact that he won.

This years Hornet Buoy was sailed in very strong winds and despite many spectacular capsizes there was no expensive damage. This event consistently generates some of the best Hornet sailing of the season.

The organisation of a 4-Race series for the Payne Cup sailed during Cadet Week attracted 10 dinghies and showed itself to be a great improvement on the previous formula of a six race series spread throughout the season. It was impossible this year to organise sufficient Mirror's for all helms and with a very young batch of helms on our hands at the moment some were still handicaping themselves with geriatric crews. With this years winner being only 10 years old, I think we can look forward to a Cadet fleet growing in Significance for the rest of this decade at least.

TRAINING

I have mentioned the promise that our Cadet fleet shows for the future and much credit must go to Colin Leveridge who again took on the Winter instruction sessions which attracted 20 cadets. Phil Gray put a tremendous effort into organising the Cadets this year particularly during camping week. Having seen his sailing performance deteriorate after Cadet week, I propose that all future Cadet Captains should be able to claim average points for the rest of the season.

The use of video equipment to help training on starting technique was so successful that we wondered at the time how long it would be before all our starts came under the close scrutiny of a camera.

In order to keep ahead of these fledglings some of the older members also had training sessions. The '420' fleet had a very successful day organised by Dave Hall and until the Autumn Open meeting, the whole '420' fleet were convinced they were going faster.

Although no formal training took place in the premier fleet the friendly and persistent instruction of Solo tail enders continues relentlessly.

POT HUNTING

The Hornet, Mirror, Solo and Dart fleets went out into the wider world for a little pot hunting this year. Most successful being Robin Smith (Dart 2606) who brings to the club its first National and European championship since Roger Hance won the Enterprise Nationals in 1973.

Neil Salmon crewing for Dave Sherwin of Leigh on Sea SC (Mirror 64203) helped him come 2nd in the National Cahmpionship and then mopped it up by winning the Mirror Worlds.

Colin Harper (Hornet 2100) did the round of Hornet Open meetings winning at Weston Sailing Club and coming 4th overall in the Hornet Travellers series whilst Graham Mead (Hornet 2108) came 16th in the Hornet World and National
championship.

POT HUNTING Contd

Three members of the premier fleet entered the Solo Worlds at Hayling Island but as in previous years their final positions were still into double figures but then standards are so much higher in this fleet.

CRUISING

Some 80 cruisers are laying up at Stansgate after a year which indicated once again that there is little demand for organised Cruiser racing. The three Barnacle Points races organised for Saturdays were abandoned, no cruisers entered the club all-in races and we had only one entry in our own Marconi Cruiser Cup. Next year it is proposed that we extract results for Barnacle Points from Mona'S Cup, Pilot Cup and the Cruiser Cup.

Dinghy sailors may be forgiven for gaining the impression that cruiser activity is limited to scrubbing, painting and launching. To dispel this myth I will chronicle this years epic voyages.

John Todds notched up a Marconi first by taking "Chimo" to the Baltic via the Kiel canal. Joan and Dave Thomas did 800 miles on their Channel Islands trip taking in Belgium and Holland en route. As for the rest of the fleet, a company of eight cruisers went up the East Coast as far as Aldebugh during August. Finally we must not forget the two Marconi Cruisers who made it round to the Medway to sample Rochester's muddy reception.

CLUB BOATS We now have a total of eight club boats:-

Working Boats Pleasure Craft
Mariner Rescue Launch Brazil
Rowing Tender Idle Vice
Fisherman Cadet
Work Boat Graduate

A mooring raft is to be added to this fleet over the winter to release the Work Boat from handling increasingly heavy mooring gear.

The cost of running club boats is high both in financial terms and the effort expended in routine maintenance and emergency repairs. We are indebted to those members who take responsibility for a particular boat since any boat which was merely club property would soon deteriorate.

It remains to be seen next year what use will be made of our four pleasure craft particularly by the Cadets. After some major repair work on the Mariner Mitsui outboard this season, the engine should be good for a few more years. However we are aware of the Mariner's limitations as a rescue launch and it is felt that we should start looking round for a more satisfactory replacement. It may prove impossible to combine the function of speed with that of stability in one vessel but the aquisition of a mooring raft will allow us to review the role of all the club working boats.

SAFETY AFLOAT

An increasing awareness of safety comes to all of us with experience and whilst it must always be the responsibility of individuals to avoid putting themselves into dangerous situations we can as a club do something to minimise the risk.

The 1983 Sailing Instructions introduced a new rule encouraging dinghy sailors to wear adequate clothing for the Easter Series.

SAFETY AFLOAT Contd ah
Our Cadets are taught safety afloat and have to demonstrate their ability to right a capsized dinghy but we have no formal training for novice adults. A natural tendency for beginners is to come down to Stansgate when it is quiet and make a fool of themselves in private. Whilst this is very understandable it is alas pretty dangerous in a tidal estuary. We should therefore encourage all beginners to contact their fleet captain who will arrange basic training as necessary. One of the easiest and safest ways to begin sailing is to join in at the tail end of a race, and follow the fleet round (some of us go on for years doing just this) Seriously though it does make it easy to decide which way to point the wretched boat and the rescue launch is always on hand if you to for a dip or want a tow back.

We have an excellent team of regular rescue launch drivers now who are not complacent about their skills and subject themselves to bouts of further training. For our major events such as the Regatta and the long distance races we are indebted to the support given by the Cruiser Fleet in providing mother ships at the remote ends of the course. The need was brought home to us this year when we had to abandon a Hornet at Bench Head in the Rum, Tub and Bung race which further demonstrated the limitations of our Mariner in rough seas.

THE RIVER

Subtle changes take place in the Blackwater each year and the first sail of the year becomes a search for the new gravel banks. The more obvious things to avoid whilst sailing are the river marks and this year has seen No 2 (Lawling Creek) edging out into the main channel and sprouting a light. The North Doubles (No 7) also received a light, but our local river mark Goldhanger (No 1) had its light discontinued.

Our "F" buoy marking the eastern end of the cruiser moorings is being replaced by a Fisheries Protection buoy which will be lit. The ground tackle from "F" buoy has been recovered and will be used to locate "D" buoy more accurately on the start line for next season.

TROPHIES

We are indebted to the donors for four new trophies this year.

To Norman Kerridge for the "Jack Kerridge Trophy" which is awarded to the winner of our new Figure of Eight race in memory of Jack who loved a ride on the rescue launch, particularly when we went up river.

To Ron Greygoose for the "Captain's Trophy" awarded to the winner of Solo Autumn points. The beautifully hand made model solo has a helm bearing a striking resemblence to its maker.

To Richard Spillsbury for the "Spring Fever Cup" awarded to the winner of Mirror Spring Points, and finally to Mike Boreham for the "Autumn Reflections Cup" awarded to the winner of the Mirror Autumn Points.

An interesting point came out this year as we prepared the trophies for prize giving, when we realised that the Pilot Cup has always been incorrectly referred to as Pilot's Cup and the Mugs Mug was first mispelt in 1968 and has remained so ever since.

CONLCUSION

The 1983 sailing year was not an unmitigated disaster, our Cadets and the Autumn Open Meetings saved us from that. However, I would ask you to reflect on the general fall off in sailing activity and let me have your considered and constructive views on whether this is a problem to be solved or do we accept it as a fact to be faced. Either way your comments can influence the construction of the 1984 sailing programme.

Malcolm Stuart
Sailing Secretary

Useful hints this month is concerned with the crew, or rather the crew-helm roles tionship. I know I have to be very careful here as this is a very touchy subject (no "double entendre" is intended here). Suppose, however, your crew turns to you at a crucial point in the race and says something like, "What on earth are you doing? That boat that's just overtaken us is not only 10 years old, but it's crewed by a 12 year old girl!" Whilst this may well be justified criticism, I would say that this is not the time to come out with it. The atmosphere in the boat will now be strained and the mental attitude of the helmsman at least will not be one that enables him to get the best out of the boat. It would be better for the crew to have kept quiet here, waited until the boat had shot past another on plane and then said something like, "That's great! We're really shifting now. Let's go for it!" _
Not, I hasten to add, that I would actually like any crew of mine to use these exact words. The atmosphere in the boat will now be harmonious and therefore conducive to better performance.

This is all pretty obvious, you may think, but it's surprising how many
people
come almost to blows in the course of a race. The same ideas apply to the helms- man as well. A good helmsman should praise a crew for doing things correctly and only criticise constructively, and preferably after the race. This is obviously a subjective point, as some people may be able to sail fastest when they are shout- ing at each other all the time. Speaking for myself, I like to enjoy the sail as well as the race and rowing (as in having an argument) spoils both for me.

Next month I shall list the points, in order of importance, that I think have helped me to sail faster over the past two years. I would point out here that I am not trying to claim that these ideas are my own or that they will work for everyone, but I am convinced that they have helped me.

SOLO —- A RECENT LOVE AFFAIR

It was back at the tail end of 1979 when, having resolved to join M.S.C. because of the enjoyment gained from crewing an Enterprise with Geoff Josey, I looked around for a suitable class of dinghy to buy. I wanted to try my hand at helming @ racing dinghy but knew of no-one mad enough to risk sailing with me, so the choice was simple. The only single-handed fleet at the Club was Solo.

Picking up a second-hand glass-fibre boat, I suppose I must have made a fairly lucky choice, for it subsequently proved fast and reliable. It seemed appropriate to name it Greenfield for, apart from the obvious connection with its dark green decking, the name also represented the street name in Dearborn, U.S.A. where we had stayed for the previous two years — the trip which provided me with the funds for boat buying, a luxury we certainly could not have afforded previously.

Launching then, with my newly-acquired green machine, into the virtual unknown, I started to learn the necessary skills and judgement the hard way, which involved the involuntary gulping of large quantities of Blackwater and frequent tests of the efficiency of my life-jacket. I was not, however, without considerable help and advice from some of the more experienced Solo helms at the Club — notably, John Rutherford and Geoff Josey, to whom I remain indebted.

It was only as I slowly and somewhat painfully began to climb the learning curve that an awareness of the virtues and potential of the Class which I had so haphaz- ardly selected gradually developed.

Whilst fundamentally a young man's boat, demanding as it does a high level of athleticism, fine balance and physical endurance but offering in return high perf+ ormance, responsiveness and excitement, it also has the unioue quality among single- handers of having a very adaptable rig. This means that with careful choice of rig and sail, and tuning to match, it is possible for people of vastly differing weights, age and technique to be competitive at Club level. ‘lhis of course is exactly where classes such as Laser and Topper fail to measure up as practical club boats, and it is perhaps appropriate here to acknowledge the great debt which M.S.C. owes to Frank Savill for pioneering this splendid class at the Club. Frank has served the Club very well in many respects, but to my mind none more so than in his excellent choice of single-hander.

A well-prepared wooden-decked Solo is a beautiful sight, both ashore and on the water, but for those who prefer the relatively low maintenance demands of glass- fibre boats they have the satisfaction of knowing that both types are very closely matched for performance, and quite competitive boats of either type can be picked up for under £500.

Small wonder then that the Solo class has for years been the best supported and most dynamic class at the Club. Anyone fed up with handicap fleet racing or crew problems could really do no better than take up the challenge offered by what met surely be Jack Holt's greatest masterpiece.

John Salmon

chain.

420 HELPFUL HINTS

This month, in the last of the series, I am going to jot down some of the things that I think have increased my boat speed over the past two seasons. I am sure that not everyone will agree with the ideas expressed here, but I remain convinced that they have helped me!

Factor affecting speed Importance rating (out of 10)

(1) Wind shifts 10

(2) Keeping boat level 8

(3) Tacking well (roll tacking) 6
(4) Mark rounding 4

(5) Tactics

(6) Boat tune 2

(1) Wind shifts - I have given this by far the most importance. It can be shown
that when two boats are travelling at 4 knots and are both tacking for the windward mark, the boat that ignores a 5 wind shift will be over 45 feet down wind of the one that tacked on the shift after only one minute. It is therefore possible to lose more ground by ignoring windshifts than by any of the following methods. There are, however, many times, especially in our tidal waters, when it is far more beneficial to tack in order to keep out of the tide.

(2) Keeping the boat level - Most people would agree, I think, that the best
boat speed can be obtained by doing this. It is particularly important when going to windward, as this is when the full centreboard is needed and any heeling is effectively reducing the depth of the centreboard. It is there- fore surprising how many people allow their boat to sail heeled over at an angle. I think the main reason is that it feels more comfortable, in that the boat is less likely to capsize on top of you.

(3) Roll tacking - Especially in light winds roll tacking can gain you a lot.
Even if you can't do it very well, it causes the sails to make a lot of noise and can disconcert other competitors who aren't trying it.

(4) Mark rounding = Now we are getting to the bottom end of the list. There will
probably only be about 10 marks on a given course, so it is only possible to lose a small amount of ground by poor rounding. One thing, however, that has been convincingly demonstrated to me is that you should always try to round a mark on the inside. If someone has an overlap on you and is calling for water, it can be beneficial, though not always possible, to deliberately slow up and round the mark behind him but close to the mark. This is especially true if there is more than one boat inside you. By doing this you will lose a lot less ground than if you allowed yourself to be pushed away from the mark by the other boats.

(5) Tactics - Except in team racing, these should normally be restricted to keep-
ing clear of the other boats and their dirty winds. Luffing matches only serve to slow down the boats involved.

(6) Boat tune — Beyond basic setting up of mast rake, I don't really understand
this subject!

Pete Chrystie

Total entry was down to 110 compared with 158 last year and 223 in 1982, not surprising perhaps with the coldest and wettest Whitsun Bank Holiday on record.

COLWYN STONE TROPHY 1984

The 1984 visit to the Marconi Sailing Club on the Blackwater by Rochester sailors was again very successful. Despite a bad forecast 5 cruisers made the trip led by Jack Pateman, the Marconi Sailing Club President,

continued

se,
2

The Rochester dinghy team was Richard Stone, Peter Belcher, Gordon Belcher (all in Lasers), with Maurice and Pam Chapman in an Enterprise and their son Mark in a Topper. The Marconi Sailing Club team was Frank Savill, Ron Greygoose and Malcolm Stuart in Solos and D. Webb and J. Walker in Enterprises.

The wind was ideal for Lasers at the top end of force 3, gusting to force 4 and in a direction to give mainly reaching courses.

In the first race the Lasers quickly pulled away, chased by the Solos. Richard Store led at the windward mark, but Peter Belcher overtook him down— wind and stayed ahead to win. The broad reaches gave some fine planing.

At the second gybe mark Gordon Belcher capsized allowing Ron Greygoose to
catch
up and beat him on handicap. Maurice Chapman, despite a prestart capsize, sailed well to beat the two Marconi Sailing Club Enterprises, whilst Mark, though last on the water, sailed above his handicap to be fifth.

For the second race the course was changed to give more beating. Despite this the Lasers again pulled away from the start. Again Richard Stone led at the windward mark but Peter Belcher's faster speed allowed him to overtake,
despite hitting a mark, Peter gradually pulled away to win the race and the
trophy for the third year in succession. Richard Stone was second end Gordon Belcher third. Maurice Chapman was close to the Lasers until the wind increas-— ed on the third lap and he finished fourth equal.

Again Ron Greygoose was the highest placed Marconi Sailing Club boat at equal
fourth, but the unusual wind direction puzzled the home team more than the visitors and they missed crucial wind shifts,

The trophy was presented to Peter by Joan Stone. The sunny weather, ideal winds, good food and pleasant company made it another very enjoyable day.

SOLO NATIONALS: 29 JULY - 3 AUGUST 1984

This year the Solo Nationals were held at Brixham, South Devon, in a joint Championship with the Seafly class.

A disappointing entry of 36 Solos was explained by the fact that a large UK contingent had travelled to the Netherlands two weeks earlier for the
Worlds,
and that Brixham was a long way from the Solo centres in London and the Mid- lands, especially in the peak of the holiday season,

John Salmon and Roger Smith were the Marconi representatives. The practice race and the first two points races were held in light, changeable winds with the water in Torbay fairly choppy. The Wednesday saw a two hour delay before the start, which with the race and the journey out and back meant seven hours on the water. The race finished in a force 4 which made Pacing a little more exciting. Strangely, on Wednesday and Thursday the two Marconi boats finished within a boat's length of each other, which ‘seemed to make the
journey
to Brixham rather unnecessary.

Friday's last race was much more exciting with a force 5 = 6 and some bigger

Overall, however, the two Marconi boats were not in good finishing positions with John Salmon 21st overall and Roger Smith 24th. The overall winner was
S. Cray (3406) from Hollowell SC with Craig Moffet second. Geoff Carveth, who
had retained the World Championship in Holland, did not compete.

The Solo A.G.M. was held at Brixham on 2nd August 1984 end this year there were no long arguments about masts, rudders, etc. The most eventful subject was a vote on the election of president, with the incumbent Gordon Walls being challenged by Craig Moffet who won the vote.

The next most eventful subject, which for some reason caused much hilarity, was a proposal that where the Nationals are held amid interesting scenery the programme should include a "lay day”. The gentleman's lady friend endor- sed this proposal,

I was pleased to see that there were quite a few young helms at the Nationals as well as the old faces, which is a good sign that the Solo is attracting young helmsmen who find it en easier boat to handle competitively in heavy weather compared to the Laser.

Roger Smith
