HORNET WORLDS 41984

Four Marconi Hornets set "sailTM for foreign parts on 3rd August. The "sailing" was done in a Townsend Thoresen ferry bound from Felixstowe to zeebrugge, and
thence to Hoorn, Holland, where we would be joined by the fifth Marconi boat with Colin Harper. The Fleet were soon found esconced in the “Viking" bar and savouring their last taste of English beer. The sailors comprised Gvnahane Mead/ Mike Turner, Pat Black/Tony Cockerell, Murray Todd/Keith Boyles and Phil Gray/ Kate Nicholson. The supporters consisted of Sue Gray, Barbara Mead (her first mention in Navigans), Laura, Becky and Geoff,

After landing at Zeebrugge, we flashed our newly acquired (and expensive) Small Ships. kegisters at unsuspecting and slichtly confused Customs Officials and then drove the 200 miles to Hoorn, The majority of the Fleet looked and felt the worse for vear cfter this first exhausting day and when, in the fail- ing light, we finally found our hotel we just collapsed into the nearest chair with a beer.

The Fleet (minus Colin Harper) had taken over but one room in a small hotel only ten minutes' walk from the boat park. The proprietor, who spoke better English then Murray, was called Basil by his friends after his uncanny resemblance to a certain T.V. character. We were able throughout the week to change in the hotel end he didn't mind us walking in and out in wetsuits. This proved a boon, as the Hoorn Sailing Club facilities were a little stret-—
ched,.

CONTINUGG. sees

«f=

The first day was taken up with boat measurements, sight-seeing and a welcome by the Mayor in a local church where free wine and beer was served! Sail meas—- urement gave several crews near heart attacks when two sets of brand new Hood's sails failed and two new Hyde genoas failed to satisfy the Dutch measurer. The Hyde genoas were quickly passed when it was established that the English rules were applied at World Championships in cases of measurement discrepancies and since the Hyde sails conformed with English rules, they were 0.K. after all. The Hood sails, however, were too large whichever rules one applied and a fair amount of on-the-spot surgery was carried out before they were passed.

The sailing was held over a triangular course some 2 = 3 miles offshore and the race instructions said we would race over 10 nautical miles. In fact, I can advise my readers that a Dutch nautical mile is probably twice the inter- nationally accepted distance. Generally, as one sailed up and down the start line to determine if there was any bias, one could not see the windward mark. The Race Officer did a fine job of setting an accurate start line for all six races and there was only one postponement for a course change and only two General Recalls all week. The longest time spent on the water was approximately five hours one day, with the shortest race (race 6) being about 14 hours when the course was shortened (probably due to worsening conditions, but possibly because the Smithers brothers were winning their first race!)

The number of boats competing was 45, of which 22 were British, the remainder being Dutch. Our Dutch hosts were very pleased that so many of us had made the journey and spent the whole week enquiring as to our well-being, etc.

I was surprised as to the gentlemanly way the boats raced, especially at the start line where it was always possible to find a spot with a hole to leeward. The racing conditions were superb right through the week, with wind strengths generally between force 3 and 5. The average water depth is only about 10 ft in.the area, so these winds produced a heavy chop which made beating difficult for the inexperienced crews. Racing through the chop with spinnaker up on a reaching leg proved to be the most exciting point with many spectacular cap- sizes to be had. With the exception of Grahame and Mike, all the Marconi boats capsized at various times during the week, but none so unluckily as Colin Harper, who capsized just before the finish line in one race when he was lying in fourth position.

As the week advanced it became a test of endurance (both on end off the water), a test of the boat and its fittings (Colin's mast fell down during one race!) and a test for the support teams who were fed up with all the sailing, the children (bless their little cotton socks) and supplying food and drink after the sailing. I'm sorry to say that Sue did not get her promised trip to Amst- erdam, which is a good excuse for us to go back to Holland one day. However, it was a lovely sight to see Sue and Barbara (second mention in Wavigens) wait- ing patiently for their loved ones (Ed's. note: And Phil and Grahame) as the exhausted sailors came in from the troubled waters,

The new World Champion is Peter Bennett from Shoreham SC and since the Chanp= ionships he has subsequertly won the Nationals, The Marconi boat positions were as follows:

MARCONI SAILING CLUB

SAILING SECRETARIES REPORT = 1984

I have set out this year's report chronologically picking up the successes, disasters and light relief as we progressed through 1984,

JANUARY:

The year started with a huge success for Marconi. We raised a total of £500 in sponsorship for the RNLI rowing race, the £350 raised by our official entry was the highest for any one boat, although it was left to our unofficial entry rowed by two St. Trinians old girls to win the race.

The first of six Cadet Winter Meetings run by Derek Hall started in January. The
meetings held at M.A.S.C. between 6.00 and 7.00 pm on Saturday evenings were well
attended and the benefit to our Cadet Fleet became obvious as the season progressed.

FEBRUARY

The 1984 Year Book came out with the promise of lots of new trophies:— ww

Points Series Trophy Donated By

420 Spring Jumbly Trophy Pete Chrystie
Mirror Spring Spring Fever Cup Richard Spillsbury
Hornet Autumn Leaf Trophy Mike Turner
Enterprise Autumn Autumn Blues Trophy Steve Evans
Mirror Autumn Reflections Cup Mike Boreham
420 Autumn Seaweed Trophy John Weedon

Only one failed to meet the Laying—Up Supper deadline but Mike Turner gave himself another year by winning Autumn Points and promised to turn over a new leaf next year. Steve Evans was seen to be handling the Autumn Blues Trophy with some trepidation. His wife revealed later that the glue was still wet.

MARCH

The main working party attempted to get Stansgate ready for another season in heavy rain. Aside from the early burly of the routine fun jobs Pete Chrystie aw and a small slave gang erected a totem pole to protect sailboards.

The Sailing Sub-Committee came up with an excellent idea to offer the use of our gravel covered hard to Tillingham Fire Brigade for routine pump tests. The request got to them a little late for this year but the idea is worth a repeat.

APRIL

The first dinghy race of the season was scheduled for All Fools Day = 6 turned up. The wind matched this effort by blowing Force 6 with occasional sleet. Commonsense prevailed and racing was cancelled for the day so that we could concentrate our resources on a first trial of the Mariner launching and recovery procedure.

The launch procedure worked perfectly in the adverse weather conditions and the 4 solos and 2 "420's" joined the Mariner in its new high visibility livery for a short thrash.

MAY

Spring Bank Holiday Monday was devoted to the somewhat novel pursuit of safety traininge Leaving the drowning activity till later in the season, when hopefully the river would have warmed up, we concentrated on perfecting the recovery of capsized dinghies and sailboards using the Mariner. After trying out everyone's

fanntiniiod

as Se

theories we concluded by making the following recommendations

Capsized dinghies lying with sails on the water are most effectively righted by the rescue launch working towards the dinghy from the top of its mast. This was shown to allow better control and to minimise the risk of damage.

- Practice towing showed that dinghies towed most successfully from a stern line,
although care had to be taken not to put any snatch load on forestay fittings which are designed for mainly vertical loads. The tow line should be clipped or looped either side of the forestay to damp down yawing whilst any snatch loads are taken back to the mast or a thwart.

- Sailboards should be de=rigged in the water-first bring the board over the side
of the Mariner followed by the rigging after releasing the clew outhaul and collapsing the boom against the mast.

- The safest method of beaching the Mariner was demonstrated using a buoy close
inshore from which the Mariner was pulled or quanted ashore after raising the
outboard.

On the Regatta I must first remind you that it was the coldest and wettest Whitsun Bank Holiday on record. Not surprising therefore to find total entries down to
110 compared with 158 last year and 223 in 1982.

We can draw some consolation from the atrocious weather, it gave excellent sailing conditions and, judging from comments made by competitors, must have been one of our most successful Regatta sailing programmes. I feel this has given us a healthy base on which to build a really good 1985 Regatta and a little publicity to those friends we have made at past Regatta’s will prove well worthwhile.

It was appropriate that the first Wednesday evening race this year was sailed in Regatta week for the Mud Trophy.

JUNE

The end of Regatta camping week brought the Rochester visit and some decent sunny weather. Rochester took the team prize by a convincing 182 to 35 points margin whilst Peter Belcher from Rochester won the individual Colwyn Stone Trophy with two firsts in his Laser. The visitors concluded that an unusual(sic) wind direction had puzzled the home team more than: the visitors and that we had missed crucial wind shifts.

The following day we entered four teams in the Maylandsea Bay Challenge Cup extracting our results for the Jack Kerridge Trophy. An excellent race this, round Osea and Northey Islands with a multitude of individual and team prizes at
stake.

We failed to reecapture the Boothby Cup this year. After a closely fought first leg at Stansgate we failed to get a team together to contest the second leg at Osea. A big disappointment in recent years has been the relunctance of some of our better helms to compete for the Club. We have the talent and ability to win many of these events but so often fail to rise to the challenge.

Summer Points 4 gave rise to an interesting debate on race abandonment procedure and it demonstrated that the Race Officer must exercise some care when seeking to abandon a race under Rule 5.1. Certainly where the situation arises because of insufficient wind it is very difficult to abandon a race where a competitor demonstrates his ability to complete within the timescale. The safest course for Race Officers is to keep an eye on the weather conditions and if necessary shorten the course either at the race box line or from a committee boat at any rounding
marke

The Rum Tub and Bung went off without a hitch this year attracting 38 cruisers and

/continued.

28 dinghies. Summer Points 5 scheduled for the afternoon was cancelled because of the late finish of R.T. & B. The trial inclusion this year of points racing on days allocated to traditional races failed on this and other occasions to attract more entries to the traditional races.

JULY

This month brought problems with the Marine Band radio at both the clubhouse end and on the Mariners “Seavoice"., A starting problem was identified on the Mariner engine but the true cause was not found until the engine was stripped down for its winter service at the end of the season. I am pleased to report that despite the extensive electrolytic corrosion the bill for winter service will be little different to last years,

The best trained fleet in the club again persuaded Dave Hall to come along for a one day session. This year he concentrated on spinnaker gyberipokery.e

The "420" and Enterprise fleets in a somewhat desperate attempt to maintain fleet racing nominated certain Sundays when they would make a special effort to ensure at least three boats made it to the start line. Unfortunately this had little effect on numbers but nevertheless seems to be a good commonsense idea. ed

AUGUST

This year's Jackpot was as enjoyable as ever and unmarred by past excesses. Nobody had to be poured back into their boat after lunch, none of the geriatrics lost their teeth and the ladies of Heybridge escaped any overwhelming displays of
gallentry.

The Pilot Cup was somewhat unusual with a Cruiser only entry. We had two Barnacle Points races this year and we seem to have arrived at the right formula of four races with results extracted from Mona's Cup, Rum Tub and Bung, Pilot Club and Marconi Cruiser Cup.

On Pilot Cup day the dinghy fleet chose to wait for Summer Points 16 despite weather conditions which would have favoured most dinghies. I have been surprised how reluctant some of our better dinghy helms are to enter one-off races. Perhaps we could encourage more entries by simply pointing out how much easier it is to win a trophy for a traditional one-off race than the long haul involved in the Points Series. ed

Robin Smith managed to gain some good publicity for the club by winning the Dart Nationals at Worthing.

The Hornet Fleet avoided any adverse publicity over in Holland and with five boats they formed the second largest contingent after Brightlingsea S.C. at the World
Championships.

The premier fleet had two representatives at the Solo National Championship. Their finishing positions were explained by the fact that the Solo is now attracting young helms who find it an easy boat to handle competitively in heavy weather.

The August Bank Holiday Series saw the resurgence of a real Cadet presence at Marconie For many years we have nurtured Cadet helms with adult crews but at long last the chickens are leaving the nest. Neil Salmon and Clair Savill won the series and another cadet pair, Damian and Lucy Boreham camefourth. Hopefully next year we can encourage more pairings and start to do battle with our neighbouring Cadet Fleets particularly Maylandsea Bay and Blackwater who both use Mirrors for Cadet
racinGe

The August Bank Holiday weekend gave us the opportunity to continue the
safety
training. Two of our more athletic rescue drivers spent an interesting afternoon

/continuede

= 2

Pishing a very game Claire Urry out of the water by every conceivable method. Claire's life saving qualifications making her performance very real.

For an unconscious casualty the optimum method evolved was to drop off the rescue crew who gave support in the water, cleared the casualties airway and gave the first vital inflations of the lungs. Meanwhile the driver brought the Mariner alongside with the ladder down on the port side, which is clear of the engine controls, then with the engine idling the crew climbs aboard to help the driver bounce the casualty over the side.

We may only get an unconscious casualty once in ten years, but when it happens the rescue driver and crew of the day must be prepared to respond efficiently.

SEPTEMBER

The Marconi Cruiser Cup this year gave us some organisational problems with a Jeaem. start from Thirslet Spit and a long line finish at Stansgate on what turned out to be a very popular weekend for river traffic. Criticism of our ability to identify finishers reliably led to a 8.3.R.C. proposal to start and finish the race at Thirslet Spit. We have countered this by proposing a start at Osea Pier with a short line finish at Stansgate but inside a committee boat rather than 'D' buoy to avoid too much action inside the moorings.

A last minute switch
of dates by the Hornet Fleet took everybody by surprise but the organising Dart Fleet coped well with what turned out to be the best attended Hornet Open of the year with 29 entries.

The Solo Open only attracted three visitors largely due to a conflict of dates which kept the Fishers Green contingent away.
However a good turnout of nine
Marconi boats and Force 6 winds kept up the interest particularly when beating down Goldhanger Creek at the bottom of an exceptionally low tide. Capsizing in a gale with only an inch of water to lubricate the hull is an experience only bettered by trying to get sailing again.

OCTOBER

The Dart/"420" Open Meeting was organised by the Hornet Fleet who were grey with Fatigue by the end of the weekend. Their task was made more difficult by not having the support of an 0.0.0. which led to the first problem with keys, then the committee boat turned out to have no obvious place to hoist flags. The rod that broke the back of these waspelike insects was the additional burden of organising
Autumn Points 9 and 10.

Despite the problems the visitors thoroughly enjoyed their racing particularly the Dart Fleets quick flash round Osea and Northey Islands which nearly ruined racing at the up=river clubs as everyone stopped to watch. Entries were 18 Darts
(7 Marconi Boats) and 14 "420's" (4 from Marconi).

The formula of a long first leg true beat created by a Committee Boat start followed by an interesting chase round the river buoys provides an attractive course for our visitors giving them some relief to the open water Olympic courses.

Helm of the Year final was sailed in Lasers of which Pete Moseley had managed to scrape together four club boats including his own. The four races turned out to be an endurance test ending in a sudden death one lap run-off between Ron Greygoose and Pete Moseley who tied for first place. In the end the overall result hung on the crucial decision of when to tack for *A* Buoy on a fast ebb tide.

Putting the club into mothballs at the end of the racing season we reviewed the use made of the club boats and whilst "Idle ViceTM had been used extensively and "Brazil" occasionally, no use had been made of the Cadet or the Graduate. It was decided therefore to dispose of these last two and consider acquiring a training
sailboard.
/continued.

NOVEMBER

With dinghy racing at Stansgate over for another year and setting out to give a polished performance at the Laying—Up Supper I noticed that whilst Cruising Prizes are listed in the Year Book none have been awarded since 1975 and few members could recall what they were for. John Witter was able to turn up his note from September, 1965 Navigans which clearly identified them as intended for a members first cruise and not as some had thought a sort of runners-up prize in the Mamgu stakese One obvious contender, which should have been recognized last year, was Ann Bates! log for their first cruise up the East Coast. I was pleased to be able to rectify this omission on Ann's birthday at the Laying—Up Supper.

Whilst keeping Ann's prize a surprise I did suggest to our Rear Commodore that since half our members owned cruisers, and the Laying—Up Supper was supported more or less equally by the Dinghy and Cruiser Fleets, we should give more awards for Cruising. Murray Bates was in the middle of finishing off some 65 hand made trophies at the time and I was perhaps lucky not to have ended up in the hot water bath with the screen prints. Nevertheless it is worth thinking about for next years; we may even see the Sea Wife's Prize back again. Despite its title and camnatations of creature comforts I understand it has more to do with climbing ew masts and remaking halliards in the teeth of a North Sea gale.

The 6 trophies, 28 prizes and 8 spoons not collected at the Laying—Up Supper will be presented at a date to be arranged, but most likely the New Year Working Party at Stansgate!

SAILING FUTURE

Looking back over the year reminds us of all the things we intended to do and of lessons learnt.

A further 16% reduction took place this year in dinghy points racing on top of last years 36% reduction. Whilst the average entry for Wednesday evening races remains around 15 the Points Series are only attracting an average of 10 boats per race compared with over 14 last year. It is interesting to compare this with attendance at Committee Meetings = the Main Committee meeting alone averages 16 and the Sailing Sub-Committee has on average more people sitting round a table talking about sailing than we see on the water the following weekend.

yy
Certain changes have already been instituted for next years sailing programme with the main objective of encouraging activity on the water. For 1985 the Summer Points series will be abandoned and Spring Points extended to the end of June. In July and August many Sundays will be occupied by traditional races but where there is a gap a half—handicap pursuit race will be run in the morning, along the lines of the popular Wednesday evening races, and in the afternoon there will be Handicap Races split into one, two or three handicap classes depending on the days weather conditions and numbers of entries.

The Summer Points Club Trophies will be re-designated as the Clubs premier trophies for each dinghy class and will be awarded on the total racing programme of Spring Points plus Autumn Points plus any other relevant closed races.

REFLECTIONS

It was 1981 when Murray Bates took on the Sailing Secretaries job after making me promise to help with some of the donkey work. I have enjoyed our four years together looking after the Clubs sailing activities, but will always remember our half-term doubts when we sat down together and wondered what if anything we were achieving I think the moment of gloom had been brought on by yet another hole in the Regatta marquee.

I pulled Murray out of this abyss by pointing to some of the things that seemed
/continuede

Yu

to be going right. Starting gently on a non-controversial issue he had to agree that we were getting the Year Book to press a little earlier each year and in sight of getting it printed in time for issuing with membership renewals. The Autumn. Points series was introduced successfully in 1982 and Wednesday evening sailors have welcomed the new pursuit race formula.

Perhaps the most significant and long lasting improvement in the last few years has come from an increasing reliance on Fleet Captains to find the resources to cover major activities. What we are finding now is that fleets have accepted an on-going commitment to specific activities making the organisation from one year to the next so much easier,

However, a group activity such as that provided by the fleets is not always appropriate to a specialist task. The sailing activity is equally dependant on the individuals who turn up quietly at the appropriate time and get on with what they have made their own job. Few of these individuals are on the Committee, or any sub-committee for that matter, so I should like to end by paying tribute to their help and by encouraging all club members to look around for some task, however small, that they can make their own.

Malcolm Stuart

420 FLEET NEWS

This will probably be my last piece for Navigans, as Anna end I will soon be moving away from the Essex area. Perhaps this is just as well, as it looks as if the hall-
owed pages are to be desecrated - I mean decimated = in order to save a few pounds.
In many ways this is a shame because a lot of people get a great deal of pleasure from the present format, although it is also true that a great many people don't even read it! However, I digress (something that won't be allowed in future?)

The 420 annual Fleet Meeting took place at my home on 5th December 1984, First item
on the agenda was to elect a new Fleet Captain. Unfortunately, the person singled out to be cajoled into the position must have got wind of it and cried off coming to the meeting at the last moment. However, undeterred, we elected him anyway and so the new Fleet Captain is Alan Woods. Alan's main worry about taking on the job was that he will not be around for a few months of 1985 and so it was agreed that Len Graves would join with Alan t© give the Fleet the considerable benefits of Joint Fleet Captaincy.

A lively discussion then ensued on how to arrange the duties. It was felt that the best way was to send each fleet member a list of duties required and ask them to take on as many as necessary. This would minimise the amount of swapping required and therefore make the turn-out for duties more reliable. There was majority supp- ort for the new format of the Wednesday evening series. A weekend cruise was svgg= ested and it was agreed that some sort of cruising activity would be arranged for 1985. The possibilities of persuading cruisers to participate as support (e.g.
to
carry gear and provide a measure of safety) would be investigated.

It was felt that a boat tuning/ race training day or days would be of use. The Dave Hall sessions were very successful but it was felt that it would be imposing on Dave's good will to ask him back for a 3rd year. Perhaps something could be org~ anised in conjunction with Maldon S.C. or maybe a "self-help" practice day could be
organised.

It was agreed to advertise the willingness of fleet members to take out any other Club members, on request, in order to encourage new members and those thinking of changing class to for the 420. This offer to be repeated on a regular basis throughout the sailing season.

There was criticism of the new rescue boat procedure. Not so much because it was a nuisance to launch and recover but more because it so often caused delays to the start of racing. Also, it does not seem to have helped the engine. It presumably has solved the problem of the double skin filling with water.

The Laying-Up Supper was very poorly attended this year - this presumably means
that the present format is unpopular with the majority of Club members. The Fleet thought it woule be a good idea to hold the prize-giving at a more popular event, say the January Barn Dance. Most people would welcome a break of about 30 minutes at half-time and the prize-giving would fit nicely in here.

Well, that sums up the 420 4.G.M. It only remains for me to thank the members of the Fleet for their support during my 2 year stint. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank all the Club members who have helped make our time with such fun. Most of all, I would like to thank whoever it was who had the foresisht to persuade M.A.S.C. to buy the Stansgate site. Teo my mind, it is the best site on the River Blackwater.and with the facilities it offers, makes M.S.C. one of the best clubs in the country.

Look us up if you are in Devon - our collection of sailing toys will be at your
disposal,

Pete Chrystie

COMMODORE'S NOTES

It is with profound regret that I report the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Eric Payne.

On Monday 4th February several members, including Eric, had assembled ready for the February Main Committee Meeting; Eric was talking, then peacefully passed away. It was a dreadful shock to us all. The M.S.C. members send sincere condolences to Mrs Payne and her family.

The Committee Meeting was postponed to the following Monday (and has not yet been held at the time of writing).

Continuing my aim to keep members informed of activities, since my last Jan- uary issue report we have continued to make much progress in readiness for the sailing season:-

A.meeting was held at M.A.S.C. on Wednesday 23rd January during which Mr G, Wignall, M.A.S.C. Club Manager, and I discussed:-

1. The problem with the water supply at Stansgate —- M.A.S.C. have agreed
to replace the old pipework and aim to complete the task before Easter;

2. Our advertising campaign — to increase the size of membership, parti-
cularly dinghy sailing members;

3. The annual contribution paid by M.S.C. to M.A.S.C.

Following the above, an Executive Meeting was convened on 29th January during which a letter was drafted to once again highlight our objections, et cetera, to the excessive levy.

In parallel with all the above, we have been in contact with the Crown Estates Commission to seek approval to extend our Cruiser mooring towards Stone.

Another successful and well attended Working Party was held on Sunday 3rd February = this has been a great encouragement to all the Executive Committee members. Several potential new members were invited to view our facilities
and meet Committee members - it is thought that possibly nine families will
join.

Progress was made on the Cruiser Park “Electrification Scheme"; the hedging and ditching party have broken the back of their task. The windows of the "blockhouseTM have been completed, the floor concreted and the roof repaired - there is only the door to be made and fitted to complete the project.

Albert Pearce and his team have positioned the three R.S.J.'s in the new garage, which has to be fitted with an up-and-over door to complete the task. If any member knows of a secondhand metal door, size 7' x 6'6", please inform Murray Bates.

Claude Emmerson has been busy painting the partitions in the Gentlemen's Changing Room and Dick Papworth has progressed the painting of the walls. Dick has also organised the replacement of the broken washbasin in the Ladies' Changing Room and is resolving the problem with the Galley sink plumbing. Our aim is to complete all the jobs before Easter. We can then, hopefully, enjoy the sailing.

Mary Greygoose and Jill Papworth have had a "purge" on all the lounge chairs
- now almost like new! Dick is now looking for a volunteer to paint the
legs of all the tables and chairs.

Soup and rolls were provided thanks to Sheila Wade and Ann Bates.

A suggestion was made that photographs of all Committee Members be displayed on the notice-board, similar to that at M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane. This has been agreed and will be organised by Steve Evans. Maybe it will help the members find the 0.0.D.

Arrangements have been completed for the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee (B.J.R.C.) Race Management Seminar to be hosted by M.S.C. and held at M.A.S.C.
on Saturday 23rd February, from 9.45 a.m. approximately to 4.00 p.m. The pro-
gramme will be presented by two members of the R.Y.A. Race Management Commi- ttee and will cover both club racing and open meeting management. The total cost, including coffee and ploughman's lunch, is £5.00. This event, hope- fully, will be attended by all sailing clubs in the South-East and should provide good publicity for both M.S.C. and M.A.S.C.

The M.S.C. Executive Committee have accepted an invitation to meet members of the Lifeboat Institution on Sunday 24th February. This meeting is to discuss lifeboat coverage on the Blackwater; all Blackwater sailing clubs are invited.

David Harper

SAFETY ON THE WATER

Just a few notes
to remind any who may need it that our sport is not without hazard, particularly at this time of year when even on a warm, sunny day the water remains very cold.

I would offer the following points for your consideration:

Dinghy sailors at this time ofyear must wear wet suits or equivalent;

Check every part of your boat thoroughly before the start of the season and replace any gear which is suspect;

- Discipline yourself to re-check your boat with care from stem to stem
each time before you use it;

- Dinghy owners must pay particular attention to buoyancy, both personal
and boat. Check it carefully yourself and get a qualified measurer to certify the boat, even if you do not intend to compete in Open Meetings;

- Do not assume rescue facilities will be on hand to help you. They are
usually somewhere else, so your salvation must always be in your own hands;

- If inexperienced, or unfamiliar with our sailing environment, please ask
advice from the 0.0.D., Fleet Captain or other experienced helms;

= One of the most sinister aspects of hyperthermia is that rational thought becomes impossible. If you reach that stage, you are really in trouble;
so, if you feel cold and tired - get ashore. There's always another day.

Take care and have a great 1985 sailing season.

John Salmon

SAILING — SPRING 1985 (SO FAR)

The season started this year with the Easter Series. The weather on the
Sunday, rain and a Force 5 Southerly, was braved by 2 Solos and an Enter-
prise who were unable to race due to the lack of rescue facilities.
Undeterred, the three boats went for a “thrash" anyway, resulting in Roger Smith looking as though he had been five rounds with Frank Bruno! Monday's weather showed little improvement with the wind even fresher than the pre- ceding day. Two Solos, a Hornet (briefly) and a Dart entered the morning race but Ron Greygoose in his Solo proved to be the only survivor. Three Solos entered the afternoon race which was sailed in a wind of increased strength, resulting in a total "wipe-out" with no finishers.

Spring Points 1 and 2 were cancelled due to bad weather.

Enterprise, Solo and Handicap fleets sailed Spring Points 3 and 4 on a day which started with light airs, gradually increasing to a nice sailing breeze by the end of the day.

The Solo "lads" were the only sailors to raise a fleet for races 5 and 6, but were joined by a Laser and a Fireball who went along for the ride. These races were Sailed once again in strong winds and Malcolm Stuart was seen plodding round sporting his specially modified reefing mainsail, which en- abled him to survive where others didn't.

Solos were the dominant species sailing races 7 and 8 and were kept company once again by Enterprise and Handicap fleets. The afternoon race called heavily on the Rescue service with capsized boats spread out gybe marks, Steve Evans in particular causing confusion by hiding one of these marks with the upturned hull of his Enterprise.

Speaking from personal experience, the water is gradually warming up now and this should encourage more of you to join in the thrills and spills and beauty of sailing at Stansgate.

See you there.

Derek Webb
Sailing Secretary

With the advent of more sailboards at the Club and recent problems encount-— ered rescuing people from other clubs, the Main Committee would like to ask all sailboarders to operate their own safety code.

The Club does supply rescue facilities in the form of the "Mariner" but this is usually tied up with the dinghy racing programme. Since it is not obvious to the Rescue Boat when a boardsailor might be in trouble and since their priority is to check on capsized dinghies (more conspicuous), it is important that board sailors are aware of their own limitations in the range of tide and wind conditions.

So, please, if you are a beginner, stay near the Clubhouse and keep up-tide with respect to the Clubhouse. If you are an expert (or an aspiring one), ask yourself whether you are not too tired to get back unaided.

RESCUE SERVICE

The strong winds encountered during the Spring Points Series and the capsizes occurring as a result have made it apparent that some members are unclear in their understanding of the role of the rescue service provided by the Club.

The rescue service is primarily intended to ensure, as far as possible, that the sailors taking part in organised racing at the Club are prevented from being exposed to any unnecessary personal danger when they are in difficulties.

The emphasis is on the safety of the human - the dinghy is of a secondary con-
sideration. It must be made clear that, on windy days, when there may be more than one dinghy capsized at any one time, the rescue boat cannot be expected to tow dinghies back to the hard. This time-consuming process will prevent it from ensuring the safety of other sailors. On these occasions, the rescue boat will check whether the crew of a capsized boat is in trouble; if it is, the sailors will be advised to leave the dinghy which will be anchored, if possible, by the rescue boat crew. If the dinghy crew is not in difficulty, or if the sailors refuse to leave the boat, the rescue boat will leave to attend to the other capsized dinghies, returning to check on the original boat if it is obvious that it is still in trouble. Abandoned dinghies can be attended to once any danger to personnel has passed. Members of the Sailing Sub-Committee are to be trained in the use of the workboat in order to expedite recovery of abandoned dinghies.

Two important points should be remembered; these are that the final respons- ability for safety always lies with the dinghy crew (who ignore the advice of the rescue boat coxswain at their peril) and, secondly, that dinghies are in- sured and therefore the decision to abandon can be made more comfortably with this fact in mind.

Finally, just a commonsense note to new 0.0.D.s = ensure that the radios are switched on and that two-way transmissions are carried out between the rescue boat and theClubhouse and between the rescue boat and the racebox prior to racing, when the rescue boat is on the water.

I hope these notes will serve to clarify any misunderstandings of the role of the rescue service.

Derek Webb
Sailing Secretary

The end of the hockey season and the start of the sailing season always clash, but with the bad winter weather we were playing league games on Sundays, so apart from the Working Party I didn't get to the Club until mid-April, when a useful Force 5 over tide got me back into the swing of things.

We've got a full rota of drivers worked out and apologies from Keith for missing out on that first Sunday. Since then the drivers have had their work cut out.

The Sunday of the Regatta proved interesting. Whilst our boats were strugg- ling in a Force 2, we were picking up an "all ships" request from Burnham for assistance. Five minutes later, the Bradwell Coastguard warned us of an in- pending line squall and then it hit us. For the next 15 minutes the river looked like the aftermath of the Battle of Trafalgar and the rescue crews,
grateful for some action, soon got to work clearing up the debris - don't
Moth masts bend easily!

My thanks to all who helped, especially the crews of "Venidia", "Suppose", "Freya" and "Rubicon" who acted as Mother Ships; Ken Hughes, who organised the replacement keel strip on the Mariner and John Pettit, who provided his usual barrage of radio equipment and supported me on Control.

Finally, this is my sixth year as Coxswain and I have suggested to the Sail- ing Sub-Committee that it would be better for the Club if a fitter person took over next year — or, as Roger would say, we can then take the wheelchair out of the Mariner!

I like to feel that during the last few years we have put the rescue and support service on a more professional footing and I hope this long notice will enable you to decide on a successor.

In the meantime, there is plehty of sailing to come and I and my drivers look forward to being of assistance.

Moorings: The question has arisen as to the liability of a mooring owner who allows another member of the Club to use his mooring. It would seem well-established practice that a member of a club using another member's mooring accepts all risks of accident howsoever arising. Even where moorings are hired out on a commercial basis, it is normally on the understanding that the boatyard disclaims all liability. The only advice I can give, therefore, is to use your own mooring. If you have to use another member's mooring, remember that if anything happens you are likely to be liable.

Sorry for the moans, but I'm only passing it on.

John Wade

DINGHY CRUISING NEWS

Initially, I didn't think that dinghy cruising would stimulate too much interest, but recent events have shown just how wrong I was. Several people have already contacted me expressing interest and even greater enthusiasm was shown at the New Members' Evening. This article will, I hope, be the first of many to tell you what is happening, when and where.

The objective of dinghy cruising is "to promote and encourage all forms of (safe and enjoyable) cruising in dinghies and similar small craft". (Dinghy Cruising Association words, not mine).

The activities currently envisaged are:-

Flotilla sailing in the Estuary;

- Creek crawling;

- Picnicking trips to such places as East Mersea or Sales Point;

- Barbecues;

- Aquateering;

- Camping cruises to "distant" sites, such as Brightlingsea.

Because such events would only be organised in a loose sense, safety is of paramount importance. We probably would not, for example, be able to count on the rescue boat being available, therefore a guard boat will be essential. To ensure that suitable safety standards are not only formulated but under- stood as well, a "package" of cruising safety notes is being compiled and will be available shortly.

If anyone is interested in dinghy cruising, please let me have your names, addresses and details of your boat.

ROCHESTER VISIT

The annual visit by the GEC Avionics (Rochester) sailors to the M.S.C. on the Blackwater took place on Saturday/Sunday 8th/9th June 1985.

The dinghy team was sailing for the Colwyn Stone Challenge Trophy. The Roch- ester team was Richard and Sharon Stone (Wayfarer), Maurice and Pam Chapman

pee Meg and Pat Fitzgerald (condor) and Gordon Belcher (Laser).
Enterprise), Mark Chapman (Topper), Alastair Macfadyen and Alick Jamieson

The wind was North West, Force 2 with occasional lulis and patches of Force 3. The course consisted of beats with the tide and very broad reaches and runs against the tide; conditions which favoured the Wayfarer and the Fireball. Richard Stone and Alastair Macfadyen took full advantage to chase the Condor round the course; Richard won and Alastair scored well on handicap. Gordon Belcher in the Laser benefitted from the gusts to stay close and was well placed on handicap.

The Enterprises suffered through lack of sail area when running against the tide and could not match their handicap. Maurice Chapman sailed fast down

continued

a

wind to split the M.S.C. Enterprises and Mark sailed the Topper well to take third place. Down wind, the Catamarans had to zig zag in a series of broad reaches but could not match handicap; however, the Fitzgeralds managed to pressurize the faster Dart into rounding a buoy in the wrong direction, which led to the Dart retiring. Overall, Rochester scored well, to go into lunch with a healthy lead.

After lunch the story changed. M.S.C. decided enough was enough and, with good Sailing by the Solos and Mirror, they attacked the Rochester lead. With a Similar course, the Catamarans, Fireball and Wayfarer led at the windward mark and , in a dying wind, bore away against the tide. In the lee of Osea Island progress for the later boats was slow.

On the second lap, the wind increased and backed, to give some planing on the broad reach. This allowed the planing boats to make up some of their handicap but not enough to prevent Richard Stone from winning the race and the trophy. Alastair Macfadyen was equal second with Mike Boreham, the Mirror's spinnaker keeping it in contention.

Ron Greygoose and Roger Smith had a private battle in their Solos, which spurred both of them to be well placed. Gordon Belcher was in sixth place, whilst the Enterprises suffered by not having sufficient sail power to plane on the last reach. The Catamaran duel was won by the Fitzgeralds'Condor, which kept out the Dart. Mark Chapman had good boat speed, but missed a buoy and had to return, thus losing any chance of a good place.

M.S.C. won the second race, but Rochester won the individual and the overall team race and so maintained their 100% record in the Colwyn Stone Trophy races.

Four Rochester cruisers made the trip, to arrive midday, and were well estab- lashed in the bar by the time the dinghy races were complete.

Joan Stone presented the trophy to Richard to round off another enjoyable day's Sailing. Once again, the visit had proved very successful with good sailing, good company and good food.

Gordon Belcher
GEC Avionics
(Rochester)

There is a mixture of good and bad news, so I will deal with the good first.

The Sailing Side of Cadet Week
—

Weather-wise Cadet Week gave us a bit of everything this year. Tents were pitched and put away in the rain and in between we had windy days, calm days, sunburn days and cold days.

The main object of the week was cadet training under the leadership and guidance of Derek Hall. The week started with ‘dry' capsize drill and instruction on rigging and reefing the cadets' dinghies (mainly Mirrors). A windy Monday afternoon added:
realism to the cadets' capsize practice, carried out off the hard using 'Idle Vice’. Thanks go to the stalwarts who spent all Monday afternoon in the water holding "Idle Vice' for the youngsters in increasingly uncomfortable conditions,

Tuesday was a fine hot day. The cadets were given some basic sailing instruction on
land, (the sea wall makes a good lecture theatre) and then spent the morning reaching to and fro across the river. Later in the morning they sailed’ off up-river escorted by the work boat, Unfortunately the wind then died away completely and a tow home was needed. Shades of Dunkirk, ten or so dinghies returning to the hard being towed by the workboat and Murray Bates' 'Candy'. The calm afternoon enabled the cadets to have some rowing practice and a swim,

The wind returned on Wednesday and with it more instruction and sailing for the cadets which was continued on Thursday morning, By now the cadets were handling their reefed dinghies confidently in the increasing winds (well, most of you were!). The wind had increased sufficiently by Thursday lunch time for the proposed sail round Osea to be abandoned in favour of a frontal assault on the island, straight across the river under jibs only. All the cadets arrived safely, although one young lady did forget to jump into her dinghy after pushing off from the hard. However she was promptly retreived from the drink and popped back into her boat to continue the voyage with the others, (I bet 'mum' still doesn't know who she was and I'm not telling). The cadets were escorted by the Mariner, workboat, fisherman, and George Robinson's Freyag A fair number of Mums, Dads, friends etc. thumbed lifts in the safety boats, and there was a good gathering on Osea beach for the afternoon. (To tell the truth we spent most of the time sheltering from the cold winds behind a big clump of gorse bushes), The trip back to Stansgate was brisk and bumpy but all boats made it in good order with plenty of opportunity to apply the knowledge gained during the week.

Friday morning was devoted to heaving-to and man-overboard drill. A fair degree of
competence was displayed although a lot of the men-overboard, (half-filled plastic bottles) were retrieved whilst sailing by at full tilt! Not quite what Derek had in mind I suspect.

The final treat(!) was a sail down to Thirslet, round the beacon and land on the spit for lunch, All the cadets plus a few others followed the workboat down to Thirslet in a brisk, cold wind, with the fisherman bringing up the rear, The Mariner popped back to the Club to collect Derek who had the morning off to scrub his boat and to collect a few packed lunches that had been left behind, I don't suppose I will ever know who decided on Thirslét as the lunch-time venue (someone in the Camping Club Boating Group I think!) but lacking the friendly gorse bushes of Osea we all stood around like penguins trying to keep warm until it was time to sail back. (It was fun though, kids, wasn't it?)
The trip back to Stansgate was a long beat along the edge of Thirslet spit and one or two helmsmen learnt another lesson, (What is lee-way, David?). The last activity of the afternoon was cleaning and putting away of boats, Derek's final duty took place on Friday evening when he presented each cadet with a small prize and they in turn presented him with a bottle of his favourite tipple.

In concluding this account it must be said that the very real and noticeable progress made by the cadets during the week reflects great credit on Derek Hall for his skill and patience as instructor and on the youngsters for sticking with it even when wet

SOLO NEWS

Solo Worlds, Pevensey Bay — see Bob Anderson's graphic account of this event - my hands are still shaking.

The beaching technique at Pevensey is designed to avoid making your trolley wet. As you near the beach they shout, "Sail it in hard!" Unfortunately, that is just the moment that the beach wind shadow takes the wind out of your
sails; nevertheless, you sail in and a number of people in the water grab your boat and run up the beach, having pushed the helmsman over the transom. They leave it on ygur trolley and all you have to do is get it up a soft Shingle bank at 45°. If you are Dutch your boat is borne, shoulder high, directly into the dinghy park accompanied by chants in strange tongues.

The event was won by Ken Falcon; Dick Batt was runner up in a borrowed boat; Geoff Carveth third, also in a borrowed boat. Skipper's Cup and Vet's Trophy were won by Tony Catchpole of Hayling Island. My position? See Solo Class Newsletter or next year's Year Book (that means it's no good).

Jack Holt had the new fibreglass sandwich boat there which he has just built using the Omega mould. It feels very stiff and he will announce price et cetera in about a month's time.

It was a shame not to have another Marconi boat there, but it was great to have the support of the Andersons = thank you, Bob and Elsie. Actually, Bob has picked up some useful tips in the dinghy park and should be considered honorary M.S.C. (Marconi Solo Consultant).

The dressing romms at Pevensey revealed some strange Sights; one chap stuffed football shin pads under the front of his wet suit; another pushed vast quan— tities of foam down the back to prolong the agony, so to speak. Some of the Dutchmen even had little strap on attachments to protect their thighs! It made them look like cowboys going for a shoot-out in the 0.K. (wash my mouth out) Corral!

We had a second barbecue on August 26th; again, the weather could have been better, but it could have been worse.

Congratulations to Cathy and Dave Nixson on the birth of Daniel on 5th August.

Stuart Pullen went down to the Chichester Harbour Federation week sailed from Hayling Island and acquitted himself well in quite windy weather.

Don't forget the Halfway Open on 14th/15th September; our Open on 21ist/22nd
September and Fishers Green on 6th October. Also, we are organising the Hornet Junior Nationals on 28th/29th September — please turn up and help.

Roger Smith

1985 SOLO WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS

PEVENSEY BAY, SUSSEX

It was during the week 26th July to 2nd August that Pevensey Bay S.C. were hosting the Solo World Championships and Elsie and I decided that we would Fede) to “sunny" Sussex to join in the delights of the week (as spectators, of
course).

ow: si

I am now glad to say that I was not competing: winds between Force 4 and
Force 7, with more than the occasional gust of 8 plus, set the conditions for most of the week. Not ideal for the faint—hearted.

Following Monday's race the dinghy park was littered with broken and bent masts, with numerous collections of other gear failures. And so it went on for race after race.

One competitor, who had to purchase a new mast, said he'd never been more terrified in his life. While on the run riding a 12 foot wave, he heard a roaring sound behind him and looked back, only to observe an even bigger wave
fast approaching. He said that he had been “pitchpoled" many times, but had never hit the water burgee first before. Listening to the conversations at the bar after the races, many similar tales were being told.

Roger will tell you how he was fifth round the windward mark and how we are
now clued up on how to race tune a Solo rig (small consultancy fees to the
Barbecue).

As a novice to Solos myself, I felt nothing but admiration as each day the competitors made for the start line in seas which, at times, only revealed the tops of the sails to those watching from the shore. I believe it was a total surprise to the organisers that Soloists were prepared to sail and survive in such conditions. The beachuastersaid that he was amazed at the high standard of seamanship demonstrated by those he described as "pond
Sailors".

I am sure that full details and race reports have already been seen in the yachting press; this is just a note of a few of the observations that I made during the week to give me the confidence to cope with the occasional
2-3.

Who knows? Next year

Bob Anderson

COMMODORE'S REPORT

Since writing my September report, we have at long last received a reply from M.A.S.C. regarding the M.S.C. contribution. As M.A.S.C. had to spend approx= imately £1,600. to improve our water heating system, they have instructed us to pay a contribution for the current year of £4,500. For next season, they are asking £5,000.

Immediately upon receipt of the M.A.S.C. letter confirming the above, an Executive Committee meeting was held in order to re-examine our financial position, review our capital budget based on a five year plan and consider Committee proposals for the A.G.M. All these items will be debated at the October Main Committee Meeting, which has not been held at the time of writing.

We are now attempting to work more closely with M.A.S.C. one landlord/tenant basis, as per their instructions. In light of this new relationship, we have replied to M.A.S.C. and tabled our capital budget requirements, which include the following significant items:

1. Sewerage disposal.

2. Road resurfacing.

3. Site security.

4. Hard -— much concern in view of recent accelerated deterioration.

5e Rescue Boat - the engine is a write-off and we are.currently examining
our rescue operation.

6. Tractor - it is envisaged that a replacement will be required in the next
few years. |

We have requested that M.A.S.C. provides the funding for items 1 to 4; in connection with items 5 and 6 we have requested an interest free loan, repay- able over a five year period.

Much thought has also been given to the future of the Club and in particular to the future lines of succession for Flag Officers and other demanding roles on the Main Committee. Our proposal is to change the rules in the M.S.C. constitution so that Associate Members will be able to hold such posts. Our proposals will be debated at the October Main Committee Meeting and, if agreed, will be tabled at the A.G.M. on Sunday 3rd November at 2.00 p.m. at Stansgate. The Executive Committee feel that we cannot continue as a dynamic sailing club without the active participation of our Associate Members in Club management.

Tickets for the Laying-Up Supper are selling very well. Please make sure you have booked your tickets if you wish to attend. Remember that there are limit- ed numbers this year.

Mr Charlie Stock has accepted our invitation to be principal guest this year and I feel sure that his short presentation will be most interesting and infor-
mative.

Pat and I look forward to seeing you all at the Club, the Working Party on
Sunday 27th October, the A.G.M. on Sunday 3rd November and at the Laying-Up
Supper on Saturday 16th November.

David Harper

Club, please contact me, lan Savage, or Alan Polley on the telephone numbers below, aS we are your representatives on the Sailing Sub-Committee.

As you may be aware, we now have a Club board, a vinta solo, which is available for use by any member. It is kept in one of the front garages and can be used when there is a Duty Officer in attendance at the Club, the key to the garage being obtainable from him. Please exhibit caution in its use. If you are a beginner, do not use it in strong winds, offshore breezes or strong tidal con- ditions. Also, let somebody know you are going out. If starting for the first time, it is advisable to attach a long line to the towing hook and have a friend on Shore holding the other end, and please always weer a buoyancy aid.

If anybody needs guidance on how to sailboard, any of the regulars or myself would, I'm sure, be able to offer assistance, but please bear in mind that the Club is not the safest place for beginners and a course on an inland lake to start with would be advisable.

If you do use the Club board, please hose it down with fresh water after use
and store back in the garage, but do not roll up the sail when wet - either
wait till it's dry or leave it draped over the board.

With increased numbers of sailboarders using the Club, I have had a couple of reports of accidents involving boards and boats in collision and of a swimmer being hit by a mast, so please could we all exhibit care, especially when launching and retrieving on beach areas, and please keep away from the hard area and sailing marks when racing is in progress. Also, be aware of the rules of rights of way, since we do not want to find restrictions being placed on our movements.

Finally, if anybody would be interested in some open races or a fun day - nothing too serious — let me know.

Ian Savage

SEA CADET BOATWORK COURSE — JULY 21ST TO 27TH

Fifty Sea Cadets from Essex units as far afield as Walton, Southend, Colchester, Harlow and Tilbury enjoyed the facilities of the Club for their annual Boatwork Course this year.

continued «<2

as Ot

They arrived, towing a motley collection of trailers heavily weighed down with their 165 ft. ASC dinghies, which in turn had tents, Mirrors, cooking gear et cetera packed within, and were soon encamped in rows in the camping
field.

For many, their regular sailing areas had been ponds, lakes or reservoirs, so, for some, the Blackwater must have seemed like a veritable ocean!

Sunday was spent mainly setting up camp and rigging boats, but a short sail
in the evening in a good breeze soon broke the ice. Monday, however, was quite a different kettle of fish, with Force 5 winds, gusting 7 at times. It soon became clear that, however deeply reefed the boats were, any further Sailing that day was out of the ouestion.
During the afternoon a GP14 cap-
Sized with three cadets aboard and in a heavy swell in the narrows just off Osea very soon turned turtle. The rescue dory at the time was having its plug "dewhiskered" (or whatever it is that "pugs" outboards at the most inopportune moments) and to our amazement a lone Mirror sailor (Peter Skeeting, we think) who was with the Camping and Boating Club plucked off the three lads who were by then decidedly frightened, and deposited them safely ashore! No mean feat and one for which we were extremely grateful.

Monday night was even more exciting .... the wind had not abated and at one
stage we had some twenty or so people parascending with the mess tent!

By Tuesday forenoon four cadets sadly decided that enough was enough and left for home, whereupon Sod's Law prevailed and the weather began to improve; the rest of the week provided first class conditions for sail training.

In terms of results obtained by way of R.Y.A.
Certificates, the Course was
an undoubted success - but probably of equal value was the experience of
operating from a sailing club where folk operate by cooperation and mutual assistance rather than by a more rigid discipline. Since many of these young men, having been bitten by the "sailing bug", will probably have their ow boats in later life, this will have been a useful introduction to club life.

Saturday afternoon saw groups of somewhat weatherbeaten boys stuffing their
dirty gear into their kit bags to take home to Mum, and striking camp, but it was unanimously agreed that all would come again next year, given the
opportunity - please!

Mike Smith

SAIL A MIRROR FOR A NEW EXPERIENCE

OR

MIRROR MANIA AND MIRROR MANIACS

Just like British Rail, we (the Mirror Fleet) are getting there, so, look out, "premier fleet"
- our fleet is catching you up! We haven't made double
figures yet, but next season could be the one for us if the Autumn Points Series is anything to go by. At the time of writing, the fleet has sailed 7 out of 10 races scheduled(the other 3 were abandoned) and the last three races have seen 6, 7 and 8 Mirrors participating. After several years of Boreham clan domination (in numbers, that is = not results!), a race can now be held without us. In fact, we can now stand on the sea wall as on- lookers and enjoy the spectacle.

I was such an onlooker on Sunday 6th October, when 8 Mirrors signed on for the morning race, with winds gusting up to Force 5. Neil Salmon, crewed by Clare Savill, had a great start and shamed the rest by flying their spinn— aker over the start line (it was a reaching start). Unfortunately, it flew too well and they capsized just @ few yards start. over the
Damian Boreham,
crewed by Peter Brown, also had a good start; in fact, so good that they thought they were the culprits who were “over the line" and had to thread a somewhat precarious return journey through the fleet to start again. Pity really; the real culprit was another Mirror who appeared to be checking the lights on "F" mark when the starting gun went off. Never mind, Damian and Pete -— put it all down to experience.

The fleet sailed down in close company to Breezy where a gybe was required, Dennis Dear rounded first, crewed by young John Dear, and was followed by Peter Collis who promptly capsized. Mike Boreham touched Peter and had to waste time doing his "720" and a certain amount of chaos threatened as Jack & Diane Rusbridge, Mike & ‘Janet Battle and Damian & Pete all managed to avoid both Peter and Mike and set off in hot pursuit of Dennis towards Goldhanger,. Dennis, now thoroughly hooked on Mirror Mania (yes, the “premier boat" has been left to sulk under its cover in the boat paxik), led all the way over to Goldhanger on a broad reach. At Goldhanger, Phil Gray and Kate Nicholson decided to set the
fleet a poser by capsizing just before the mark and drift-— ing into the path of the onrushing stream of Mirror Maniacs. This time, chaos not only threatened but actually occurred and out of the melee emerged my dearly beloved husband, Mike, crewed by Lucy Boreham, scarcely able to believe his luck at going from 5th to 1st in one fell swoop (of a Hornet)! Mike Battle was close behind (in "Battleship", would you believe) and these two remained in that position around "A" mark and into the second lap.

Eventually, by dint of much hard work and superior windward Sailirig, Mike Battle took the lead and led around "A" mark by a few yards, only to lose it again to Mike Boreham, who blew into his sails a little bit harder and reach- ed the finish line just two feet ahead of the "Battleship". Jack & Diane Rusbridge sailed a good race to take 3rd place.

In the meantime,
other exciting things had been happening on the course. for a start, Chris & Stephen Thorne's gaff fell down, Peter Collis again capsized and Neil & Clare also lost their gaff. Finally, Damian & Pete cap- Sized and, all in all, the rescue boat had quite a lot of work to do. I think Mike Wellington (rescue crew) actually enjoyed his swimming as a rescuer more than his swimming as helm the day before, when he took part in the Helmsman of the Year Final. Peter Collis obviously righted himself because he came in

COMMODORE'S REPORT FOR A.G.M.

Since taking over as Commodore last year, I have at least achieved one personal objective; that was to improve communication by keeping the membership totally informed of all developments.

=. M.S.C. membership has been signif-
TANS icantly increased and I am sure you gh A YS will agree that we have re-intro- duced a better sense of belonging in the Club.

continued

mn Oa

I take this opportunity to thank the Executive and Main Committee members for their support and encouragement, and I also extend my thanks to the other Club members who have assisted us in achieving our objectives.

Every sailing club has problems; we are no different. My approach has always been to consider problems as opportunities and thereby reduce hard-
ships.

The following comments relate to significant Club events in chronological
order.

At the start of the season we were concerned about the decrease in interest in dinghy sailing and the increase in subscriptions to M.A.S.C. and M.S.C. necessary to balance our books. We soon realised that our solution to both Situations was to increase the size of our membership. Consequently, we mounted a recruitment drive and, in parallel, started negotiations with M.A.S.C. re our section levy.

I was also burdened with the task of chairing the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee and running a Race Management Seminar for them. I am indebted to Pat and Malcolm Stuart for their support in this direction. As it happened, we used the M.A.S.C. facilities for the seminar; 69 delegates attended and we gained much publicity for M.S.C.

The winter/early season working parties were very well attended; this gave us much incentive to work harder on behalf of the Club. The Cruiser Christ- mas Party on 15th December 1984 was most enjoyable and a New Members' Evening was introduced. Both events were well attended.

At the end of the pre-season working parties we had provided ourselves with another garage: converted the "blockhouse" under the race-—box into a large, secure storage area: organised five 13 amp. double power sockets in the Cruiser Park; and cleared most of the ditches and the sides of the road to the Club.

An early decision was to make more use of the site - hence the venue here
today. To reduce costs, we no longer have a front picture on "Navigans"; maybe we can debate this later under "Any Other Business". The Barn Dance on 26th January was another success. I must thank Sheila Wade for a most excellent term of office as Social Secretary.

Just before our Main Committee meeting on Monday 4th February a dear old friend, Eric Payne, died. Eric has been a great loss to the Club.

February brought problems with the water supply.
We also had further dis- cussions with M.A.S.C. about our levy.
Application was made to the Crown
Estates Commission for permission to extend our Cruiser moorings towards
Stone.

Early in the year Claude Emerson and Dick Papworth completed much painting inside the Clubhouse and we are generally quite pleased with the result. By early March most jobs had been completed and on Sunday 24th March we held our "Fitting-Out' working party. During the winter two of our members, Peter Sayer and Arthur Hodges, spent hundreds of hours refurbishing the tractor. A microwave oven was purchased and the installation co-ordinated by Dick Papworth.

Essex Police telephoned me about thefts on the Bleckwater. Action was taken to inform all members. The replacement of our magnetic card lock system is now high on the list of priorities for capital expenditure.

We exhibited at the National Dinghy Exhibition once again - my thanks to

continued ceecee

-3-

Derek Webb and Steve Evans for organising same. Several new Associate Men-— bers joined the Club as a result of this exercise. The Fitting-Out Party on Saturday 30th March was also another success.

The Regatta was excellent from the sailing point of view, although we would still have liked to have seen more Marconi dinghies participating. However, the event brought some problems. Just to mention a few:-

1. Sewerage;

2. Shortage of spotters;

3. Not sufficient hot water;

4. Snags with the toilets;

5e Aggravation from certain (albeit a small percentage) of visiting dinghy sailors and their spectators.

6. Problems with the telephone and electricity supply.

7. Lack of interest from Club members.

Just prior to the Regatta, h.A.S.C. (Gerry Wignall in particular) organised a re-plumbing exercise for our hot water system and to overcome problems due to low cold water pressure. Unfortunately, the wrong size boiler was instal- led, but this was soon corrected and has worked satisfactorily ever since. A safety audit just prior to the Regatta was about as untimely as one could ‘have wished.

At the last Committee Meeting we decided not to hold a Regatta next year, as there does not seem to be enough support to administer and control the event. Tomorrow evening we will hold the first meeting of the new Main Committee and the following week there will be a Sailing Sub-Committee meeting, during which we will decide upon an alternative to the Regatta.

There has been certain concern about safety on the water and much time has been spent debating the subject.

The annual visit by Rochester on Saturday and Sunday 8th and 9th June went quite well. Rochester won the individual and the overall team race. I am looking to Phil Gray, Peter Clayton and the Sailing Sub-Committee to redress this situation next year.

The Barbecue was not blessed with fine weather. However, four hundred tickets were sold, thereby creating a good profit and marking the start of Cadet Week. Fifty Sea Cadets and their instructors joined us for Cadet Week. I hope this visit will be repeated next season. Derek Hall did a remarkable job teaching and entertaining the M.S.C. cadets during the week. Whilst on the subject of our cadets, we have now decided to allocate Garage No. 3 for their use.

A new lawnmower has been purchased. I am sure that you are all pleased that the site now looks more inviting and well kept.

Now to the problems and opportunities:-

1. Towards the end of Cadet Week, the engine of our Rescue Boat seized and
is now beyond economical repair.
The quotation is in excess of £1,300.
We have contacted many other sailing clubs to talk about their choice of rescue boats and to seek their advice, et cetera. The concensus of opinion is that we should purchase 4 displacement type hull with inboard diesel, rather than a planing hull with outboard engine.

2. Sewage disposal. The worst problem we have, but I am pleaseé to report

continued

-4-

that Dick Papworth has taken this task on board and is making excellent progress. My concern is the cost, which could amount to many thousands of pounds.

3- We have agreed with M.A.S.C. that our contribution for this year will
be £4,500. and for next year £5,000.

We also have agreement with M.A.S.C. that they will finance the following
items:

1. Sewerage;

2. Road resurfacing;

3 Site security;

4. Repairs to the hard;

5 Replacement rescue boat.

Of course, we will endeavour to keep costs of all of the foregoing to a minimum and provide as much labour as possible. No doubt the N.A.S.C. Chairman, Mr Tony Mayhew, or Mr Wignall, the M.A.S.C. Club Manager, who are both here with us today, will comment later.

We have given much thought to the succession and future leadership of M.S.C. We need dedicated persons who will adopt a professional attitude and feel that we must now change our rules to allow and encourage Associate Members to hold senior posts. Of course, any agreement will have to be ratified by
M.A.S.C. Rules Committee.

I will now table objectives for next season, irrespective of the constitution of the Committee:-

1. Encourage more dinghies on to the water.

2. Increase even further the utilisation of the Stansgate facilities.

3- Organise fund raising events in order that we can keep subscriptions at an acceptable level.

4. Help Maureen Ball, who has done a most marvellous job looking after the
Galley, by finding some more volunteers to man the Galley each weekend. Maureen is resigning as soon as we have found a suitable replacement. Any offers of help will be very much appreciated.

On that note, I thank you all for your support and apologise for not being able to spend more time in your company here at Stansgate this year. Pat and I hope for a better year in 1986, with fewer family problems.

Lastly, my thanks to the wives of the Executive Members, who have been so understanding regarding the time we have spent on Club affairs, and a special thank you to Pat Black, our Secretary, and Neil Pembleton, our Treasurer, for keeping us on course.

David Harper

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT - 1985

There were several developments affecting sailing before the season started.

continued

Fw

One of these was the demise of the Hornet fleet, which suffered a sudden and
dramatic loss of boats at the end of last season.
Another, more positive event resulted from the decision to advertise the Club at the London Dinghy
Exhibition. The emphasis was placed on attracting more dinghy sailors
and
the venture proved to be successful in this end.

A new format for the year's sailing programme was planned. This consisted of extending the Spring and Autumn Points Series and extracting points from
the closed club races held during the summer to form a Summer Points
Series.

The weather during the spring and summer months was not conducive even to the
more experienced helmsmen to compete, let alone the novices, and as a result the turnouts for the Spring Foints Series were low, with the 420 fleet
not
managing to complete one race. The Solo fleet were an exception to this trend and maintained a steady attendance.

The number of entrants to the Regatta returned back to its usual level this year and a successful sailing programme was organised.

Strong winds during Cadet Week prevented the Cadet Series from being sailed and serious damage was incurred by the Rescue Boat engine at the end of the week. This disabled the nescue Boat for the rest of the season and prevented some of the Club's longer distance races from being sailed.

The new format for summer sailing enabled points series to be formed for all classes except Enterprises.

The Cruiser Cup was well supported by M.S.C. boats, which is a strong indi-
cation that the Barnacle Points Series could be reinstated in the future.

Wednesday evening racing was as’ popular as ever, the simple format being
enjoyed by both race organisers and competitors.

The autumn brought better weather, which encouraged many more sailors to participate in the racing, with the Solo and Mirror fleets in particular showing large increases in competitors. The growth of the Mirror fleet should be taken as an encouraging sign for the future, when a progression should be made up to a larger two man dinghy, thereby filling a gap which presently exists within the Club.

The organisation and effort laid on for the Hornet Junior Nationals was extensive and the Championships were run very smoothly, but the entry was disappointingly low.

The Solo and Dart Open Meetings were as well organised and the higher number of entrants made the events enjoyable for both competitors and
organisers,

Derek Webb

Treasurer's Report.

During 1985 the Club's finances have improved substantially over previous years. This is generally due to two factors. Firstly the substantial rise in subscription rates approved at the last A.G.M.; however if the membership had stayed at last year's level this would have only raised £16,000. As can be seen the rise in membership this year has raised a further £2,440 and is the second reason for the improvement. The actual membership figures are:-

1984 1985

Ordinary 202 209
Family 34 40
Associate 111 133
Honorary 2 10
Cadet 3 1
Student 5 3

TOTAL 307 396

This is a welcome and significant achievement as it allows the overhead costs of the Club to be spread amongst more people and hence hold down subscription rates.

In general the individual Accounts show the level of spend and income as predicted in the budget for the year. It is in the area of Capital expenditure that the effect of the increase of membership had the greatest effect. Here it was possible to use some of the extra income for improvements around the site and the facilities, although the road has not been resurfaced. The reason for postponing this will be seen when looking at next year's expenditure. As a consequence of this the Club has achieved a modest surplus
of £2000 to £2500 as opposed to the loss which was predicted at this time last
year.

Looking forward to 1986, there are a number of significant points. As was explained last year the expectation that 'Exceptional Items' of spend will ever end is false. Currently the Club is faced with funding a number of urgent capital projects. As you are aware the Rescue Boat engine has to be replaced before next season. In addition the actual hull will probably need replacement within the next 4-5 years. It has therefore been decided to examine a number of alternative combinations of engine and hull. While this may impose a greater requirement for funding at this moment, the longer term benefits should be a substantial reduction in running costs.

There is also an urgent need, indeed Maldon Council are insisting, to improve our sewage facilities; the Hard needs reconstruction; the road needs resurfacing; and security on the site needs improving. The estimate for these items is:-

It is not practical for the Club to raise these sums of money in one year nor would it be right to do so. However it is also essential to avoid the trap of running a permanent deficit account (as most Nations do). This however requires that the Club is able to Budget for a number of years into the future and that the Club can raise the funds to pay the bills on some form of loan basis. It is for these reasons that the Committe has approached the M.A.S.C. for a short term loan. However the initial response appears to be that while they will fund the work it will not be on a loan basis but on an increase in contribution, which as we all know is never reduced when the ‘loan' is repaid.

This raises the whole question of the basis on which the contribution is calculated. We as a Club have very little control over the level. The constitution of both Clubs does not permit us to run our own bank account; we have to use the M.A.S.C. as our bank. Therefore if we fail to agree on the contribution effectively the M.A.S.C. can simply withold the sum required in their opinion. During this year the Committee have been attempting to resolve two points with the M.A.S.C.. Firstly the current level of the contribution and secondly the basis for the future increase in its level. It is the second of these which is more important to allow future budgeting to be carried out
effectively.

Turning now to this year's proposals before the meeting and dealing first. with subscriptions. Last year I said that I hoped to hold the increase this year to the level of inflation. Due largely to the increase in membership the proposed increase has been held to an average of 6.2% approximately, which is in line with inflation during the year.

The second and separate proposal relates to the level of contribution to the M.A.S.C.. The Committee feel that a mandate from the Club is necessary to help in the negotiations with the M.A.S.C.. If passed the motion will stengthen our position and should it be necessary we will ask for your further support during the year on this matter.

Finally let us look at the longer term future of the Club financially. The Club now has a turnover of £30,000 per year which is the equivalent of some small businesses and therefore has to adopt a more business like approach to its financial dealings. It is not unreasonable to forsee a continuing Capital spend of 10-15% per year. It is also obvious that costs will continue to rise due to inflation. The increased income required can be generated by a number of methods. Firstly simple subscription increases; secondly by
