membership increase. This year we have been very successful in recruitment. It is considered that the Club can expand to 500 members with the present basic facilities and as can be seen from this year the improvement in financing would be dramatic.

The other area which must be pursued is reduction of costs. Again this year some savings have been achieved; most notably in the area of Navigans and the Year Book. However the biggest single cost in any project is labour. The wiring of the Cruiser Park this year would have been two or three times as much if it had been all done on a contract basis. However it is not only the one off project where labour costs are important. We all like to enjoy the facilities offered by the Bar and Galley on sailing weekends. To supply thes services requires labour. Yes they could be subcontracted to an outside organisation; however the profit on them would probably not even pay the outsider, let alone give the Club any return. There are approximately 30 sailing weekends per year and, if it is assummed that the Bar requires 2 people and the Galley requires 2 people, to man this 2 days ever weekend requires 240 people on a One Day basis. In other words with a membership of 400 people it only requires each of us to give up ONE days sailing every YEAR AND A HALF. This is an area of the Club which can generate a very substantial level of income and profit for the Club. I would ask you all to consider giving up just the one day to help keep the Clubs costs down to a minimum.

Neil Pembleton

ENTERPRISE FLEET NEWS

Well,as most of you will know by now, I shall not be sailing at the Club next year; Derek Webb and myself are moving to another club with an active racing fleet. It was a hard decision, as we have both been members of the Club and the fleet for about 8 years now. But, at the end of the day, we are both inter- ested in competitive Enterprise racing and, after this year's racing, or lack of it, we have decided upon a move.

Over the past 8 years we have tried hard to build up the fleet, but must con- clude that, although we have some 13 boats, most are content to potter.

In September of this year I sent out a questionaire to all fleet members, asking what sort of racing they wanted next year and whether anybody would take on the job of Fleet Captain. Apart from the “active three", I had two replies. Need I say more!

I have therefore reccomended to the Sailing Sub-Committee that fleet status is withdrawn next year and that the Enterprise Fleet sail as part of the Handicap Fleet. If in future anyone wants to take on the job of building up the fleet again, they should contact a Sailing Sub-Committee member.

I hope we shall see an knterprise “leet at the Club again. It's an excellent
boat, and the Club has had a fleet for many, many years - it would be a
shame if it disappeared forever.

Good sailing.

Steve Evans

Ed.'s note: Steve, we'll miss you, June and Derek. Good sailing at your new club.

MIRROR FLEET NEWS

The Mirror Fleet Meeting, which was held at my home on 11th November, was exceedingly well supported, especially by new members. All the items were discussed at length on a very informal basis, with all fleet members putting forward their own ideas and thoughts. For those fleet members who could not attend, you can still make your views heard if you would like to contact me (telephone [redacted]) or perhaps put an article into Navigans as Maggie Boreham did so well recently. (d's note: Hear, hear!)

The main views of the meeting were as follows:

1. That we would like to re-introduce the Cadet Series and Ladies Race into
the sailing calendar.

2. That we feel duty cover can still only be given to one complete weekend
by the fleet.

3. We would like to hold a Mirror Open Meeting during 1986.

4. We would enter with 4 boats into several other Clubs' Open Meetings in
our area.

5. The Mirror Association would be contacted with a view to 2 of our fleet
members becoming Class Measurers.

6. Great concern was expressed about the efficiency of the Club's radio
communication system, i.e. the number of times it seemed to be inoperable.

7» A “Mirror Fun Day" would be held, possibly on the first Saturday of Cadet Week,

8. A Fleet Winter Meeting would be held during February 1986; venue and
time to be arranged (hopefully to follow from a Cadet Meeting).

Finally, the meeting was interested to know why our dinghy park is full of ‘Mirrors which never seem to move from one sailing season to the next. Can anyone let me know if they would like to see anything introduced into the Club which would tempt them onto the water?

On a more personal note, I would like to say that 1985 has definitely been one of the better years for our fleet (even if the weather hasn't). We have seen an increase in members and, more importantly, an increase in the number of Mirrors on the water. The friendliness and Willingness of the members to help one another and the Club in general has been very evident this year and I hope it will continue to grow and strengthen during 1986.

Chris Thorne

COMMODORE'S REPORT

My apologies for not reporting to you in the December issue but, as Sue in- formed you, I was abroad on business.

First, I take this opportunity to wish you all a very happy 1986 - let's
hope for a better summer than last year!

We all enjoyed a very well attended Laying-Up Supper at the County Hotel, all tickets being sold well before the
an
event. Sheila Wade has booked the
MR.N.~F.TOVEY, same venue for this year. Charles NAVAL DIVISTON, Stock was our principal guest -I feel M BLOCK, sure those who attended will remember
WRTTTLE ROAD WORKS

continued

it OF

Recently we had the Christmas Working Party, which was once again very well
attended. Two of the scrubbing posts were replaced; a base plinth for the new winch was cemented in position; part of the Sewerage herringbone system was excavated to establish the problem associated with the cesspit
system;
the ditch in the Cruiser park was cleaned; and Dick Papworth completed even more jobs in the Clubhouse.

An Executive meeting was held just before Christmas to prepare a purchase specification for the new sailing support boat. This meeting was also att- ended by Geoff Josey (Ford Motor Co.) who is providing us with invaluable help and assistance a propos the engine and installation of same. The spec- ification was finalised, agreed with M.A.S.C. and work has now been put in hand with the boatbuilder at Deal, Kent. Our eventual choice was for a "Sea Worker 22" which is a Colvic Marine hull, wheelhouse and foredeck et cetera by Brian Cory Boatbuilders and will include a Ford FSD 425 4 cylinder direct injection marinised engine, rated at 70 BHP at 4000 r.p.m. We hope to con- duct sea trials during mid to late March and take delivery on Saturday 29th March. The total cost will be in the region of £8,500. We are in the pro- cess of arranging a loan from M.A.S.C. which will be repaid over the next
4 or 5 years.

Murray Bates has suggested we run a competition for naming the new support
boat - yes, we will give a prize and the winner can have the honour of break-
ing a bottle of champagne over the new boat (except it might have to be a cheap sparkling wine, due to our financial state!)

As I mentioned briefly above, we are still making some progress with our sewerage problems. Dick Papworth will now be talking to a land drainage engineer and then with Maldon District Council for approval of our proposed rectification scheme.

In parallel with the above, we have also been considering ideas for improving the appeal of the Satnsgate site, particularly for those members and friends "left on the shore". An initial suggestion is to build a veranda out from the North wall of the Clubhouse with access from the lounge. This would be a very attractive area for spectators and sun worshippers alike and provide a ready made area under which we can site the outside bar for the Barbecue and Open Meetings. A Sub-Committee has been formed under the Chairmanship of George Robinson, who presented his first report at the last Main Committee meeting. In this issue you will find an article from George which I hope you will find most interesting. Please answer his questionnaire so it will help us decide upon future developments at Stansgate.

I hope to see you all at the Barn Dance on 25th January at M.A.S.C.

David Harper

COMMODORE'S REPORT

During February we at last made considerable progress regarding the sewerage disposal problem. Two separate meetings were held at Stansgate attended bv representatives of Effluent Engineering Contracts, our consultants, and the many local authorities involved in the exercise. It is now clear that we have no sensible economic alternative but to introduce a proper treatment system. The output of such a system would be to a standard such that it could go direct into the Blackwater. Obviously, before we depart upon such an expensive long term solution, we have to obtain planning permission and then clearance from all the appropriate authorities. This will also include satisfying ourselves with regard to all aspects of hygiene and safety. The planning approval, et cetera, will take until at least the end of May 1986; consequently, we are seeking approval for a pilot scheme which will form part of the final overall project. This initial scheme is to link the pre- sent and the old Clubhouse cesspits so as to increase our holding capacity. Until the overall scheme is completed, we will arrange for the tanks to be emptied by local contractor.

I am pleased that we are now in a position where we can at least implement our sailing and camping calendar. During the abovementioned meetings, we also took the opportunity to arrange visits from British Telecom re the tele- phone and Lander Alarms re the magnetic esate and door locks.

(Because it's not a Japanese word as far as I know)

By the time you read this article, 'the season' will probably have already started and those few hardy souls who worked on their boat during the recent ice-age will, no doubt, have taken
part in the first rites of the Spring Points Series. As I sit here writing this in front of a roaring (gas) fire, all those house-hold jobs I put off last season seem a more attractive
proposition than painting boats in cold garages. Those of you with long memories and time to read the whole of Navigans might remember a few seasons ago that I was allowed to use our front room to store the Mirrors over winter. Now Maggie has got this funny idea that the room ought to be put to some 'good use'. Consequently, Mirrors are ‘out! (or rather never 'in') and the room houses a (mini) snooker table, Maggie's sewing machine (courtesy of Japan) and
a
whole load of junk (mostly mine so I am told). However, it is not the purpose of this article
to reveal all that goes on in the Boreham household. - you'll have to buy the unexpurgated
paper-back to discover that. No - the purpose of the above rambling is~ just an excuse to
ask those who race , and those who race officer, to perform a few simple tasks to make life easier all round.

Helms - please ensure you sign on with your name. The boat number, ot simply "Fred, does not
mean a lot to me. If you can't remember who you are, how do you expect me to know?
Besides
in the interests of safety both the Race Office and 0.0.0. must be certain who you are in case you run into trouble on the water. Apart from that you might qualify for a prize sometime.

Crews - the same goes for you. Don't forget, it's not the helm who gets all the glory.
You earn points in your own right towards the prize for winning crew, irrespective of whether you sail with the same helm all season or not.

Race Officers - please, please, fill in all details on the Signing On sheet. It's not too
difficult to discover what race it is supposed to be or the approximate wind strength; at
the very least you ought to know what the course is - after all, you set it ! However, of
more importance is the requirement to time-in all boats in all races - not just the handicap
races. The information is wanted to try and work out some ‘personal handicap' numbers.

Signing Off or Retiring - don't forget to ‘sign off' at the end of the race. If the Race
Officer has forgotten to put out a Signing Off sheet, then get one out of the folder yourself. If you retire before the end of a race, apart from signing off please let the Race Officer know before you go off for your pleasure sail (or go home). If the R.O. doesn't know you have retired, he might think you are 'missing, feared drowned' even in the calmest weather.

So what does SOSOTTI mean ? - I'm not sure, but I think it means:

SO - Sign On (that means both helm and crew)

SO - Sign Off (or you will automatically be disqualified)

TTI - Time Them In (please Mr/Mrs/Ms Race Officer, time in all
boats in all races, not just the handicap class).

Best wishes for a good sailing season to one and all.

Code of Practice for Launching and Recovery of Gruisers

Large Boats - boats above 2/ft. length will not be allowed on
the hard when dinghy events are in progress, At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight,

Tractor - Only to be operated by authorised drivers,

Ninches - «hen dinghy events are in progress the winches
must be under the charge of an authorised operator, Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the Nest half for dinghies.

the 0.0.D. will be informed and suitable notices must ve displayed for the information of dinghy sailors

At other times the following code should be observed:

When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Vinching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed,

Avoid sharp bends in winch cables-shackles must be used for attachment to trolleys.

DO NOT shackle winch wire back on itself.

It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers,

If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the boat owner must provide a rope or cable of suitable strength and sufficient length that the tractor may remain level and always clear of loose shingle,

Boat Trolleys - If left submesged should be adequately marked to
avoid damage to other boats,

COMMODORE'S REPORT

This month I am writing to you later than usual as the Easter Weekend caused us to delay the Nain Committee Meeting to 8th April. I was hoping that by now we would at least have experienced some reasonable weather. However, on the brighter side, we have again made good progress with jobs at the Club, and I consider us to be in good shape for the sailing season.

The Solo Party held on Saturday 22nd March was an outstanding success and I sincerely hope that we may see many more similar functions. The following day we held the Working Party which was well attended and achieved much pro-
gross despite the awful weather - Arthur Hodges and his team even started
work on the base for the new diesel store.

Murray Bates and I have visited the boat builder to inspect the sailing support boat and we are delighted with the quality of the workmanship —- it should be finished within one week of the time of writing, undergo sea trials on Saturday 12th April and be delivered to Stansgate by Saturday 19th April. CRUISING IN COMPANY

There is no Sailing Regatta at the Club this year and our Fleet Captain had hoped to organise a cruise to St. Katherine's Yacht Haven, London, to cover the Spring Bank Holiday weekend. Unfortunately, there are no berths available over that period, so this idea will have to be put off for the time being.

Continued. iéé«ex

However, there is no reason to abandon the idea and, if there is sufficient ‘ interest, the trip can be made later in the year.

In the meantime, there could be some form of Cruiser Rally over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend, which can be continued into the following week for those members who have the available time. The suggestion is that Cruiser members and their crews meet at the Clubhouse at about 8.00 p.m. on Friday 23rd Ma , when a destination can be agreed.

With at least three days available, this could be the River Swale, Medway or any of the Essex/Suffolk waterways. Subject, of course, to weather, the Walton Backwaters would make a good destination as there will be ample moor- ings available at the Titmarsh Marina or there is good free anchorage. can
be discussed for the benefit of members with limited experience and any

CRUISER MOORINGS

Last year, as in previous years, a number of moorings dragged and the presence of barnacles on the anchor flukes indicated that the anchors had landed on the bottom with the flukes uppermost. The weight of the ground chain holds the boat and it is only in strong conditions that the problem is apparent.

I have spoken to members of the Chelmsford Diving Club and they are prepare
d
to visit the Club to check individual moorings. It will require at least two divers for safety and one would swim down the scope to follow the ground chain

continued

to each of the two anchors. The points of the flukes would be correctly posi- tioned and bedded as far as possible. The main thing is that the flukes would be the correct way.

There are of course expenses and the charge would be £3.00 per complete mooring, irrespective of position. This is payable by the individual and I expect that the job will be done sometime towards the end of April. If you want your moor- ing checked, please let me know. I will then Supply the Diving Club with a numbered list of the moorings to be checked and receive back a list when the job is done.

Arthur Hodges

SOLO NEWS

By the time you read this the season will have started, with the premier fleet first on the water, I expect.

Things look good for Solo sailing in 1986. We have some good new sailors joining the fleet; Phil Gray is selling his Hornet and will look for a Solo; Malcolm Gandy had bought John Murphy's boat to return to the sailing scene; Colin Willsmore is a new face who we are pleased to welcome; George White has bought Bob Anderson's old boat; and the one-third owner of the red and white boat is Mr Weston.

We had a pleasant evening at Marie and Dennis Dear's house in February, which made a nice break despite the snowy weather.

In January, Bob Anderson arranged with Dick Batt to give a winter talk, which he did with great enthusiasm.

Recently, Malcolm Stuart organised a fleet party at the Club. This was a ‘great success, due to much hard work by Malcolm. The Solo helms cooked the meal and, as for as I am aware, everybody is fit and well! The highlight of the evening was a Victorian melodrama featuring that dastardly fiend, Sir Mountifield Dickbatt!

On the sailing scene, four Solos went to the first Open Meeting of the year at Chess Sailing Club. It was a very good turnout, but the Marconi results were not of the highest order. It must be said, however, that there were seven or eight helms present who had been in the top ten in the Nationals in the past two years. Ron Greygoose was the top Marconi helm, with his new Batt sail looking good for the new season.

Happy sailing.

Roger Smith

MIRRORS ON THE MOVE (HOPEFULLY!)

In October last year I came to the conclusion that, unless I did something soon about the paint flaking off my boat, then by next season there would be none left at all! So, one cold October evening, I set to work in the garage with an electric paint stripper. It shouldn't take too long, I thought; after all, most of it is flaking off anyway. Some hope!
later Several hours
and with only a small indent made into the wood, I realised that I had under- taken a longer job than I had first anticipated. Why didn't I buy a G.R.P.
Mirror?

It was around Christmas when I finally had the hull filled, sanded and generally ready to paint. I decided that, as Spring was on its way, with bright flowers and sunshine, black was the colour to have. So TI returned to the garage with

continued .....

= TO? me

a new brush and a couple of cans of International's best black. Halfway through February and after four months of working in a freezing cold garage, (I think I've got frostbite!) I finally had it finished. Okay, so it has a couple of runs and it's a bit blotchy, but it's finished now and that's that!

Having consulted the Mirror Year Book and fixed up a crew, I decided that it was time to hit the water and the Bough Beech Open would be the boat's proving ground. So, on March 23rd, I set off with Nigel and the dad to Kent. I'm beginning to think it wasn't such a good idea. After getting up at 6.15 a.m., we arrived only to find the gates locked and nobody about — the first start was an hour later than I had thought! Eventually someone showed up and let us in, only for us to find a howling gale sweeping across the reservoir.

The three races turned out to be survival lessons and, in the first race, after a broad spinnaker reach, we came to a sticky end, upside down in a bit of a vi- cious squall. After two races spent freezing at the back of a quickly dimin- ishing fleet (20 boats in ist race, 9 in 2nd!), we had had enough and decided to retire for the day without any idea of whether the boat was going any better
than last year - the peak of which was an amazing 4ist at the Nationals!

But don't let me put you off visiting the local Opens - how could 1? Itisa
lot of fun and does your sailing a lot of good to get amongst larger fleets aad and harder competition. I intend to visit a number of Open Meetings this year
and hope that some other (keen and adventurous - there must be some!) Mirror
sailors will join me.

wm WMhat exactly is MARINE WATCH ?

Well for a start let's make it quite clear - IT IS NOT A VIGILANTE GROUP

The aims of a Marine Watch are:-

1. To reduce local opportunities for crime by deterring would-be
thieves and vandals.
2. To establish a community spirit so that everyone can contribute
in the protection of their property by mutual co-operation and
communication.
3. To inform the police or the liaison persons of any suspicious
activity.
4. To make everyone more aware of local crime problems and more
security conscious about their own boats.

The successful operation of a Marine Watch Scheme would soon have obvious
advantages:

1. Crimes such as vandalism and thefts of and from Boats should be
reduced.

Now I know the meaning of being ‘hoist by his own petard' ; just as I thought nobody, but nobody, was interested in Personal PYNs, some clown decides to ask me when the results are going to be published. I suppose some might say I'm the bigger clown for suggesting it in the first place and I guess they're right. Things are not helped very much by the fact that my own Personal PYN looks distinctly sick -- as I said , hoist by his own petard
(or is it 'on' his own petard - what is a petard anyway ?).

After juggling with the Personal PYN 'rules' and rehashing the 'method', a result of sorts has been achieved. So, for what it's worth, the table below sets out, for all to see, the horrible truth about the Solo fleet. Why the Solo fleet you’ask ? Well, they seem to be the only fleet to sail regularly. Apart from that, I reckoned if they're hard enough to go ‘frost-bit.ing' then they're hard enough to suffer the ignominy of public exposure of their PYN.

Now to the table - if we start out on the basis that virtually nobody sails to their PYN
standard, then we're halfway to understanding the table. To make it easy, we assume that only one person (ie. the person who finishes 3rd on corrected time) actually sails up to the Class PYN standard. That obviously means that the two who finished in front of him/her must have sailed better than the standard whilst those behind clearly did not achieve such
excellence.(it gets worse as we proceed). Let the doubters consider - if we all sailed to
the class standard, we'd finish in a gigantic dead-heat.

For any one race, each elapsed time was compared to the corrected time of the person who came third and this produces a unique PYN for that race for each competitor. This is added to the aggregate of previous unique PYNs calculated , divided by the number of races (+1) considered and a new personal PYN is the result. In the table:

Column 1 = Standard class PYN attributed to all before they compete, or complete, a. race

Columns 2-5 = Easter Series

Columns 6-14 Spring points races (except 9 & 10 which were not timed)

Columns 15-16 "Psuedo-races' based upon the combined Handicap, Mirror and Solo fleets who competed in Spring 13 & 14, having sailed the same course in the same conditions.

NB. Where a helm has not taken part in, or completed, a race, it is assumed the unique PYN for that race is the same as his/her Personal PYN , and so the personal PYN doesn't change. This is fair enough since there is no evidence to show it has changed. £G. to date, Colin Willsmore hasn't completed a race

due to either not entering or due to retiring. Consequently, he retained the full class PYN of 122; this would obviously be a distinct disadvantage if the race results were calculated on the
basis of the Personal PYN. The lesson is there to be seen - you must finish the races (ie be
timed in) to get a more favourable personal PYN (unless you're the champion and you're then likely to find your PYN getting somewhat onerous as the season progresses).

It is worth noting that a very good (or very bad) result has a more dramatic effect early in the season than it does later on in the year since those later in the year are masked by the aggregate PYNs of the past.

A PYN which is rising with each subsequent race would suggest the person is sailing below (ie.worse) than the current personal PYN attributed to them. Conversely, a falling PYN indicates sailing better than the personal PYN. No prizes for guessing that a substantially unchanged PYN indicates you are sailing up to (your) standard compared to others in the list.

Conclusion

No conclusions . As with all handicapping systems, nobody is satisfied except the winner. One could argue the merits, or otherwise, of a particular handicap system for as long as it takes to find the

The thing is, the personal PYN is not a measure of personal skill, only an indicator to past performance. Thus although Jack, Dennis and Mike did not finish a race, we continue to attribute the class PYN of 146
to them - because there is nothing to say it should be anything else..,

THE RIVER BLACKWATER

If you've ever felt you'd like to know more about the River where you sail, I can recommend reading 'The Salty Shore' by John Leather. He writes of places so familiar to us by name such as Mersea, Bradwell, Tollesbury etc.

A couple of years ago while visiting St Peter's Church by the sea wall at Bradwell we found a charming cottage nearby and wondered who it had once belonged to. It turns out that it was once lived in by a Walter Linnett, a professional wildfowler, and the last surviving one on the Blackwater by 1947.

John Leather has also written an excellent book, '"Barges', about the sailing barges of South East England. We are still privileged with the frequent sight of these gracing our river and this book should be able to tell you all you'd want to know. M.S.C. Spring Cruise

On Friday 23rd May at 8pm several Cruiser members met in the Clubhouse to discuss 'Cruising in Company' as suggested by Arthur Hodges in the April edition of Navigans. Following a few drinks and a lot of chat, it was decided that we would head for Titmarsh Marina the next day. The wind came up in the night and it was none too comfortable on the moorings. We still had the high winds Saturday morning so a council was called ashore at llam and the decision made to sail down-river under head-sails, I was glad to be off; although I have not suffered the miseries of sea-sickness I was beginning to feel decidedly queasy, and some other crews felt the same way.

Eight Cruisers left Stansgate between 12.15 and 12,30 and enjoyed a comfortable
sail up the Wallet. Pye End is just one of the buoys we have trouble finding, but our boat, Veruna II, was saved from sailing into Harwich by the crew of Kellys Eye, 4.30 found us all at Titmarsh with Viridia aground in the entrance, but not long after there was enough water for all boats to enter, We were soon safely berthed, as crews helped each other with fending off and tying up. Everyone had a good night's rest, and Sunday morning was spent relaxing, pottering about on our boats. Ron decided to put his inflatable on the coach roof of Tekin Two, and the crews of Kellys Eye and Veruna II were engaged in the same task. Pete and Kelly were somewhat surprised to find a swordfish in their inflatable that they had been towing. I can't say I saw the fish, but can vouch they had not had a drink at that point in time. Unfortunately, Snoopy had a sick little boy on board which was rather worrying, but I am pleased to say he soon recovered.

At 4pm the crews of Viridia, Kellys Bye, Tekin Two, Two Jays and Veruna II walked into Walton to be met at 6.30pm by the crews of Snoopy, Sandpiper, Olaf and ; Ebony Rose for dinner in the Walton and Frinton Sailing Club, We can all thoroughly recommend the cuisine at under £3 a head. After dinner, discussion was the laying of plans to sail to the Deben the following morning. Two Jays and Sandpiper could not stay any longer, so would be heading for home on the Momay morning. We bid them good night and safe journey, and I understand both crews had enjoyed cruising in company.

10am Monday mormming our flotilla of six were motoring out of the Marina, making for the Deben and the dreaded bar!! lpm found us at Felixtowe Ferry with every- one telling us that was the calmest they had ever known the entrance to the Deben,. I was pleasantly surprised, or more to the point relieved, after the tales I had heard. Tekin Two came on the radio, Ron and Joyce were enjoying their sail, and would meet us later, That later turned out to be the next morning! All the other vessels went on to anchor at the Rocks, but when the tide went out Veruna II was sitting high and dry on the shingle, so out came the bucket and brush for a scrub- down, It was a lovely, warm,calm evening so Arthur and Irene from Viridia, along with Pete, Kelly, Malcolm, Helen, their two children plus Malcolm and I, strolled down to the Ramsholt Arms. We managed a couple? of drinks and it was so pleasant getting to know one another. Coming back in the dark was good fun, Pete was telling me a creapy story which made me cry with laughter, not fright, sorry Pete! Arriving back at the Rocks we found Viridia with all her cabin lights on and it was suggested to Arthur that motoring up and down the river for 2 or 3 hours would charge the batteries, but I'm not sure he found this amusing, Sorry Arthur! Malcolm and I had to stay awake until 1.30 am until Veruna II came afloat so we could move her into deeper water. It was a dreadful night, every boat had a fair amount of anchor chain out but the wind was so strong the boats were swinging around and no-one managed to get much sleep.

At the first light of day Viridia and Snoopy upped anchors and went on to Waldringfield. Veruna II had dragged her anchor, and was almost in mid-channel. Kellys Eye had anchored on the opposite shore and had spent a comfortable night. Here was a lesson to be learnt, Pete had experienced anchoring at the Rocks, so

CRUISER NEWS

It is quite a common sight to see cruisers anchored between Bradwell Power Station and the Baffle, and one of our new members decided to drop his hook there whilst he made a cup of tea, On leaving he found the anchor snagged and after a great deal’ of effort managed to get the anchor to the surface together with a very obvious Power Cable, He had no choice really but to pass a rope under the Cable whilst the anchor was released with a great sigh of relief, Yes! The Cable is live, I am told 415 volts, and there are notices on the land and on the Baffle, but thought I would mention the incident to prevent a recurrence,

Night Sailing

I think most people who have sailed at night can recount some incident, and one gentleman from Brading Haven Yacht Club (I of W) reverted to verse, The following appeared in the Newsletter of the above club and I thought some of our members might appreciate it:

When both lights you see ahead
Port your helm and show your red,

When to your starboard red appear ‘Tis your duty to keep clear
But when upon your port is seen
A steamer's starboard light of green,
There ‘s not so much for you to do
For green to port keeps clear of you,

Green to green and red to red
Perfect safety, go ahead,

When in danger or in doubt
Always keep a good look-out.

When in danger with no room to turn,
Ease her, Back her, GO ASTERN.

Cadet Week Activities

Sunday First day, and a list of over 30 cadets was drawn up, followed by capsize
drill on dry land. In the afternoon we did the capsize drill on water using ‘Idle Vice’ tied to the mooring raft, also practised rowing and paddling, Evening: Rounders.
Monday Not much wind, sailed up by Osea and back again. Afternoon: sailed by
Osea again, got bored, sailed back! Evening: Non-stop Cricket, it rained,
Tuesday Cadets divided into Groups 1 and 2, Group 2 continued the week as follows:
Barely any wind, sailed through moorings and back again. Afternoon: No wind at all, we practised tacking and gybing inshore with someone holding the boat. Tried to
sail up by Osea, no progress, so came back, (Ed. - Yawn!) Evening: Volleyball.
Wednesday A strong NW wind blew up which was wonderful after Tuesday's calm, Sailed
a simple triangular course a few times, A few capsizes, Afternoon and Evening:
Royal Wedding celebration games, high tea in the Lounge, and a disco, Water fight and disco enjoyed very much,
Thursday Another good strong breeze meant that we were able to sail by Osea and
go round a course, Afternoon: Sailed to Osea for lunch (all cadets), afterwards a race round Osea = some made it and some didn't!
Friday A very strong SW wind which was against the tide making it choppy and rough.
One boat turtled but righted and sailed on. Practised heave-to and man overboard. Afternoon: Races from the start line, Evening: Prize-giving after watching video of afternoon racing.

All the cadets greatly appreciated the work put in for them by Derek Hall, Mike & Maggie Boreham and all the other people in the rescue boats, Thanks also to Chris & Graham Boustred for organising so many of the activities on land for Cadet
Week,
Jennifer Ball, Cadet.

'Travels of a Calor Gas Bottle' Dave Thomas.

What a holiday!! Two weeks in the Scottish Highlands sounded OK and the people looked nice but, oh dear, the weather was awful.. I was strapped to the front of a caravan and looked forward to some scintillating scenery, but beyond Watford Gap the heavens opened and remained that way. By the time we returned to Maldon I was exhausted and beginning to show signs of rust. Time for a re-charge and a general
face-lift.

I refer to myself as Dora - well Dumpy Dora actually, as my shape as a gas container
has long been referred to as a 'Dumpy' by all the people I have worked for. Somehow I have been diverted since my recent service and now find myself highly charged and in company of other friends at a Yacht Chandler's in Bradwell. There is an atmosphere of anticipation and excitement but I am somewhat apprehensive at the prospect of what will be my first sailing trip. Indeed the thought of so much water brings on some painful memories,

By Saturday however I have been exchanged and almost lovingly installed aboard the yacht 'Marinero'. I am impressed. The boat hardly rocks at all except when the elderly couple stumble aboard late at night singing some hit from the 1930s,

From the final clinking of the Geneva bottle it seems no time before they are up and untying ropes. The engine has erupted and we are moving off into what looks like very deep water to me. After about an hour the engine stopned and I was disappointed that the journey was over so soon — but no, there is activity on deck and contrary to some of the rumours I had heard in Bradwell, sails were being hoisted. Three days later having touched down briefly in Ramsgate and Brighton we were in Cherbourg and the boat began to sink!!

Well, it seemed like it to me as a constant procession of Frenchmen called out for Marinero and deposited box after box of what they referred to as ‘ship's stores' onto the deck and into the cockpit. Now I can tell you there was nothing edible in the whole consignment and either we were destined for a voyage well beyond my capacity or an army of guests were coming for a long stay. I was not aware at this stage of the drink problem called "Becketts" which emanated apparently from a travelling companion named 'Northerner'.

In due course all stores were stowed reverently away and we sailed to Guernsey and thence to Lezardrieuy in northern Brittany. The river approach was magnificent scenery of steep rocky’ hills on both sides and without exception all the natives gave a friendly wave or call.

My services were not called upon too much during the next few days as the owners were enjoying the gastronomic delights of true French cuisine ashore,

About a week later we sailed north again in brilliant sunshine upwards but thick fog sideways and I for one was pleased to arrive in Jersey. 2 Although by now I was beginning to feel a little drained it was again a relaxing few days for me, Then we left for Cherbourg and I did not enjoy the conditions round the Cap de la Hague although I gather that 'those upstairs' judged it a good sail and celebrated in their normal manner.

It was in Brighton that I had my first tummy rumble, that feeling of emptiness that signals the need for a re-charge. Before I could blink I was yanked roughly upwards and shaken and the adjudged to be fit for a bit longer, then dropped unceremoniously back in my box.

contd...

There never is a convenient time for a gas bottle to run out acnarently. ‘ell, I won't be treated like that and I've learnt = trick or two over the years,
-

That night the flag officers of alcoholics anonymous came over from 'Northener' and amidst the drinking there was obviously some attempt to cook dinner. I know because 2 gas rings, the grill and the oven plays havoc with my insides and ordin- arily I would have quietly given in at this stage, Not this time though. I strained and sucked and held on until I could smell the pastry starting to rise and then I switched off.

The singing eventually stopped and there was an awareness through the haze that
all was not well in the galley - then came the language, totally unrepeatatle,
and from such nice ladies too,

I chuckled then and I still do in my new paint, waiting at Dan Webb & Feezey for my next purchaser,

Dumpy Dora.

COMMODORE'S REPORT — AGM 2nd November 1986

A year ago I was able to report that the MSC membership had been significantly
increased during the 1985 season - I now have to inform you that despite all of
our efforts, we have experienced a 4.2% decline. However it is with much pleasure that I am able to inform you that the majority of the problems previously highlighted to you have been addressed and resolved.

Before talking about the events of this season, I must remind you that there is a national decline in dinghy sailing activities: in fact, some well established clubs have had no alternative but to close their dinghy sections. I1 feel sure that our success is based on maintaining varied interests and promoting a friendly and helpful atmosphere throughout the Club. We have achieved a better sense of belonging into the membership and made huge strides to unite our dinghy and cruiser
sections,

Incidentally, following the last AGM we wrote to the MASC confirming the two AGM proposals —- Agenda Items 9.2 and 9.3 regarding:
1. Levy imposed upon MSC by MASC
2. The amendment to the rules to permit Associate Members to participate
fully in the running of the Club, i.e. to become Flag Officers.
Although no formal written answer was received, Gerry Wignall showed me copies of the MASC Committee Meeting minutes where discussion took place on this subject. The MASC ruling as interpreted by Gerry Wignall is that the Commodore, the Hon, Secretary and the Treasurer must be Ordinary members. This is now a subject to be steered and handled by your new Committee.

From within our membership we again received requests for reduced subscription rates for retired members. This subject has been debated and agreed by your Main Committee and is tabled vefore you as a proposal today. You will also see proposals introduced to overcome certain other problems apropos Club operational management.

The following comments relate to significant events in the 1986 season. I will avoid talking about the weather this of course, no doubt played a role with respect to the reduction in our membership levels,

CONT 6s ais

Sewerage I will not dwell on this topic as I have kept you informed through Navigans reports. We are pleased that at long last we have approval from the six authorities and that approval has been given by MASC, and work commences tomorrow, The project will be completed and working before the start of the
1987 season.

The 1985 Laying-Up Supper at the County Hotel was a great success - all tickets
being sold well before the event.

Next followed the Christmas Working Party during which two of the scrubbing posts were replaced: a base was prepared for the new winch: part of the old sewerage herring—bone system was excavated; the Cruiser park was cleared and further Clubhouse decoration completed.

We next addressed the problem of replacing the Sailing Support Boat. Although this was a tortuous exercise, we eventually took delivery and commissioned the boat in time for the more active part of our racing season, A competition was organised to name the new boat which was formally launched on Saturday 19th July
1986.

Our next objective was to examine our position in order to maintain our membership level and establish our viability. We therefore debated ways of improving the appeal of the Stansgate site. A significant consideration was to those members and friends ‘left on the shore’, Initial suggestions were to build a verandah on the north wall of the Clubhouse and provide a 'play area’ for children. We also decided to consider catering and manning the bar on certain
Friday, Saturday and early Sunday evenings. The play area was completed but the
verandah project hit a snag when we were informed that due to the Thames Barrier Scheme it is planned to increase the height of the sea wall on the south bank of the River Blackwater by three feet. Our planning approval has been held up but the retiring Committee envisages that this is only a temporary hold and that approval and implementation of the project should be achieved in 1987, or 1988 at
the latest.

The Barn Dance held at the MASC on Saturday 25th January 1986 was another total sell-out and a very enjoyable event.

Unfortunately we then had bad news with the sad and sudden loss of our dear friend and colleague, Jack Bigden a former Commodore,

A new telephone was installed at Stansgate and a '100 Club' introduced. My thanks to Alan Goss for organising the Club. I will leave it to Niel to report on the Club —- if he has the courage! Personally I feel that the '100 Club‘ has been the best scheme I have ever joined!

The Solo Fleet party was held on Saturday 22nd May 1986 - a super event. Pat and I
feel all sections should consider a party. Maybe Malcolm Stuart could take on yet another job and become Party Manager. We are sure you would all enjoy them. The winter series of lectures were all very well attended despite the weather. Murray and I offer our sincere thanks to all the organisers, The Fitting Out Party on 5th April 1986 was exceptional with most members joining in the spirit of the fancy dress, Another success down to Sheila Wade and her team. Let us hope that we find another energetic replacement to follow Sheila's excellent term of office, On 10th May we held the New Members' Evening. This must now surely become an annual event. This year we had a cabaret provided by a flock of sheep! The stage was the dinghy park and there was quite a remarkable performance by a number of animals on Malcolm Stuart's Solo. This was to the delight and amazement of our new members and Committee members alike — Malcolm was not so delighted!

Our extended bar and snack service commenced on Friday 30th May 1986, and on balance is considered by the retiring Committee to have been an overwhelming success. I feel sure that the membership will all join me in thanking June and Robert for the excellent and much appreciated service. Unfortunately, June and Robert will not be able to help us next year, so I appeal to you all for volunteers.

Bank Holiday Weekend 25th - 26th May brought the Catamaran/Solo Open Meeting,
an alternative to our normal Regatta, Fifteen Catamarans and nineteen Solos entered, the event being very well run, mainly by the Mirror Fleet. During the weekend we collected £50 for the Sport Aid Fund, The next Committee will have to decide upon the formula for next year. I feel that our active dinghy members will plan fora Regatta revival, probably in 1988.
Mrs Connie Bigden formally launched the'"Jack B." - Doug Field won the prize for
naming the boat. His suggestion was supported unanimously by the Main Committee.

On 14th June the team from Rochester visited us - at least MSC won, if only by a
narrow margin, It is unfortunate that Jack Pateman will not be able to attend
our forthcoming Laying-Up Supper .... something about "he who laughs last..."
remembering his comment to me when Rochester won the previous year, The Cadet Week
followed by the Camping Week, 18th - 26th July was again very popular this season -
my particular thanks to Derek Hall, our Cadet Skipper, for all of his efforts, energy and enthusiasm, On 19th July of that week we had the Barbecue —- an excellent evening, a record attendance and thoroughly enjoyed by all concerned, Let us hope that the verandah project is completed without too much delay as this should also reduce the burden of setting up the Barbecue bar. On Friday 25th July 1986, the Doha team arrived and, as I have recently reported fully in the September issue of Navigans, I will only remind everyone here that MARCONI WON and that we have been invited back to Doha next year for another return match.

Our future Projects are: 1. Road resurfacing.
2. Repairs to the Hard.
3. Implementation of the verandah project.
4. Improvements to the catering facilities.
5. Re-examination of all aspects of site security.

To complete my report, I must inform you that Murray Bates has declined the nomi- nation of Commodore. I confess that I was deeply disappointed and concerned when ke informed me of his decision only a few weeks ago. Murray and I and the Executive Committee had formed a very good working relationship and at last were realising the rewards of our efforts. We felt that most of our problems were over and that the way ahead had been paved for a good future of the MSC and a sensible term of office for Murray. I respect Murray's reasons for not continuing and am delighted that he has agreed to accept nomination for Vice-President. At least we can now rely upon his continuing. interest albeit not as active as in the past,

Peter Clayton had previously agreed with me to complete this year's term of office and then retire from the Executive Team, As usual, Peter has very kindly helped us out by agreeing to stand as Vice-Commodore for one year, with George Robinson acting as his assistant. George is very capable and has been a most active member of Committee. I hope to see him as Vice-—Commodore in the not too distant future,

Our main problem was to find a new Commodore. Murray, Peter, Pat Black, Neil and I are indebted to Robbie Sims for agreeing to accept nomination. Robbie is a well established member of the Club am was Vice-—Commodore in 1962 when the Club was at Heybridge. Also he was instrumental in the procurement of our present site. We
have had to introduce a rule change to allow Robbie to become Commodore - this is
included in your AGM notice.

TREASURER'S REPORT.

During 1986 the Club has continued in a sound financial state.
However we have failed to achieve the budgetted surplus for the year of £4000.00. In practice it appears at present that the surplus will only be £2300.00 approx..
Looking at the individual accounts, the noticeable failures to achieve budget were:-

CLUBHOUSE
This was due to the heavy expenditure on sewage disposal, approx £750.00 during the year. However the new phone must have been working better as the income has more than doubled.

SAILING
The expenditure includes the first purchase of diesel and the fitting out of the JACK B. The income has mainly come from the fees charged during the Camping Fortnight. The Sailing Sub Committee have done well to contain the expenses in view of the late delivery of the JACK B.

SOCIAL
An excellent result with an increased profit due to the efforts of Sheila and the support of the membership at the events.

NAVIGANS
The increased expenditure has largely been due to higher printing and postage costs.

OPEN MEETINGS
Again an increased profit due both to the organisers and the support by people attending.

SUBSCRIPTIONS
This has been slightly disappointing. The failure to increase the income

13

results from a slight drop instead of an increase in the membership. Hopefully the proposed increases in next years rates will not deter members and we can continue our efforts to expand the numbers.

RATES
As you are aware the block mooring fee was renegotiated during the year and an increase of 33% is likely. This increase relates to the figure at the commencement of the last five year period.

GALLEY and BAR
The analysis of these figures is particularly hard. This is caused by a number of factors. Firstly there is the lost income of the Regatta Weekend to consider which is estimated to have cost about £1800.00 in profit. Secondly the experiment of the Galley opening has cost Galley profit, however the better use of the Club on Fridays and Saturdays has contributed to the Bar profit.

RESERVE ACCOUNT MOVEMENT
The original budget for the year anticipated a Capital spend of £2500.00 approx. This was overspent by £1500.00 mainly on the opportunity to purchase the farm equipment from Osea, the necessity to put Roll over cages on the tractors and the Scrubbing posts platform. In addition we failed to budget for the trailer for the JACK B.

Generally I believe that we contiue to have a healthy situation and that the Reserve will increase during next year.

Looking forward to next year, the M.A.S.C wrote to us in April and
asked us to budget for a contribution of £5250.00 compared with £5000.00
this year. The Committee accepted this figure. However the basis of the contribution is still the subject of negotiation to determine the ground rules for the years after next. During next year there are a number of projects which may be able to proceed if the budget allows. These may include the provision of a CB radio system with a semi portable unit, the construction of the veranda, etc.. In addition both the Road and Hard are in need of repair, however the expenditure on these last two items is part of the discussion on the contribution to the M.A.S.C..

The ONE HUNDRED CLUB at present has a membership of 17 and needs at least 25 to break even. It will therefore be necessary to subsidise the prizes from the general club funds unless there is a sudden increase in
membership.

Solo News

The Fleet AGM was held on 14th November with 11 members attending.
Roger Smith resigned his fleet captaincy because of his new appointment as Sailing Secretary of the Club. During Roger's term of office the fleet activity has increased as has the membership and he deserves most of the credit for this happy state of affairs. His energy, enthusiasm and constant good humour has been an example to all, and deserves our sincere thanks.

I was elected as the new Fleet Captain and have resigned from the Main Committee as a result. This meant that a new Committee member was needed to represent Associate Membership and the dinghy sailing activity. John Rutherford has agreed to do this so Solo interests will be well represented on the Main Committee. Associate Members should channel their concerns through hin.

A few of the other key points from the AGM are as follows:

It was agreed to count finishing order in local open meetings towards our 1987 Summer and Autumn points series (Results Secretary please note). We have done this for several years now in order to actively encourage our Fleet to support these meetings as this tends to stimulate the growth of the class in this area. I believe this adds variety and enjoyment to the sailing season whatever your standard of performance. I will publish meeting dates as soon as they are confirmed and recommend you note them and give it a try. In 1986 the meetings concerned .were:

Halfway Y.C. and Fishers Green

but in 1987 it is possible that:
Dabchicks, Up River and Berwl Valley

may be added.

A vote was cast on the desirability of staging a Regatta on Spring Bank Holiday
1988, Result: 10 in favour, 1 abstention.
It was recommended to modify the proposed 1987 sailing programme as follows:

a) take the last 2 races from Spring Points and add them to the Summer Series.
bd) extend Autumn points by adding 1 additional week to end of season,

Our Open Meeting entry fees are excessive compared with other clubs. Bar/Galley 1987

One of the aims of the current committee is to improve the facilities at the club generally and to create more of a Club atmosphere. In order to do this we need to make more use of the Clubhouse, Last season we made a start by providing an extended bar service and meals facility. Members may be interested to know that the increased bar profit achieved has gone a long way towards keeping us solvent this year.

The excellent service provided by Robert and June last season has taught us a lot of lessons, not least the fact that we need to provide ‘professional’ catering equipment if we intend to provide an efficient service.

It appears to be the general concensus of opinion among members that the bar/galley service be continued and perhaps even extended if there is sufficient demand. However before we can do this and invest in the necessary equipment we need someone, (preferably @ couple) who would be prepared to operate it.

oTM I would like to ask ALL MEMBERS to consider whether or not they know of someone (not necessarily current club members) who may be interested in doing this. In particular members living in the Stone, Steeple Southminster areas may know of people looking for a part-time interest.

A retired couple would seem eminently suited for the position, so don't forget to ask relatives and friends.

It is too early to give specific requirements and dates but we would anticipate running the service from approx thé end of May to the end of August.

Anybody even vaguely interested in taking on the task or who can think of someone we might approach should contact me at the earliest opportunity.

George Robinson, [redacted]

A WINTER'S TALE (continuing the tale of Dumpy Dora).

Dumpy Dora was glad to be spending the winter in the chandler's- it was very cold with thick snow made crunchy by a daily coating of ice and a biting wind that stirred the gas bottle from her hibernation each time the chandler's door opened, as it had just then. A customer was asking for gas and the chandler obligingly lifted Dora from his stock rudely awakening her from her dormant state. The customer carried Dora out into the cold air and into his car,

In the car was a pile of clothes and blankets, but as the man drove away he started to talk to the pile,

‘New, you know the plan, you will work on the outside of the boat, while I concen- trate on the cabin interior.’

The pile answered in a strange language but the man seemed to understand:

"No, my dear, you can't doinside the cabin, you're net experienced, and no you have not got frost bite, you haven't get out of the car yet.’

After a short journey the car stepped and the man got out saying:

"Right I°11 get the cover off the beat and this gas bottle hitched up, then every so often we can have a hot drink.'

Dumpy Dora blinked to see a woman appear from the pile wrapped up like an eskime w and sniffing in a most unbecoming manner. The man set to work cheerfully while the woman sniffed leuder and staggered from car to boat with armfuls ef tools.

"We want all this old paint and varnish off, here's a new Skarston scraper for you and I'll get cracking inside.’ With that the man disappeared into the cabin with the gas bottle, calling out:

"Don't put any nicks in the wood, my leve.'

The woman eyed the scruffy little boat Palefully then, wrestling with a ladder in the wind, eventually managed to bash it onto the boat, climbed up and started to scrape and sniff.

So the winter wore en, all::week Dora and the little boat lay warm beneath the heavy cover, but come the weekends, the couple arrived to rub and scrape,

‘They are wearing me out,' Dora told the boat. ‘Every hour ‘er out there knocking to come in for a hot drink and mean about her cold and chillblains. Did you hear it this week?'

("How's your cold?* asked the man.
"Gone to my chest,‘ she said w 'That's why it's best you work outside, the fresh air will de your lungs good. Are your chillblains any better?’ he enquired, ‘I've made medical history with them,’ was the doleful answer, ‘The doocter said he's never seen them in places where I've got them," ‘All that rubbing and scraping should help your circulation,’ the man told her.) ’ "He's a decent chap,’ Dora told the boat another time. ‘Do you know, this week he bought her a new blade for her scraper and a tin. of Nitromors, and she never even smiled,’

As spring approached the smell of paint and varnish enveloped the little boat and Dora hoped the better weather would cheer the woman up, but,as yet another cup of tea was being made, her hopes were dashed when she heard the reply to the man’s conversational question:

‘Did you have a good week at work, dear?’

"No, the manager called me into his office and said that punk-rock may be in style for the younger generation, but he expected a woman of my age to have a little "taste". I explained my hair was red and blue from anti-fouling, but all he said was "I suggest you change your hairdresser."'

Well, the festive season is behind us once again, 1987 has arrived as promised, and our thoughts can begin to turn once more to plans for the coming sailing season,

A FAMOUS VICTORY

This is a story of courage; a story of achievement; of men against the elements in intense competition against the best helms in the Blackwater.

Dawn breaks. Some hours later the Solo team from Marconi Sailing Club make the final adjustments to their highly tuned machinery on the hard at Stansgate.

In a fresh Force 4 the intrepid team sail to the distant shores of Osea Island where the teams gather for the start of the Maylandsea Bay Y.C. Challenge Cup.

At the start the Marconi team of Solos helmed by Malcolm Stuart, Dave Nixson and Roger Smith put into action the well honed plan, rehearsed over weeks of secret practice, The plan was to go round Northey, then Osea and avoid going up Lawling Creek (sorry, Phil) as fast as possible!
The race was finished in a decreasing wind after a pleasant sail in pleasant company. Only later were we to learn that for the first time for many years Marconi had won the Challenge Cup.

Roger Smith

CATAMARAN FLEET BRAVE THE ELEMENTS TO BE THE FIRST ON THE WATER IN 1987

Report from Gur On The Spot Correspondent

In conditions far beyond those normally endured by other members of the Club, (S.1s), the Cat. fleet dipped their paws on the first Sunday of the New Year.
Force 6 - 7 winds over a strong tide, whipped up to a steep chop, which
together with horizontal rain provided the ideal sailing weather.

The race course was set from the slipway, up-river to Osea Pier (no extra points for sailing through the gap in the pier!), down to Fisheries mark and back to the slip.

Three boats turned out for the event, two Darts sailed by Mike and Tom Duckmanton, Andy Rimmer and Anthony Prior, and the Stampede with Trevor Milton, John Nickalls and Morris Brill.

The Duckmantons got away first but half way up the beat, Tom was involved ina dramatic incident, As conditions deteriorated Tom decided 30 knots was a bit fast for Mike's Dart. He bravely sacrificed his personal comfort by breaking his trapeze wire and plunged into high seas to provide a sea anchor in an attempt to help his helm control the boat. He clung, white knuckles straining to the jib sheet for a full two minutes, The boat slowed down and his helm, not wishing to lose such a valiant crew to hypothermia, insisted Tom came back on board the boat,

Meanwhile the other two boats were sailing hard behind them, Andy Rimmer, well known for his autocratic streak, had wrested his crew from his sick bed for one of the most demanding events of the season. Anthony was later heard asking if water-proof paper-hankies were available,

Trevor turned out a strong team on the Stampede, using the weight gained over Christmas to best effect, After the first half he made a quick pitstop for technical adjustments and a replacement crew as Sarah Brill became the first lady on the water in 1987.

The race result left little to question —- Mike and Tom had to retire as, despite Tom's valiant efforts in slowing the boat, he was in breach of Dart Class Rule No. 7(a) which states that the person using the trapeze shall have at least one foot in contact with the boat. Andy Rimmer was disqualified under RYA . Rule on fair sailing for dragging his crew out of bed whilst suffering from flu, a sore throat and a cough. This left Trevor and his crews to take line honours with the Stampede,

So with sacrificial sons, the risen dead and adjustable crews, the Fleet is
ready for 1987 to be - The Year Of The Cat,

Adventures Of A Gas Bottle

It was late in the season when George and myself, carrying enough supplies for |
a fortnight's sailing holiday, got on board 'Sagtob', George's Warsash One Designy We purchased two bottles of gas, one of which was brightly painted. Once on board we stowed the maps, food and drink. We connected the painted gas bottle to the cooker, lashing the other one in a locker,

The easterly wind was fresh and, as we had arrived at Bradwell Marina early, we left almost immediately. The sun was brilliant and we made a good fast passage to Ostend, needing to make only two tacks. The next day's offshore trip to Flushing was an easy one and prior to entering the Walcheren canal we stayed overnight in the small yacht harbour and purchased duty free drink. George liked gin. Every day of the holiday started with a breakfast of boiled eggs and toast and the highlight of the day was ‘opening time’ at twelve noon. Drinks but little food! No wonder we were hungry come the evenings,

Our journey through the canals was therefore enriched by good restaurant food. We ate well in Were, where we had moored, nestled in the fisherman's harbour right in Wy the centre of the town. Kortgene marina in the also had a good restaurant as well as showers, Willemstad will be remembered for its Victorian hotel and marvellous a la carte.

We had sunny weather as we sailed (and motored) through the canals and had only two minor mishaps. After coming through the enormous lock gates into the Maas we kept inshore to avoid the many large ships and barges. At a bend in the river we went aground on a submerged slipway. Luckily we were quickly pulled off by a motorboat. The other fright was an engine stoppage coming up the river to Rotterdam. The Warsash OD had a Vire engine and, as is usual, the plug oiled up at the most incon- venient time. Until we reached the Yacht Club in Rotterdam I sat ready with a fresh plug in my hand in case of further breakdown, as the river was as busy as Piccadilly Circus.

We had an expensive meal in a small exclusive restaurant before I flew back to England — penniless! George's wife was joining him for the second week.

A week later I had a telephone call from George. He had returned to Burnham slightly slightly early and was doing some painting and varnishing inside the boat but would I join him for a weekend sail. So on the Friday afternoon I joined him aboard
ww
'Sagtob’ to clear the holiday gear. We changed gas bottles and, before going ashore for a few minutes, George lit a small gas heater to help dry the paint, We had nearly reached the slipway in the Club launch when there was an explosion and we could see that ‘'Sagtob' was ablaze and sinking. There must have been a small leak of gas from the new cylinder, We were lucky that no lives were lost. Broken- hearted we cleared away and went home after leaving the empty gas bottle at the- Burnham chandlery.

George bought an identical boat with the insurance money, and gave it the same name, I wish this story were fictional, but unfortunately it is not. George has never had gas on board since that time and neither have I,

Geoffrey Bond

COMMODORE'S NOTES

Your Navigans has been bereft of these notes for several issues now. This was a deliberate ploy on my part because I felt that until I had given myself a chance to work myself into my unexpected role I would be guilty of being a trifle presump- tuous if I launched forth my opinions on some subject or other. Oh, very well then, perhaps I can also plead guilty to being a little lazy also — but only a very little.

Since the A.G.M. we have had two full Committee Meetings and three Executive Meetings at which I have been very much the new boy learning the business and I now feel I am beginning to glimpse the shape of our coming seasons. Coming in fresh as I do to the running of the Club I can appreciate that we have some quite difficult
situations with which to deal - all, of course, revolving around money. It is the
usual dilemma, we want to expand and improve our facilities but we want to do it without over-—burdening our costs.

HOMEWARD VOYAGE

The morning of the third day was as calm and windless as the past two days during which we had motor sailed the entire distance from Poole to Dover, Naturally such conditions are not acceptable to any yachtsman, let alone one schooled in the tradi- tions of the East Coast, where the wind blows with exuberance and periods of calm are considered monstrous, offensive and even unholy. This persistent lack of wind and the prospect of yet another full day of motor sailing was, not surprisingly, regarded by the crew with distaste which manifested itself in slow, sullen and dispirited activity as the boat was prepared for sea,

When the tide served we slipped through the Western entrance and set a course for the Downs. It was dawn. Movement through the water was reluctant, deliberate and sluggish, Now and again the helmsman would glance in at the cabin clock, not with anxiety, but merely to please himself with the thought that each minute gone by made it nearer the time when this ordeal would come to an end. So it was,in an atmosphere of gloom and despondency which hovered over the boat like a sea fog, we came, some two hours later, to Ramsgate.

In Ramsgate we refuelled, collected vital stores and within the hour had once more put to sea. But now there was a change for during that hour the accursed calm had
ended.

At first we stared stupefied, unable to comprehend the scene which now confronted us. Then quite softly someone said, "It's wind," and someone else, as if this observation needed confirmation shouted, "It's wind, it's wind, a westerly wind!" A passion of intense physical activity now afflicted the crew so that before we had reached the Quern buoy, which marks the deep water channel to Ramsgate, the big genoa was up and sheeted in, the engine was off and we were SAILING!

At the Quern buoy, where there was more sea room, we headed up into the wind and jubilantly raised the full mainsail. We bore away on to a broad reach,and with the boat moving at near Ats maximum speed, headed toward the Longnose and N.E. Spit buoys in the Thames estuary.
The hiss of disturbed water as the wake streamed astern, the exciting sensuous rhythm as the boat plunged forward into a sunlight sea, heeling to the wind, combined to produce an assured complacent air of deep satisfaction which rapidly erased all memory of the tortuous movement of the past two days.

The Westerly wind posed a problem because a course following any of the principal channels of the Thames estuary would have involved sailing to windward adding many extra miles. To avoid this a course was plotted which would bring the wind fair, but in so doing involve a passage across the notorious sands that encumber these waters. It was a bold plan for no one except fishermen,who are accepted to be foolish, crossed the sands. It was a plan which depended upon exact timing and to have any chance of success our first objective, the North Edinburgh channel, needed to be entered just as the flood tide commenced,

Sailing is an activity which is both repulsive and attractive. Repulsive because it is dangerous, mostly frustrating, wet, cold and uncomfortable. It is attractive because it brings adventure and exciting rewards at any moment, and because there are moments which elevate the spirit to peaks of supreme ecstasy. As we sailed in a silvery sea, under cloudless skies with a fair and constant wind we experienced one of these peaks. Very soon the Longnose and the N.E. Spit were astern and just ahead,at the time we wanted, was the Tongue Sand Tower and the Edinburgh channel. The first part of this channel is quite short and in less than forty minutes we were heading out into shoal water towards the Knock John. A dramatic change of depth from 40m to 2.5m was recorded just beyond the buoys marking the northern edge of this channel. The surface of the water which had all the characteristics of shoal water running off a sand bar caused some anxious moments, but the depth was adequate for our moderate draught.

The Knock John was the first of the drying sands, reported to be .6m in 1973, but no sand showed now. About two cables to seaward of this drying area a shallow rill with

8.

a minimum depth of 1.2m was shown. We estimated that as the tides were half springs, and the flood tide had been making for an hour, there would be sufficient water for us to pass safely. We stood on towards the sands. The colour of the water changed from deep blue to sandy yellow which streaked out East to West along the length of the sands. Ahead, only a hundred metres away, we could see the Barrow Deep with its usual traffic of commercial craft plying to and from London.

Slowly the depth decreased until it was almost 1.2m, the draught of the boat. It remained at this figure fully five minutes as we skimmed across the bank, then quite suddenly in deep water again. When we looked back a plume of disturbed sand could be seen drifting across our wake. The keel had ‘smelt the bottom’ as the bargemen would say.

Hazards of sailing in shallow water were now temporarily replaced by the problems of navigation in restricted waters. At least three ships were close enough to require a constant check on their progress towards us. A tanker and a container ship were approaching from the starboard and a Swedish timber boat from the port side. We took bearings every few minutes, with the hand bearing compass, on their respective bridge decks and in seamanlike fashion passed safely between them. The last of the ships had barely crossed our stern before once more we were confronting the shallow waters at the edge of the channel.

Before us now were the East and West Barrow Sands. We cleared the West Barrow easily but we touched on the East Barrow close beside the Barrow Beacon. Undaunted, in the Swin now, we maintained our course toward the Maplins and found the edge of these sands halfway between the N.&. Maplin and S.W. Middle,

We now faced the most critical part of the voyage and once more depth was the principal - concern, Those calculations, so carefully checked and recheched and upon which the decision to cross the sands had been made, were about to be tested. We were fast approaching the Ridge,a great hump of sand raised by the ebb and flow of the Crouch as it scours its course between.the Foulness Sands and the Buxey. Depths here are unreliable because with every gale the sands change, so with trepidation, tinged with no small amount of panic, we drew closer to this final barrier. Failure to cross would entail a long detour, also if we grounded the taunts and smirks of other yachts— men would be intolerable.

The belief this sand bar could be crossed was encouraged by a certain familiarity,that is, I was acquainted with these waters as I had sailed in the Crouch for many seasons and often sailed past the Ridge, but I had not tried to cross it before. As we drew near I could see,two cables distant on the port side, the surface of the water dancing in Pyramidical confusion suggesting a concealed underwater obstruction. To starboard the sea was green, the surface untroubled and smooth like a pond. I chose this way Ww and freeing the headsail to slow the boat,steered purposefully towards it,

The Gods were benign for there was no sudden shock, no bump or brating sound as sand and shingle ground beneath the keel. Instead we found a fathom, two whole metres, and swept across the fearsome barrier into the Crouch.

I offered silentprayers to those Gods whose whims and fancies determine the success (or otherwise) of our more desperate schemes, With deep sighs of relief we sailed on congratulating ourselves on our audacity.

Without further anxiety we reached the Blackwater and somewhere near the Nass beacon made our first tack in forty miles. As we passed Bradwell there was barely thirty minutes of favourable tide remaining, but the wind held and we beat up river to pick up our mooring just twelve hours after we had left Dover, Then,as if satisfied all was well, the wind fell away and a tranquil evening peace suffused both boat and crew, Never had here been such a day, and as we swung to our mooring we drank a toast to all the Gods who command the elements upon which our sailing is dependent.

"And me — Dumpy Dora — how do I fit into all this? I was taken aboard at Ramsgate and stowed in the cockpit locker where I shared all these anxieties and excitements of the crew. During the following winter the owner sold the boat and me with it. The
new owner, I have to say, is less adventurous - or should it be foolhardy?"

Bill Chrystie

CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LAUNCHING AND RECOVERY OF CRUISERS

Large Boats — Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight.

Tractor — Only to be operated by authorised drivers.

Winches -- When dinghy events are in progress the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies.

The O.0.D. will be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors.

At other times the following code should be observed:

When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the handle removed.

Avoid sharp bends in winch cables-shackles must be used for attachment to trolleys.

DO NOT shackle winch wire back on itself.

It is the responsibility of the boat owner to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing a sufficiently strong team of helpers.

Leave winches tidy, return shackles, strops, etc. to garage after use, rewind cable tidily riding turns can damage the cable.

Report any damage or wear of any equipment to an authorised tractor driver.
