TREATMENT OF HYPOTHERMIA - Reprint from Navigans, June 1981

Just a few minutes in the Blackwater doesn't do some people much good, so imagine what half-an-hour would do to a sailor (not properly protected) after Capsizing - the rescue boat could be unaware of your trouble because he is helping another sailor elsewhere on the river.

If you are called to a hypothermic casualty, this is what you are likely to find:

The Patient Will Be:

Blue with the cold.

FPWwWNrF
Stiff with the cold.
Immobilised with the cold.
Unconscious or semi-conscious with the cold. Possibly able to nod his head weakly in the affirmative to the question 'Can you understand what I am saying to you?" He is likely to be irrational.
His respirations will be shallow,

AN U
slow and irregular,
His pulse will be weak, slow and difficult to feel.
His rectal temperature is likely to be below 31 “6.
8 His blood pressure, if you could record it, would be very low.
9 Since he is exposed to the cold and long boat the stage of shivering his deep core temperature is likely to be below 31 °c. I am not suggesting that you should stick a thermometer up his anus to find out! In any event, unless you take immediate action his temperature will accelerate downwards to death by heart failure,

What You Should Do:

1 Treat him very gently. Rough handling may precipitate heart failure in a dangerously cold person.

2 Get him into the warm, out of the cold and away from the wind.

3 Keep him horizontal. His heart is weak and his blood pressure is low. Blood supply to the brain must be maintained at all costs to avoid irreversible brain damage.

4 If local conditions permit, get him to the nearest shelter and stop his heat loss.
Remove his wet clothes — dry him — put on warm clothes - wrap him up in warm blankets
with a‘warm human being beside him.

5 Do not waste time giving him hot drinks unless you are sure he can swallow. If he cannot swallow you may drown him, Unless he is getting warm and beginning to shiver do not give him alcohol. Alcohol dilates surface blood vessels and increases heat
loss.

6 Trained mountain rescue teams carry special breathing apparatus capable of admini- storing heated, oxygen enriched, air.

7 Take him to the nearest available HOT BATH.

8 The water should be at Test it by putting in your elbow, if your elbow will
accept it - so will the patient.

9 Lower the patient gently in. If sufficient help is available attempt to keep his upper and lower limbs out of the water. It is his trunk that needs reheating. The limbs have a larger surface area in relation to their mass than does the trunk. If immersed it is possible to reduce markedly an already low blood pressure by inducing vasodilatation over the skin of the limbs and, to make matters worse, excite the return to the heart of a pool of very cold blood in the extremities. This could prove to be the last straw that broke the camel's back and arrest cardiac function by lowering still further Deep Core temperature,

10 Do not forget to top the bath up with hot water to maintain the temperature
at 42-44 "6,
ll The first sign of positive recovery to look for is the onset of shivering. At that moment the patient will start dynamically to re-heat his own body. Continue to re-heat him passively with the bath treatment. His bodily functions will begin to

nant

return, When you are sure he can swallow in spite of severe shivering, this is the time to give him hot grog. Alcohol is good fuel and quickly absorbed from the
stomach,

L2 You have now saved someone's life. Hopefully by this stage the patient is in hospital or medical help has arrived. Hand over, for the patient is not out of the wood yet.
Lots of complications could occur - for instance a common one is pneumonia, Your
patient is going to need expert medical care and devoted nursing.

The practical aspects of survival training will now be considered under the following headings in decreasing order of importance:

1) Protection 2) Location 3) Water 4) Food.

DUMPY DORA

Dumpy Dora was fed up since her last trip at sea. She had been returned to the greatw dumping depot where all gas bottles are eventually sent when they are beginning to show wear and tear. Here they were either thrown on the scrap heap or smartened up to live another day.

Dora was right at the back of the shelf looking forlorn. Her paint was chipped and she looked dejected. She was worried. From her position on the shelf she could see a large pile of gas bottles destined to be melted down, They were crying and groaning.

A man was sorting out the shelves and throwing bottles on the heap with a crash, Nearer and nearer he came putting some bottles in a neat row on the floor and others on the ever growing scrap heap. Dora felt sick, all the sea air had got to her paint - it was peeling and she felt so drab, She could see her reflection in an old piece of broken mirror standing on the shelf. She looked awful and a tear rolled down her face, Suddenly a large brown hand came down on top of her and heaved her up in the air. Two large grey eyes stared at her. She trembled and tried to smile puffing out her chest and fluttering her eyelashes. The old man gazed at her. "You look a sorry old thing,' he said. Oh dear, she thought. ‘Still there might be life in you yet. Your body's not too bad.' Dora swelled a little, 'A might rusty though.' She felt sick again. ‘I guess with a new coat of paint you'll do, there are no holes in you.' Withy a big sigh of relief she found herself in a neat line of bottles waiting to be
renovated.

She was left like this for two days. It was cold and draughty on the floor and what was worse she would occasionally get kicked by people passing. I hope they don't have a dog here, she thought. She didn't fancy a hot shower, After two days she was heaved up and taken into the paint shop. Dumpy Dora felt quite embarrassed as wire brushes were vigorously rubbed up and down her until she was completely bare of blue paint. Then she was lightly rubbed over with sand paper, this tickled and she laughed. Then a man with a mask over his face sprayed her with a light grey flat paint.
Dora was left for four hours to dry. She felt better with her underwear on and waited excitedly for her final coat of paint. When the paint sprayer came again she closed her eyes and mouth and sat very still while she was sprayed a nice blue.

When she was dry her inside was refilled with gas and she was put back on the shelf, at the front this time. She felt wonderful, she swelled with pride and smiled at everyone who came near her, She knew it would not be long before someone bought her and she would be off on her travels again. She might even meet a nice Dumpy Daniel, after all those little Gaz bottles must come from somewhere.

She smiled - suddenly the future looked very rosy,

Julie Bloomfield. ‘Juliet

SOLO NEWS

I had expected to be able to report the start of the Club sailing season in this issue but regrettably, although eight Solos turned up at Stansgate on 29th March, the high winds had prevented completion of mark laying and safety facilities. Although racing was offered in the afternoon, none of the fleet accepted the
invitation.

Many thanks to those who gave their time to helping with the Sailboat 87 stand. The stand was very well prepared by John Nickalls et al. and attracted considerable interest in the Club — hope this is translated into new membership.

Roger Smith and I started our season on 15th March at Chess S.C. (Rickmansworth) where the first Southern Area event was held on a small pond. About 20 boats competed in gusting and variable conditions. I found reasonable boat speed but
lacked the mental agility to compete in that company - incurring so many penalties
I got dizzy doing 720s. Roger sailed rather better but did not get amongst the prizes. I can't quote actual finishing details as I was busy rebuilding my trailer while the prize-giving took place. What with that and punching a hole through the bottom of my boat I could have had a better start to the season,

Where were you when the Club held its ‘Rules and Tactics' evening? Lots of good material was prepared and the standard of presentation consistently high — my congrat- ulations to all concerned, Regrettably the Solo Fleet apparently thought they knew it all already! We shall see!

I'm happy to say the turnout for the Race Officer Training evening was very encouraging and hope this was found to be useful to some of you. My thanks to Ron Greygoose for his time and skill in assisting with the preparation and presentations,

My thanks also to those who turned out for the Working Party and made light work of the tasks. An informal Solo Fleet meeting at that event discussed how the Eastern Area Open Meetings should be handled and concluded that only the 2 events already nominated (Fishers Green and Halfway YC) plus our own Opens should count points towards the Marconi Series. However I am very keen that all of vou who are able also attend the other events in order to ensure they are repeated next year, and to encourage attendance at our events.

CRUISER NEWS

The last of the current series of Winter Meetings was held on lst April 1987, and the next series will not start until the end of the coming sailing season, More about that later.

Last year, as many of you know, I arranged a number of organised cruising trips which were termed ‘Cruising in Comvany'. ‘Organised! gives an impression of discipline but anyone who participated can tell you that the only organisation was the decision on destination and the time table. Even this was a joint decision taken after a meeting in the bar and everyone had been heard. There were once two schools of thought as to a destination and this was finally decided on a show of
hands,

Some of the people who took part had never been out of the river with their boats before and I am sure that we all benefited in some way as well as having a very nice time. I have been asked to organise something similar for the coming season so the first outing will be on Saturday 23rd May 1987.

This is the Spring Bank Holiday Weekend when there will be a large open dinghy sailing meeting at the Club and it would be very convenient for the majority of the Cruisers to be elsewhere, If anyone wants to come along, we meet in the ww Club House on the Friday evening 22nd May 1987, sleep on the boats, and leave about High Water on the Saturday morning.

As previously mentioned the decision as to destination will be democratic but we have been invited to the Walton & Frinton Sailing Club on the Saturday evening. The Steward will arrange a meal and there are good mooring facilities at the Titmarsh Marina. The Sunday can be a lay day or some may choose to return, whilst others may travel on to the Rivers Orwell or Deben as we did last year.

Nothing has been finalised as yet and it will not be until the day, but for many boats this will probably be the first voyage of the season and a coastal trip will or should identify those little things we overlooked when fitting out. There will always be a friendly boat in sight and if anyone is thinking of coming along but feels a little apprehensive then speak to me or to someone who was involved last year.

DUMPY DORA

Christina's Tale

The snow swirled around as Dora dozed in her snug locker on board ‘Moontide’. Although comfortable and well insulated from the elements, she was irritable and bored and wished that the winter would end so that she could be afloat once more,

Then suddenly she was wide awake, disturbed by the regular crunching sound of . approaching footsteps. A great fear spread through her liquid and left a lump in her valve, for she knew that the locker door was broken and she was therefore easy prey for a robber, She turned for help to Clive, her key, hanging on his usual clip, but he slept on, snoring contentedly, unaware of the drama.

The crunching stopped outside and was followed by the banging of a ladder against the hull and the sound of boots climbing the rungs. Something dropped into the cockpit and the boots returned down the ladder and crunched their way back into the gloom. Dora waited a few minutes and then nervously opened her locker to see what had been delivered in such a disturbing way.

Dora's fluid gurgled with glee as she saw the envelope with a Greek stamp and recog- nised the strange hand of Christina Calabottapopoulos, her pen friend. Her sudden cry woke Clive and with his help the envelope was soon opened. Dora started to read and as she did so, the cockpit seemed to become sunny and the sound of swirling snow was replaced by the gentle lapping of warm sea against the hull. "Dear Dora,

I just had to write and tell you what a terrible season I have had serving on a charter boat this year.

There I was, minding my own business on a shelf in George the chandler's in Nidri, Lefkas, which is an island in the Ionian sea, when Captain Birdseye comes in with a very sorry looking bottle. Her body was all dented, the paintwork chippved, and she was covered in various dead creatures: the smell was unbearable, This was a premonition of my fate. I was exchanged for this poor wretch and rudely swung through the streets of the town on the way to the quay.

New 'Alkadi' is a trim Aloa 27 and I was pleased to be installed in the vast port
locker, especially as I was the sole occupant - luxury indeed! Birdseye stomped off
muttering that he intended to "get yamassed at Nicks" and I settled down to a quiet snooze in the warm sun,

Suddenly all hell broke loose. The boat lurched and Alkadi reverberated to the stomping feet and shrill voices of Birdseye, Boozy Suzy, Krystos and Julie, my companions for two terrible weeks,

To my dismay, the locker was thrown open and I was showered with a bucket, warps, boat hook, flippers snorkles, deck shoes, frisbee, fishing lines and a vicious octopus worrier.

The next half hour was chaotic, as supplies were stowed aboard. Anything which could not be placed in the cabin lockers was heaved in on top of me, particularly Retsina bottles and containers of draught Metaxa.

Eventually the engine, called Donka for some strange reason, was started and we eased our way astern, helped by Birdseye hauling in a line which led down deep into the clear water. Suddenly Birdseye fell back into the cockpit, followed by sodden rope and chain and the liberated kedge anchor, a performance to be repeated many times during the next two weeks. Then, horror of horrors, the anchor, chain and warp were
thrown in on top of me, closely followed by the fenders - oh misery.
There follows a precis of my two weeks as often described by Birdseye:
'The shakedown cruise to Paleros on the mainland passed without incident, except that Suzy's first rule of sailing was established, i.e. the angle of heel allowed is directly proportional to the amount of RetSina consumed,

GONG, «4

Dumpy Dora contd, 8,

Paleros will be remembered for the destruction testing of Ouzo and the enterprising Greek taverna owner who flushed his toilet with this spirit because of a water
shortage.

The voyage from Paleros via Kalamos to Astakos was noteworthy, as a sudden squall off Mitakos blew a hole in the mainsail and put Suzy's first fule to the test - she slept the rest of the way.

Astakos is not one of the flotilla calls and is a bustling, lively ferry port. After much searching, the worst tailor in the world was soon found and he agreed to haul out his ancient machine into the main street and repair the sail. We couldn't bear to watch the appalling artisan at work: we thought he had a limp until we learnt that he was wearing one of his own suits, so we explored the town,

A dingy bar was soon discovered which we christened "The Last of The Summer Retsina", The wine was served in copper jugs from vast barrels packed floor to ceiling. All four of us managed to become seriously yamassed for 50p.

Many adventures were to follow in places with names straight from the pages of Homer:
Sami, Fiskardo, Assos and Argostoli on Cephalonia, Frikes, Kioni and Port Vathi on Ithaca. Ah,the joys of bare boat charter! ed

The time swept past and soon we were making a late evening run up the Meganissi channel, past Christina Onassis's island of Skorpios towards the lights of Nidri and the welcoming party at Nicks.'

Christina continued - They may have had a good time, but my life was a misery,
having all sorts of debris hurled into my locker. And as for that kedge anchor, no manners at all.

Anyway in true bottle tradition, I gave my all and helped produce many delightful meals and I now await my fate in George's chandlery for next year: I pray for a gin palace to be my next berth and I hope you never have to serve Birdseye and his appalling friends.

Hope you are well,

Christina"

Dora read the letter over and over again and each time she became more embarrassed, She was thankful that her locker was only large enough to accommodate Clive, herself and a few cans of beer during the season and that the kedge anchor on ‘Moontide’ was stowed in the starboard locker. However, how could she face Birdseye when he fondled her tap at the beginning of the season, knowing that he had upset her penfriend in Greece?

Birdseye, *Noontide'

CLUB DINGHY, ‘IDLE VICB'

The Club's Challenger dinghy ‘Idle Vice' has now been fitted out for the season and has been allocated a space in the Handicap Fleet dinghy area.

As she was leaking badly last season, the opportunity has been taken to give hull and rigging an overhaul, As well as the obvious work, such as revarnishing, a lot of effort has been put into resealing hull fittings, providing new aluminium keel bands and filling holes and damaged areas.

Some running rigging has been replaced and a sailbag donated so that all Idle Vice's gear can be kept together and stored in one of the garages when not in use,

To make this work (and the expense to the Club) worthwhile, I hope that maximum use will be made of the boat. Item 5 on Page 13 of the Year Book refers to use of Club Dinghies,

Idle Vice is simple to rig but like all boats has a few 'quirks'. When the boat is ‘parked' the gaff is stored in the boat, projecting into the forward buoyance tank. Remember to replace the forward hatch cover before sailing and also check that the aft tank cover is in situ.

To slot the gaff onto the mast, loosen the gooseneck fitting and remove the boom, slide the plastic 'slug' into the track and replace the boom (pushing it fairly high up the track). Hoist the sail until the gaff fitting is close up to the mast, secure the main halliard, pull the gooseneck fitting down the track to tension the luff, then tighten the gooseneck locking nut.

I hope that considerably less work will be required on Idle Vice next year and she should be available for sailing earlier in the season. The assistance of users is requested to help keep her in good trim by observing a few simple rules.

PLEASE: Do not allow the hull or rudder to be scraped or bumped on the hard or
beach,

Ensure that the boat is placed centrally on the trolley so that weight is taken on the chine and bilge keels (a look underneath will make it clear what I mean,
Do not cut or alter the rigging in any way. If you have trouble rigging the boat, ask an experienced club member,

When you have finished sailing, wash the boat and gear, return the boat to the dinghy park, tie down to stakes provided and cover up. Put sails and loose gear in sail bag and return to garage.(Consult 0.0.D. if in doubt)

PYN-man returneth - repent ye sailors before 'tis too late.

Those sinners/sailors (delete as you feel appropriate) who can remember back as far as March and June, 1986, might recall the articles on the Portsmouth Yardstick Numbers (PYN) which appeared in Navigans. Although written with a certain amount of, hopefully, obvious light-heartedness it was still the intention to test the reaction to the idea of the Personal PYN.

In all, I received four responses to the articles; one indirectly from Eleanor Witter who seemed to have been enthusiastic (unfortunately Eleanor no longer sailed at MSC), a second from Maggie (who
hinted I ought to do something useful - like slaughter the weeds in the garden), another from an
MSC member who wasn't, however, included in the list (he thought it a good idea) whilst the last response was torn from a rather reluctant sailor who was included in the PYN list and who seemed to
suggest the whole thing should be dropped - preferably on my head (not really that bad - just
author's licence). The point is, no positive response was received from anyone involved so the whole thing was dropped .

I was therefore somewhat surprized (and rather pleased) when one of our leading Solo sailors asked what had happened to the personal PYN, said he personally found it interesting and would be pleased to see it revived. Thus flushed with renewed enthusiasm, I have revived PYN-man.

My idea is to post on the notice boards a list of race-by-race ‘Performance’ PYNs, together with a "Personal' PYN calculated for every 4 races you complete. With luck, by the time you read this article, the notices will be on the board and I might also be able to publish some ‘unofficial' race results based upon the Personal PYNs. Don't worry, the 'official' results (and prizes) will still be calculated using the standard class PYN.

Performance PYN - this is calculated for each competitor in each race by taking the Average Corrected
Time (ACT) of the top two-thirds of the placed yachts in the race, then multiplying the ACT by 1.05. Let's call this the New ACT (NACT). We now take the NACT figure and eliminate (from the calculation) those yachts in the top two-thirds whose Corrected Time is greater than the NACT. The Corrected Times of those yachts stil] left are now averaged to produce the Standard Corrected Time (S_ ) and it is this S which is divided into the Elapsed Time for each yacht in turn to produce the 'Performance' PYN for each yacht placed in the race . All this supposes that the Race Officer has remembered to time in all boats (SOSOTTI !). It also supposes that I have read the instructions correctly.

Personal PYN - after the first four Performance PYNs obtained for any particular helm, the personal PYN
is obtained by taking the average of the four Performance PYNs and then using this (new) Personal PYN for édlcutating the helm's Corrected times for his/her next four races ; we then repeat the calculation of yet another new personal PYN and soon.

Will it work ? - I haven't the foggiest notion; all I can say is that if you understand the above
then you're a good deal cleverer than me - and I wrote it !

HOW TO QUALIFY FOR THE 'HELMSMAN
OF THE YEAR' FINAL.

Each fleet (ie. Dart, Solo, Mirror and Handicap) each provide one finalist for the Helmsman of the Year final series on 10 October. The fleet finalist is the helm with the maximum points taken over a majority of the qualifying races. The qualifying races are all Spring, Summer and Autumn Points races up to the end of September. The number of races to count in the ‘Qualifying series' is the nearest whole number above half the races held. Thus if the Mirror fleet hold, say 27 races, then

the number of races counted for determining the Mirror representative would be 14.

In previous years, the Helmsman of the Year has been raced in single-handed lasers.

SUNDAY ‘Ye went over all the parts of the boat we could think of. One group came

CASUAL SAILING

I recently witnessed a disturbing but not unusual incident when two dinghies were launched in a Force 5 wind with a strong ebb tide. Neither dinghy was properly rigged and three of the four sailors were inadequately dressed for the weather conditions. Being midweek, no OOD was present to give advice and it was fortunate that both boats eventually got back to the hard without harm, one full of water and the other dragged in from Ramsey Marsh bay.

If you are inexperienced, please admit it and seek help and advice before you venture out. Do remember that you need adequate clothing for sailing even in summer and particularly in a summer like this. It is a fine line between staggering back. tlue with cold and not getting back at all.
To enjoy sailing you need a well—found boat and you need to be properly kitted out.
The last thing we want is to lose members through disillusionment - or worse,

This year's Cadet Week saw an increasing number of adults joining in and learning how to sail properly. For next year we will consider setting up in parallel with Cadet Week a special course for those adults who would like to learn how to sail but are not necessarily interested in going through the full RYA training scheme,

part of a series of ten races for the B.J.R.C. Cruiser Section, there were 21 yachts on the Starting Line between Osea Pier and the 'Jack B', These varied from the fastest boat with a F.H. of 95 to one with a 7.H. of 137, and was quite a sight for the interested spectators on the sea wall,

With a force 3 wind from a N.E. direction and an evbing tide, the course went as far as the Bench Head, the Sagle, The Colne Bar, the North tagle, and the N.. Knoll. With such a variety of boats, there was some exciting racing as several groups of boats fought it out for positions. The first boat home returned in just over 5 hours and finished second on corrected time, The overall winner was ‘Dizzy Lizzy' from

Cruiser Cup contd.

M.L.S.C. who began with a4 F.H. of 97. Many thanks to the Race Officer and his

crew of assistants,

SOLO TEAM RACE —- Saturday ist August
Which could be retitled ‘Nine brave fools get blown into oblivion

Team racing takes place between teams of three boats where the winner is decided on the TOTAL score of all three boats. The scoring is the standard 3/4 pts for ist , 2 pts for 2nd , 3 pts for 3rd, etc with 7 pts for retired and 10 pts for disqualified boats.

The basic principle of team racing is to prevent members of the opposing team overtaking any of your team members, or to enable a member of your team to overtake a member of the opposing team, without losing a place yourself.

By a wonderful piece of luck the Solo team race took place on the first really windy sailing-day of the summer. Starting with a modest force four the wind gusted up to a steady five by the mid-afternoon.

Out of mine enthusiastic entrants three team captains were picked ; Roger Smith, Dave Nixon and myself. The other two members of each team were placed by the team captains picking their names from a hat.

This gave teams comprising ;

Roger Smith Dave Nixon Stephen Rutherford
Dave Payne Colin Willsmore Steve Keeble
Bob Anderson Malcolm Stuart Dennis Dear

The COURSE for all three races was : E.st , Nor.st , F.st , Finish with D.st

First Race - Dave/Colin/Malcolm against Stephen/Steve/Dennis

A very scattered start left Dennis and Dave with a good lead ahead of the rest of us. With the wind blowing against the tide the beat proved slow and bumpy, producing little opportunity for team tactics . The following reach was little better, where boat-speed and control (or lack of it!) were most important. No it was the gybe mark which everyone completed without incident. The following run was a good test of tactics and I got myself in a_ diabolical position, stuck on the outside of Malcolm with Colin approaching fast from behind. At F Colin slipped round the mark right behind Malcolm and overtook me before I reached the line. Up ahead Dave had already managed to beat Dennis’ for first place.

Second Race - Roger/Dave/Bob against Dave/Colin/Malcolm

This race began with a very keen start that left three boats ahead of the line at the gun; Dave Payne, Colin and Bob. Although Colin turned back toward the line he was still a good twenty feet away from it when he decided to rejoin the
race.

It didn’t take long for the two teams to split into three fiercely competing pairs . Once on the reach the solos screemed across the river, all keeping surprisingly close. Because of a slight change in wind direction it was now

possible to gybe anywhere between 1 and F.
Gybeing however, proved easier said than done, with the lumpy seas and gusty winds. The resulting capsizes where as spectacular as they were frequent. Due to either his enormous talent or good luck Malcolm avoided capsizing, but wasn’t quite fast enough to beat Roger to the line.
Once everyone had returned to the hard, it was agreed to take a long lunch.

Third Race - Stephen/Steve/Dennis against Roger/Dave/Bob

By this time the wind was blowing at a constant force-five. After missing our first start due to lack of upright boats we managed a second, reasonable start. With the tide coming in, the beat was hard-going but fast with Steve Keeble going particularly well. Once on the reach Steve was just ahead of me, with Dennis and Roger both well ahead. Once out of the cover of Osea Island the boats really howled along.
At No.1, I thought it best to tack around, allowing Dave and Bob to catch up with me. On the run to F Dave capsized and I nosedived, leaving us both in the middle of the river with a boats full of water. Steve managed to gybe at the emark, then almost sailed over Bob‘s boat as it capsized in front of him. The result of all this was Steve getting a third, Bob a fourth and myself (after plenty of messing about) a fifth. Dave capsized again at F and had to be towed back to the hard.

Conclusion

Judging from the response of those taking part, the day was a success despite the weather. It also seems that when approached in an unhurried manner’ team racing is a lot simpler and less ruthless than most people expect. Another point to be noted is that to be a success any team competition needs a whole day allocated to it.
I personally hope the Solo team race becomes an annual event (possibly with its own trophy) and that other fleets in the club try a team racing event
themselves.

- From Stephen Rutherford, our mobile correspondent.

COMMODORE
'S NOTES

Here we are in September; the season is nearly over and the period of mellow fruitfulness is upon us. Was anyone quick enough to catch our summer?
Let us away with frivolity and think only of such jollifications as 'working parties' and ‘laying up’ and next summer.

The first of the new season's working parties has already taken place and I offer our congratulations and thanks to the environs party for their splendid efforts in the Cruiser Park which is now free of all extraneous lumps of iron and material and is quite ready for its quota of winter custamers. I am assured that every boat has been allocated a place and we require owners to use those spots only. If there are any difficulties, please refer to Arthur Hodges who will be happy to resolve them for you.

We have had one or two unfortunate incidents this year which make it necessary for me to bring to your attention our rules and bye-laws of which every member is expected to be aware. These regulations are the result of thirty-five years worth of experience and have evolved from this accumulated wealth. They are there to allow us all to live in harmony and SAFETY with one another. In this connection I must remind members that they must have insurance for themselves and any guests using their equipment. In an effort to to emphasise this need, members will be asked to identify their insurance company and policy number at subscription time.

One further safety point I must make is to tell you that children must NEVER be allowed to ride on the tractors. A child was doing so recently, fell
off and was nearly run over - such an event must never happen.

Another lot of unsung heroes of whom I must make mention are the crews who man our rescue facilities. They do a splendid job involving very long days and all that I would ask is that those who go sailing just as a long day is caming to a close should do so with due regard to their own safety and not stray so far as to require the further services of our hard-pressed rescue crews.

Finally, on a happier note, I am sure you would like me to offer our thanks and appreciation to the Jessops for their imaginative menus of nutritious grub on offer to us these past few weeks. Thank you, we needed that.

Robbie Sims,

Tales from Stansgate (1)

THE TAIL OF TERRY LINN

There was once a field mouse named Terry Linn who lived in the farmer's field near to the Big River. Also by this river was a sailing club named after the famous inventor Guglielmo Marconi. Terry Linn would often sit and watch the sailors having a wonderful time sailing in, and falling out of, their boats and he resolved to build one for himself.

He searched for materials fran which to build his boat, and had no trouble at all finding same scrap wood. Being a rodent with big strong teeth he soon gnawed a perfect little Mirror Dinghy complete with a little mast, gaff and boon. He found same discarded whipping for sheets, halliards and painter, but he could not find any suitable material from which to make his sails, until one day in July, same Camping Club Boating Group members set up canp in the field next to that in which he lived.

One of these campers, after a particularly wet day sailing, left his Mirror Dinghy sail spread out to dry on the ground in his caravan awning. In the middle of the night Terry Linn crept in and carefully nibbled out a piece just the right size to make a sail for his little boat. So now if you look carefully when the MSC Mirror fleet is out racing you will often see, right
at the back, Terry Linn in his little boat - Sail No. Mouse 1 - and if Terry's
friends can find enough sails left where they can borrow same pieces, then maybe next year Marconi's will have a Mouse Class fleet.

THE END

TERRY LINN

NOTES FROM THE SOLO A.G.M. - 27th AUGUST 1987

1. The AGM for the Solo Class Association was held during the World Champ-
ionships at Mumbles Yacht Club.

2. The subscription is to go up to £10 next year with a view to holding
it for two years after that.

3. The National Championships will be held at Whitstable next year, presum-
ably on the long weekend formula.

4. The Meeting was chaired by Nick Yeomans in a brisk, constructive way.
He was eventually elected President as Paul Hemsley resigned.

5. Most of the meeting was taken up by discussion of proposed rule changes,
notified to members in advance. These had been proposed to update the rules to reflect modern construction practices and remove ambiguities.

6. No-one wanted the Solo to become a class where the ability to buy the
most expensive equipment was the key to success.

7. The official situation is that where the AGM gave approval in principle
to the rule changes, the Class Association will now get RYA lawyers to draft the changes in legalese before applying to the RYA for formal ratification of the changes. The basic information is as set out in the pack sent to members, I shall comment on amendments, etc.

8. Transom flaps may be side hinged.
- Instead of measuring mast weight plus C of G, the tip weight will
now be specified. (Like Enterprises, apparently).
- Internal (T-piece) fittings for shrouds were ruled out. It was felt
they could be dangerous in a boat like the Solo with a slack rig.
- It was stressed that shrouds must be removable; Jim Gates said that he
would rule out shrouds connected directly to the hounds.
- Wooden side tanks would be allowed on composite boats, they would
have three buoyancy compartments like a wooden boat.
- Centreboards and rudders may be glass sheathed in future. Most dis-
cussion on this point - many people thought it could lead to very
expensive construction, but it was thought this could be overcame by a minimum weight limit.

9. Bill Loy and Michael Barnes were elected on to the Committee. There
was one space left unfilled. Nick Yeanans thought this could be filled by someone to represent the Eastern Area. Meetings are in London on Friday
evenings, about once every six weeks or so - Any offers?

Roger Smith

AUTUMN BANK HOLIDAY HANDICAP SERIES 1987

To be honest, at the time of typing this article, I do not actually know for certain who has won the Autumn Bank Holiday Handicap Series; it's a job for the Sailing SubCommittee to adjudicate upon. Hopefully, by the time I reach the bottom of the page, the Sailing Sub will have decided in their wisdom what is to be done, and then I'll be able to fill in the gaps I left on the page. Just think, if I hadn't mentioned it, you'd never have known of the drama I've experienced in preparing this report.

Race 1 was 'sailed' in little or no wind; an occasional puff helped those fortunate enough to be in the right position at the right time but 13 out of 18 didn't manage to finish, mainly due to lack of wind. Several of us spent a very frustrating 15 20 minutes only a few feet from the finish but the adverse tide thwarted our efforts. Dave Nixson, however, persisted with his characteristic single-mindedness, as did Colin Willsmore, and they both finished some 15 - 20 minutes after the winner, Ron Greygoose. When you consider that Ron was only about 50 yards ahead of them, you can understand the situation.

Race 2 did at least have some wind, even if not a lot. The course was good in that it gave a true beat from Goldhanger to Breezy and this provided an interesting choice of route. As usual, I chose the wrong one and lost out badly, as did Peter Collis and Damian Boreham in the Mirrors. Mike Taylor, however, chose the right course and won the race; the point of this tale is that both Peter and Damian had a good lead over Mike at the time they chose the wrong way so, who knows, the Mirrors might have had 1, 2 and 3 in this race had they been as wise as Mike. 'Ah! if only....' ought to be emblazoned in bottle tops over the club bar, for such are the tales of woe to be heard every week in the changing room and what would be the 19th hole if we were a Golf Club.

Race 3 saw not only a much better wind, but also the first appearance of the catamarans. Trevor Milton won it in his Stampede, Joan Hardie was second in her 420 and Dave Nixson sailed a canny race to just beat fellow Soloist Malcolm Gandy by 31 seconds on elapsed time. Again, the beat from 'E' mark to 'D' mark provided a choice of route - and again I chose the wrong one; it's getting to be a habit with me.

Race 4 was sailed in the best wind yet and the catamarans won easily over the monohulls, filling the first three places with Mike Duckmanton providing his son, Tom, with another win towards his 'Mug's Mug' tally.

A rush to pack up tents and caravans saw little time for frivolity, ending a weekend's sailing which saw varying fortunes as well as extremes of wind strength, a multitude of hard luck stories as well as a whole host of 'might-have-beens'; by the time you read this it will have all faded into the Club's history.

Don't forget, the hero who sits at the sharp end of the boat (well .- usually) earns points towards the ‘crew's prize' in the Spring, Summer and Autumn Points Series in their own right. Just because 'your' helm wins a Points Series, it doesn't mean you automatically get the crew's prize. It pays

each week. Similarly, a crew can win a Points Series prize even if their 'normal' helmsman doesn't receive one; take a look at who receives the lst place ‘crew's prize' for the Summer Mirror Points and you'll see what I mean (helm-husband ‘Jack came 3rd).

EDITORIAL

Now the Cruiser field is filling up with boats for the winter, it is becoming obvious that the season is coming to an end. The Working Party and the A.G.M. are upon us once again, and even if you only glance through Navigans you won't fail to notice the fact that the Laying Up Supper is also coming
up!

CRUISER MEMBERS

Firstly, apologies for not expending very much time with the Fleet this year, but as most know, I had an illness early in the Season. I was advised to stop sailing for same time and as a result made a calculated decision to sell
Viridia.

Initially I thought I could carry on as Fleet Captain but found it very difficult without a floating base and particularly when "Cruising in Company" needs the organiser to go along.

I am therefore relinquishing the position as from the A.G.M. To date a successor has not bee found, although Malcolm Yeoman has kindly agreed to arrange the Winter Meeting programme. He has also offered to organise the Discount Paint Order, and you will be hearing from him about the details.

The Laying-Up plan for this Winter is desplayed on the Club Notice Board and this should be 99% correct. Slight inaccuracy has arisen through two boats remaining at the Club after initially giving notice of leaving, but if any member has a problem please give me a telephone call.

That takes care of everything except the trip to the Boat Show in January
- so I am asking for a volunteer to make the necessary arrangements. Not
a difficult task but preferably requires saneone who will be going along.

Next Season we should have a new Fleet Captain to take over the tasks and hopefully the "Cruising in Company" which has sadly been hit by the weather this year. Thank you for your help and support, particularly during my illness and the offers of a sail which I will be taking up next year.

I am not leaving the Club, and fran the date of the A.G.M. will probably be taking over a job on the shore where I can keep in touch albeit without a
boat.

Arthur Hodges, Fleet Captain, Tel.[redacted] (See Page 10 for Mooring Lifting Dates)

MIRROR NEWS

The Summer (what summer ??) Points Series has now finished and the Autumn Series has begun; results for the Summer Series are to be found elsewhere in this Navigans (I hope!). Whatever the results, it was nice to see Mike Taylor and his daughter, Helen, sailing again in the Autumn Bank Holiday Series in which
they proved themselves the leading Mirror - and won one of the races.

The weekend of 19/20 September was the club's Mirror Open Meeting and I'm happy to report that 5 MSC Mirrors
took part, along with 6 visiting boats: The club helms were Debbie Yorston, Jon Yorston, Mike Battle, Damian Boreham and Mike Boreham . The winner was Michael Wright (from our near neighbours, Maylandsea Bay Sailing Club) who not only won overall, but also won the first three races (he didn't sail the last
race). However, he didn't have it all his own way all the time and some good racing was enjoyed
throughout
the fleet. The best MSC boat was Damian, crewed by Katy Rutherford; who finished 3rd overall.and the full results are set out below.

Our thanks to the Catamaran Fleet who organised this open meeting so well (and, as always, with good humour
and friendliness) . Our thanks also to the Jessop family - no, not just for doing the catering, but for
wm providing Mike Boreham with a crew for races 3 and 4 (he went single-handed for 1 and 2); Susan Jessop had her first taste of sailing in the Mirror image and apparently thoroughly enjoyed it. Rumour has it that
Susan is now trying to persuade her Dad to buy her a Mirror - let's hope she is successful and that she is
able to join the Mirror Fleet in 1988.°

Autumn Points 3 saw 7 Mirrors racing whilst, in the afternoon, race 4 had 8 Mirrors sailing (and we could have had 10 sailing !). There's no doubt about it, we're growing in strength and s‘owly but surely catching up the Solo Fleet with our numbers. **

Vic Braybrook returned to the fold on the morning of 27 September with "Flaming Pest', complete with his
crew-daughter Kim, and they proved that a long break hadn't affected their sailing skill - except for Vic's
timing ! He was a long way over the line at the start of Autumn 4 but by the 2nd mark had overtaken all but Damian, Roy Woods and Dave Onyons. The lead then changed between these 4 boats until the final leg when Damian crossed the line lst, Vic 2nd, Dave 3rd and Roy 4th. However, an eerie silence greeted Damian from the Race Box as he optimistically waited for 'the hoot'; what a pity he'd forgotten to sign on Thus, Vic was the well deserved winner after all, everyone moved up a place and Damian discovered he'd literally never been in the race in the first place; I bet that's something he won't do again, at least for a while.

By the time you read this, the sailing will be over for another year, so let's hope all the Mirror people
who sailed in 1987 will continue to do so in 1988; perhaps some others will join us on the waters in what
must be one of the most pleasant of sailing areas.

COMMODORE'S REPORT - A.G.M. 8th November 1987

When I came to write this report for you I was at first under the impression that in many ways the year has been a non-Year. Principally I think this has been the result of the non-summer of wet and not particularly warn weather we have ‘enjoyed' culminating in a hurricane the likes of which we have not had in the past century, or two, or three!

Some serious losses have resulted from the hurricane to some members while others have had lucky escapes. I should like to express our sympathy to those who have suffered losses and offer felicitations to those who were lucky. There, but for the Grace of God, go any of us.

I do not propose in my report to deal with a load of statistics of our events as I am assuming that these will be the basis of the secretarial reports which follow mine. My task as I see it is to deal with policy and to try to make myself sensitive to the wishes of the membership as a whole. In this connection T have found it to be an extremely difficult year since I found myself precipitated into M.S.C. politics after a break of 24 years. So I have had a lot of catching up, learning and re-organising of my thoughts to do before being in a position to offer the lead you could expect from my predecessors. ww

My first impression of the Club was that it was well run by a core of able, well motivated, active members operating a well-established routine, developed over many years. This impression I have discovered to be well-founded. You do have such a core of enthusiasts to whom we owe a great debt of gratitude for their work and dedication and without whom we would not have survived so long. Thank you from us all. I refer, of course, to all those members of committees, sub- committees, project groups etc., both official and unofficial who have for so long dedicated their lives (not too strong a term) to our better enjoyment of our chosen sport/pastime, call it what you will. What is worrying though, to me aS a new boy is the impression that we need far more active involvement from our younger members. SO come on you younger ambitious ones, help us to identify

you and so harness your energies and ideas to the greater good!

I should like now to turn to our ongoing sore which we are still truing to resolve and that is the question of our contribution to the MASC for the facilities which we enjoy here. We have so far signally failed ever to achieve a sensible dialogue with the General Committee of the MASC with whose philosophy and approach in this matter we disagree profoundly. To this end we have invoked the aid of the Trustees to see if they can offer some acceptable arbitration. Your committee does notTM object to making a contribution, or even its magnitude,Wthe MASC for our facilities
which we think is only fair - but only to the manner in which the MASC wants to
assess this hurden and with which we disagree fundamentally as being wrong. There is a resolution for you to consider later which, with your support, may help us to precipitate a solution to our difficulty. A solution to this difficulty is fundamental to our future development since we are coming to size and activity level when our tradition of self-help may no longer be possihle or even relevant. This will give rise to a great deal of serious thinking on how to go forward as additional substantial funding may be necessary and if we cannot have an acceptable, fair and predictable arrangement with our parent how can we expect to plan ahead?

Your committee is nothing if not optimistic though, and I am very pleased to announce that 1988 will see us once again holding a Regatta at the end of May. This result is due in no small way to the dedication and imagination of Malcolm Stuart who has driven this project forward overcoming all the difficulties to produce a package which will make it work in practice. So I hope we can now unite 100% behind him to help the project exceed our expectations. As a spin-off we will be trying

oS)

certain re-organisation of the garage areas and from this experience we hope to learn and then promulgate a 5-Year Plan of development where it will be possible to correlate funding and spend in a way which will do most good. It is terribly easy to blue a lot of money on eating out at the best restaurants when, perhaps by planned restraint, we should be planning to buy the restaurant.

Another aspect of our Club which your Committee has recognised as a growth area is that relating to Winter Storage of boats which I can only see increasing both for Cruisers and Dinghies. This means improved storage facilities will be a must if we are not all to sink into a quagmire. This will need funding, and we have taken the initial step of proposing differential storage fees for Cruisers based
on length - for want of a better yard stick! We hope you can support this important
measure because the Cruiser fleet is growing in size and influence and, by definition needs additional facilities like hard standings, power, space etc. which we will try to provide as fast as funds will allow.

One area which has become a bit of a minefield is our Rules where certain changes, particularly over the past few years have not (perhaps?) been properly ratified by the MASC. This is my fault because I did not really appreciate the extent
of the situation early enough. (Sorry, Malcolm, you did kick hard enough - but
I was too thick!) However, I have now had discussion with Gerry Wignall, and Pat is preparing a new corrected full set of rules which we will then submit to the General Committee of the MASC formally. I do not expect more than one or two changes will be necessary.

Implicit in a lot I have been saying is the underlying need to increase our membership substantially and I would like to take this opportunity to promote the idea in each of your minds the resolve to say out loud on January Ist 1988 "This year I will find and introduce a new member to the Club." To succeed in this resolve would, at a stroke, dissolve many of our financial and funding worries and we could then do most of what we need to without having tag raise any additional funds.

Before I conclude I am pleased to announce that Eastern Electricity has undertaken to divert our power lines underground (somebody must have worked hard on them) and because one of the new stays comes on our ground they will be paying us rent of £1.19 p.a. for the privilege.

In conclusion I would like to say what an honour and a privilege I have regarded being your Commodore this past year. We are the best Sailing Club around and we
can all take pride in being members and for my part - I thank you.

Further news on the MSC Sailing Instruction 6 (the 'one-horse race' rule).

Following the short trial period for the application of the 'one-horse race' rule to all classes, the Sailing Sub-committee has decided that for 1988 a minimum of two starters will be required for each race. As explained in the September'87 Navigans article, the one-horse race was introduced some years ago into the Handicap Fleet because most of the time there was never more than one starter in the handicap series races - kinda discouragin' for even the most persistent of souls.

It is interesting to note that in 1987, the number of one-horse races in the Handicap series was as follows:-

Handicap Spring points - 1 out of 9 races
Handicap Summer Points - 1 out of 13 races
Handicap Autumn Points - 4 out of 11 races

Hopefully, we will have enough Handicap boats entering each race in 1988 to make it a good season's sailing. With promises of more 420s, we might even start awarding the 420 trophies again.

COMMODORE
'S NOTES

Christmas has come and gone and here we are at the start of a bright new Leap Year and may I wish you all a very Happy and Prosperous Year.

In many respects the Sailing Club is facing a year in which I foresee not a few pitfalls and difficulties which we will have to address and overcome. As I said at the AGM your Committee would like to take time to discuss and draw up a plan which looks at the development of the Sailing Club on a longer term basis so that we have a chance to arrange priorities and finance in a controlled manner including having discussions and obtaining the full backing of all the Members. The way forward, however, is being frustrated right from the outset because we do not have enough volunteers to fill the vacancies on the Main Committee, particularly from Marconi employee Members. Being a member of the Main Committee need not take up much of your time, only as much as you want to give. Your views, however, in that forum are vital to the future of sailing as we know it. If you are interested then phone me NOW at [redacted]
Ext 437, or at home on [redacted] - or contact any Committee Member. Your
Club Needs YOU.

We have had our post-Christmas Working Party on what was a mild and pleasant day which, speaking for myself, helped to blow away many a cobweb. It was well attended, much valuable work was accomplished and it gives me much pleasure to thank everyone who came for their efforts, which are much appreciated.

I have always been very proud of our Club and one ofthe principal factors which has sustained that view over the years has been the spirit of independence demonstrated by the degree of self-help shown by the Membership. We are a self-help Club and we get things done because WE do them. I recognise that as the Club activities expand the work-load becomes more onerous and a time will come when we will need to consider some full-time assistance. With the departure of Claude into well-earned retirement, perhaps now is the time. Do you have any views? If so, please talk to me or any Committee Member urgently.

HAPPY NEW YEAR

ROBBIE SIMS

THE ANNUAL RNLI ROWING RACE

MALDON LITTLE SHIP CLUB

(Sunday 3rd January 1988)

Never leave a meeting even for the most urgent reasons, because those that remain have a nasty habit of volunteering you for something. It happened to me at the Sailing Sub-Committee Meeting when I returned from a short walk down the MASC corridor to find that I had volunteered to join the M.S.C. crew in the Annual Rowing Race to be held on January 3rd. As I have a cruiser, (they said) I must be good at rowing. (Have they never heard of outboard motors?)

The final crew line-up was Malcolm Stuart (team leader), Roger Smith, Ian Lindsay and yours truly. Malcolm decreed that we needed a practice, so the date was set for Sunday 20th December. So rapidly did our fame spread that my sister and brother-in-law flew in from Virginia, U.S.A. to witness the practice session. (They did stay for Christmas as well, but I am sure the initial attraction was the rowing race practice.)

Ian could not make the practice session (he must have known a thing or two!) so David Ball substituted as helmsman. The Fisherman was launched and we managed to row it up to No.2 Buoy against the ebb tide and a fresh westerly breeze. I enjoyed the trip back resting on the oars. All this time brother-in-laww (like a true American) was clicking away with his camera ("Hey, you guys are
crazy!")

The practice session showed that fine tuning of the Fisherman was required. Some new '‘'go-faster' rowlocks were required, a pair of oars had to be shortened and new grips fashioned (technical stuff).

Christmas was spent gathering sponsorship and manufacturing the obligatory Viking helmet.

Sunday January 3rd dawned after a very wet and windy night. "Tt's a waste
of time driving to Maldon this morning, it's too windy, they'll surely postpone the event," I told myself, turning over for my second sleep. However a sense of duty overcame my inertia and complete with family (for moral, and possibly later, physical support) I arrived at Hythe Quay roughly on time. The rest of the crew were already there sporting a variety of Viking helmets. The Fisherman was equipped with mast and M.S.C. Flag, lowered by crane into the water and secured on the pontoon ready for the start.

The race plan was to down a drink at Maldon Little Ship Club, run to the boats and row to Maldon Yacht Club, run to the clubhouse, down another drink andTM@ collect a balloon. Then it was a run back to the boat and the long row up to the Fullbridge for another drink and balloon. Here we had a problem as
the pub was upstream of the bridge and our boat had a mast..... The final
leg was back to the M.L.S.C. and a run into the clubhouse to sign-off. (No-one said anything about this running).

There was a good turn-out of boats and crews for the event, many in fancy dress and a lot of fun was had by all. The West Mersea Lifeboat and Dick Townshend in his Mobile Coastguard Vehicle and quite a few spectators turned up to provide a bit of extra support.

We achieved 3rd place in some class or other and over £100 of sponsorship. Many thanks to all of you who donated to this worthy cause.

RAY BALL, Usually Bosun.

SATURDAY 2nd MAY 1987 Martin and I flew fran Heathrow on the 18.25 T.A.P. flight to Lisbon. The food
was good and the drinks were free, and as I had never visited the capital of Portugal, I was looking forward to the trip.

The boat, a Trident Challenger 35' long-keel sloop, had left Palma Mallorca two weeks previously and had last been heard fran in Gibraltar. We were met at the airportby a tired looking skipper and crew. Spirits revived after a good seafood meal and a visit to a cafe in gardens right in the centre of Lisbon. The four of us sat drinking beer and watched the world go by, still in au shirt sleeves until 2.30an. This was a real transformation having left England enjoying a rainy Saturday in one of the coldest springs I can remember. We took
a taxi aout to the marina, and rowed aut to the boat. We were moored next to
a Swan which was bristling with winches.

SUNDAY 3rd MAY This was a make and mend day. We worked the engine and prepared for sea in the
morning. Weather was glorious and sunny. In the afternom we walked a way alamg the banks of the River
Tagus. My camera seized up at the top of an eight storey sum dial monument. We then caught a 1930's
vintage tran (all cast irm and wood) to the city centre where we took in the sights of Lisbon - the
architecture
and the senoritas. There being no food shops open anywhere, we boarded a trolley bus back to the boat for aftermmom tea in the cockpit beneath the awning. A taxi was ordered in the evening for another
hit at the seafood, which
is plentiful and good everywhere in Lisbon. We still had to water and provision for the first leg of 150 miles north to Porto.

MONDAY 4th MAY We shopped at the Co-Op first thing - fresh food for three days. Bought stamps but
could not find postcards. Breakfasted and filled up with water. It was 10.30am when we slipped our
berth and moved out into the river. We set our mmber two jib and were som doing 6 - 7 knots with
the wind behind
us. The sun was scorching
hot. Rubbing my factor 5 suntan oil in, we were fighting
for the best positions in the cockpit - look out Atlantic, here we cane! As we passed Estoril in the
flat calm river I could see a line of white alag the shore beneath the cliffs ahead. Could they be breakers? They were! Lunch-time and we tumed northwards and the wind was now on the nose, and we encountered the Atlantic for the first time. The engine was tumed qm and we were doing 5 knots in a la@g swell of 20 feet top to bottan. As me who had never been physically seasick before, I scoffed my lunch of tinned salmon with asparagus and salad, feeling slightly uneasy.

At 14.30 I caild not navigate any more, and had a total paralysis in putting my head down into the locker to get my Oilskins and seaboots aut. The wind and the seas head risen and so was my lunch about to. Once oilskinned and harnessed up, I practised the mariner's ancient call to "Hughiee!!!

The swell had growm in size to something I had never encountered before. We sailed up and up and up the side of each swell, and then down and down. They were very lag and we collectively estimated then
to be 30 - 40 feet fran top to bottan. All I could do was steer the boat with the spray coming over
the bow, over the boat, over the sprayhood and then over me. I was still heaving my heart out regularly, but eating the odd Ryvita. The night wore @ and I finally went below at 0400, wet, tired and still very ill. Martin had also been sick since teatime and many plastic bags had came up and over the side fran my berth where he lay prostrate. My relief at 0400 was very perky with a cheery "Good Morning!"
- I won't repeat
my reply!

TUESDAY 5th MAY 0800 I was fast asleep in the pilot berth when I was awakenend as the engine was
shut off with claxis of smoke. The engine water inlet seacock had broken off and overheated the engine. The top of a mastic tube cured the problem. We sailed for fair hours to cool off the engine. The winds were still strong and the seas still rough.

1000 There was a lad crash as our radar reflector crashed down aon deck and then over the side. The rivets a the crosstrees had pulled aut. We had eight attempts to get alagside it and it took all
four
of us to get it a= board. TI think we were all thinking
how difficult it would be if it was me

of us, but no-one said anything. I was cold, wet and sick, and my gear below had got wet. Oh what had I let myself in for?

2100 Nearing Oporto, the evening meal was served up and I tried my first meal for a day and a half. Cannellani an Ryvita. The seas were flattening out and I felt a lot better.

2300 Secured in Oporto after having a devil of a job finding the entrance. We were now pumping the bilge every half an hour. 167 miles logged so far. I didn't think much of the first leg!

WEDNESDAY 6th MAY The morning was spent finding the leak and curing it. We also had to change the
altemator
which was putting too much charge into the batteries and boiling them up. The boat was also in quite a mess after the heavy weather. Brunch and went shopping. Tasted a super crab salad in a local restaurant. We were so tired after brmch a sleep was called for. Late aftemom, provisims were bought in the port area where the ladies kept smiling at us? The Oporto Yacht Club visitors' books made fascinating reading of all the worldwide ocean voyagers who had called there.

In the evening we caught a bus to take us the 14 kilanetres into town. We were directed to a tourist
restaurant by a policeman, but we decided not to eat after qe beer. They wanted 350 escudos for the beer and 1800 escudas cover charge. CRUISER NEWS

For the March Cruiser Meeting I have arranged a talk and video film covering an event of a slightly different flavour. The subject is '‘'The Three Peaks Yacht Race' and the speaker will be Duncan Phillips.

As an introduction to this event I have included Duncan's comments providing some background to the race:

"The Barmouth to Fort Willian Three Peaks Yacht Race was the brainchild of the famous explorer and venturer, Major H.W. Tilman. At the time, 1977, he was living in Barmauith in West Wales, and two local doctors conceived the actual details of the Race. The Race has been canpeted each year since then and has grown in number of entrants and is now a fiercely contested sailing and manning race.

An outline of the race is:

Yachts of any size or type may canpete with no handicapping.
Crews to number
5 in all, with any 2 to mum and climb each mountain.
The overall sailing distance is about 400 miles, and running about 74 miles, with maintain ascents totalling
11,176 feet.
Boats have to sail fran Barmouth to Caemarfo - mxunners ascend Snowiao, 3,560 feet and distance of
24 miles, retuming to boat totally unassisted.
Fran Caemarfon to Ravenglass Cumbria Coast by any route; mmners scale Scafell Pike, 3,210 feet and 32 miles, —
Then to Fort Willian (Corpach) by Mull of Kintyre to climb Ben Nevis, 4,406 feet and 18 miles. The Race finishing
when runners return to boat.

Total number of boats restricted to 35 because of berthing problems in the harbours.
Boats must canply with D.O.T. and Yacht Racing Standards for Category 3 Offshore Races.
Runners' equipment must contain minimum for mountain survival.

The race is run in June - usually the nearest Saturday to mid-summer with a convenient late aftemom
high tide. I have personally canpeted sane 6 years now, skippering a boat for 5 of these and taking part in the running. We have had various results fran finishing 10th to not finishing at all.

The important point is that anyone can enter. The purpose of the Race is to prove endurance; capability of finishing at whatever place is a tremendous achievement for those taking part."
DUNCAN PHILLIPS.

These and several other poems, all with a '‘watery' theme, can be found carved on some of the paving stones by the Thames near the Royal Festival Hall. TI believe they were put there when the Royal Silver Jubilee (1977) Walkway was laid out. I liked these two so much that I scribbled them down,

Down the stream the Swans all glide,
It's quite the cheapest way to ride.
Their feet get wet, their tummies wetter,
I think after all the bus is better.
(Spike Milligan)

Enjoy thy stream O harmless fish,
And when an angler for his dish,
Through gluttony's vile sin
Attempts, a wretch, to pull thee out,
God give thee strength, O gentel trout,
To pull the raskall in.
(John Wolcot; 1801, which accounts for the spelling)

MIRROR NEWS

Happy New Year to all the Mirror Fleet.

Now is the time to start thinking about the coming season and preparing your boat. We are not much further than the thinking stage ourselves. Damian ventured out to the garage one day where Bumble is in residence awaiting attention but soon returned requesting a heater. My reply was unhelpful and Bumble is still waiting! Lars Tinn is up on a rack above Bumble so will probably have an even longer wait for attention. ("Thank goodness for fibre glass boats," I can hear some people
saying!)

The season starts early this year - March 27th - but it would be nice to see some
red sails out with the Solo Fleet. Their Fleet Captain, by tradition, buys all the intrepid Solo helmsmen a pint on that first day. Perhaps we need that sort
of incentive - how about it, Mike? A mug of soup would do and probably be more
appropriate!

The Dinghy Park is being laid out in a slightly different way this year; the Club will be providing stakes for your boat. If the positions are wrong then blame Malcolm Stuart who organised a few of us at the Christmas Working Party to measure out the area and put in posts and string to his measurements! This was done so that John Rutherford can easily place the stakes. I believe that it will be "first come, first served" as to where you actually park your boat; another reason to sail the first Spring Points races.

The Cadet series is longer this year, 8 or 9 races instead of the usual 6, and some of these are being held on a Saturday. I hope the Cadets will be able to manage a Saturday as well as a Sunday. I don't know if we can but we'll try! I mention this here because a lot of Mirrors are sailed by Cadets and I hope you
read this article. (...as well as my other reader!)

See you in March,

FRIDAY 8th MAY 0400 My watch began. We had been dodging the inshore fishing fleets all night and
we had now rounded Cape Finisterre (I had always wondered where it was) with our diesel mmning lo. At Cape Villano lighthaise we altered course eastwards. We were now round the tip of northem Spain and entering the Bay of Biscay. A decisiam had been made to pull in somewhere for diesel although nme of our charts had any details of approach. We had large scale charts of only the places we were to visit. Our present charts covered Gibraltar to the Bay of Biscay, sane 500 miles. After a day's nm
at 54 knots average, we moved only several inches the charts! Not like navigating on Thames estuary
charts. On our approach to the most beautiful bay in which the town of Comme is situated we were directed across the bay to the village of Laxe where a fuel pump had been seen aon the end of the jetty by a passing
Moody.

1030 No qe could be famd to sell us diesel, until, with a lot of sign language, we ascertained that it was tokens only for the local fishing fleet. The sun was very hot by now after being at sea. I had drawn the short straw and, amned with a five gallm can, I climbed aboard the fish collectio lorry “mon a ane way trip inland. The driver spoke no English and me no Spanish. He was taking me sane 16 kilanetres to a service station at Cabanas. I had my piece of paper with the name of the village where I started from firmly in my pocket. It seamed to me as if he were taking me to Madrid. My head was spinning fran lack of sleep and no food, but the scenery was beartiful and lush. I was dropped off at a garage where I bought 25 litres of gas oil at a cost of 1300 pesetas. I then started thumbing a lift, much to the amsanent of the garage staff. Thirty minutes later the lady in the garage fixed me up with a lift with a lady and child in a Renault 5, again I had a language barrier, but, with lots of smiles, off
we went. I was dropped off 3 kilanetres from Laxe and the boat, and started walking the last two miles carrying the five gallos of diesel. There were no cars around as it was lunch time. The soinds and smell of the camtryside in summer were breathtaking, the vegetation was green and lush and the scenery was beautiful. At last I got a lift from a Spaniard who spoke English. He got me back to the boat and my breakfast at 12.30. The others had been shopping and had sampled the local hostelry. I had been up since 0345 and was now sanewhat cheap crackered.

1300 To sea again. launch was fresh grilled sardines, with the grill pan tied into the cooker as we
met the Atlantic swell again. Delicious! - followed by fresh strawberries and yoghurt. I slept the
aftermmoanaway happily. I was third in line to shower at teatime as we approached La Carma. TIwas all soaped and lathered up when the water ran out —- oh bother!

om1930 Secured at a pontoo for the first time this trip, we then went ashore and re-showered and telephmed wane. La Carona was a very lively place as we ate a hearty evening meal ashore. Everyone was aut
pranenading or sitting
in the many cafes. The atmosphere was very friendly.

SATURDAY 9th MAY After a good night's sleep we spent all morning working an "Ocean Challenger", cleaning,
repairing, checking, refuelling and watering. We all went into tow for brunch of Paella and beers
followed
by a walk aromd town. The shops were closed in the aftemoa, But they were impressive
and
expensive for Spain. We faimd a supermarket open and spent £45 on food, and then lumped the six-bags-full back to the boat. Talked to three people who had just arrived from Falmouth in a Westerly Corsair. They'd had a force 9 wind up the backside all across Biscay, it didn't sod too good. We met many other voyagers, sane going north like us, but most going south. We had a good yam with all of them,
swapping experiences. Yau do meet interesting people who cruise - three of them had arrived just behind
us in a traditimal thirty footer called "Mrs Muir" en route for Southampton. She was crewed by two guys fran Liverpool, and skippered by a chap fran Chester. It was their first delivery job.

Saturday evening was spent in the company of "Mrs Muir's" crew. We had a most disjointed meal with
large helpings of wine followed by a taur of the town ending in the waterfront cafes with local brandy and cigars. The is sanething special about the Liverpudlian humour.

SUNDAY 10th MAY Today's The Day! 7099 Awoke after a sound night's sleep. A thunder stom was in
progress
and nobody wanted to get up.

1000 Preparations in progress, but it was still raining heavily.

1100 Slipped La Carma after eating our first meal all sitting rod the salom table. The rain had stopped and we were all full of hope as well as breakfast. We headed north with a bit of west across the Bay of Biscay.

1300 Two hairs out and what little wind there was, was an the nose. The sea was calm,only 300 miles
to go before we get to land again. I slept the aftemom away - the calm weather was a real treat.

1800 It was my watch now. The sea was still flat, but the day had became more and more overcast. It
looked
as if there was a lot of rain about. No more lying an deck sunbathing. Everyone now in hats,
jumpers
and oilskins. We were now 42 miles aut and the wind was just picking up from - guess where
- northerly! We were in radio camtact with "Mrs Muir" who had left several hours after us. They were
steering 018 degrees true, more directly across the bay than we were. We intended altering to a north- easterly course the next day, when we were expecting to pick up a NW 3 4 wind. Not a thing in sight
as I looked forward to my dinner of corned beef hash.

2200 All alme mTMm Deck. No.1 genoa still was up, but with the engine still ticking over. Darkness fell with overcast cold clear weather. Wind was still mm the nose. Y

MONDAY llth MAY 0400 Not much shipping around, although we had encountered a giant floating crane
lit up like a Christmas
tree. I understand we were slow at altering course, our helmsmen of the hour was mesmerised, thought it was a block of flats! Whilst aon my own I looked at the chart and saw that we were in a position where we had 5,000 metres of water beneath us. That's over 3 miles deep! Not at all the Thames estuary.

& Sparks their food is very good. We were getting silly with the boat's standing jokes, the skipper hid the foot away whilst Martin and I were
always hungry. Don, the other crew member, was permanently asleep when not an watch.

1600 - 1800 My watch again. The wind had finally arrived, we were tranping along at 7 knots.

2000 We now had five rolls in the mainsail and a full genoa, and were doing eight knots. We all sat
and discussed
the sky and claxd fommatim and thumbed our weather books, all agreeing it to be a wan
front caning through.

CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LAUNCHING AND RECOVERY OF CRUISERS

The O.0.D to be informed and suitable notices must be displayed for the information of dinghy sailors.

Large Boats Boats above 27ft. length will not be allowed on the hard when dinghy events are in progress. At other times they should be handled with great care due to their weight.

Tractors Only to be used by authorised drivers.

Winches When dinghy events are in progress, the winches must be under the charge of an authorised operator. Only the East half of the hard may be used, leaving the West half for dinghies.

At ALL times the following code should be observed:

e When winding up the slope always use the ratchet. Winching down the slope should be done by use of the brake with the winch handle(s) removed.

e Avoid sharp bends in the winch cables.

e DONOT shackle the winch wire back onto itself. USE THE CHAIN PROVIDED.

e tis the responsibility of the BOAT OWNER to ensure that the operation is done safely. This includes providing an adequate trailer and a sufficiently strong team of helpers.

e Leave winches tidy, return shackles, strops etc. to the garage after use, rewind cable tidily as riding turns can damage the cable.

e Report any damage or wear of any equipment to an authorised tractor driver.

e REMEMBER, it is your responsibility to check for the safety of any equipment in
use, if in doubt - DO NOT USE!

e _ If the tractor is used to pull boats up or lower them down the slope, the WIRE STROP MUST BE USED to allow the tractor to remain on the level and always clear of loose shingle.

Boat Trolleys _ If left submerged should be adequately marked to avoid damage to other boats.

MOORINGS INFORMATION 1988

The system we adopted in 1986, which is outlined again below for reference, was largely successful. We again did not receive any criticism from the River Bailiff for being too far out in the fairway. C row was marginally too far inshore but this will be rectified this year.

One boat went adrift in 1987 due to a scope failure, so check your mooring tackle in
plenty of time. Replace anything which is worn or suspect, IF IN DOUBT - RENEW.
New gear is a small price to pay for peace of mind or against the real cost of damage to your own or other boats.

Make sure your mooring buoy is of adequate size to support the additional weight of scope and bridle.

During 1987, dinghies have been damaged by striking submerged trailers whilst approaching the hard. Trailers must not be left submerged. It is the responsibility of the owner to ensure the trailer is recovered immediately the boat is launched.

Dave Thomas undertook a survey at the end of 1985 which confirmed that C row has a fairly constant depth but that A and B rows get significantly deeper towards Stone. So to allow for this please note the changes to recommended bridle lengths etc.
