CRUISER DOES & DON’TS

Over the last twenty years the Cruiser Fleet has developed from one of just a handfull of 18’ to 20’ cruisers to the present 120 plus fleet of boats up to 45’ in length. During this time a code of practice, based on practical experience, has been evolved, some parts of which are now Club Bye-Laws others are custom and practice. The purpose of this booklet is to acquaint new members, and remind existing members on how the Club operates with respect to cruisers, what equipment is available to you and how to get access to it.

Moorings The Club leases the moorings area from Maldon District Council. The moorings are laid in six rows, three are deep water (rows A, B &C) and three drying (rows D, E &F).
Rows A, B and C are laid in the spring and lifted in the autumn each year to ensure that they can be properly inspected and maintained. This is done in teams over a number of weekends, the dates of which are published in Navigans and in these notes which accompany the Year Book. Members will also be notified by their Team Leaders, see page 2, and they or their representative MUST be present on these occasions.

Mooring buoys must be of an adequate size to be afloat at all states of the tide and be marked with the mooring number. Mooring strops, if made of rope, should be protected against chaffe by polythene tubing. Anchors in A, B and C rows should preferably be of the CQR or Danforth type, but if Fisherman types are used then provision must be made for lowering themin the correct plane. Chain sizes and lengths are given on page 3. It should be noted that 9/4 inch chainis the maximum size that can be laid at the Club. Shackles should be wired, and shackles and swivels should be of the largest practical size as they are THE WEAK LINK in any mooring.

Tenders All tenders should have some form of identification on them. Tenders must NOT be parked on the sea wall (Anglia Water Authority Rule), or on the foreshore by the White Hut (Obstruction of a Right of Way). During the winter, tenders are to be stored with the cruiser, only one rigid tender per member.

Cruiser Park It is the resposibility of each member to keep their allocated area tidy-PLEASE put any rubbishin the bins provided. DO NOT park your car in the cruiser park if you are going out sailing, it may obstruct the movement of boats or tractor. If you need electric power, this is availablein the park from the standpoints and you must use the correct 15amp
waterproof plug - LEWDEN Part No PD 160/3.

DO NOT ATTEMPT TO USE THE OLD DOMESTIC ROUND PIN TYPE.

High The high pressure hose is available via the 0.0.D at weekends and by prior arrangement Pressure with the Cruiser Fleet Captain during the week. Please read the operating instructions Hose carefully and always ensure that there is oil in the reservoir.

Scrubbing At present there is no booking system to use the posts, this may have to be reviewed in Posts the light of the current Anti-Fauling legislation. Drinking water is available at the posts, the stop cock being situated by the green Bio-Pack.

Jack There is a 15 tonne toe jack in garage No. 5. Key available from the O.0.D or any tractor
driver.

Trailers It is the responsibility of each member to ensure that the trailer used for launching and recovery of his boat is suitable, not only for the boat but also for the conditions at the Club.

e Axles must be big enough to take the weight of the cruiser.

e Uprights must be strong enough to cope with the effects of the tide.
Pea sticks and string will not do!

e Wheels must be suitable for the hard and the field.
Small solid wheels will not do!

e Good steering is needed. With the increasing number of boats laying up at the Club it is important that trailers have reasonable steering as space is becoming
limited.

IF IN DOUBT - ASK!

The third and last instalment of Cadet Skipper Derek Hall's log from his sailing trip last year from Lisbon to St Helier.

TUESDAY 12th MAY Midnight + 5 minutes, my watch again. It had taken me 20 minutes to get aut of
my sleeping
bag, dress into full oilskins and hamess up. We were being throw about samnething awful.
I decided the genoa must came down. We put the working jib up, not an easy job in the dark with the seas building up, and every third wave caning on board. We all now knew we were in for a a blow!

0630 Called up on deck again, I had not been able to sleep. We landed the mainsail, the seas were getting
bigger
by the hour. We were doing 6 knots under the working jib only, the wind was up to a NW 7, they
had said it would be a NW 3 - 4, oh hell! The seas were getting bigger but were much shorter between
waves, very uncanfortable.

1030 Skipper managed to do beans an toast, followed by yogturt and biscuits with hot coffee.

1130 It was now up to a full Force 8 and the boat is being flung aramd everywhere. "Sea Scout", a
large
bilk carrier, altered course for us, but didn't answer our VHF call. Our positign was now very
approximate. "Mrs Muir" had caught us up, we met up in the middle of Biscay and were now three miles astem after a photo call. My writing in my notes at this point is almost illegible due to the rough seas. Biscay was really getting its revenge now. Very cold and wet an deck: now and we were two to a watch,
both an deck. We are hand steering as our Autohelm 3000 cannot cope.

wy
WEDNESDAY 13th MAY There is nothing worse than getting out of a wazm sleeping bag, putting danp
clothes and wet oilskins to face a contimous Force 7 and 20-foot waves with sameone throwing cold water at you for four hours at a stretch. Night watches were now very cold. The other three were now all
sharing
my gloves. Mostly we went over the beam waves which were now huge, although every now and then
the dam things broke as we reached the top and and were sent crashing down, which shook every filling in my head. Sometimes when we were at the bottan, the force of the wind blew the crest off and dow onto us. It is great fun trying to fix our position as we are now approaching Ushant. We sighted land after breakfast. I had never seen so many evil rocks and as many lighthouses in one area. Ushant is
certainly
a treacherous place. After a lot of time and effort we finally identified the correct approach to Brest (no roan for mistakes here).

1430 We entered the Part of Camaret in France, very glai to be there too. Our. log had recorded
388
miles. I stayed awake during the afternoon to have an early evening meal at a local hotel with our
friends
off "Mrs Muir". For 95 francs I started with half a dozen oysters which were scrumptious -
although I had trouble opening my throat to let them slide down - followed by Cordm Blew chicken with
cheese, coffee
and brandy. This was followed by one of the best night's sleep I had ever had.

THURSDAY 14th MAY Up at 0800 ready for the off again as we were @ a tight schedule. The weather
was awful, blowing
a hooli, with poor visibility. We poked our nose out and ran down-channel to find, the entrance to the Dufore channel, "Mrs Muir" had decided to stay put.

1130 We were back again having had the only dissent of the trip over the decision on whether to continue or return. My decision was to return, which was what we did. The rain was caning don in sheets and the visibility very low as we were cleared by the Port Authorities and the Custans after we had secured alongside and had dropped off to sleep. The day was spent reading and sleeping and exploring the village of Camaret which was picturesque and still very sleepy even in mid-May. Our evening meal was cooked
an board followed by drinks ashore.

FRIDAY 15th MAY 0800 We were ready to try again, our forecast was Northerly 4 - 5, visibility good.

1000 Slipped Camaret after paying mooring fees and a further visit from a Coastguard boat. We were
followed out by "Mrs Muir" and a Swedish boat who was heading for Brightm en rate to Gothenburg. The narrow channel Dufore is not so bad in good visibility.

1400 After tacking for two hours we were into the English Channel. Wind was still the nose after thirty miles logged, only one hundred and ten to go to St Helier.

1500 Amazing, we had freed off the wind and were sailing well.

2000 Off watch and was not @ again until 0200 to 0400. Still creaming along at 7 knots off the Brittany
coast, really fantastic sailing and we were knocking off the miles with a strong tide with us. Oh no, it was lasagne again for dimer. Taight was to be our last night at sea and we were allowed an extra tot after the weather forecast and evening news. The forecast was good and we were just beginning to pick up lighthouses. It was more demanding again allowing for tides and strong anes at that.

SATURDAY 16th MAY 0145 Up to relieve the skipper. It was very cold. To think I was due hame that
day, it seamed impossible I could make it. We were still sailing well, logging 6 knots, but we were now against
a foul tide.

0400 A good watch with brilliant sailing @ a very cold but clear night, although I had been unable
to get a good fix the small scale chart. Had to get my sleep now to be fit for Jersey later in the
day.

0830 I was up again. The engine had been started at 0545 when the wind died. We were approaching
Jersey
which looked good in the clear visibility. We entered through the Middle Passage, passing a type 42 Destroyer anchored in the bay.

1100 Secured in the marina at St Helier, just scraping over the ledge. I was looking forward to a good shower, several pints of Jersey's cheap beer, a slap-up lunch followed by an aftemoon's kip and Saturday
evening
an the town. As it tumed aut I got the shower and lunch time pints, ate lunch in the Wimpy bar as everything had closed after air drinks. I went shopping in the afternoon for gifts and caught the evening flight back to Sauthend. There were no flights left Sunday or even Monday to either Sauthend,
Stansted,
Gatwick or Heathrow.

In two weeks we logged 885 miles spending six nights at sea. An enjoyable experience although hard
work at times keeping up a tight schedule. Cruising is my thing, I would go again tanorrow if I could.

Don't rely too much an electrmics though, our Sat. Nav. never worked; our VHF gave trouble, and our
Autohelm
gave up an the last two days.

CAVITATION
& VENTILATION are camoanly confused with rubber bush damage but it is entirely different and costs consideraby
less to rectify.

Cavitation could be the result of poor propeller design, wrong blade area, or pitch for the application for which the propeller is being used. Usually the result of cavitation can be seen by metal "eaten" or “bumed" off the propeller surface or gearcase. These "bumed" areas are the result of vapour bubbles which have been formed by the water's inability to flow over or around poorly developed areas, such as damaged propeller blades, which impede the natural water flow. These bubbles attach themselves to a surface of higher pressure, such as the propeller blaje face, and cause mimite but high pressure impacts which erode the surface where they collapse.

Ventilation is the effect of extemal air or exhaust gases being made available to the propellers. The propeller blades, during their operation, have a pressure- and a suction side. When air is induced
into
the propeller's
working area, the suction, or back side, of the blade will accept any migrant air, thus causing loss of thrust, increase in motor rpm and poor performance.

Causes of Cavitation and Ventilation
are:
Too high a transan setting
Severe
tuum when in use
Wrong motor angle
Damaged and out-of-balance propellers
Fauled boat bottan or lower unit
Loss of converging ring fran a thru-tub exhzist propeller
In general, incorrect boat ‘set up'

Although it is not possible to repair cavitation bums it is possible to reduce cavitation and therefore reduce the production of cavitation bums. This is dme by cupping the propeller. upping is a slight tum on the trailing edge of the propeller. This reduces cavitatim, increases acceleration and reduces vibration. Cupping is also the equivalent of increasing the pitch of the propeller by me inch and this Should therefore be taken into camsideration when thinking of cupping a propeller. Cavitatim can also
be reduced by having the propeller blade thinned down as this reduces the high pressure build up.

ELECTROLYSIS

eeeeehhy is a propeller beyond repair when it has electrolysis?
Because the metal structure of the propeller becanmes so weak with fatigue that it would be dangerous to use it an a boat because considerable damage cauild be caused to the vessel, namely by a whole blame being “thrown off". It is also impossible to weld onto a propeller when it has electrolysis because the zinc, which would nomally be present in the metal of the propeller, is dram out and this zinc is needed to weld. w

---.eHow is electrolysis
caused?
Water, even fresh water, can act like acid in a battery. Two dissimilar metals immersed in water may fam an active "battery" actually generating a small current and eating away ane of the metals. This is called galvanic corrosion which is a wasting process that can go on all the time the craft is afloat and can attack all metal canponents immersed in water, especially the propeller.

Propellers painted with anti-fouling paint, especially anti-fouling which is high in copper content, may react with the metal of the propeller and cause electrolysis, render the propeller
inguseless. Bronze
Propellers should not be covered in any way. This is because an oxide layer builds up naturally over the top of the metal which renders the propeller slightly corrosim resistant. If there is no oxygen getting to the propeller metal, then no oxide layer can be built up and thus no “self protective skin" is present.

is electrolysis
ow stopped?
To stop electrolysis
all you need to do is fit an anode. Many boat builders fit Cathodic Protection (anodes) as standard
on new craft. It may be canpletely absent, or need renewing on older craft. There
are many
different types of anode available. There are anodes which attach to the hull of your craft, directly onto the rudder or skeg etc., or to the propeller shafts themselves, and also hanging anodes.

eeeeeWhat do Steel Developments Ltd recommend conceming electrolysis?
We strongly recamend that anodes be fitted to all craft. Installation of anodes to GRP and wood boats is simple and straightforward and can be undertaken by any owner or boatyard when the craft is hauled out. The anodes
must, however, be correctly fitted to the boat or it will not protect
the propeller ani
stem gear, etc. Every time the craft is hauled aut, the anode should be checked and, if corroded, then replaced. The propeller should also be overhauled ready for the next season ahead.

PROPELLER
CARE AND SERVICING

Why have your propeller Serviced and Repaired? Roughness, Cavitation, Corrosion and surface damage to @ propeller reduces its efficiency and hence raises fuel consumption. Steel Developments have canpiled
a list of useful hints about propeller care and maintenance:

Propellers are made usually of either Bronze, Aluminium or Stainless Steel but it is vital that all are fTMnaintained properly.

A propeller not only pushes the boat alamg but regulates engine rpm of which the rpm is directly related to horsepower
and the propeller
pitch is related to mpm. An example of this would be if your engine should have an rpm of 2500 but you can qmly get 2300, your propeller has too coarse a pitch. This ca bealtered by having
the pitch reduced by 1" which will give you the needed 200 rmm tobring the engine to its full revs and efficiency and so reduce fuel costs.

On your propeller there will be the propeller's measurements. If these are, for example, 10 x 12 then this means the first mmber (in this case 10) is the diameter, which is determined by doubling the distance
between the blade tip and centre of the hub. The second mmber (which is 12 in our example) refers to the pitch. Pitch is the blaje angle, and the 12" pitch indicates that in each propeller revolutia the
boat theoretically would advance 12" - but due to slip loss the actual advance is sanewhat less.

Using a damaged propeller will not only reduce the boat performance but can cause costly engine damage.
To obtain
the best possible performance fran your vessel you should have your propeller serviced at least
ance a year - and every time you damage it - by an expert. frying a "do-it-yourself" repair could well
cost
you more in the lmg mn.

alte following hints should be followed in order to achieve the best possible performance fran your vessel:

lt. ADWAYS CARRY A SPARE PROPELLER TO USE IN EMERGENCIES.
2s Propellers and stem gear must NEVER be coated with anti-fauling or metal-based paints, to avoid
Problems
of severe corrosion.
3. A suitable propeller puller should always be used when removing an inboard propeller.
4. NEVER run
a vessel for lag periods with a damaged propeller as you may cause same severe damage to your engine and stem gear.
5. Make sure you have an anode fitted to your vessel so yau reduce the risk of your propeller
and stem
gear fran electrolysis.

CRUISER RACING

Now that we are working up to a new season, it is time to give som serious thought to what type of sailing will allow us to obtain the most from our yachts and from our time available. Often, due to pressures of work and family commitments, we find we are forced to plan our sailing and we are not always able to go as far, or for as long as we would like.

Racing on the Blackwater is an excellent way of having an enjoyable day out and of using your yacht to its full potential whilst developing your sailing
skills.

The B.J.R.C. (Blackwater Joint Racing Committee) run a series of ten races through the season from May to September, aimed at the family cruising man and woman as well as at those who are committed racing helms. Races are timed to go out to sea on the ebb tide and return on the flood, having sailed around a series of navigation marks in the Blackwater and Colne estuaries.

Entry for the B.J.R.C. race series costs £5 regardless of whether you enter one or all ten races. This nominal charge also includes all the information necessary, such as the basic rules and race courses. You must, of course, comply with a few safety rules. Races are run using the P.Y. handicap system. Yachts without a recognised handicap would be rated by the B.J.R.C., and therefore no yacht is excluded.

In addition to this, there is also our Marconi Barnacle Points. This year there
will be two races held on the weekend of 23 - 24 July. With more than 100 cruisers
in the Club, I am hoping for a good response. Don't forget, racing is a good discipline. It checks your ability and sorts out those weak points, boat and personal, as well as being good fun.

As the Cruiser Racing Captain, I am interested to learn how many people would like to join us racing this year. Therefore I would be very grateful if all Cruiser owners would complete the form below and return it to any sailing sub- committee member.

I will be only too pleased to answer any questions you may have, so please do not hesitate to contact me any time.

SAILING IN ROUGH WEATHER

In the spring and autumn at Stansgate we frequently experience strong winds and. when these blow against the tide we can get very choppy and confused water, particularly between Stansgate Point and Osea Pier.

In such circumstances the Race Officer, the OOD and all members who have turned up to race will be faced with a decision.

Firstly, irrespective of what the Race Officer decides, members remain responsible for their personal safety and should not sail if they judge the conditions to be well beyond their present level of competence. The Race Officer will, in reaching his decision, assume that members have considered the weather conditions and have reached the decision that they can survive them when they sign on.

fee Race Officer's job is therefore not that of deciding what is suitable for the least experienced and worst equipped member, but only that of deciding whether or not it is safe to start a race for the more experienced members. We must recognise here that the only way of getting experience in sailing in rough conditions is. to get out and do it and we are only going to improve our skills by pushing ourselves a little. The Race Officer has therefore to make the difficult judgement on how far to let those who sign on for a race push themselves.

In circumstances such as this the Race Officer will consult with the duty Coxswain, the Fleet Captains and the oOoD. Any course set for racing must take account of the ability of the rescue facilities available on the day to recover crews who may get into trouble. He may therefore restrict sailing to the shorter courses, and faster boats like the Catamarans will have to put up with having their wings clipped.

The ultimate authority for all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of club members is the OOD, however in practice he will normally only exercise this authority in response to a request from the Race Officer for guidance, and would in any case take any decision affecting racing after consultation with the Race Officer.

fo summarise what is a cautious justification of racing in conditions that prompt thoughts of more comfortable hobbies:

1. Competitors must decide themselves whether or not they are competent to
go out in rough weather.

2. The Race Officer must consult the duty Coxswain, Fleet Captains and OOD
and set a suitable course or postpone until such time as a suitable course can be set.

BOSUN'S LOCKER

I would like to add my personal thanks to Murray and Peter for replacing Jack B's prop. shaft bearing, and re-aligning the engine. To replace the bearing (a 5" bronze cylinder with rubber lining), without removing the engine and shaft was a tricky operation requiring considerable thought. As well as spending a couple of evenings planning the job, Peter and Murray gave up a day's leave to do the work, I confess to having had doubts that the job could be done, and certainly did not expect that Jack B would be ready for the Bank Holiday weekend. (I even went as far as phoning a local marine engineering firm for
a quote - THEY did not want the job).

When an item of club equipment is found damaged one weekend, but is ‘miraculously' repaired and back in service a week later, it must seem to many members that the club has a ‘fairy godmother' with a magic wand. I hope the above notes will dispel such thoughts. The Club's ‘fairy godmothers' are usually, guys in boiler suits wielding, not wands, but tool kits (or on the admin. side, lounge
suits and pens).....

That was the enjoyable part of my article, now for a gripe! The failure of the shaft bearing was a ‘mixed blessing' because upon hauling Jack B out for that repair it was found that the boat had suffered some damage to the hull. Damage to the port bow had removed some of the glass fibre covering the edge of the foredeck, exposing an area of unprotected and splintered plywood. Chipping of the gel-coat on the corner of the transom had laid bare small areas of glass-fibre, None of the damage was in itself serious and a few hours' work and a fiver's worth of materials put things right. BUT despite requests in Navigans I was not actually informed about the damage. If Jack B had not been brought ashore and repaired, rain and spray would have soaked into the damaged areas possibly causing delamination, etc., etc.,

Please, if you damage a Club boat, or notice a fault in it or in its gear, please let me know as soon as possible.

I know it's embarrassing confessing to making a mess of things and I will probably growl and mumble in my beard, (I enjoy a good moan before getting on with the job), but at least I will be able to put in hand the necessary ‘stitch in time'.

‘nuff said. End of gripe.

MIRROR FLEET NEWS. .

The sailing season started on March 27th - but racing was abandoned for the morning because
of strong winds. However, on April 10th, Spring Points 3 and 4 were raced with five (I think) Mirrors turning out; is this a record for the Mirror fleet so early in the season ?

A longish course was set,for the morning race which was sailed in a good breeze. Alec Pembleton and Damian Boreham were single-handed {with Damian managing to capsize twice) but Steve Keeble, crewed by daughter Melanie, were well in the lead and looked all set for a good win. Unfortunately, the leading boats in the Catamaran Fleet discovered that the Goldhanger ('C') mark was missing and so all races were abandoned. Also taking part in the Mirror race was new member Alec Goodwright, with Georgina as crew. A warm welcom to Alec and Georgina who soon discovered the delights of mud walking by capsizing in the shallow waters just around the corner of the Stansgate Point. No harm was done and Georgina didn't appear to be bothered at all in this (her first) race. Lucy Boreham with Jenny Ball as crew maintained an upright stance throughout to make up the quintette of Mirror
Maniacs.

The afternoon race was won by Janet Keeble (single handed) to end a day which very definitely belonged to the Keeble family with Steve and Melanie finishing 3rd, just behind Alec Pembleton's 2nd place.

Spring Points 5 and 6 were sailed in very strong winds and and-adverse’tides, Again a good turnout with 6 and 5 entries respectively. This time, Damian had his crew, ‘Katy Rutherford, with him and they won both races . Janet’ Keeble was 2nd, Lucy 3rd and Jack and Diane Rusbridge 4th in race 5, whilst Lucy ftnished 2nd fn race 6 and the others suffered disasters of various sorts and all retired.

Spring 7 and 8 were held on Sunday, 24th April, which was bright and windy - and cold. Just how wy
cold that wind really was showed after the races with everyone complaining of numb hands, blue feet, pinched faces and wondering if a sunny, but sheltered, spot in the garden picking up weeds would have been a more sensible plan for the day. However, pleasures are relative; how wonderful those hot showers were -- you have your choice and takes your pick. It just proves how essential a wet or dry suit is for dinghy sailing at this time of year.

Race 7 was postponed until 12.15 because the Jack B was out of action (prop shaft bearing’ gone - or
something), and then a short course using 'F' mark was set. Only two Mirrors took part with Damian and Katy finishing lst with Lucy and Jenny in’2nd>position. This was repeated in Race 8 with Lucy
reckoning she-was a little closer to her:brother this time - but not a lot. For both races, the
wind was quite brisk, around 3-4.

A good start to the season and hopefully more of you Mirror Mariners (makes a change from Maniacs) will join in the fun and games of racing with Steve, Janet, Melanie, Alec,P, Alec G , Georgina, Jack and Diane, Lucy and Jenny, Damian and Katy in what is, undoubtedly, a marvelous place to sail.

Maggie Boreham

Jolly Boating Weather or The Spring Bank Holiday Cruise

The Cruiser Fleet's first Cruise-in-Canpany of the season was a visit to Brightlingsea over the Spring
Bank Holiday Weekend. The organiser/flotilla leajer for this event was Malcolm Yeoman in VARUNA II. TARA's crew consisted of myself as skipper/cook, Cadet David Ball as First Mate/Washer-Upper and Cadet Stuart Golding as everything else. Having a small boat and a yamg crew I intended to be quite choosy about the weather
so, like a respmsible yachtsnan, I visited the Landm Weather Centre qm the Friday before the cruise and paid £1.50 for a 5-day weather forecast. The forecast was for predaninantly
southerly
winds until Bank Holiday Monday, when the wind was to strengthen fran the south-west.

Malcolm had called a pre-cruise meeting for 10.30 am the Saturday morning bit unfortunately our car chose to have a flat tyre so aur arrival at the club was sanewhat delayed. However we arrived in time to load the boat, make a quick phone call to the Colne Yacht Club order dinner and to depart for Brightlingsea in bright sunshine at about lpm. The southerly wind ('Super, a reach all the way to the Colne') lasted
as far as Bradwell when it went easterly and freshened - right qm the nose! Waves getting
bigger - to
go on or WM into West Mersea or Bradwell was the question. Decided to put in a reef and plug (axe again I blessed the day I fitted slab reefing). We som settled don to the motim and devoted ourselves to a bit of navigatim. Name of this 'Down to the end of the Blackwater and tum left for us! To be honest, ane bit of sea looks much the same as another to me so we used charts and compass to find the cardinal mark marking the 'Molliette' wreck an Mersea flats and were then able to bear away for Brightlingsea.

By 5pm we were safely tied up almgside another yacht in Brightlingsea. Another 10 or so Marconi boa’ were already there. At 8pm we all gathered for dinner in the Colne Yacht Club and as usual the Col® laid an an excellent
meal.

Qn Saturday night the wind freshened and the rain cane down. The boat inside of us wanted to move aut at 8am qm Sunday so it was a reluctant sortie to move aut at 8an into wind and rain to let him art. The rest of Sunday was spent in Brightlingsea eating and taking the occasional walk ashore. The weather forecasts were unfavourable for days ahead and I was beginning to think of leaving the boat at Brightlingsea until the next weekend. Watching a small yacht being towed in by the Lifeboat at Sunday lunchtime did nothing to inspire me to leave the shelter of Brightlingsea creek.

By Sunday evening the crew of the good ship TARA were getting a bit 'cheesed off'. The midnight shipping forecast was for more of the same (strong south-westerlies) on Monday so I resolved to have a lie-in m
Monday morning.

I awoke on Monday morning at 7an to find the friendly face of Niel Pembleta@m peering through the hatch. It appeared that there was to be an easing of the wind for a few hours, did I fancy heading back to the Club? The initial reactio (from a wan sleeping bag) was No! However a sense of nautical responsibility
prevailed and rapid arrangements were made to leave - no time for breakfast.

We. broke the good news to the boat an the outside of us and they let us out. The wind was southerly
which
meant plugging against the wind and tide down the Colne but a reach up the Blackwater - not a bad bargain. J

An hour was spent motoring down the Colne against* the wind and rain, and as som as we could set a course for the Blackwater, the mainsail was set, double reefed, and about half the jib unrolled. A very brisk, if bumpy, sail was enjoyed until Bradwell was reached, when the wind dropped! Was this the lull before
the storm? Engine an for a quick dash back to Stansgate, and still it rained!

The mooring was reached about llam when a hearty breakfast was enjoyed before tidying up. The cooker heated the cabin and allowed my lag-suffering crew to thaw out.

Thanks are due to Malcolm Yeoman for organising the cruise and the evening meal at the Colne Yacht Club. This was a well-supported Club event which was only marred by the weather. Let's hope for better weather next time.

Ray Ball, TARA

Rescue Boat Competition -— Saturday 28th May 1988

This year saw the introduction of what we hope will become an important annual event giving some recognition to the valuable service provided by our rescue boat coxswains and crews.

We were fortunate to get a very professional judging panel led by Dick Townsend (Bradwell Coastgard), two representatives from the Essex River Police and David and Ione Saunders from st Johns. David went out on the water to monitor closely how the casualty was treated.

The brave casualties James Brill, Emma Henderson and Debbie Yorston jumped in from the scrubbing post two or three times each and stood up well to the manhandling. Its not often you see a drowning person smile.

The seven teams demonstrated a variety of different techniques for recovering the casualty but the most impressive by far was Trevor Milton in his catamaran whose very smooth pick up brought a spontaneous round of applause from the spectators. This years entries and the first three placings awarded by the judges were:-—

Malcolm Grant MSC Jack B
Dave Onyons MSC Jack B
Brentwood Sea Cadets Baddow Star

John Chandler MYC Jacomar 3rd
Barry Parker MSC Jack B
Bill Fletcher SSC Zodiac 3 2nd

Mike Battle gave our predicted entry of 100 boats in the Essex Chronicle
May 27th — he was one boat out, we only achieved 99. Our publicity officer
more than made up for this error in getting 24 column inches of write-up on the Regatta into the Essex Chronicle on June 3rd, and 17 column inches in Yachts and Yachting.

Frank Saville and Mike Hellewell played computer games on the hard over the weekend in the dry half of Charles Anderson's caravan, and came up with race results in record time. No problems with power failure thanks to the new cable provided by Malcolm Grant. Mike Battle's new token system also worked well, and avoided the problems of interpreting soggy signing on sheets. MIRROR REGATTA REPORT

Where were you all ? The turnout of Mirrors was either apathy or charity - apathy because you weren't interested or charity because you all thought it was about time your fleet captain had a chance to win something.

A meagre five Mirrors entered the Regatta, four club boats and one visitor. Liz Ballard and son Adam from Maylandsea Bay joined Janet and Melanie Keeble, Jack and Diane Rusbridge, Elizabeth and Anne Goodwright and yours truly, who with a choice of three crew decided to opt for the heavyweight version, Janet, due to the prevailing strong southerly wind on Sunday.

Capsizing was the order of the day on Sunday with both the Keebles and the Ballards taking a dip. Again this was a charitable jesture I'm sure, to give Janet and me a good chance in both races 1 and 2.

The Monday however was not the day for the more portly crews and helms. Having said that, the first wins must have gone straight to my head because on the first mark at A buoy, I decided it was best to sail back through the cruiser lanes rather than head out towards No.1. Both Janet Keeble and Liz Ballard stormed away and on the long haul from C to B they tussled against one another to gain tactical advantage with Liz just coming out on top.

With 2 wins and a third place for Battleship we decided to sit out the final race, which started in the lightest of breezes. Mike Turner (RO) put in an extra mark off Osea Island for the Mirrors. The conditions were a westerly wind (such that there was) and an outgoing tide. Having conquered the Stansgate spit, the Mirrors had to sail almost to Osea pier to take A mark and E mark to starboard. Liz Ballard came out the winner in this the final race but with Janet Keeble second, her fourth in the series, Liz Ballard was beaten into 3rd place overall.

So the Battles marked up their first major win and collected first prize - a
bottle of Gin! Not that we are ungrateful to win anything, and that it is the competing that counts not the winning, but I do think bottles of booze for winners of the "premier" event in the club's calendar is a bit OTT, especially for a fleet primarily made up of cadets. I've scoured every page of "Clubs and Classes" in the last three editions of Yachts and Yachting and in not one article or photograph have I seen winners presented with alcohol. Perhaps the Sailing Sub-Committee believe that it should be consumed and Che CompletelieDed 3 sealed again with a message saying "' I won Saltlor this at Marconi's Regatta" and then Lee thrown into the Blackwater as a promotional

Summer Points Racing: This has now started and it's fun, so where are you all?! So far, of the 20 registered Board sailors, only 6 have actually competed to date. Our earliest starting time is 11.50am on a Sunday and there are 10 races in total (see Yearbook for dates). There is no need to enter them all to do well. If there is sufficient interest, there should be no problem in participating in the Autumn Points as well.

Procedure is very simple: entries need to SIGN ON and identify their sail (not the board) by any visible marks or colours (so far this has proved sufficient, but if the numbers increase I will see about acquiring some stick-on numbers). On finishing or retiring, SIGN OFF. The race start is preceded by a 10-minute warning gun when our
class flag is raised - a yellow and blue vertically halved flag. Lots more
information in the Yearbook - read it! NOTE: I have been infommed that it is
etiquette to keep out of the way of other classes starting before us - races usually
start at 5 minute intervals.

Helms and crew had to face a fair old wind on Saturday, 2nd July, for Cadets Races 1 and 2, and sailing conditions were both exciting and testing. In Race 1, Richard Battle capsized (twice I believe) but David Ball (crewed by Janet Keeble) sailed into a good 2nd position behind Lucy Boreham (1st) and Debbie Yorston (3rd but catching up fast as they approached the finish). In the afternoon, the number of entries increased to 6 when 'the morning mob' were joined by Greg Hall (sailing PATCH) and Damian Boreham (released from duties at his local Gateway Supermarket). David Ball got a superb start, trapping Damian to leeward and spilling dirty wind onto Lucy astern. With the course of 'Jack B' mooring, D, F, and 'E' (somewhere near B) David held the lead to E with Damian 2nd and Lucy third; unfortunately, tricks of the tide got both David and Damian into trouble and, much to her surprise, Lucy found herself in the lead which she held to the finish 1½ laps later. On the way, Greg hall's mast fell down and Damian provided a spectacular spinnaker capsize with screaming accompaniment from his crew, Maggie Boreham. Richard Battle finished but retired (hit mark) and again Debbie Yorston was catching up fast in 2nd place, Damian was 3rd and david Ball 4th. Debbie's crew for both races was Melanie Keeble.

CATAMARAN NEWS

The more observant amongst you will notice that this is the first Catamaran newsletter this year, entirely due to the fact that the scribe's duties have been delegated by the Fleet Captain. This allows him more time to indulge his propensities for amour, female wrestling and amateur radio, not necessarily in that order.

The Cat Fleet is undergoing a healthy resurgence in numbers. A recent count showed a total of thirty boats, not counting those which the writer has never seen on the water. of these thirty, nineteen are regularly sailed. By far the largest class is, of course, the Dart 18, of which there are currently seventeen. Has anyone noticed the phenomenon
amongst our Dart 18 sail numbers? We have 2626, 3131 and 4747. The Dart 20 (Stampede)
section of the fleet has recently doubled its numbers, no less. That is to say that we
now have two instead of one. |

Whilst on the subject of numbers, it must be noted that whilst we have this large fleet . the boat park, rarely do we get many boats on the water at race time. So come along, helms, you will never discover your true talents until you pit them against others.

It gives us great pleasure to welcome the newcomers to the Fleet, namely, Clive from Leigh Sailing Club, Keith an ex-Windsurfer, Graham Baker and Steeve Keeble. Before someone else says it, I am well aware that there are newcomers that I have missed. Some I do not know about, some I am aware of but do not know names and origins. So my apologies to those. Please come and give me the facts and you'll get a mention next
time.

Graham Baker and Steve Keeble are the more notable newcomers for the fact that they are recruited from other classes within the club, Graham graduating from Mirror to Dart, and Steve from Solo to Hurricane. (The wind of change?) Now the Hurricane has_ the reputation of being very sophisticated, amongst other things. So ‘hi tech' is it, that we hear it will be christened "Fly By Wire" (but only in very small letters.) The word is that once the in-mast water ballast system system is sorted it will be something to watch. Go for it Steve and Dave.

Qn the racing front the summer points season is upon us, although there do not seem to many races taking place or people taking part. Nothing changes does it, and Trevor Milton seems to win them all (well, almost all.) Within the Dart class the normally all-conquering Duckmanton boat has developed a tendency to couple with racing marks. The age-old remedy of a well directed bucket of water hardly seems appropriate here.

At the time of writing the Piers Race is almost upon us and by the time you read _ this,
will be over - God and meteorology willing. Barrie Palmer will then be free to answer
queries on next year's race. There will be one more order of commemorative sweatshirts, and orders, complete with ten pounds cash should be passed to the writer.

The writer would also be grateful for any items of interest to the Fleet, e.g. news, requests for information, rumours, lies and scurrilous gossip; you know the kind of thing. As an example where are the photographs of Regatta Days promised by Andy Rimmer?

Your roof-top reporter,
Peter Flook (Dart 4747)

ADULT TRAINING 1.- 5 AUGUST 1988

As an alternative to the arduous routine of the full Cadet Week course we offered this year a rather laid-back course for adults which attracted a total of 17 with the four men well outnumbered by the fairer sex. We spent a very pleasant five days drinking coffee, socialising and, when the mood took us, learning how to handle sailing dinghies.

The course fell into a pattern of morning chats over coffee, with sailing in the
afternoon:

MONDAY Tiller Waggling, or how to make the boat go where you want it to go.

TUESDAY Capsize Drill, or how to get back in the boat when it decides to go its
Own way. Sailing practise round the buoys.

WEDNESDAY Resucitation Practice with St John Ambulance.
Man Overboard Practice, but only with plastic bottles because we had done the getting wet bit on Tuesday.

THURSDAY Basic Seamanship - getting the dinghy away from the shore and back again
without hitting anything on the way.

FRIDAY Cruise Day - not a lot of wind so we sailed to the nearest ice-cream shop.

Many thanks to the instructors Mike and Maggie Boreham, Janet Keeble, Caron Stuart and Bob Anderson, and to Niel Pembleton and Peter Coote who let us use their boats for the week to supplement those that course members and instructors managed to hide from the cadets.

CADET SERIES 1988 il.

Races 3 & 4 - the weatherman certainly had it in for the Cadets when he ( presumably a ‘he' ?)
followed up the fairly stiff winds of Races 1 and 2 with even stronger winds of Force4-5 plus for Race 3. The Race Officer set a prudent course of Jack 'B' mooring buoy, ,OD_ (three times around), thus keeping the boats within a confined area within the lee of the Clubhouse and sea wall. Even then, the waves and winds proved difficult to contend with and, of the four starters, only one managed to finish the race. Richard Battle (Mirror), Nigel Leeder (Laser) and Lucy Boreham (Mirror) all retired but Damian Boreham (Mirror) completed the course which was shortened to one lap.

With winds very soon Force 6 gusting, the Race Officer abandoned Race 4 without setting a course, not least because the Jack 'B' was, by now, busy assisting with the rescues at the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championship at Stone. In fact, the Jack 'B' spent the rest of the afternoon on this task and it is understood that at one time in the afternoon some 12 dinghies were capsized, whilst Yachts and Yachting reported Force 7 winds and 8 broken masts.

Races 5 & 6 - these races were held on 6 August at the end of the camping fortnight and, in contrast
to the previous four races, the Race Officer had a hard job to find any wind at all. Race 5 was
schedulled for 11.30 but was successively postponed to 13.00, 14.30, 15.00 and finally started at 16.00.
in pretty light wind conditions. This race was won by Lucy Boreham (Mirror) with David Ball (S/H Mirror)

The Ladies Cup - 1988

For the second year running the Ladies Cup was contested as a series of 3 races on a single day (ie. Sunday, 31 July) and some 14 lady helms signed on for the first race. The classes of boats taking part were Stampede catamaran (1), Dart Catamaran (2), 420 dinghy (3), Wayfarer (1), Solo (1), Mirror (5) and Embassy (1). Our thanks to the Race Officer, Rescue Boat Driver and their assistants.

Race 1 - a somewhat short race (KF1) of about 1½ miles taking approximately 20 minutes to complete. The 'sausage' course meant that the race was sailed pretty well in the lee of the sea wall with a dead run to Breezy and a beat in the reverse direction. This course was a severe handicap to the catamarans and they finished well down the list, two retiring and the remaining Dart finishing 10th out of 11 finishers. However, the course and short duration did have the advantage that all boats sailed in similar conditions of wind and tide and this resulted in a close finish with only 101 seconds on corrected time covering the first 8 places. Those helms who took the inshore course up to Breezy (in order to cheat the incoming tide) found they had to gybe to reach the mark - a manoeuvre which appeared to worry their menfolk ashore more than it did the lady helms. However, the men needn't have worried - most of the ladies competing have helmed before but (as usual) give up the driving seat to the men for the 'serious' racing.

Janet Keeble (Solo) kept very close inshore up to Breezy and won the race by 7 seconds from Lucy Boreham (Mirror) who, in turn, finished 11 seconds ahead of her mother Maggie Boreham (Mirror). Debbie Yorston (Mirror) must have thought she had got 3rd place ahead of Maggie because, as they both raced neck-and-neck for the finish line on a dead run, Debbie's bow was actually ahead of Maggie's bow - but Maggie was flying her spinnaker and presumably it was the spinnaker which reached the finish line first. If you've read Eric Twiname's book on the sailing rules, he illustrates a similar situation in his definition of 'finishing'.

Race 2 - the problem with a single lap race is that you don't get a chance to correct the mistakes you made on the first (and only) lap. Thus, Race 2 with its course of KT2 was welcome news - not only for the two laps but also for being able to get away from the lee of the sea wall and sail some reaches. Certainly Rosie Duckmanton (Dart) found this course more attractive to sail and she came 1st, 31 seconds ahead of Maggie Boreham (Mirror). Lucy Boreham finished 3rd (23 seconds behind Maggie) and Debbie Yorston sailed consistently to again finish 4th (12 seconds adrift of Lucy). Then followed the two Janets - Janet Battle (Mirror) in 5th place and Janet Keeble (Solo) in 6th place.

Race 3 - this time the course was further extended to 3 laps (KT3) and Rosie Duckmanton again came 1st - this time by a rather bigger margin of 2 mins 20 secs ahead of Caron Stuart (420) and Charlotte Burck (Wayfarer) Caron and Charlotte always look as though they enjoy their sailing and both improved considerably on their previous results. An interesting (and significant) deadheat for 4th place between Irene Hellewell (420) and Janet Keeble (Solo) meant that they shared the combined points for 4th and 5th places, each having 4½ points to their credit.

The much slower Mirrors and Embassy found the extended course of 3 laps too much as they battled with the increasingly adverse ebb tide on the last lap. None managed to finish the course, the best being Lucy and Maggie who managed to struggle round No.1 but couldn't get round 'A' mark; none of the others managed to get around No.1 and all retired.

Overall result - Rosie Duckmanton (Dart) was a very convincing winner with two 1sts to count and the 10th position from the 1st race as her discard. Lucy Boreham and Maggie Boreham both scored a 2nd, 3rd and Retired and so tied for second place overall, just 1/4 point ahead of Janet Keeble. Had Janet managed to beat Irene Hellewell for that 4th place then she would have come second by 1/4 point ; as it was, that extra ½ point made all the difference. It is not often that a dead-heat in the lower ranking places plays a real part in the overall result but, on this occassion, it made a difference. For those interested, IYRU Rule 11 applies. Full results listed elsewhere in this issue of Navigans.

Sue Fletcher (Embassy) was probably the youngest and most inexperienced sailor taking part but, nevertheless, had a good sail and came ahead of her mother, Val Fletcher, who was sailing the family 420. Irene Hellewell usually serves at the sharp end but, having swopped places with husband Mike Hellewell, no doubt enjoyed the experience and was pleased with her =4th with Janet Keeble. Pat Stuart (Mirror) had Adrian White as crew and one wonders if Adrian was tempted to stand on the gunwale, grab the boom and try to crew the boat 'sailboarder-wise'.

Family Note - did this year's entry establish some sort of record ? Have you noticed the three sets of mother and daughter helms ? In order of mother/daughter, they were Val/Susan Fletcher, Pat/Caron Stuart and Maggie/Lucy Boreham . How about trying to break that record next year ?

Report by Lillie of Lagoona and Little Annie Fanny

CATAMARAN NEWS

The event looming largest in the memory during last north must, of course, be the Piers Race. The event will, no doubt, be well chronicled by other correspondents but we have some comments of our own.

It is reported that those left behind were somewhat disappointed at the end, when, joyously greeting the returning sailors, they were met with deflated, perhaps disinterested, attitudes. It should be remembered here that the spectators saw two peaks of frenzied activity and in between nothing was happening. The sailors themselves had been on the water for around eight hours, and when returning to dry land the sensation of getting a sore backside off the hard deck led to relief rather than elation. So we apologise for not seeming to appreciate your support.

For my own part the lasting impressions of the race are how long it seemed to take from Clacton to Walton on the way out. There are wide spaces of open water out there. With other boats only visible on the horizon it was hard to suppress feelings of fragility and insecurity, particularly as the last rescue boat seen was at Bradwell. This was not helped when, at the turning mark, the sea-fret descended and a Visibility was severely reduced. For all that, it was a great day and all seemed to have enjoyed it, courtesy of the weather.

I won't attempt to re - thank all those helpers who have already received their
thanks. However, I am asked by the fleet to say a special thank you to Mike Battle and his army for the sterling services that they provided.

Last Sunday saw the final two races in the Summer series, when we actually had ten Catamarans racing. Someone must read this column. Congratulations must be offered to Graham Baker for winning his first race. Next Sunday sees the opening of the Autumn series, so let's keep up the numbers racing.

Don't forget the approaching Solo open meeting (Sat/Sun 17th/18th September) when we are duty fleet. Lots of bodies will be needed so please leave these dates open and communicate your availability to the Fleet Captain as soon as possible.

Your Catamaran correspondent, Peter Flook

CADET SERIES

The conlusion of Race 7 (on 7th August left the Cadet Series very much 'wide open' with 4 competitors in with a chance to take the trophy for 1988. Best chance was that of Lucy Boreham who needed only one more win to make sure of being the overall winner but other possible winners were Ian Fletcher, Stuart Golding and Damian Boreham, all of whom needed to win the last 3 races to win the series. For Lucy, the cancellation of one of the remaining races would have been good news; alternatively, if she could not get a win then the remaining races being won by different people would also have guaranteed her overall first place. However, it was not to turn out that way......

Race 8 was scheduled to follow the Jackpot but the Club's rescue boat was so busy dealing with capsized dinghies that it could not cover the Cadet race and it would have been unwise to set a course without adequate rescue boat cover. Given the presence of a rescue boat, it would have been possible to set a course in the lee of the sea wall which would have been a good test of sailing ability, and certainly there were Cadets willing and able to take part. However, given the wind strength and the fact of the Jack B being fully occupied with the aftermath of the Jackpot, the Race Officer wisely decided to postpone Race 8 until Sunday 21st August, when the last three Cadet races could be completed.

Races 8, 9 and 10 - come 21st August, the wind strength was predicted to be Force 5-6 rising to Force 8 offshore, but at the Club it was nearer Force 3-4 and sailing conditions on the water were really quite flat. Although the number of Cadets present promised some 6 boats, only 3 actually entered for the three races 8, 9 and 10. They were, Stuart Golding (crewed by Richard Carlisle); Lucy Boreham (crewed by Jenny Ball); and Damian Boreham crewed by Katy Rutherford); all of them sailing Mirror dinghies.

Damian won all three races quite clearly and so ensured his hold on the Cadet Cup for 1988; as crew, Katy secured three more wins to put her at the top of the Mug's Mug league table for the crew who sails most times in a prize-winning boat. The interesting bit was the close racing between Stuart and Lucy with some good tactical moves by both - plus some errors. Although Stuart took 2nd place in Race 8, Lucy reversed the position and got two 2nd places in Races 9 and 10.

Overall Result - the overall result was the closest for some years with Damian just winning the series by ¼ point over his sister, Lucy, whilst Stuart got his well-deserved 3rd place.

by and, before you know it, another navigans dead-line has passed by. As you read this, the Summer Points Series will probably have been completed and we can look forward to the Autumn Points Series before finally putting the boats to bed in mid-October.

Congratulations to Mike and Janet Battle on winning the Mirror Class in the Regatta - it was quite windy
at times so I am told. I wouldn't really know because I must confess that we were on a canal boat holiday with another family and, I must say, it was one of the nicest, most restful and most peaceful holidays I have ever spent.

Congratulations to Damian and Katie for winning the Spring Points Series; hard luck to Lucy and Jenny
for coming 2nd but getting no prizes - the Mirror Class was the only one which didn't manage an
average of 4 entries for the series and so lst place prize only was awarded.

The camping fortnight (inclusive of Cadet Week) was, aS usual, very enjoyable and equally most successfu 1. This was the 7th (or was it the 8th) Cadet 'Week' we've attended and all have been well-worth the effort This year 'the effort' not only covered teaching sailing to the very young, but also the somewhat older members who, in their spare time, carry out the duties of being parents to the Cadets. Although the lst week was a bit windy at times, the weatherman was kind to us for the following Cadet Week with its programme of sailing instruction. The wind was just enough to sail pleasantly, the sun hot enough to give us a tan and the number of people enough to keep things lively. Even our ‘traditional' thunder-
storm (yes - we usually have one at night) was a very muted affair and hardly anyone noticed the rather
weak lightning and the low-level growl of thunder which followed it.
.

More significantly for cadet Week was the large number of Mirrors which took to the water - there must
have been 12 -15 sailing .. At one time, as I looked towards Osea Pier, there seemed to be so many Mirrors sailing there thatI thought Maylandsea Bay must have been holding an open meeting but not at
all - it was our members having a fine time sailing on the mighty river Blackwater. The point is,
if you can get your boat on the water every day for the ‘once a year’ week of sailing tuition, it seems apity not to consolidate what you've learned by taking part in the Sunday racing programme.
So don't pack your Mirror away until next year's Cadet Week - keep it sailing and join in the Sunday
racing.

The club's Mirror 'open' event is to be held on 10/11 September. This is an event that definetely needs your active participation and it's worth having a go. We usually only get a few visitors from local clubs so you are not going to find too many Mirrors buzzing around. In fact, most will be the same people you sailed with during cadet Week.

DON'T FORGET - OQUR MIRROR OPEN NEEDS YOU

10/11 SEPTEMBER

Happy sailing
_

Maggie Boreham (Honorary Scribe to the Mirror Fleet)

The Jackpot 1988

This year's Jackpot started its 1st leg (to the Jolly Sailor) in Force 3/4 plus and finished the 2nd leg in Force 4/5 plus. Most of the Solo entries (except for Ron Greygoose) capsized sometime or other and 'hairy' moments were 'enjoyed' by most participants. Unlucky duo were Mike and Janet Battle (Mirror) who were caused to capsize after a close encounter of an alarming kind with a port-tack boat from a neighbouring race. Their exhilarating journey back towards the clubhouse on a glorious starboard-tack planning reach was suddenly and unexpectedly brought to an end near Osea and they finished in the drink and were thus deprived of a good 2nd leg result. As the Solos approached the end of the 2nd leg, the view from the racebox was, to say the least, interesting as we saw various helms capsize at high speed. Colin Willsmore and Ron Greygoose looked set for a neck-and-neck finish as each approached the finish from opposite sides of the river but Colin capsized as he reached the cruiser lines - only a little short of the protective lee of the sea wall. Barry Newboult suffered similarly, whilst Malcolm Gandy and Peter Collis capsized a little further up river between the pier and Steeple Point. Perhaps the thought of being so near the finish (after an exciting ride) caused a momentary lack of concentration; any suggestions of over-indulgence at the Jolly Sailor is strenuously denied.

Mona's Cup 1988

This year's Mona's Cup was rather sparsely populated with entries, only 6 boats taking part compared to 16 in 1987 and 26 in 1986. The Mona's Cup is an 'all-in' race (ie. cruiser and dinghy) and, for this reason, the 'long line start' is used. The 'long line start' is indicated by the letter 'L' after the course code letters and means that you must start between 'D' mark and No.1 but in line with the triangle on the race box and the mete pole . Those with long memories might recall that in the 1986 race some 21 out of the 26 entries were disqualified because they started between the mete and 'D' mark; this year only one boat made this mistake.

Of the 6 starters, 4 were catamarans and 2 were Mirrors, thus the entries represented the very opposite ends of the 'speed spectrum'. In fact, it was reminiscent of the Hare and the Tortoise fable and could well have been a re-enactment since Mirrors often do quite well in this race.

The wind was Force 4/5 (forecast rising to 6), the water was rough and there were plenty of 'white horse' to be seen off Osea. Mike Battle and Derek Holroyd (Mirror) found their weight both an advantage (keeping the boat flat) and disadvantage (slower speed, no spinnaker) whilst similarly Damian Boreham and Jenny Ball (Mirror) found themselves having difficulty in keeping the boat upright and consequently they shipped water up to the gunwales (without capsizing) and had to 'sail' into the shelter of the smoother water by Osea Pier in order to bail out. Their lightweight advantage was boat speed - plus spinnaker. The catamarans had a fine old time and they didn't take too long to get up to Heybridge and back. The finish leg was to round Breezy to starboard and finish into the wind between 'D' mark and the mete. Graham Baker showed distinct signs of not being able to find Breezy and, in the race box, we were taking bets on whether he would (a) sail to Stone (b) round Breezy to port or (c) capsize. However, he did none of these things and finished correctly having, as always, thoroughly enjoyed his sail (this time crewed by Dave Onyons). Rob Stahl was the unfortunate cat disqualified for incorrect start and it seemed a shame to have to deprive him of a finishing 'hoot' having sailed all the way up the river and back again. However, he was 'timed in' and would have finished third. Steve Keeble shows every sign of mastering the techniques of sailing his Hurricane every time he goes out and he certainly looked as though he was enjoying himself, as was his crew Dave Payne. Trevor Milton found the going very much to his liking and won the race; if he can tell me the name of his crew then he/she will get a 'credit' in the Mug's Mug League Table.

CADETS - BRADWELL FIELD STUDIES & SAILING CENTRE

My daughter Jenny and Lucy (Boreham) went to the Bradwell Sailing Centre for a week in August with the aim of achieving their RYA National Dinghy Certificate Level 5 to top up on their qualifications earned with Derek Hall's excellent tuition of our Cadets over recent years. They succeeded in gaining their Level 5 certificate, and enjoyed their week so much that they intend going back again next year if possible.

Ir case there are other Members who might be interested in their Cadets trying this course I have typed out below all the relevant information on what the Centre offers, taken from its own literature. Jenry's one week residential course cost £60 which we
considered very reasonable for 6 full days at the Centre - from llam Monday till 2pm
the following Sunday (though Jenny and Lucy did leave at 10am to hurry back to the Club to take part in a vital Cadet Race!

The Centre is situated beside the Creek at Bradwell Waterside on the River Blackwater. There is a main residential and administrative building, boat yards, workshops and a laboratory for field studies. The Centre can house 40 studerts plus six accompanying staff. Accommodation is in centrally heated rooms with full toilet, shower and drying facilities. There is also a lounge, dining/lecture room, ard a recreation room with table tennis and juke box. The meals are cooked by permanent catering staff but the students are required to assist ir other domestic duties. All equipment, including protective clothing for the various specialised activities, is provided by the Centre. (Ed's note: You'd need to take along your own wet suit if you usually wear one for dinghy sailing, they are provided by the Centre for those doing the Boardsailing Course only.)

SAILING Instructior is given in Toppers, Yachting World Day Boats, Oysters, Wayfarers, 505's and Bradwell 22's. Teams of experienced helmsmen and instructors enable complete novices to receive expert tuition. A safety boat is always in attendance. The Centre also has a 26' auxiliary sloop, in which all off-shore sailing, coastal and foreign cruising is done. Basic equipment for courses in seamanship, navigation and meteorology, covering the theory of the RYA/NSSA Proficiency and Coaching Scheme is also offered. The Centre is recognised as a Royal Yachting Association/National Schools Sailing Association Examination Centre.

CANOEING instruction is given in a variety of single-seater kayaks. Expeditions by canoe can be arranged on request.

CAMPING: Sailing and canoeing camping expeditions are also arranged, using modern lightweight camping equipment and craft suitable for sleeping aboard. All the necessary equipment is supplied.

BOARD SAILING. The Centre is equipped with a variety of boards, also with junior and intermediate rigs for the beginner.

ELIGIBILITY AND SAFETY REGULATIONS Courses at the Centre are open to all aged 13 and above. tudents who are candidates for a sailing or canoeing course must be able to swim 50 metres in light clothing. All persons using the Centre must abide by the Education Committee's safety regulations and accept the guidance of the Warden and his staff during the course.

CATAMARAN NEWS

Event of the north this time goes to the Catamaran Open held on the weekerd of lOth/llth September. An overall entry of 23 Cats. looks encouraging until it is realised that 14 of them are Club entries. Our Cat men must be complimented on this turnout whilst bemoaning the lack of visitors in any numbers.

The weather was not kind to us over this weekend, bursts of reasonable wind strengt always quickly abating to nothing at all for long periods. This weather of course did nothing at all to assist the administration of the event which was being run by our Solo colleagues and the courses can only be described as interesting. Thank you, Solos, for a job well done in difficult circumstances. Results as follows:

First: Stampede 63 Trevor Milton
Second: Dart 4469 D. Lloyd (Stokes Bay)
Third: Tornado 290 John Nickalls

An interesting innovation was the donation of a new trophy for Marconi Sailors participating in this event by Steve and Janet Keeble, entitled the "Old Codger's" Shield. Its concept is brilliant, Steve, quite the best thing you've done this year. Modesty prevents me from publishing the names of the first winners but carn I just add that if anyone knows of a 72-year-old trapeze artist, please put them ir touch with me.

The following weekend gave us the chance to be useful at the Solo Oper Meeting wher we hope we ran a successful event. On both days we were able to field 3 rescue boats which were not needed because, once again the wind did not appear. Thanks to all Cat men and women who turned up to help.

By the time this appears in print, sailing will have officially finished (although rumblings are heard of a potential winter Cat series.) It is to be hoped that everyone has enjoyed the season and looks forward to the next one. Do not forget the winter's social events, the first of which is the Laying Up Supper on the 19th November. Let's have a good attendance and show that we are surely now the largest class in the Club.

Your Cat correspondent

Peter Flook

THE MARCONI CATAMARAN OPEN MEETING - 10/11 SEPTEMBER
(through the eye of the hurricane)

(This is not meant to be an unbiased view of the evert, as from on the water it is impossible to see all of the action throughout the fleet.)

Saturday dawned bright with a force 2 wind blowing from the West. Owing to confusion
over first race start times the meeting was reduced from 4 races to 3, but to keep the troops happy Ron Greygoose, our intrepid Race Officer, set a practice race up to No.8 Buoy.

The race got under way after postponed start, and Janet (my better half who was crewing in place of Dave) and I had an excellent view of the rest of the Fleet streaming from us towards the first mark. By the time we got to No.2 we were in the lead and pulling away from the Fleet. The run back from No.8 to No.1 was fairly uneventful except that the wind was gradually fading. A quick reach to C and back “brought us into contact with Paul Metcalfe who was just rounding No.1 on his way to
C. We reached across to round A only to find that the wind had died completely and
we were forced to slowly tack up the shore by the Club.

As we reached the middle of the Hard, a voice cried out 'race abandoned!' and there on the Club flagpole was a limp ‘abandon' flag. At least we didn't have far to go to get ashore. Paul Metcalfe crept ashore about 15 minutes later ard most other boats drifted in on the falling tide.

After a leisurely lunch we dragged ourselves onto the water for the second race. Again the wind was very fickle and we made one of our yet to be forgotten lousy starts. John Nickalls_ shot straight into the lead. He started to cross the river towards the Club but the wind died and he tacked to the Osea_ shore. We were following a similar course but the wind held up and we made it across. We were accompanied by two Darts and the three of us spent the next ten minutes trying to get around the corner. The Fleet was now divided into two halves. One on the Osea shore and one in the bay. The wind made the race a lottery as it varied from force nil to force 2 and boats ten yards apart could experience the extremes. We swapped places with our little group, losing out by our slow tacking. A Dart led the way round No.2 eTMclosely followed by John Nickalls and Caroline. Two more Darts followed and then us, closely followed by another Dart.

As we drifted with no wind towards No.1 we watched Trevor Milton and Tom _ sail serenely up and round No. 2 with their own personal breeze. They must have gained 600 yards on the leading boats and then continued on towards the leading group containing John and the first 3 Darts. The rest of us? We still had no wind, just
tide.

Rounding No.1 and heading for C the leading group were in line astern. The wind was very localised with both Trevor and I managing to lift hulls at some point whilst others were just coasting slowly towards the mark. The shallow water forced me _ to bear away as the rudders were grunching on the bottom. This forced me to put in a tack at C and the yellow hulled Stampede shot past on his own personal gust. From C to B was again a procession and then followed the usual short tacking duel to the Club finish line. Although we overhauled the yellow Stampede, it was a race in which the Darts took the honours.

CONT.

10.

Cat Open contd.

Sunday was a lot better with the wind blowing 3 gusting 5. After a much delayed
start, the Fleet headed to No.2. This was our most disastrous start, with me actually falling off the boat! John and Trevor made their usual good start with Rob and Matthew not too far behind. We had Graham Baker and Dave Onyons for company as we set off to catch the rest. By the time we got to No.2 we had passed everybody except John, Trevor and the leading 2 Darts. Mike Duckmanton and Rosie were trying to make life difficult by trying to catch us on a port/starboard meeting. At No.8 just John and Trevor were ahead. JI do wish Johr would get a more colourful sail as it is almost impossible to pick him out from a distance, and a distance is about the closest we ever got!

Downwind to No.1 we chose a different route from Trevor. We were behind him and had nothing to lose. It paid off as we were first to Osea pier, where we promptly found @ hole in the wind. John and Caroline were well on their way to the E mark and the end of the first lap as we crossed them when tacking between No.1 and C.

"They will Finish after one lap," we thought. We had been racing about 90 minutes and the Sparks were a long way back. But no! There was John and Caroline goirg around again! By now the river was filled with boats and as we headed for No.2 we thought we could see the Committee Boat. But alas no. As we came up towards No.2 we found ourselves slightly to windward of an echelon of cruisers. We were all on starboard and in front were 2 Windsurfers crossing on port.

"Starboard!" we cried as one. "Starboard!" again. No reaction from the Windsurfers.

"Starboard!" we cried. - "You don't own the river!" came the reply. They were very
lucky, as a Hurricane is 8ft wide and they must have been $8ft 6ins apart. The cruisers were all trying to take evasive action as well, but we were clear so we left them to have an accident with some other unfortunate boat owner.

The rest of the race was uneventful, except that as we passed Osea pier on the way back, there were Sparks still heading for No.2. Janet and I were pleased to finish ahead of Trevor although he beat us on handicap (28 seconds in 3 hours).

Race 4 was a short affair and after our usual bad start we did not see the leaders at all. We spent the first part of the race trying to get through Peter Flook's dirty wind and the second part catching and passing Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine and _ the yellow hulled Stampede. Although we crossed the line ahead, they murdered us on handicap. JI understand that Trevor beat John across the line by 1 second, which gave Trevor and Tom the meeting overall. John and Caroline finished 3rd overall with Janet and me 5th. Typical, they only had prizes for the first 4!

The highlight of the presentation was the award of the 'Old Codger' trophy to Peter Flook. It couldn't have happened to an older (and nicer) man!

Thanks must go to the Solo fleet for running the event and to the people who manned the Galley and Bar, and we look forward to returning the compliment with a couple of 3-hour races in a force 5 wind.

Steeve Keeble (fly by wire)

P.S. I understand that those little wooden wash tubs with the red flannels on a broom pole were also racing. Did anybody see them?

I would like to start by thanking all Members for the continuing success of the Club during the last year, and on behalf of the Club I would also like to wish Joan and Robbie All the Best for the future.

On the sailing side, the last year has been marked by some notable achievements.
