MARCONI SAILING CLUB - 1988 A.G.M.

Commodore's Report

Fellow members - friends - another year has gone by since I last gave you my report.
Little did I know then what a traumatic year it was going to turn out to be both personally and Clubwise.

Over the past year we have had quite an eventful time which started with the retirment of Claude Emerson to some well earned rest in the middle of England. This resulted in two abortive attempts to recruit a single replacement, with us finally finding two people to share the job viz: Dave and Darren, with all its attendant difficulties in effective control and we are back to one again now!

For some time past now, members have been increasingly suggesting that the load of work, or rather chores, falling on their shoulders was becoming unacceptable and as a result we asked the MASC to investigate the possibility of being able to offer a full-time steward accommodation. As a result, planning permission for a house was
sought - rejected - and is now on appeal. Whether, if the appeal is successful,
the house is ever built will depend entirely on us the members because the cost will not be insignificant. The only help against this will be increased membership and
-~if you remember, this was one of my messages to you last year - each of you recruit
one member and our financial worries sink into the background. As Pat will no doubt be telling you, the recruitment drive was beginning to show some success, but we do need more.

Over the years I have always been adamant and vehement that our Club was successful because the members belonged and they belonged by being involved and were involved by supporting the essence and spirit of self help. This support must continue and
we will remain successful - BUT I think the time has now come, because of our size,
when we must seriously consider removing the burden of chores from our members by having a full time steward. If you agree then give your new Commodore your support by recruiting one more, at least, new member each by Easter. Remember though, I
said CHORES - not Working Parties - you are and will continue to be essertial work
units for these belonging activities!

We have made a start in trying to drain the Cruiser Park - but it obviously still
needs some more work done on it - but at the end of the day I think we will have
to spend a great deal of money and have it done properly.

um There were for me three highlights this year. First we had a Regatta which, with Malcolm's energetic input should continue to improve over the years especially if we build on the new conditions and procedures we introduced this year. Second, I actually managed to spend the whole of the camping fortnight at Stansgate which I found very instructive and enjoyable despite never having a minute to myself. z think a lot more members should consider attending this camp. Third we had an inaugural Piers Race which, thanks to the clemency of the weather, allowed us to see and learn our mistakes without getting into a serious sailing incident. Long may it continue and become the prestigious East Coast Race it deserves to be.

You will note from the papers already issued to you that your Committee has managed, I think for the first time in several years, to announce Committee nominations for all positions. This is excellent and it is essential that everyone will offer their services from time to time without being specifically asked. In particular your committee must have visibility of ordinary members who will be prepared to ‘do their bit' So do not be bashful, drop broad hints to Officers and Committee about what you may like to do.

You will note that your President, Jack Pateman, is relinquishing his post and that we have been very lucky in securing the services of Martin Jay for this position. Our grateful thanks to Mr Pateman for all he has done for us in the past and a rousing welcome to Mr Jay for taking on the mantle.

One note I had hoped I should not have had to announce to you. We have still failed

4.
to reach a final agreement with the General Committee of he M.A.S.C. for the use of the assets. On two occasions in the past 9 months we thought we had an agreement only to find the General Committee would not ratify the plan. We were trying right up to Friday evening to come to some compromise. In this respect Gerry Wignall has worked very hard to arrive at a settlement and we have found him helpful and constructive. It is now obvious we must have some representation on the General Committee, and to this end, John Weedon offered himself for co-option during the summer, but now faces an election this coming week. WE MUST ENSURE JOHN IS ELECTED so please every ordinary member of the Club make the effort to go to the M.A.S.C. to vote. Voting is all week, so do take your MASC membership card, and take the few minutes it needs. You will have up to seven votes to cast, but you need only cast one for John. We are on the last legs of the negotiated compromise and I think that if we had not been up against an election next week we may well have had a settlement for a five-year term with an extension of two years if a new five-year term had not been agreed by the end of the fifth year. But in case of difficulty Niel and I intend to brief Mr Jay in the next week or so. What we can say is that the total figure is known to within a few hundred and this should enable us to formulate reasonably accurate budgets.

I have kept you all long enough but I cannot conclude without paying unstinting tribute to the other Officers, Committee and Members for the wholehearted support I have enjoyed over the past two years as your Commodore.

And finally, if I may turn to the personal trauma I alluded to at the beginning of
this report. It is not unique to me - there are many others here today who have
suffered; are now suffering; and unfortunately still others who don't know it, like me last year, yet to suffer. I mean of course the indignity of redundancy or redeploy ment. I mention this not to raise any oohs and aahs but to try and show you all
the strength and support our Club - or which should more appropriately be called
our Community - can afford to its members. The true empathy which emanates from
its corporate being and which can be so effective in combating depression is priceless -guard it well -it is what makes our Club GREAT. Continue to show my successor and
all his successors the same support you have shown me and you will - No, we will
- have a still greater Club. I hope my family will be able to remain members for
many years to come and if we can escape from Lincoln, the Sims' tent will be with you for Regatta and Camping fortnight.

Robbie Sims, Retiring Commodore, A.G.M. 1988

SOLO NEWS

At the end of another successful sailing season I would like, on behalf of the Solo Fleet, to express my appreciation to Dave Onyons and the other Rescue Boat Drivers for the excellent support provided for the racing this season. Our thanks also go to those members of other Fleets who supported our racing programme with Race Officer and other duties.

The Fleet AGM took place at MASC on October 12th and I will summarise a few of the key decisions taken here:

1. The Fleet would support the Eastern Region's attempt to field a team for the Inter-
Region Championship at Littleton S.C. on 6th November, even though this clashed with the Club AGM. For this and other reasons the Fleet felt that it would be more appropriate to hold the AGM at MASC midweek.

2. The provisional 1989 sailing programme was found to be generally acceptable although
it was felt that pursuit-type racing on a Sunday should be kept to a minimum.

3. More Sunday evening barvecues would be organised in 1989 - Ron Greygoose to arrange.

4. John Salmon agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for a third and final year. Dave
Nixson agreed to continue as Vice-Captain. ew

5. The September 1989 Solo Open meeting should be a single day event (on a Sunday)
with three races in a day. In order to achieve the tight timing of such a programme it was felt that the meeting should be for one Fleet only.

6. John Salmon (Fleet Captain) and Malcolm Gandy (Spring Points Series Winner) were
charged with deciding who should receive the Frank Savill Trophy which is awarded each year to the Fleet Member showing most improvement. The 1988 winner is Janet
Keeble.

7. The January Solo Supper should be repeated, preferably at the Cross Keys again
- Pat Stuart agreed to investigate.

8. A provisional date of April 8th was fixed for a repeat of the Solo Fleet Dinner
Party at Stansgate but this event will only be held if someone volunteers to organise it. Any Fleet member who would like to take this on should let me know.

The final Eastern Area Open Meeting of the season took place at Fishers Green on
2nd October with the usual minimal breeze. The event was won comfortably by Joly,
Reece from Broadwater SC. Seven MSC helms competed, gaining finishing positions
of: 2nd John Salmon, 3rd Ron Greygoose, 5th Malcolm Gandy, 6th Dave Nixson,
8th Roger Smith, 10th Janet Keeble, 14th Colin Willsmore.

This left Alan Burrell of Half Way YC as Eastern Area Champion with MSC helms filling the next five places in the order: Malcolm Gandy, John Salmon, Ron Greygoose, Dave Nixson, Roger Smith.

The Mirror Fleet AGM was held at MASC on Friday 11th November.

1. Mike Battle agreed to continue as Fleet Captain for one more year only, with Debbie
e~Yorston as assistant, Debbie to take over as Fleet Captain at the end of the year.

2. To encourage a larger turnout for Mirror Racing, it was suggested that a Mirror
Teach-in would be held in the summer - less confident sailors to be put in with
experienced ones to help them improve their skills and learn about racing. Also it was proposed that advanced sailors could be shown tuning of their boats for best
performance.

3. Mike Battle said he would like to put up a Prize for the lst ‘Beginner Cadet'
over the line in the Mirror Open to encourage Cadets to enter the race who have not done so in the past as they felt they had no chance of winning the race. It was also suggested that the Mirror Open should be a series of 3 races on one day, instead of over a whole weekend.

4. It was decided that the Cadet Races should no longer be held on Saturdays because
this can be less convenient and makes the Cadet Series seem not as important as that
of other Classes - which of course is not true! It is intended that on each of two
Sundays there would be 3 Cadet races, with the rest of the Series fitted in as normal. On these two Sundays it was proposed that Pursuit Races would be held for the other meTMFleets. It was also hoped that a Mirror Fleet Barbecue be held after sailing on these two Sundays and that the Mirror fleet might hold one or two other social
activities.

5. The Fun Day during Camping Fortnight was a success and it was hoped it would be
an annual event. The Club's Regatta had also been a great success though Mirror involvement was disappointing and it was hoped that more would take part in the future.

Finally, it was generally accepted that 1988 had been quite a good year, but next year we are going to boost our numbers and get more of those sixty-or-more Mirrors sitting in the park out on the water!

LOWESTOFT COLLEGE - SURVIVAL COURSE FOR SMALL BOAT USERS

This is a one day basic Sea Survival course designed for the small boat user. Instruction is divided into two main Parts:

a) Theory and demonstration of raft and equipment in classroom, Survival problems
and solutions!
-

by Practical wet drills with liferaft and jackets.

The course is based on the inflatable liferaft, but it also covers aspects where a liferaft may not be available. The actions required at any particular stage during an incident are dealt with so that threats to life are minimised.

Courses are normally held at Lowestoft College where there are purpose facilities, including a heated training tank and a wide selection of survival equipment.

The course starts at 0900 hrs and finishes at 1700 hrs with a lunch break of about an
hour. A lounge area is available for use at coffee and lunch breaks, and coffee machines are on site. Meals are not normally available.

A swimming costume and towel are required and if you would like to test your protective clothing and lifejacket please bring them along provided they are clean. There are lifejackets etc, available at the College.

NAUTICAL BRAIN TEASERS

Below are some nautical terms and an imaginative attempt to describe their origin. These attempts bear no relationship to reality. Why not send in a few of your own.

Jib Sheets : Named by a bosun, in Nelsons time, who compared the quality of the rope to bed clothes in a Gibraltar doss house.

Mizzen Mast : Caused by confusion at English Harbour, Antigua, when a short sighted local talking to the captain of a ship of the line, mistook his ship to be a 2 masted vessels and said, "If you've got a 3 masted ship, you've got a mast missing!"

King Post : When sailing ships transported Official letters to the empire they used to store the sacks close to the main deck support beams for increased stability. As the term Royal Mail had not yet been coined, the area became known as the King Post.

Fore Deck : In the sixteenth century it was common practice for ships to have bow and stern castles. The purpose of these castles was to give the best advantage to the ships weapons (arrows). Each castle had many floors (decks) but for stability reasons four was considered to be the maximum. Hence the exposed deck at the front of the deck became known as the Four Deck.

Tiller : In early times it was considered that a ship travelling through he water made a motion like a plough through the soil. The man who steered the plough was called the Tiller as that is what he did, and this name was applied to both the man and the steering device on the ships.

HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR FINAL

Saturday 8th October saw the top Helmsmen from the four major fleets in the Club assemble at Stansgate for the 'High Noon' of the season to decide the Marconi Sailing Club Helmsman of the Year 1988. Damian Boreham represented the Mirror Fleet, Mike Boreham was to have represented the Handicap Fleet but pulled out to be substituted by Mark Savill, Malcolm Gandy was the Solo Fleet representative and John Nickalls from the Catamarans.

The contestants are the helms who achieve the most consistent performance throughout the season up to the end of September. Again this year the Sailing Sub-committee agreed to sail the Final in Lasers, arranged that each helm has a sail in each boat.

Boats were provided by Mark Savill, Mark Strong, Derek Webb and Derek Holroyd. I would like to thank the owners on behalf of the Club and the Contestants for making the event possible.

October 8th saw a Force 4-5 Westerly making life difficult. All except Malcolm Gandy had an involuntary swim to freshen themselves up and John Nickalls enjoyed it so much he kept going back for more. Either that or he was looking for the other hull! Malcolm and Mark had a close race with Mark getting line honours and Damian battling to a gallant 3rd.

At this point, much to the disgust of the Race Officer, the combatants decided that gardening was much more fun on such a day and downed tools to come back another day. Needless to say Murphy's Law applied and as soon as the boats were put away the wind dropped to a benign 3.

So episode 2 of this mind-warping suspense thriller was staged on 22nd October when the weather was Southerly 1-2 at most. Thanks to Graham Baker, Colin Willsmore and Debbie Yorston for rescue and race-box duties. John Nickalls jetted in from the States to participate but obviously had difficulty in adjusting to the time zone.

Race 2 was easily won by Damian and we all thought that his skill combined with the lighter weather would make it his day. All apart from Mark Savill who won Race 3, which was a particularly well contested race. This made race 4 almost a formality but Mark came in first once more to confirm his status as 'Helm of the Year 1988'

BRADWELL SAILING CENTRE

Lucu (Boreham) and I spent a week at Bradwell Sailing Centre where we were trained and tested for our Level 5 (this now replaces Seamanship 2). However, we got a fun holiday out of it as well which you can see in the following write-up of our week there.

MONDAY
We arrived at the School about 10.45am having had some trouble finding the entrance. Lucy had arrived already and had managed to get hold of a room for just two. All the other dormitories in the girl's section were for four people and these were mainly taken up by the Basildon Swimming Club who were there on their week off from training
At about 11.30 we all met in the TV room where the warden told us about the school and the rules about meals and the fact that the girls' rooms were out of bounds to the boys and vice versa!
In the afternoon we all went out for a sail with the instructors in Wayfarers and Oysters. There was a strong breeze at first and we all sailed to Stone where the wind conveniently dropped totally, leaving us all to drift (or row) back with the tide.

seTUESDAY
Breakfast was at 8.15 and so by 9.30 we were all down at the boat-yard across
the road to get our gear. Lucy and I were put in a Dayboat and left to get on with rigging a boat we'd never even heard of before, let alone sailed in. All the dinghies there are moored up on the water making rigging quite difficult as you have restricted space. Luckily, two boys who were also doing their Level 5 were on the next Dayboat and they had sailed in it the day before. This meant they would be able to tell us what to do if we could not work it out. However we did not have too much trouble and the only questions asked came from the bovs wanting to know how come we had ended up on the best Dayboat and why had they got stuck in the one that was the worst? There was barely any wind so we rowed out of the creek and drifted along with about four other boats. (Most of the Swimming Club had gone in the Toppers, canoes and sail boards.) We drifted about a bit and then had lunch after which a sea breeze came up and we sailed all the way out to sea just past Bench Head and back agair:
in about a Force 4.

WEDNESDAY
Today was when Lucy and I really took our Test. We went through everything; sailing without a rudder (not as hard as it sounds), sailing without a centreboard, @sailing a triangular course, man-overboard drill, hove-to and sailing backwards. We managed everything except sailing backwards which we just could not master. What made it harder was that the sail has to be pushed out against the wind and as the wind had increased from a steady Force 4 to a strong 5 it became almost impossible to hold the sail out against the force of the wind. However we completed the other tasks without difficulty and with much more success than the two boys in the other
Dayboat!
All the people involved in the Level 5 testing had lunch (the others in the Toppers had eaten ages ago!) and we set off again to practise coming alongside and sailing a tight circle around the rescue boat. Both Lucy and I were now very cold and tired having fought the elements all day, and the boys were too. We were all sent ashore to swap round (Lucy and I were supposed to be showing the boys how to sail without a rudder, however the wind was too strong) and we just sailed all the way out towards sea, turned round and came back again. As we were nearing the entrance to the creek I heard several voices calling my name and I saw our very own Jack B motoring past with my family aboard and a couple of my brother's friends as well! I though they had come all the way just to see me but I was wrong, they had come to fetch 'A' mark after it had wandered downriver and been towed for safe keeping into Bradwell Marina. We moored up and went ashore very tired after a long day.

THURSDAY
The boys had been told, much to their relief, that they were not good enough, so now it was just Lucy and I doing the Level 5. We had spent all the previous evening poring over a chart of the river, phoning up Lucy's parents for the weather forecast and tides, and asking the advice of one of the instructors, working out where we would go for a day's cruise. We had worked it all out as a part of the Level 5 and set out, with one of the adults from the swimming group as ballast, in a Wayfarer expecting to have to actually go on the cruise, but we did not have to in the end which was a relief! During the morning we finally mastered sailing backwards as it was only a Force 3 breeze.
By this time Lucy and I were sick of dinghy sailing, we both wanted to go in the Toppers as everyone else was really enjoying themselves so we were pleased when we were told that we could go in the Toppers in the afternoon. During lunch there waS a massive shaving-foam fight where everybody, including the instructors, got totally covered! After we had washed ourselves off in the water (which incidentally is not warm at all, despite the rumours!) we sailed about in the Toppers. The wind
had steadily increased and was now a Force 4 - 5. This and the fact that there were
not enough Toppers to go round meant that there were two people to each Topper. Everyone was capsizingall.round but Lucy and I stayed upright without much difficulty. That is until my helm (i.e. Lucy) slammed the tiller across too hard when tacking and we went straight into irons. I am not sure quite what happened
yy
(probably something my helm did) but the next thing I knew was that I was floundering in the freezing water while my helm had struggled over the top in an attempt at a dry capsize. However, while standing in triumph on the daggerboard it bent under her weight and she slipped off and fell into the water which saved me the job of pushing her in! By now we were thoroughly enjoying ourselves and were not too happy when everyone was told to come in because it was too windy.
Reluctantly everyone packed up the Toppers which were towed back and we all walked back along the sea wall, back to a nice Silower.

FRIDAY
We woke up to what seemed a howling gale on Friday morning. The forecast was for a strong Force 6-7 and there was a gale warning until Sunday evening. On days like this the Bradwell 22s are used and so all of us rowed out and rigged these massive dinghies. As the name tells you they are 22' long and are built at the School's boat yard across the road from the school itself. They have the foredeck of a Wayfarer, a huge steel centreplate and four sails (two jibs, a mainsail and a mizzen), and are very sturdy and strong.
Lucy and I ended up doing most of the rigging as the Instructor decided thar if we were good enough for Level 5 then we should do all the work. We motored OUw
- each Bradwell 22 has am outboard engine for emergencies - and then began the struggle
down towards Osea. In all my time on the river I do not think I have seen anything like it. The waves were enormous, there was spray everywhere and the wind was howling fiercely. The wind was so strong that even the Bradwell 22's were heeling (gasp!) and the Instructor heartened us by saying that one had even capsized before (double gasp! ) Apparently it took three people oan the centreplate as well as two on the skeg to stop it from turning turtle!!!
Our destination was to be Osea Island, and although we enjoyed it at first, by the time we had been thrown about, continually soaked to the skin by the spray and been out in the freezing wind for ten minutes, we were all ready to go back. However, the powers-that-be in the nice warm cabin of the safety boat, with their cups of coffee, had other ideas!
Tacking was an awkward affair. The centreboard case is just below waist height so getting over it was extremely difficult, and trying to control a flapping jib that was determined to catch itself on the other jib, the mast fittings and everything

else, was almost impossible. In the end we worked out a system of two people either side of the centreboard case (one for each jib), and when we went about we just unwound the jib sheet from its bollard and handed it to the person on the other side. It got so windy that in the end all three boats took down their mainsails, (another job for Lucy and me) and just relied on the other three sails.
When we got as far as Stone we beached, because our safety boat had spotted someone in trouble. Just off Osea we could see a dinghy on its side (hardly surprising) and our safety boat spent a good half an hour before they had even got the boat upright, and it took a long time then to tow it back. These two totally mad people had set out from Stone in this wind, which personally I thought rather stupid because if we had not been there, no-one would have been there to help them out and they could have ended up a lot worse than just spending a long while in the freezing water.
Nobody could face turning out again, even for the short part of the trip just across to Osea as we had all slowly frozen up just sitting there cold and wet waiting for the safety boat to bring our lunches across. After lunch we back on a broad sailed reach. By now the sun had come out and because the wind was us, we all felt behind a lot warmer and everyone fell asleep, including the Instructor, apart from the four of us who were watching the jibs and the poor boy who got lumbered with helming. I do not think that I have ever enjoyed a hot shower as much as I did that day and wmI hope I do not get as cold as that ever again!

SATURDAY
As everyone had been so cold on Friday and the weather was still rough it was decided that we take the motor boats and go across to West Mersea. The ex-Liverpool
class Lifeboat had broken down (sob!) so we all piled into three motor boats - one
similar to Jack B but smaller; one similar to the work boat but bigger; and another that was a cross between the two. However the boat similar to Jack B broke down outside the Power Station which meant that those on board crammed into the other two boats which were already well loaded.
We went up the river to West Mersea and were just working out where to moor up along the slipway when we ran aground on it. Local teenagers had struck up a good trade ferrying people from the shore to their Cruisers in huge tubs with engines and one had just zipped before us into our selected space and as we turned around we grounded on the slipway. It did not help when another lad came by in his boat and said "Don't hang around here or you'll go aground!" We all scrambled out and waded ashore to have lunch and spent part of the afternoon looking around before we motored back to the Sailing School. The broken-down boat had been repaired in time to come and collect us.
On the last evening it is the tradition to march off to some woods nearby and have a Barbecue, but because it had been raining, the food had been pre-cooked and we took it into the recreation room to have our feast there. We all played silly games like passing waterbombs along a line from under chins etc. and needless to

RESCUE DRIVERS

Roll up! Roll up!.... Once again the sailing season is upon us and it is time to
think about planning and resourcing the Club's Rescue Services which, thankfully, have so far enabled our activities on the water to continue in relative safety and with the reassurance that assistance is near to hand.

Whether one is venturing out for a tentative first try or is a hardened competitor, the knowledge that the Club is providing these services is a much welcomed aid to one's confidence.

Last year the response to my ‘recruitment campaign' was first class, and has enabled me to establish a solid nucleus of experienced Rescue Boat Drivers. To enable us to provide an even better service this year, it will be necessary to recruit additional volunteers and organise further training sessions.

Aside from providing a wider service - perhaps by having two boats out at a time -
with sufficient manpower we will also be able to lessen the burden on the _ stalwarts who have provided the service to date.

At present there are four boats which are used for rescue purposes and training:
Jack B
Baddow Star
The Workboat
The Fisherman
Primarily we use Jack B, with Baddow Star as back-up. It is the Club's intention to complement the above with a fast inflatable in the near future. The communications are by CB and VHF, and although there is an increasing array of equipment, the maintenance is taken care of for us. All we have to do is drive the boats - although obviously there is a training programme to enable would-be drivers to attain the required level of competence.

Further to this I intend to arrange some training in the correct use of the Communications Equipment and some First Aid sessions with the help of the St John Ambulance Brigade. It is envisaged these will be held both at the MASC and at Stansgate (more news on this in a later edition of Navigans.) We will also be sending some representatives to the Bradwell Field Studies Centre for specific
training in handling rescue craft - although places are very limited.

In a lighter vein, there will be the Annual Inter-club Rescue Boat Competition which last year served as an excellent opener to the Regatta. If anyone is interested in entering a team please let me know.

Finally, if you haven't already, you will soon be receiving a copy of the Sailing Schedule. This once again promises to be an eventful mix of Opens, Regatta, Team Races and, of course, the East Coast Piers Race, not forgetting all the normal Points events. As a small Club the organisation of these events necessitates a great deal of work by a small number of people.

JURY RIG FROM ST PETER PORT

Some of you know that Geoff Vines was unfortunate enough to lose the mast from Seabrume last Summer. He was entering the Big Russell between Sark and Herm and the wind was SW 5 when a lower port-hand shroud parted at the deck causing the mast to buckle at the cross trees and fall to starboard. The mast was recovered and Seabrume limped into St Peter Port under engine.

Most of us would have put the boat into a yard at that stage and left it for the insurance company to sort out. There followed a period of several days of much telephoning and letter-writing when the extent of the damamge needed to be surveyed and negotiations with the insurance company started.

By this time Mike Vines had joined his father and the decision was taken to set a jury rig and sail the boat back to the mainland. The boat would be much more accessible in Portsmouth than it would be in St Peter Port. The remains of the mast were cut in two and the upper portion rigged with cordage salvaged from the original rig and other bits and pieces which were on board. The genoa was rigged so that the foot was set to the improvised forestay and the peak led aft to the jib track with a sheet to the winch. The rig was evidently sound because Geoff and Mike arrived safely at Portsmouth having sailed across the Channel in 5's and 6's.

Now Geoff Vines is a member of the RNSA and a fellow member had observed his activities in St Peter Port. It turned out that he left at about the same time as Mike and Geoff and was also headed for Portsmouth. The result of this coincidence was that Geoff's efforts and successful voyage back to Portsmouth had been monitored and Geoff was subsequently nominated for a seamanship award of the RNSA which was duly presented at a ceremony in January. I feel sure that the Club would wish to congratulate Geoff on his well deserved award. Incidentally the trophy, now in pride of place on Geoff's mantelpiece, is known as the Sex Pot. I have been repeatedly assured that it really is an award for seamanship.

Seabrume is currently being repaired and fitted with a new mast and it looks very much as though Geoff will be in the water well before the rest of us for the 1989
Season.

Dave Steward

THE PINOCCHIO TROPHY

For those of you who didn't know, it was my 40th birthday in early January. As befitting such an august occasion I was treated to a surprise birthday party, cunningly arranged between my devious wife and that 'snake in the grass' Dave Payne.

The Party, of which I had not the slightest inkling, was full of surprises, least of all being a package hand-franked 'Grafham Sailing Club'. On opening the package I found two small shields, one for me and one for Dave, engraved 'Pinnochio Trophy,
ist, 1.1.89"
So what is the Pinocchio Trophy?

Our story starts the previous week on Monday of the New Year. Along with Robin and Lisa; John and Caroline; Trevor and Christine; Tam and Mike Duckmanton; we dragged ourselves to Grafham
to compete in the Grafham Grand Prix. Meanwhile Janet went to my mother's for the day.

Dave and I were back hame by early afternoon and about 6pm Janet rang me to find aout am how we had done.
"We were up-wind of everybody right from the start. Trevor and Christine got close but were just behind; Paul Smith (a friend who sails a Hurricane) was about ten yards
behindssas”

When Janet had finished talking to me, she rang Dave to sort out the surprise party. She also asked him about Grafham and he told her the same things as I had. From all of this Janet believed that we had won the Grand Prix, but was surprised to see that we had left the boat at Grafham.

After intensive interrogation the following day, I finally admitted the truth. “There was no wind and racing was abandoned without the boat ever going in the
water."
But every word we had said was true. We were furthest to windward of all the boats waiting to launch; Trevor and Chris were next to us, but our bows were slightly
ahead: Pawl Smith was parked behind us, etc....

I didn't think any more about it until we received the trophies.
The significance of the ‘Pinocchio Trophy' was that Dave and I told the most _m velievable pack of porky pies Janet had ever heard, and that she was completely taken in by our consistent stories. The ‘Pinocchio Trophy' was her revenge.

It has pride of place on the shelf amongst all of her genuine trophies.

Steeve Keeble, Fly-by-Wire.

Captain Keeble on his yacht, found his crew a Payne
So decided, singlehanded, to sail his Hurricane
Said Steve, "I'll follow Chichester and Chay
I'll sail both Capes and Roaring 40's on the way."

Preparation over, dawned the long-awaited day
To see our Steve afloat, and safely on his way.
A man whose name was Hobie shouted same advice "If your mast fills up with water, send for us in a trice."

The sail progressed quite smoothly when alas, alack and zap The compass, map and sextant fell from poor Stevie's lap As if this was not enough for any man to face,
A Tornado had been forecast, Stampede-ing at a pace.

"Oh, Dave. Oh, Dave, Where are you? Wish you were here with me.
There's Shearwater everywhere, just me the boat and sea."
No Spark of inspiration, No 'A' Class thoughts were there, Nacred into the bargain, Steve started to despair.

Just then a gust filled the sail right to overflowing.
He Catapulted in the air, oh where , oh where's he going?
He Darted here, he Darted there, but to no avail,
He lost all his provisions, 'cept for same olde tyme ale.

They found poor Steven later upon a desert isle,
Alone, shipwrecked and legless, but still he had a smile.
The moral of this story, if to sailing you aspire,
Don't take your 'cat' to sea alone, takes two to FLY BY WIRE.

Christine Milton, Cat Fleet

SAILING IN SAFETY _
About this time last year Malcolm Stuart wrote an article for Navigans on Sailing in Rough Weather. The article is reproduced here as advice to new members and a reminder to existing ones. Malcolm's notes are mainly directed towards racing, but much of the advice is relevant to non-racers as well. Adrian Wright also offers Similar advice to Salboarders (see Page 8).

Do remember at all times that, although the sun may be keeping things warm ashore at this time of year, the water is still very cold, and this could put life in danger for the sailor who is in the water too long.

If you are inexperienced, do let saneone ashore (e.g. a friend or the OOD) know that you are going out. The moral is: Get out there and enjoy your sailing but do make sure that you and your boat are properly kitted out and that the conditions are suitable for your own level of experience.

SAILING IN ROUGH WEATHER

In the spring and autumn at Stansgate we frequently experience strong winds and when these blow against the tide we can get very choppy and confused water, particularly between Stansgate Point and Osea Pier:

In such circumstances the Race Officer, the OOD and all members who have turned up to race will be faced with a decision.

Firstly, irrespective of what the Race Officer decides, members remain responsible for their personal safety and should not sail if they judge the conditions to be well beyond their present level of competence. The Race Officer will, in reaching his decision, assume that members have considered the weather conditions and have reached the decision that they can survive them when they sign on.

The Race Officer's job is therefore not that of deciding what is suitable for the least experienced and worst equipped member, but only that of deciding whether or not it is safe to start a race for the more experienced members. We must recognise here that the only way of getting experience of sailing in rough conditions is to get out and do it and we are only going to improve our skills by pushing ourselves a little. The Race Officer has therefore to make the difficult judgement on how far to let those who sign on for a race push themselves.

In circumstances such as this the Race Officer will consult with the duty Coxswain, the Fleet Captains and the OOD. Any course set for racing must take account of the ability of the rescue facilities available on the day to recover crews who may get into trouble. He may therefore restrict sailing to the shorter courses, and faster boats like the Catamarans will have to put up with having their wings clipped. —

The ultimate authority for all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of Club Members is the OOD, however in practice he will normally only exercise this authority in response to a request from the Race Officer for guidance, and would in any case take any decision affecting racing after consultation with the Race Officer.

To summarise what is a cautious justification of racing in conditions that pramnpt thoughts of more canfortable hobbies:

1. Competitors must decide themselves whether or not they are competent to
go out in rough weather.

2. The Race Officer must consult the duty Coxswain, Fleet Captains and OOD
and set a suitable course or postpone until such time as a suitable course can be set.

3s If these two points have been properly addressed, then racing will only be abandoned in the most extreme conditions, or in the absence of rescue cover.

EASTER-EGG SERIES, 1989

(guaranteed free of salmonella and curry)

Easter 1989 probably saw the best of the weather for this year and what marvellous weather it was for the first sail of the club's '89 sailing season. Though the Gate Lock broke down completely on 7th May (design fault), it is hoped it will be repaired by the time you read this.

pushing or leaning on the gate in any way while you are operating the lock.

2. Insert key fully -= and remove it in one continuous motion, (ensure that the key
cames to a stop against the reader frame before removing it).

tell you the lock has operated, allowing you to open the gate. (This is more useful sometimes than looking for the green light which can be difficult to see in strong
sunlight.)

4. If the lock fails to operate at the first attempt, wait a short time before
inserting the key again. (The instructions with the keys say: Do not insert the key
into the reader if the red light is on - which is probably saying the same thing.)

SOME PEOPLE HAVE ALL THE FUN

A rather unusual title that! It was prompted by Malcolm Stuart's rather serious article in the last Navigans about safety and the responsibilities of the inidvidual, the Race Officer and the OOD. What Malcolm said was absolutely spot on, but don't let the serious side of officialdam spoil the fun you can have if you are Race
Officer.

The Race Officer has the ideal opportunity to get his own back on all of his rivals, both within the Fleet or in other Fleets. What is a good course for one Fleet can be
a B...... awful course for somebody else. So - if you are Race Officer, what must
you consider when setting the courses:

The relative speed of the Fleets. Obdviously the Cat Fleet proceeds around the course at approximately twice the speed of the Mirror Fleet, (difference in PY numbers indicates this), but that is not always the case. If there is an average wind and a strong tide, then the speed differential between the fast and slow boats will
increase.

e.g. If the tide is 3 knots and the Mirrors can only do 5 knots then their speed will vary between 8 and 2 knots, depending whether they are sailing with or against the tide. (In fact the boat speed will vary also with the tack of the boat, but for the purpose of this explanation we have taken a fixed speed). If a Cat can do 10 knots then its speed will vary between 7 and 13 knots depending on the angle to the tide. The ratio is now not 2:1 between the Fieets.

contd....

6.
This example highlights that a course with legs into the tide favours the Cat Fleet (ratio 3.5:1), but that a course with lots of down-tide legs favours the slower boat (ratio 1.625:1). Unfortunately life is not this simple, as courses are a combination of up, down and across tide legs, and boats vary their speed with the legs of the course. So that it is at best an indication that strong tides favour fast boats.

However, light winds favour slow boats. If a fast boat is stationary for any length of time then it has to make up that time on the slower boats by the ratio of their Py numbers. However, if the Race Officer shortens the course, the fast boat will find it almost impossible to make up the time.

e.g.- If the Fleet is windless for twenty minutes at the start of the race, and the race is shortened to one hour, then the Cats need to make up that 20 minutes (times the difference in PY) plus the difference in PY for the forty minutes sailed. This means that a Hurricane would need to beat aMirror by approximately 55 minutes in 40 minutes of sailing! Time ticks faster for fast boats when there is no wind.

But then again, a dying wind favours the fast boats and a strengthening wind favours the slow boats, for obvious reasons.

Having disposed of the impact of the wind and tide, let us consider the sea _ state. Flat water favours the boat with the least wetted area, as there is less friction with the water. This is why it is important to lift the storm going upwind, and to plane with the bows clear going downwind. If you look at the record-breaking Windsurfers, they are designed to have minimal wetted area when planing downwind. I have heard quotes of as little as 200 sq am being in contact at any one time. That is about 2/3 of the sole of your foot!

As the waves become steeper and the wave tops closer, then the longer boats are favoured, as they do not dip into the thoughts as much. If the distance between the waves is 12 feet, then a Mirror will fall into every trough, but an 18-foot Cat will generally ride across the peaks. The hull shape also is impacted (just the word) by the waves. A pointed bow will cut through the waves, whereas a flat bow will slam and slow the boat down. A flared bow will lift the boat over the waves, whereas a sharp bow will tend to nosedive into the face of the wave.

The final part of the equation is' the characteristics of the boats themselves. Monohulls can tack more quickly than Cats, so a course that requires a lot of tacking favours a monohull. Trapeze boats are favoured by long legs in strong winds as the crew expends less effort in keeping the boat upright. High aspect ratio sails are favoured in light winds, but can be difficult to manage in strong winds. Fully battened sails are favoured in light winds as they hold their shape better.
Spinnakers are favoured in light winds as they provide extra drive.

So where does this bring the fun into being Race Officer? Well, it depends on your dd

point of view. If you hate the Cat Fleet you set a course with lots of tacking. ibs you hate the Mirrors the course has legs into the tide or the waves, etc. However if you want to set good courses, then the Cats want long legs in good winds and the tide can generally be ignored. The Mirrors want legs where the tide assists them to the next mark and where they are out of the waves. The Solos want similar courses to the Mirrors but with less emphasis on avoiding all of the tide; while with the Handicap
Fleet you payS your money..... The Windsurfers prefer to avoid downwind legs in
steep waves.

Setting courses can really be fun, especially in Club racing where the Fleets can be given courses suitable to them individually. It only becomes difficult in a Handicap race where the boats are mixed. One other thing, same helms/crews have poor memories, sO you can always send them around odd-shaped courses to further confuse them. Sailing the same old courses, week in week out, becomes very boringl

I love it when my turn for Race Officer comes around. I like to see the Fleets work, so the courses are always unusual.

I look forward to seeing what courses you set.

Steeve Keeble, Cat Fleet

NEW RACING RULES

Every four years the International Yacht Racing Union revises the Racing Rules. The last changes in 1985 were mainly to clarify the existing rules, this year however the changes will affect every sailor.

These new rules came into effect on lst May this year.

A brief description of the rule changes that effect yachts at this club is’ given below. The new RYA rule book (YR1/89) should be consulted for a more detailed and definitive description of the rules.

Rule 4.1
The individual recall signal is now the display of the 'X' flag instead of lowering the class flag to the dip.

Rule 5.4(c)
The Race Committee may now abandon or cancel a race when it considers that to continue would be unfair, even if this has come about due to a change in the weather
conditions.

Rule 25
This rule, which defines the sizes of class insignia and sail numbers, has been changed but will only apply to sails made after lst January 1989.

Rule 26
Advertising and Sponsorships: This rule has been rewritten. A further description of this rule and how it will affect this Club will be given in a future edition of
Navigans.

Rule 32
Avoiding Collisions: The change to this rule has put a new obligation on the Protest Committee when serious damage has occurred. The Protest Committee MUST now penalise the right-of-way yacht if it finds that the right-of-way yacht had the opportunity but failed to make a reasonable attempt to avoid the collision.

Rule 42.3(c)
This rule which was about luffing another boat the wrong side of a mark has been deleted. For a boat to be allowed to luff another boat the wrong side of a mark, the leeward boat must have luffing rights and the leading boat must not be about to round the mark.

Rule 43.2
When two yachts are approaching an obstruction close-hauled on starboard tack, and the yacht to leeward or ahead needs room to tack and hails the other yacht for roan to tack; if the other yacht shouts "you tack” and the yacht requiring water tacks -
under the old rules the hailed yacht (on starboard tack) had to 'keep clear' - now
she simply has to give room for the hailing yacht (on port tack) 'to tack and clear (the starboard tack yacht.)'

Rules 45, 52 and 51.2
A yacht is now required NOT to touch a mark, this was not actually specified before. If a yacht does however touch a mark, the standard exoneration procedure has changed from re-rounding to doing a 720° turn. The offending yacht is required to sail well clear of other yachts to do the 720 as soon as possible after hitting the mark.

Rule 54
The ‘pumping and rocking rule has been reworded and a definition of sailing added. Ooching (sudden movement of the body forward or aft) is now always prohibited. When roll tacking or gybing the mast must now not move away from the vertical more than

Contd

Racing Rules (continued)

once. A Protest Committee may now disqualify a yacht for infringing rule 54 without a hearing, although if one is requested by the yacht, one must be given.

Rule 68.4(b)
Protest flags. If after a collision oe of the yachts involved displays a protest flag but does not subsequently lodge a protest, a third yacht having witnessed the collision may lodge a protest even though she herself did not display a flag.

Appendix 3
The 720 rule has been rewritten such that a yacht that infringes a rule in the preparatory period must take the penalty as soon as possible after the infringement, instead of waiting for the starting signal.

Mike Hellewell, Sailing Secretary

On the record - but off the wire ! ed

During the May Day Bank Holiday Handicap Series, Richard Willmot ‘slipped his leash' on the trapeze of Graham Baker's Dart and plopped into the water. Rumour has it that Graham sailed on all unknowing and engaged in lonely conversation with himself that is the hallmark of those who choose to sail solo. Having finally realised he had lost the 'helmsman's best friend', Graham returned to pick up his errant crew and, all now safely gathered in, continued the race and no doubt wondered whether ‘the rules' would have allowed him to finish without the company of his companion-in-arms. I can certainly ‘feel' for Richard since, many years ago, I did the self-same things whilst crewing in Suva harbour. The problem was that I fell off just a few yards short of the finishing line; I still held the rather Tong length of jib sheet and was dragged over the line mindful of the fact that, very occassionally, (small) sharks were to be seen in the harbour. I must admit I got back in fairly sharpish.

The above reminiscence was sparked off by a snippet in The Times which reports that the Royal Naval Sailing Association (organisers of the Whitbread Round the World race) has apparently decreed that any boat finishing without having picked up, ‘dead or alive', a crew member who has been swept overboard will be disqualified. Time was when such a boat wold have been generally expected to respectfully retire but obviously times have changed. However, the mind boggles at such a situation; does a

disqualified yacht appeal against the Race committee ? what comes first, the coroner's inquest or the race committee meeting ? Could a helm, having lost his crew ‘dead or alive’ in an inland reservoir race, wait for an uncomfortable race committee to disqualify him (unlikely to be a ‘her' I’think) if he

chooses not to retire ? I must admit that when avidly reading the descriptions of the Round the World
races I've never considered the terrible dilemma facing skipper and organisers - it makes you think.

MAYDAY AT MAPLIN 7.

The mens were bad from the start. The bank holiday cruise was for at least a week
to posh places - and I'd forgotten my shaver.

As is well known, it is almost impossible to get bits of rope like moorings, painters, etc. hooked up around a saildrive with folding prop; and we managed to avoid this, but a deep spade rudder and shallow skeg can be lethal for mooring buoys which are too buoyant to depress to free. It was freezing cold in swimtrunks battling with the buoy and the elements, and in the end it was a knife job.

We motored down to a mooring in Bradwell Creek which seemed preferable to bouncing about on the Club moorings, so at least the first night was OK. Next morning we rejoined the fleet near the Bench Head Buoy for the beat to the Spitway.

Once through the Spitway it was a more-or-less dead run in the direction of the Medway and Thames, but the wind reduction hoped for when everything was going the same way was not very obvious.

I had chosen my largest Genoa (a lightweight cloth) for the season and omce on the headfoil this was not likely to be changed as the joins in the foil luff groove were no longer perfectly aligned. In order to protect the nearly new lightweight cloth I decided to use the main only and make a series of donwind tacks after controlled gybes. The conditions were such that it could easily be described, after a few Grinks at any Club bar, as a Yachtsman's Gale but realistically it was only a good
Force 5.

My crew on this occasion was the better half, who now sails only against medical advice due to an assortment of mechanical problems. This meant I could not leave the tiller in such conditions and no way would I trust the Autohelm. My previous practical experiences have included strong wind and an uncontrolled gybe and, yes, it does bring the mast and supplementary gear down to deck level.

Apart from the occasional change of tack when the echo sounder suggested it, the only other excitement was the antics of the Avon being towed astern. The three main modes of behaviour were: steadily filling up with water and acting as a good sea anchor if only the painter glue joint holds; upside down; and airbome, attempting a fly-past.

Nevertheless there was no apprehension and the use of harnesses or the washboard to shut up shop was never considered. Anyway, at this rate, it would soon be peaceful again. The conditions were modest compared to a never-to-be-forgotten incident, surfing in on enormous breaking waves some years ago in Holland, when precise rudder control and hence my ability to take the seas just slightly on the quarter (Cape Horn style, never dead square,) left me with 100% confidence in the underwater details of my boat.

At the Maplin Bell Cardinal I aybed for a port tack about due south. The echo sounder, mostly on 10' flashed 8' a couple of times, but the alarm set for 7' (twice our draft) was not sounding. The waves were looking nasty and we were rising and falling more than the 2' indicated by the echo sounder.

Then it happened. About three horrendous crashes. Nothing else occurred to me other than that we were aground on sand as hard as concrete and no boat would take that for more than a minute or two in such waves. The fact that I spotted the remains of the rudder aster and the crashes had ceased should have told me we were still travelling forward, but I'd lifted the engine hatch and saw water coming in from the direction of the transom.

The Prospect has many attributes, that's why I chose her. Among them are the inner mouldings in the hull and topsides; super for insulation, but it does mean that it

GOntd.s:.<s«

MAYDAY contd...

takes a lot more than lifting the berth cushions to see the inside of the hull and
confirm the presence of keels - or otherwise. Frantic activity inside while upside
down, attempting to evaluate the problem, also caused seasickness and I subsequently abandoned the task to despatch what must have been an unusual Mayday format.

My brain had just about managed to work out that if we were breaking up and about to sink, the rest of the fleet could not approach us in such seas, and taking to _ the Avon would have been difficult for me and impossible for Joyce. With hindsight I'd probably do the same things again, as to delay until it was too late could have been an even greater mistake. .

The crisis lasted about 10 seconds, but I managed to pad it out for a couple of minutes. Derek Hall of 'Staggers', with a calmer appraisal suspended the ‘'Mayday' action until the need was confinmned and since we were still afloat and not aground, he managed to carry out a difficult tow to Thames Haven Yacht Club, where I could dry Out and assess the damage and temporary repairs necessary.

Many thanks once again to Derek and also to Peter Bloanfield for standing by.

The plywood, saws, drills, clamps, Isopon paste etc. were ordered from home, pranptly~ delivered and after a night-shift duty spent sitting and lying in the mud, _ ‘'Tekin Two' returned to base the following Monday.

A new rudder is required; the hull/transan join requires a complete new section; the port bilge keel needs rebedding and tightening up; but it could have been a lot worse. The sounder was used for a survey of the area on the return trip, without
result.

I have not learnt anything from the incident I didn't know before and I am still uncertain about the possibility of a large log in the water, or same similar obstruction. In a sudden crisis, time is vital for major decisions, 10 seconds or even a couple of minutes are inadequate unless you have all the facts.

I have been once before adrift without any form of control or propulsion. The elements were the worst ever recorded in the area, anna domini was not a factor in
September 1951, and I had 9 full days (and, worse still, nights) to consider the only
variable, for all the use it was.

This long-ago incident does throw up same analogies for the small boat scene, so ITM pass them on for what they are worth:

1. Once out of control, ships and boats are beam-on to the seas and that's the worst
attitude.

2. Roll angles of over 90° (over 45°heel) can occur and can never be got used to.

3. Revise your Physics. The future depends on the relative positions of the ship's
(and its cargo) centre of gravity and its centre of buoyancy, which is called the
Metacentre.*

4. Always have a large reserve of fuel on board for long trips, in bad weather it is
possible to use it all up with no progress over the land.

5. The last 10-15% of fuel in a low tank is generally unuseable, sediment and sludge
on the bottom become disturbed and that's your lot.

contd.

MAYDAY contd...

6. Never rely on outside help in extreme conditions, sometimes even aeroplanes can
take days finding you.

7. Oil on troubled waters, sea anchors, even lifeboats (if they are still in the
davits) are useless, they are only for story books. A small boat sailor may try a sea anchor from the bow if he's not too paralyzed to move.

See, I've experienced all that and I still don't know what happened! Here's to the next time, Father Neptune.

Ron Phillips, Tekin Two.

Ed's Note -

I believe there is an automatic membership of an Association for people who have used a parachute to save their lives. I wonder if an equivalent group for those who have ever been rescued as a result of a Mayday call would be very popular. Perhaps’ the numbers qualifying would be too great. Or would those eligible very much prefer to keep their heads down and not take part in an annual get-together when hair-raising yarns could be swapped!

* The following from the Oxford Campanion to Ships and the Sea:

Metacentre. The point of intersection of a vertical line, in relation to the ship's structure, drawn through the centre of gravity of a ship when she is lying upright and a vertical line drawn through the centre of buoyancy when the ship is heeled. To make certain that a ship is stable so that a righting moment comes into play when she is heeled, the metacentre must be above the centre of gravity.

@CAT FLEET NEWS - ROUND TEXEL AND ALL THAT

Whoops! Saneone in the Hurricane Fleet really stood on Peter Flook's toes by the sound of it. A pity to see a petty personal disagreement brought to Navigans though. A third Marconi Cat went to Texel and in spite of being forgotten in the "“well-wishes" list, it was Hurricane 101 'Flying Colours' that put Marconi SC high in the honours list.

Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton crossed the line 5th behind the 'Specials'; were first production boat to finish and when the prizegiving was finally held at 12 noon on
Sunday, were placed second overall from 950 starters.

Texel is the first Friesian Island off the North coast of Holland, is only 3 miles from Den Helder on the mainland at its southernmost point, and is served by a gqocd, if mot expensive, ferry service. The event started same 12 years ago when 5 boats challenged each other to a race around the Island o Catamarans. From there it
quickly escalated. In 1980 there were 410 Cats in two starts. Now the format is for
one mass” start. 1988 saw 870, and this year a massive 950, to race the 100
kilometres - 60 miles - around the Island. The biggest Cat Race in the world without
doubt.

6.
Round Texel contd...

The island is long and thin, surrounded by shallow water and shifting sand banks. The western shore is straight, runs approximately North-South, and has long, sandy beaches pounded by the North Sea surf. At the top of the Island is a lighthouse at the entrance to the sound between Texel and the next Island, Vlieland. Here the water is very shallow but with a very strong current. As the shore curves around the back of the Island, the course follows a line of withies eastward same 15 miles to the 'VC' buoy, where the Cats turn southward to close the shore again about one-third down. The water is too shallow to navigate inside the line of withies. From here to the bottom of the Island the shoreline is very much like the edge of the Blackwater, marshy, but like everywhere else in Holland, backed by a sloping dyke or sea wall. The course then goes back up the western shoreline to the finish about half-way along at Strand 17.

The organisation is superb. On arrival at the beach road, competitors are marshalled on to a hardstanding area where trail©&TMS are unhitched from the cars and immediately picked up by oe of a fleet of 20 tractors, to be towed along the beach where each class has its own area. When you are ready to leave the beach you simply queue a few minutes at the marshalling point for a tractor and direct it to your trailer.

The start line is between two huge trawlers and is over a mile long. At the ten, five and start signals a helicopter flies along the line with white, blue and red smoke respectively to complement the signals from the Cammitttee boat. There are no general recalls. With strategically placed video cameras at both ends, and in the air, they get your number.

The weather was glorious with a breeze of around 12 to 15 knots from the north-east, which meant that everybody started om the same tack of the close fetch up to the lighthouse. This drastically reduced collisions compared with last year's event, but the start was delayed for 1 hour because the wind was holding the tide out around the top of the Island, across the shallow sands between Texel and Vlieland.

Most of the Hurricanes and faster boats started at the outer end of the line, which had a slightly favourable bias. From here these crews were able to twin trapeze immediately. showing amongst the early leaders was Rob White and Jeremy Newnan while 100 yards to weather, Robin Smith & Lisa Gatton tailed the Dutch team of the Hoekstra brothers. Slightly further ahead the Hurricane Turbo with wing mast and new extra-long racks sailed by Reg White and Steve Olle was doing battle with the giant Roberts 27s. ew

Towards the lighthouse a number of singlehanded 'A' classes, Hurricanes and Tornadoes, that had started further inshore, found a band of stronger wind just off the surf line, and these boats led around the light to start the beat across the top of the Island. Robert White and Robin Gnith steadily worked their way through the pack, and in fact passed the Roberts 27s when they ran aground near the 'VC' buoy. Robin & Lisa were the first Hurricane round the mark on to the long downwind leg behind the Island, in 5th place behind 3 'A's, a French Formulae 20 and a Tornado.

Down the back of the Island Robin & Lisa overtook two of the 'A's, the Formulae 20 and the Tornado, but were in turn passed by the faster 'Specials', the Roberts 27s and the Hurricane Turbo, when they hoisted their huge spinnakers. At the bottom of the Island Robin & Lisa started the twin trapeze beam reach back to the finish same mile behind the leading 'A'; and with helicopters clattering overhead and chase boats to leeward, ‘Flying Colours' was pushed to the limit as the gap was reduced. But at the line the 'A' Class was still 50 yards ahead. A few moments earlier, Reg White &

Round Texel contd... 7.

The Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championship.
(Through the Eye of the Hurricane)

This event is held annually at Stone Sailing Club and consists of a number of different races.

On day one, there is the Stone Dinghy Challenge, which is effectively a practice race for the following series, followed by the first race of the championship proper. Day 2 has the rest of the championship and is followed by the "Cock o' the River" race. This last race is a pursuit event between all of the class winners in the championship event.

Many years ago, the two premier sailing events on the Blackwater were the Marconi Regatta and the Blackwater and Colne championship. However, in recent years the Stone event has seen a falling off of entries, although a revival is taking place.

It was disappointing to see so few entries from Marconi, although I do not believe that we had any entrants at all in recent years.

This year, the Marconi fleet provided entrants in the Cat Menagerie andw the Laser fleets.

Mark Savill was our sole entrant in the Laser fleet and despite some excellent and consistent sailing was unlucky to place only third. Mark scored two second places and a forth out of the three races but was beaten by a first, second and DNS by the winner, and a first, third and fifth by the eventual second overall. That is close racing by any standards, and I am sure that we will see Mark amongst the pots ( and not just beer and toilet) in the very near future. Well done Mark!

The Cat fleet was represented by Fleet Captain, John Nickalls accompanied by the ever blushing Caroline (It's not often that a good looking young lady gropes my thigh under the table!); Current European Hurricane Champions Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton, myself (wearing the loudest trousers in the competition) crewed most ably by Mike "Crocodile' Duckmanton and on the Sunday Trevor Milton crewed by Chris and Paul Ellis. Trevor was taking the opportunity to test drive the demo Hurricane.

Race one on the Saturday afternoon got off to a bad start, as John had broken the goose neck on the Tornado and everybody (thanks Darcy) was trying to help get him on the water in time. The effort did not succeed, but did mean that Mike and I missed all of the signals and were about 50 yards behind the line when the gun went. It was only because we saw Robin screaming in, that we were even facing the right
way.

Needless to say Robin and Lisa screamed into the lead, followed by a couple of Unicorns and about 4 Shearwaters. It was a reach to the first mark and Mike and I had passed all except the leading Unicorn, who we passed at the second mark. It was then a chase after Robin and Lisa. We maintained our distance on them to the next mark, after which we had a long reach up to the Baffle. At this point John and Caroline joined us and we both chased Robin and Lisa. John stayed down to leeward and claimed after the race that he was under powered, whilst Mike and I tried to pitchpole on several occasions. Unfortunately, we had knocked

Blackwater & Colne contd...

the port rudder back and every time I tried to bear away, the rudder just acted like a brake, sending up a spectacular plume of spray.

Meanwhile Robin and Lisa had reached the paffle and fallen into a hole in the wind. Both John and I had been gaining on Robin, but when he reached the Baffle the distance was dramatically reduced. However, despite our best efforts, we both fell into the same hole! The wind was going through all points of the compass, but Robin snook round and was off on the reach back to Stone. John rounded second and raced off, and after two involuntary gybes Mike and I began the chase.

There is no way you can catch Robin and Lisa when they have got a 100 yard lead, so Robin took line honours, John crossed second and we were third. Meanwhile the leading Unicorn seemed to sail straight around the Baffle without stopping. Robin won the race, the Unicorn was second by 7 seconds and we were third.

Race 2 was on Sunday morning. Robin got to the line a little early and consequently had to dip back. John Nickalls and I made perfect starts and John led by about 10 yards at the first mark. Around the second mark we went, with Robin and Lisa breathing down our necks. You just can't keep that man back, and he sailed over us on the reach. John kept him at bay, and the two of them fought tooth and nail (or is it forestay and tiller) around the course. Mike and I held our position about 100 yards back until about halfway around the second lap, when two ‘dead in the water tacks' lost us about 400 yards.

We had just passed Mark Savill when we did the first bad tack and he proceeded to sail effortlessly passed as we floundered about. He had requested a tow as we overtook him; we could have done with one when he went passed.

John managed to hold Robin off to the finish, but Stone were sailing the Tornado off of a lower handicap than the Hurricane, so Robin took the race on handicap.

Trevor Milton had taken the Demo Hurricane (Robert Whites Boat!) out to race, but was forced to retire at the first mark when the tiller , extension broke. He's a strong lad that Trevor!

A liberal application of brute strength and lashings of adhesive tape meant that Trevor, accompanied by Christine, were out for the second
race.

The one advantage of a fast boat is that you are back with plenty of time for lunch. When the second race times were reached, a large portion of the monohull crews were still in the galley queue, so a postponement was signalled. Unfortunately, 3 out of the 4 Marconi cats were already on the water, so for 30 minutes we practised heaving to. John Nickalls claims he is faster than me even when he is hove to!

Mike and I made a dream start to the third race. Well, anyway, I woke up when I hit the water after bouncing off of the mainsail! Robin and John rushed off into the lead again, whilst Trevor rushed ashore to pick up Paul Ellis in place of Christine. (Sailing is now getting like football, with substitutes on the touch line). Mike and I pulled the Hurricane up and proceeded to chase Trevor around the course.

CAMPING WEEKS

One interesting spectacle that hasn't been at our camps before was the presence of a dolphin amongst the moorings. He had already been seen in the river earlier in the season and during our fortnight spent time up at Stone and also visited our own moorings on most days. If we were at the right place at the right time (perhaps about an hour or two before low water) we might see him leap right out of the water a times, and fall back with a huge splash. I've been informed that he (or they - for there may have been two of them) was probably feeding on fish who graze am_ the weed growth on mooring chains and boat bottams. Perhaps the warmer water attracted him or it may be a more desirable spin-off from the grossly overpriced and totally ineffective new environment-friendly anti-fouling the yachtsman is now legally obliged to use!

There was lots of interest playing 'spot the dolphin’ by people both afloat and ashore. He usually kept a respectful distance from boats but if you kept stationary and patient afloat you could get quite a good view of him. Peter's cartoon arose from the frequent discussions among us on whether we were seeing a porpoise or a
dolphin - I'm sticking to dolphin!

Our fortnight's weather was warm and dry except for the middle Sunday which was rather grim. For the rest of the time, though it varied occasionally from too much to too little wind for enjoyable sailing, those of us mm site had enough variation to allow everyone to have same of the sort of sailing they liked. Calm hours allowed everyone to safely swim, paddle and generally play around in the water.

CADET WEEK

Cadet Week followed the patter established over the last few years with dry land instruction, capsize drill in a dinghy attached to the moorings barge, a trip to Maylandsea for lunch, a trip to Osea for lunch, and a First Aid lesson for sane younger Cadets. On Tuesday there were two separate Raft Races organised, one for younger Cadets and one for the older oes. Each of two teams were given 2 long pieces of rope, 3 barrels, 4 planks, and the task of assembling a raft and propelling it out to the moorings barge and back. The whole task kept them busy for some hours.

The last day, Friday, was rather short of wind but there was no rest for the Cadets who had a busy programme of organised games on the water all day. All their activities during the week were videoed by Maureen Bigden and Janet Battle, and there was just time for the results to be shown on the Friday evening after the Presentation of Prizes.

The Presentation was made more interesting by the use of a 'Sin Bin' - any Cadet who
had supposedly ‘stepped out of line' during the week had his nose held over a barrel containing seaweed liberally dosed with, I believe, pickled onion vinegar. The audience decided how long the poor victim suffered by electing how long the count
should last - anything up to a (sometimes very slow!) count to 20. And by the end of
the evening there was a new saying - if anything at all to do with sailing ever goes
wrong it's now always “Ben's Fault" (Holroyd, that is).

Thanks are due to Ione & family and her friend who came along with their First Aid skills and the St John Ambulance Caravan for Cadet Week. Ione was much less busy last year, but there were one or two custamers, and it was peace of mind for us

CADET SERIES

The Cadet Racing went very well this year and had a pleasing turnout. The first day of racing was 'good weather', force 3, but the entry of a Dart in with the Mirrors posed a problem for the Race Officer who had to fit in three races. All these races were won by Lee Harrison and Debbie Yorston in the Dart.

The next set of races were due to be held om the first Sunday of the Camping fortnight. There was barely any wind and plenty of tide and everybody retired except Damian Boreham who finished the course eventually, and won. In the afternoon there was a bit more breeze but not much. Only 3 boats entered, Damian (Mirror), Lee & Debbie (Dart), Lucy Boreham & Jenny Ball (420). There was not enough wind and too much tide for the Mirror which got into trouble at A Mark and ended up drifting round the corner and finally retired. However the 420 did well and managed to cross the line before the Dart and therefore had a clear win. The 3rd race was put off to the next Sunday due to lack of wind.

The next Sunday the 2 races were again postponed, this time due to too much wind, it was blowing a Force 5-6 gusting occasionally to 7. The next Saturday when the 2 races were due to be sailed, there was again no wind but by the afternoon it had picked up enough to have a race. At very short notice Ray Ball, and Mike & Maggie Boreham stepped in to provide rescue cover and Mike Battle agreed to be Race Officer
- many thanks to them. More boats joined in the races and by the 2nd race the wind
had picked up to a force 3-4. Both races were won by Damian Boreham am_ handicap. The winner of the Cadet Series was Lee & Debbie in the Dart with Damian coming a very close second by just one point and o countback.

CADET SERIES, 1989

The winner of the 1989 Cadet Series is:-

LEE HARRISON (DART 18)

Many congratulations to Lee Harrison (Dart 18) on winning the 1989 Cadet Series in what turned out to be a ‘nail biting' finish and all hinging on the last race. This is what a race series should be like and the 1989 Cadet Series must rank as one of the best for some years.

Cadet Races 1,2 and 3 were raced on Sunday, 2 July, in Force 4-5 with at least 5 entries in each race. Lee Harrison won all three races very handily and, truth to tell, the Cadet Series looked

to be well and truly ‘wrapped up' for 1989. Apart from Lee, the other entries were Jon Yorston (Dart 15), Jenny Ball, David Ball, Lucy Boreham and Damian Boreham (all Mirrors).

Cadet races 4,5 and 6 were scheduled for Sunday, 23 July. For race 4, the wind was somewhat lacking in strength, very patchy and very variable around the course, so much so that only Damian Boreham (Mirror) and Michael Fletcher (Topper) managed to round Breezy mark to complete a shortened course. Unfortunately, Michael inadvertently infringed a rule at the start and was disqualified.

There were only three starters for Race 5 which was sailed in slightly windier conditions but was still pretty light and made it difficult to make way against the tide. This race was won by Lucy Boreham (420) with Lee Harrison (Dart 18) second. This time it was the turn of Damian Boreham (Mirror) to be frustrated by lack of wind at 'A' mark and he eventually retired.
The Race Officer
decided to postpone Race 6 until 30 July (when Cadet Race 7 was scheduled, together with the Jackpot for the club's senior citizens).

The gods deceeed that Sunday 30 Ju'y brought with it a wind of Force 7 - occasionally observed to
touch Force 8. Problems with the Jack B delayed the start of the Jackpot and eventually the Race Officer postponed the Jackpot to a later date and the Cadet Races 6 & 7 to Saturday, 5th August.

Despite Lee's three previous wins,the Cadet Series was now still far from over ; Lee could be beaten by Damian if he (Damian) won both races 6 and 7 and Lee finished no higher than 4th in each race. Thus Cadet races 6 and 7 promised to be very interesting.

Cadet 6 was raced in Force 3-4 and was won by Damian (Mirror) with Lucy Boreham (420) 2nd, Ian Fletcher
(420) 3rd and Lee (Dart 18) finishing 4th. Clare Davies (Mirror) and Sian Caruth (Mirror) both
retired whilst David Stewart (Topper) unfortunately missed out a mark and was disqualified. So, the scene was set for a nail biting finish with all depending upon the last race.

Cadet Race 7 was sailed in Force 4 and, although Damian again won the race, Lee won the series by
finishing 2nd with Lucy 3rd, Ian 4th, David Stewart 5th and Kirsty Jolly 6th.

The Final result - since both Lee and Damian had 4 1 ' points
each, the series
was decided
on
countback; Lee's vital 2nd place in race 7 overtook Damian's 3rd place in race 2 and so Lee emerged the overall winner.

The 1989 Cadet Series came to a marvellously exciting end , having been sailed in a wide variety of condition of course, tide and wind, thus providing a good test of all round sailing skill and knowledge. Lee dealt with the varying conditions with great competence and thoroughlydeserved his win but he had to fight hard for it. Lucy Boreham (helm) and Jenny Ball (crew) discovered they liked sailing the 420 and came 3rd overall; alas, no prize because the Average Entry fell just short of the magic number of '6' required for the award of 3rd prize. With 4 races to count, only Lee, Damian and Lucy competed all 7 races. David Ball and Jon Yorston each competed 3 races, Jenny Ball 2 races as helm (but she also crewed for Lucy) with Ian Fletcher and David Stewart also competedin 2 races. Stuart Golding, Richard Battle, Michael Fletcher, Kirstie Jolly, Clare Davies and Sian Caruth all sailed one race, some of them taking part in their first race ever. A total of 14 helms took part in the Cadet Series which is not a bad total compared to some previous years. However, in view of the large number of cadets taking part in the Cadet Week training programme it would be nice to see more cadets taking part in 1990.
