COMMODORE'S NOTES

It is extremely unfortunate that the fine weather of the summer broke on the August
Bank Holiday weekend when we ran the second major event of our calendar - the East
Coast Piers Race. While Malcolm Stuart, John Nickalls and the rest of the organisers tusselled with the problem of the course to set, I was at Walton listening to the wind howling in the rigging and I whole heartedly support their decision to _ shorten the course despite the pressure of the event and the natural desire to sail the course. The events of the actual race demonstrated the correctness of their decision. On behalf of the Club I would like to thank all who helped for making a success of the event despite the conditions.

We still have the Autumm Series to be sailed, the Solo and Mirror Open on Sunday 17th September and the Helmsman of the Year Final om Saturday 7th October. All of these should provide good sailing and I am sure that the Helmsman Final will provide interest for any spectators who are there.

These events are followed by the Working Party on Sunday 5th November when the Club TM is dismantled for the Winter and prepared for the winter maintenance activity. Following the pattern of last year, the Main Committee will be contacting each Fleet Captain to arrange for them to carry out a specific task and the Fleet Captains will be looking for your support. By using this method last year, a great deal was
achieved.

The Laying Up Supper is on Saturday 11th November. Because of the increasing number of people attending, we are holding it at the Heybridge Moat House at Ingatestone this year. Peter Bloanfield has succeeded in booking the same popular band as we have had at the last two events. Please book your tickets early to avoid disappointment, either via your Fleet Captain or the normal ticket sellers (see
below).

Finally, to round off the year we have the 'Last Fling' race on Sunday 19th November followed by the Annual General Meeting and Prize Giving.

Would all members please note that:

COASTGUARD COMPLIMENT

Having survived the rigours of Marconi's East Coast Piers Race, I was aroused fran reasonably deep slumber to answer the telephone. In a matter seconds I was of
briefed with the details of an incident at the Club by the Duty Officer of Thames Coastguard at Walton. I was requested to rendezvous with the Bradwell Marine Rescue Unit (MRU) at the Sailing Club. Mersea Inshore Lifeboat had been launched and an ambulance had been requested to stand by from Burmham-on-Crouch.

As I pulled into Stansgate Road, I was aware of the blue lights of the MRU fast approaching and we both arrived at MSC together, approximately 6 minutes after the initial call, quickly followed by the ambulance.

Having identified the yacht involved, which was on its mooring, the casualty was a 44-year-old male who had been loading stores from the boat to the dinghy alongside, had inadvertently slipped, upturned the dinghy and ended up in the water. The amily other person on board the yacht, the Master, quickly threw the main sheet to the casualty who tied himself securely under the arms to it. The Master had made several attempts to raise the casualty by using the boamn, but because of the physica’ exhaustion of the casualty, was unable to get him on board. A call was made tw Thames Coastguards who raised the initial alarm and hence our attendance at the Sailing Club. The Lifeboat arrived same 8 minutes after us and put the casualty ashore, where he received immediate medical assistance.

My reason for writing this note is that it may serve as a lesson for all - the
casualty was fortunately all right although hospitalised for the night, but in the space of a very short time he became close to hypothermic on a flat calm night while the yacht was at anchor.

It had been impossible to get him aboard and it was aly through the skill and presence of mind of the Master, who attempted in every way to recover the casualty, acted in text-book fashion to ensure that he was safe and secured to the yacht and called for assistance, all of which, had he not done so, could have ended in a very sad evening.

I trust he is not embarrassed by my mentioning his name, but credit must go to the Master, Mr Derek Hall, for his commendable action in saving the life of his crew.

Charles Anderson _

EAST COAST PIERS RACE

(or "Thank Goodness we didn’t go to Clacton......")

With a forecast of "Force 6/7 occasionally 8" one has to look on the bright side; a wind direction of NNE, whilst not bright, was at least less gloomy, so we took the plunge by setting the full course. The buoys were already in place, the spotters had set off for the four gates, and Roger Smith Ml ah to tell the competitors that they were to sail down to the mouth of the river, up the coast to Clacton and Walton, and then back to Marconi’s.
Perhaps the competitors had suspected what we were going to ask them to do and found an excuse to be elsewhere, or perhaps their families had simply demanded their presence at some other Bank
Holiday activity - either way, there weren’t as many faces at the Briefing as we’d have liked, and the
reasons for this are still a subject for some conjecture. The preparations had been based around
accomodating 150 boats, trailers, cars and tents - the site looked quite empty as a near-gale rattled
through the dinghy park.
As the fleet gathered for the Briefing the so far unaccomodating weather did us a favour. A particularly strong squall threw itself at the clubhouse, the water turned streaky-grey, and the race committee's hearts fell. A quick rethink, the course was shortened, and the Commodore in Titchmarsh Marina became ten years younger in a trice.
Even with the strong wind course in use only 38 of the entrants were adventurous (foolish?) enough to venture out to the start, but the race set off a few minutes late from Osea Pier, with the boats fetching up toward No.1 before beating up Goldhanger Creek. This first beat saw the first real evidence of the wine cena as Reg White’s Hurricane Special’s mast broke in two- it wasn’t to be the White family’s
weekend.

The reach from Goldhanger to Mill Beach threw off most of the ‘fast’ rescue boats, and they rejoined the leaders as the fleet emerged having passed behind Northey Island. By this time Rob White had
assumed the lead in his standard Hurricane - Will Sunnucks, also sailing a Hurricane, was lying second,
and we'd let our Tornado drop back to third place. Past the club in 31 minutes and on toward Bradwell the cats with less sail area were able to pick up valuable time against the more powerful boats struggling to stay upright on the tight reach. The wind increased as the leaders passed through Bradwell Gate, and the spotters watched as half a dozen boats capsized in quick succession. With a multitude of rescue boats having volunteered their services for the day all the casualties were quickly attended, although a number of boats suffered minor damage and several retired.
The beat across the river to the Nass Beacon gave a brief respite from the stinging impact of
high-speed salt water and a chance to re-establish communication with the crew - even if this was
limited to the expression of mutual interest in keeping the mast out of the water. Bearing away at the Nass was exciting, and the downhill ride back to the Club gave the water a chance to numb the other side of the face. Downwind, the cats lost their tendency to lift one hull clear of the water in a gentle attempt to deposit slow-witted sailors in the water; instead they adopted a more effective bow-down attitude. Every gust pushed the lee bow further under the waves, threatening to trip the boats (now travelling at over 20 knots) forward into the spectacular, but most disconcerting, “pitchpole". On our boat, Caroline took the helm, leaving me with both hands free to haul on the mainsheet, and with four eyes glued to the port bow we careered upriver.
Rob White was leading as we passed the Club, and Will Sunnucks was still ahead of us, but the second White mishap of the weekend happened as Rob rounded No 2 mark in the belief that it was a large
inflatable near No 4. The Race Officer didn’t approve of this - indeed | understand a mild panic set in as
Will Sunnucks followed Rob on the wrong course and visions of the entire fleet failing to complete the race arose in the organisers’ minds. Luckily (mainly for us !) we psa the mistake, rounded the correct mark, and screamed back to the finish line. Although Paul Smith very nearly passed through our lee as we pinched up to the windward end of the line (anticipating a second lap), a scream from Caroline sent us reaching down to a two length lead over the line.
Was the event a success? Well | certainly think so. All those who sailed enjoyed the race: several
thought that we ought to have had another lap, but we were very pleased that we hadn’t! The
organisation seemed to go well - several visitors observed that we had clearly planned for a lot more
entrants, and that we’d have been able to cope without any real difficulties with over a hundred boats. Whether to hold any future Piers Race on the Bank Holiday weekend must be a critical question, and
we've learnt a lot to apply in the future. However, several aspects were particularly satisfying - not the
least that we had 24 rescue boats of assorted types covering the course.

Sincere thanks are due to all those who helped out at the weekend: to the cat fleet members who helped with the setting-up and taking down; to the other Club members who put in a lot of time and effort to provide rescue cover, to marshall the competitors, to staff reception, and to make the event run smoothly in a hundred and one other ways; to the Solo fleet (and in particular Roger Smith and his team on the Piers Race day and to John Salmon for providing the additional races); to all the Club members who weren't directly involved yet tolerated the inconvenience that the race inevitably involved; to all our sponsors for removing the financial burden and allowing us to make a generous donation to the RNLI and Sailing for the Bisabled: and to all those members of the other clubs who willingly gave their time and services to bring us all safely back to shore.

My own special thanks must go to Malcolm Stuart, who (as always) was tireless in his efforts for the event, to Charles Anderson who put all his local knowledge and organisational skills into making sure we achieved such an effective rescue cover (and what a seductive radio voice he has!), and to Mike Duckmanton whose calming influence rescued me from many a panic!
And what of next year? Well, we have a good foundation on which to build. We’ve built up a broad range of contacts, and we've seen many (but I’m sure not all) of the pitfalls. The final decision remains
to be made, but personally | hope 1990 will see the best Piers Race yet. It’s unlikely to be faster (we
everagee 16 knots), but a warm sunny day, flat water, and an on-board store of cold beer would let me orgive that!

DISTRE FLARE
The Piers Race Sailing Instructions insist that all competitors carry a certain level of safety equipment. Part of this requirement is that at least one distress flare should be carried, and the most popular choice has been the ’miniflare’ pack made by Pains-Wessex. This pack contains a launcher and 8 shells, each of which rises to a height of 80 m and burns for 6 seconds. The pack can be carried conveniently in a pocket.
Pains-Wessex made a number of these packs available for sale in support of charity for the Piers Race, and we have a number remaining in stock. They have come direct from the
manufacturer and thus have a long shelf life, and we are selling them at a price of £15... the
standard chandler’s price is £20.
Although the Piers Race is a long distance race over quite exposed water, many of the Cat fleet have chosen to carry these flares whenever they're sailing a distance from the Club. During the Piers Race it was educational to hear that an upturned catamaran not far from the Bradwell gate
became totally invisible to watchers on the shore... and we've experienced a number of
instances lately when sailors have become separated from their boats.
These flares are equally useful to cruiser sailors; whilst they are not suitable for use offshore, they have the distinct advantage of being able to be slipped into a jacket pocket and thus offer direct personal protection.
Should you be carrying some? .
Only £15 a set, all proceeds to RNLI and Sailing for the Disabled.

WEIL'S DISEASE

The national rat population is increasing and between 50 to 60% of rats carry and excrete the organism Leptospira ictero-haemorrhagiae in their urine. Infection with the organism causes an illness which has been known to result in death of 10% of
cases. There has been a recent increase in the incidence of the disease - 133 cases
were notified in 1988 compared with amily 68 in 1987 and 32 in 1986. Formerly
occuring mainly among sewage or abbatoir workers and miners, recent records show that the majority of fatalities are now related to water activities. In 1989 there have been 19 deaths of which no fewer than 13 were associated with water users. The nature of leisure water activity means that the average age of this at-risk group is
fairly young with most cases occuring in the 13 - 42 age group.

ABOUT THE ILLNESS The organism enters the human body through breaks in the skin such as cuts, blisters and abrasions or via the lining of the nose, throat or
alimentary tract. The incubation period is 7 - 13 days and the disease starts with a
fever, muscular aches and pains, loss of appetite and vomiting with prostration. It is vital that the doctor be told of any water-borne activity as the symptans are easily confused with those of flu and if the patient has a 'clean' occupation the possibility of Weil's Disease may be overlooked in the early stages. Subsequent bruising of the skin, sore eyes, nose bleeds and jaundice may occur. The fever lasts about five days and may be followed by significant deterioration.

Laboratory testing of blood will confirm the diagnosis but this may take undue time — in an ordinary hospital. Send samples direct to:
The Leptospirosis Reference Unit, Public Health Laboratory, County Hospital,

Hereford, HR1 2ER. Tel. [redacted]

here they will be tested within 24 hours. Treatment is usually by Penicillin
Antibiotic.

RATS AND THE ILLNESS The rat is a creature of the water's edge. The leptospira organism is passed in urine and, while it does not live long in dry conditions, can survive for same time in water. Salt water soon kills off the organism but there is a significant risk in tidal waters such as lower parts of the Thames and other rivers. The risk increases upstream and is greatest in canals, ponds or areas of slowly draining water. There is a significant risk to users of river banks or reservoir edges.

WATER USERS Sailors, board sailors, canoeists, oarsmen, swimmers or fishermen are at risk in any area with a population of rats. Any skin wound or blister, old or new, may be infected if immersed in water polluted with the organism.

GENERAL CARE

Handrails, steps and walkways should be checked for gaps, nails or rough edges that may Cause minor wounds.

ALL MEMBERS: Every effort must be made to see that food residues are removed from the Clubhouse, boat and trailer parks or picnic areas. A happy well-nourished rat will produce more rats.

Wear shoes to protect the feet from cuts.

Don't allow water to collect inside your dinghy, it may be wet but it may not all be water! (Ed's note: The same caution also necessary with pools of water collected on the outside of boat covers i.e. don't let it come into contact with any wounds.)

Cruiser Owners: Don't think it is solely a dinghy sailor's problem. If you ever have to come ashore clutching at the jetty from your tender, you too are at risk.

Waterproof surgical plasters of an adequate size should be used to cover old skin wounds before going afloat or to the dinghy park. Such protection will also apply to club workingparties when members may be clearing old structures or other hazards.

Every sailing club should have available to members at all times a supply of clean fresh water to wash wounds and a shower for those who may have fallen into suspect
water.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

As the Sailing Programme draws to aclose it is time to start to think about the
future.

This begins with the election of next year's Committee at the Annual General Meeting and there is a nomination form elsewhere in this issue of Navigans. The only restrictions that apply are that the Canmmodore, Secretary and Treasurer must be Ordinary Members and that the Canmodore, along with the Vice and Rear Commodores, must have served at least one year in the last three on the Main Committee before being elected to these positions.

Under the Constitution and Rules of the Club the Main Committee can, via Rule 10.7, make nominations for any position and increasingly over the last few years, these have been the only nominations. Whilst this helps with continuity, it should not exclude others from seeking nomination. Early next year I will attempt to give an indication of those people serving on all the Committees who may be intending to retire, so that others can came forward. You will see from the nanination form that very few of the positions are elected if you compare the list with the Committee in the front of the Year Book. Again, volunteers are always required to fill these positions and if you are interested, please contact the relevant Sub Committee Chairman. Regarding this year, I an pleased to say that members have came forward to fill all the positions.

There are however a number of other positions to be filled by election, namely, the Fleet Captains and the Dinghy and Cruiser Representatives on the Clubhouse and Social Committees. These are elected at your Fleet Meetings, so do consider volunteering and attend the meetings. I hope that the dates of these meetings will be published in Navigans.

Winter Tasks Over the winter there is a considerable amount of work to be carried out, ranging from erecting the Tractor Shed and Tender Rack through refurbishing the Entrance Hall, redecorating the Galley and Bar, to work to replace the old sewage-system covers and remove the trees to increase the size of the dinghy park, and same work on the road; these activities will be arranged on a Fleet basis as last year, when we made a tremendous improvement in the site.

In addition to these, there are a number of items which will be carried out using professional help, which includes an electric shower in the Ladies' Changing Roan, and an updating of all the radios to allow us to use Channel M2.

Beyond these activities, the Main Committee have made a definite committment to a second Rescue Boat and the Sailing Sub Committee are producing a proposal so that we can approach the MASC for the funds. At the same time we will be asking the MASC to replace the water pipe. Finally, next summer a series of working parties will be needed to start work on the Cruiser Park drainage.

Obviously the costs of all these schemes are much less if we, the Members, carry out as much work as possible, but it does require help from everyone and not just a dedicated few. I ask you all to contact your Fleet Captains during November and arrange to help however you can.
If there are any Members who are able to lay bricks or can carry out same carpentry or electrical work, could they please contact Chris Davies as soon as possible to assist with the winter work.

Finally can I remind you all that the tickets for the Laying Up Supper on Saturday lith November are now available and the Annual General Meeting is on Sunday 19
November.

N.J. JAMES

Many old friends in our Club were saddened to hear of the death of Norman (Jimmy) James, Jimmy had not

enjoyed good health for several years and passed away on 14th September. He had a long association with Marconi's, at Baddow and then at Witham, with the Marconi Microelectronic Company.

With his family he sailed a GP 14 for many years and more lately enjoyed cruising in his Centaur "SONYA" which

unfortunately he had to sell because of his health. Jimmy was a very popular Club member, always willing to help. He will be missed very much by his fellow mariners, and we send our condolences to Peggy and his sons Roger, Peter and Nigel.

BLACKWATER '89 5.

The Marconi Sailing Club have been trying to win the Colwyn Stone Challenge Trophy since it was first awarded in 1981, However each year Rochester have managed to win by a mixture of good luck and good sailing. On
Saturday 24 June 1989, the luck finally ran out. On a warm sunny day the combination of a fickle wind, a
strong tide and a well sailed single-handed Mirror finally managed to do what world champions, fast boats and national level sailors had failed to do: Damian Boreham won the Colwyn Stone Trophy for MSC, It was like John Bertrand winning the America's Cup for Australia.

The MSC team was: Ron Greygoose in a Solo, John Weedon in a Laser, Mike and Maggie Boreham in a 420, and their son Damian in a_ single-handed Mirror, The Rochester team was: Richard and Sharon Stone in a Wayfarer, Christopher and Alexander Jibb in a Mirror, and Peter and Gordon Belcher in Lasers, On paper it was a strong
team - Richard had won the trophy four times; Peter had won it three times; Gordon had sailed in the event
for fourteen years; whilst Christopher showed great promise last year.

The wind was light and from the West, the tide was coming in from the East. The Rochester team made @ good start and on the second leg were in first, second and third places. However the wind stayed light and as the fleet ran downwind against the tide, the single-handed Mirror was too close for comfort; Damian somehow managed to control three sails and kept close to the fleet, staying out of the tide, to win. Rochester packed
well with Peter Belcher second - first on the water but just eight seconds behind on handicap. Richard Stone

was third, Gordon Belcher fifth and Christopher Jibb sixth, At lunch Rochester were 4? points ahead and ready for the sea breeze to cane in and blow the single-handed Mirror's chances,

rm, was not to be - the wind for the second race was even more fickle, After a long beat with the tide the
fleet had to run against it along the island shore; John Weedon, now in a Kestrel crewed by Lucy Boreham, pulled away and appeared to have an unassailable lead, Peter Belcher and Richard Stone were chasing him hard and Gordon Belcher was trying to keep Ron Greygoose under control. Damian Boreham was out in the tide and appeared to have blown his chances. Once again the final run against the tide changed everything. The boats at the front of the fleet sailed into a hole with Peter Belcher and Richard Stone overtaking John Weedon; then the wind changed direction to the East and freshened as, belatedly, the sea breeze came in,

Peter and Richard were first and second over the line, but the slower boats were now sailing in a good breeze and easily beat their handicap, Damian won the race, with Ron Greygoose second (despite almost capsizing at the last mark). Rochester's placings were three, four, five and eight with MSC placings one, two, six, seven, thus MSC won the second race by 4% points,

Overall Damian Boreham won the Colwyn Stone Challenge Trophy with two firsts, whilst Rochester retained the Medway Cup for the team event,

Again a very pleasant visit with good interesting sailing, good company and good food.

-- The results of the 'HELMSMAN OF THE YEAR!
Final for 1989

The winner of the 1989 'Helmsman of the Year' series :-

MALCOLM GANDY

Congratulations to Malcolm Gandy who won the Helmsman of the Year trophy after what must rank as one of the closest and most keenly contested H.o.Y finals for many a year. MalcoJm.saw an almost certain runaway
victory suddenly turn into near defeat - only to snatch a well deserved but-hard-earned success in the last
moments of the competion. Certainly, those of us who were able to watch the 1989 final witnessed a fine performance by all who took part, with victory and defeat being governed by the capricious activities of the
wind and tide - aided and abetted (as always ) _ by the helms making the wrong decisions at the wrong time.
Enough of poetry (poetry ? what poetry ?), let's get on with the report.

Those taking part in the H.o.Y were :-

Malcolm Gandy (Solo Fleet) Lee Tridini (Sailboard Fleet) Mike Duckmanton (Cat Fleet) Mike Hellewell (420 Fleet) Damian Boreham (Mirror Fleet) John Weedon (Handicap Fleet).

All races were around 2 laps of the course D, A, E, No.1 and F marks, all passed to starboard with.a N-Nl!
wind starting out at Force 4 - 5, later dropping to Force 1-2 and then picking up again to Force 3-4.

"E' mark was placed near Osea island and directly to windward of 'A' mark and I reckon Graham Baker, driver of the Jack B, made a good job in positioning it just about right. It certainly provided a choice of route on the windward leg between A and E which undoubtedly proved crucial to the outcome of the Elimination Rounds.

The formula for 1989 was that the 6 finalists were divided into two groups of three, each to race an Elimination Round of 3 races in Mirrors (swopping the boats for each race). The winner of each group would then meet in the final as a Match Race sailed in lasers, the winner to be the first to score two wins.

The Elimination Round (single-handed Mirrors) - the two groups were :-

Group 1 - Malcolm Gandy, Mike Hellewell and Lee Tridini
Group 2 - Mike Duckmanton, John Weedon and Damian Boreham

For obvious reasons, Damian was not allowed to sail either of the Boreham-owned Mirrors (Bumble and Lars Tinn) and these boats were allocated to Group l. Malcolm, John, Lee and Damian had all had experience of sailing Mirrors and Mike Duckmanton took the wise precaution of getting some Mirror experience during the Jackpot on
the previous Sunday. Just as well - a Mirror handles somewhat differently from a Dart 18 catamaran ! Mike
Hellewell stepped into the Mirror for the first time but was well used to mono-hull sailing in his 420. He did wonder why the jib kept failing to tack, that is until he realised he didn't have his usual crew (Irene) to do it for him. Races 1 and 2 provided much sport for the spectators as near victory turned into even nearer defeat with each tack and gybe. Mike Duckmanton capsized in Race 2 and Mike Hellewell spoiled a brilliant start in race 1 by going back because he thought he was over the line. At the end of race 2, the Elimination Round was still wide open with:-

(a) Lee Tridini needing a win the the 3rd race of Group 1 in order to beat Malcolm Gandy and
(b) John and Damian needing to finish ahead of each other (but not necessarily win) in the 3rd race
of Group 2.

Race 3 was a fine race with much swopping of the lead and lesser places all the way around. The outcome of the Elimination Round was that Malcolm (Group 1 winner) and Damian (Group 2 winner) went forward to face each other in the Match Race Final.

The Match Race final (single-handed lasers) - Damian won the start of Race 1 but was soon overhauled by
Malcolm who went on to win by almost 2 minutes. Race 2 saw Malcolm in the lead from the start and soon well ahead at the finish of the lst lap. These races were really a procession and, to be honest, a bit of a bore after the thrills and interest of the Mirror racing. So confident were we in the rescue boat that Malcolm would win the 2nd race (and the H.o.Y) that we planned to pick up 'E' as soon as both had passed it . Then
an apparent miracle happened - the wind started to drop and Damian started to catch up. Gradually, inexorably,
Damian caught, matched and then overtook Malcolm to win the 2nd race by 30 seconds. One win each and all to play for on the last race. Malcolm lead the 3rd race initially but lost the lead on the broad reach and run legs. An incident at 'F' mark on the first lap saw Malcolm doing a 720 which enabled Damian to establish a
handy lead. Now another miracle - the wind started to increase again and Malcolm gradually whittled away
the lead until, as Damian rounded 'F' mark to start the beat for the finish line, Malcolm was not many yards behind. With 156 yards to go they were level and the previous victories and defeats now counted for nothing.

Malcolm eased his way ahead and won the race, and Helmsman of the Year, by 8 seconds.

A MAGNIFICENT SERIES - A FINE WIN - A PLEASURE TO WATCH
